The Śrī Lakṣmī Tantra, page 1.
First Chapter.
Salutation to the eternally faultless one, the universal cause of the world,
to the waveless consciousness whose self is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.

I bow to the horse-faced one, whose splendor is like the snowy mountain, who is adorned with garlands of *tulasī*, and who bestows the Sarasvatī of horses. We worship Hayagrīva, the god consisting of knowledge and bliss, whose form is like pure crystal, and who is the foundation of all sciences. || 1 ||
In this commentary,
we pay homage to the Goddess Śrī, whose friend the Lord sports by casting the snares of Brahmā and others upon the variegated board of the three *guṇas*.
For those seeking the jewels of reality within the great ocean of the Lakṣmītantra,
this commentary, the Tattvaprakāśinī, strives to provide assistance.
1. *Namaḥ* is the designation of the specific means (*viśiṣṭopāya*), which is the essence of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and of the specific goal (*viśiṣṭopeya*).

By the term *nityānavadyāya*, the possibility of Nārāyaṇa undergoing modification—which might be suspected due to His being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world—is refuted, and His distinction from both bound and liberated souls (*baddha-mukta-jīva*) is stated. [Salutation] to Him who is the cause of everything in the world.
Thus, the doctrine of the Upanishads regarding Brahman as the non-different material and efficient cause, as well as its distinction from the eternal individual souls (*jīva*), has been stated.

By the term "for the sake of knowledge" (*jñānāya*), the fullness of the multitude of qualities conducive to being the cause of the world, as well as the attribute defining its essential nature, has been stated.
By the term "waveless" (*nistaraṅgāya*), the absence of the six waves (*ṣaḍūrmi*) and its distinction from ever-changing consciousness (*cit*) have been stated.
We worship that which has the bird as its seat, which is the support of compassion, adorned by the moon, possessing the stainless moon, sun, and fire, and having the form of Lakṣmī. (2)
2. "Of such a form," and so forth; the meaning is "in the form of the letter *ī*. "Stainless," and so forth;

by this it is stated that the Goddess has the nature of speech (*vāk*), being in the form of a syllable that pervades both vowels (*svara*) and consonants (*sparśa*). As it is said in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The sixteen are declared to be called vowels (*svara*), and the twenty-five are called consonants (*sparśa*)."
"And these ten are pervasive; they consist of Soma and Agni respectively.
Thus [it is said]. [He is] one who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedāngas, and is proficient in all the scriptures.
He who knows the reality of all philosophical systems and has mastered the arrival and transmission of all phenomena.
He had conquered his senses and mastered their foundation; he was no longer subject to passion or hatred; he was established in the fourteen-limbed yoga and devoted to higher discernment.
4. "Fourteen" means by means of the yoga of the placement of devotion (*bhakti-nyāsa*).
2) In ancient times, when the sun was pierced by Rāhu, it attained the state of being a burner [of darkness].
The source of all austerities, a mass of splendor, and free from all affliction.
5. Regarding the word "pierced" (viddha): here, one should refer to what is stated in the 260th chapter of the *Anuśāsanika-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata*:

[He pierced] the sage who was endowed with the three qualities of Atri, established in the three aims of life (trivarga), immutable, performing the morning twilight worship, and who had offered oblations into the fire. 6.
6. By the words "devoid of the three qualities" (*atriguṇa*) and so forth, the etymological significance of the name of the great seer Atri is revealed.
[She was] the most eminent lawful wife of those devoted to their husbands, illustrious, and the mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa for a specific reason. 7.

7. Regarding the passage beginning with "brahma": In ancient times, the three deities endeavored to test the chastity of Anasūyā. Enraged by this, she transformed them into two-year-old infants. Thereafter, propitiated by her queens, she restored them to their former state; this Puranic narrative is to be kept in mind here.
Constantly praised by the gods, ever-peaceful and ascetic,
she was wise, a knower of all dharmas, and eternally devoted to her husband.
Having heard various teachings on dharma from her husband,
Anasūyā spoke these words preceded by a prostration.
Anasūyā said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, my protector, lord of the world!
From you alone have I heard those various kinds of dharmas."
And there are various types of knowledge, distinguished by differences such as their fruits and essential natures;
among these, the Dharma of the Blessed One has been upheld by me as the most distinguished.
11. The Dharma of the Blessed One. The dharma of cessation has the attainment of the Blessed One as its fruit.
As you have spoken those various discourses connected with the Dharma of the Blessed One, the supreme majesty of Lakṣmī has been indicated right there in each instance. 12.
Because it is a secret and because you were not asked, you did not reveal it;
nevertheless, I desire to hear that supreme majesty of Lakṣmī.
13. Regarding the phrase "because it was not asked": the injunction intended here is that one should not speak to anyone unless asked.
For what is the nature of that Goddess, what is her form, from what does she arise, what is her measure, what is her support, what are her means, and what is her fruit? 14.
Therefore, O best among the knowers of Brahman, I wish to hear this from you, so that through the yoga of its realization I may have fulfilled my purpose. (15)
"Show me that path; I have approached you, O Lord, please teach me.
Having heard these words of hers, [he spoke].
The Blessed One spoke thus three times. || 16 ||

16. Regarding the phrase "to him who had approached": the intended meaning of the Vedic text is that "to him who had approached, that wise one duly proclaimed that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence. Regarding the word "path" (*panthānam*): it means the correct means, as in the common saying, "The path is that by which great men have gone."
Atri:
O knower of dharma, O practitioner of dharma, I have been well enlightened by you today.
Thinking, "I must speak when questioned," I did not reveal it previously. || 17 ||
O auspicious lady, you are worthy to hear the supreme majesty of Lakṣmī— the eternal [truth] residing in the heart of the series of the Upanishads.
Formerly, sages dwelling on Mount Malaya were devoted to dharma;
they had heard the Sāttvata wisdom from Nārada, who has the vision of the gods.
They questioned the Lord Sanātana,
Nārada— who resembles Brahmā and knows the dharma of the Blessed One— regarding this very same matter.
The Sages said:
"O Blessed One, we have heard from you that the Sāttvata is the refuge of all beings."
The Dharma of the Blessed One is pure, characterized by having liberation as its sole fruit. || 21 ||

21. *Sāttvata* means one who takes refuge in *sattva*. The meaning is that *dharma* is the sole preeminent principle among the group of *sattva* qualities. By this, the etymological derivation of the word *sāttvata* is also indicated. For example: *sattva* refers to the quality of *sattva*; one who possesses this is *sattvataḥ*. The suffix *-ta* (in the sense of possession) is applied here just as in the case of *parvata* and other words. From *sattvata* comes *sāttvata*. Of that very [dharma]...
The commentary states: "The pure Bhāgavata Dharma is [the subject].
3) In that explanation of the true meaning, the greatness of Lakṣmī is supreme.
It has been indicated here and there, but it has not been revealed because it was not asked.
We desire to hear this account which enables one to cross the ocean of worldly existence;
may your lordship explain to us the entire glory of Padminī. (23)
We bow our heads to your feet, which deliver one from the cycle of worldly existence. O Sage, please instruct us; we have sought refuge in you for a long time. 24.
24. Regarding the word "long" (*ciram*): the intended injunction is that one should not speak [the secret] to someone who has not resided [with the teacher] for a year. Nārada says:
"O sages of firm vows, I have been well enlightened today."
Being pleased, I shall today proclaim the eternal Lakṣmītantra.

25. *Lakṣmītantra* is the name of the work. It will be stated right here (in verse 44) that this *tantra* was taught by extracting the essence from the root *Lakṣmītantra*, which consists of one hundred crore verses: "Where that Goddess is seen in her true form, qualities, and majesty..."
Padminī, born from a lotus, was the queen of Padmanābha. || 26 ||
Formerly, when Purandara was overcome by the curse of Durvāsas,
the three worlds were deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of vaṣaṭkāra, and their prosperity had fallen away.
27. "In former times," and so forth. This narrative is to be found in the first part (*aṃśa*) of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
The lack of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and the absence of the *vaṣaṭ* call are the causes for the loss of prosperity.
When the host of gods is impoverished and dharma is emaciated and has ceased to continue—
When the Grandfather had gone to the Ocean of Milk together with the gods.
28. *Nisaṃtate*: the meaning is "severed.
Having performed intense and great asceticism for many groups of divine years (*bahūn varṣagaṇān divyān*).
When Janārdana, the Lord of the World, the God of gods, had been awakened; || 29 ||
When the matter had been reported to the God by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
[the churning was performed] by the gods in the Ocean of Milk, following the path thus commanded.
When the Pārijāta tree, the best of horses, the lordly elephant, the host of Apsarases, the Kālakūṭa poison, the Vāruṇī wine, and likewise the nectar had emerged. (31)
Immediately thereafter, when the goddess rose from the great ocean together with the moon,
she was like a lotus-plant situated upon the chest of Padmanābha.
When she had beheld the host of gods who had attained glory, and when she had not looked upon the host of Daityas who were formerly defeated; || 33 ||

33. By means of these positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka), it is established that the casting of a glance by Lakṣmī is the cause of all prosperity. "When this exists, that exists" is the positive concomitance, for which the example is "as among the gods. "When this is absent, that is absent" is the negative concomitance, for which the example is "as among the Daityas. This very [point]...
He will state the subject matter immediately in the thirty-fifth verse.

While Purandara, having attained complete sovereignty, was rejoicing, Bṛhaspati approached him in private and spoke these words: 34. While Purandara, having attained complete sovereignty, was rejoicing, Bṛhaspati approached him in private and spoke these words.
Bṛhaspati said:
O Purandara, I shall inform you at the proper time; listen to these words.
Through both positive and negative concomitance, the nature of Fortune has been explained to you.
...was spoken of in the past. || 35 ||
O Lord, the greatness of the great extends through that [state],
so that your own stability may never fall away.
The stability of the kingdom is supreme. || 36 ||
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, strive thus: go for refuge to Padminī;
for she is indeed the root of prosperity, and she is the supreme goal. (37)
And that very same eternal Goddess is the intention of the Vedas;
she alone is the life-breath of the worlds, and she alone is the activity of the worlds. (38)

38. Regarding the phrase "of the Śrutis": the meaning is that, according to the statement "I alone am to be known by all the Vedas," [the Lord] is the ultimate ground where the purport of all the Vedas culminates. Since there is no distinction between the two (the Lord and the Veda), there is no contradiction in their statements.
This indeed is the desire of the worlds; this is knowledge, both supreme and inferior.
This very one creates at the proper time; she protects the three worlds.

39. Even according to the established doctrine that the status of being the cause of the world is unique to Brahman, since that [causality] is of the nature of His power (*śakti*) and is non-distinct from Him (*apṛthaksiddha*), it is entirely appropriate to designate even that which is produced by the power as being produced by the possessor of the power.
And this will be stated very clearly by the Goddess herself (11.6, 7).
At the end, she withdraws the universe while remaining established in its respective causes;
how can one attain greatness without propitiating this Mother of the worlds? (40)
This indeed is the abode of Viṣṇu, from which the ascetic does not return;
this is that supreme goal of the Sāṃkhyas who have realized the Self. 41.
This is that final goal of yogins, having attained which one does not grieve;
this is the final goal of the Pāśupatas, and this is the destination of those who know the Vedas. || 42 ||
This is the eternal culmination of the entire Pañcarātra;
this is the goddess Nārāyaṇī, established in the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
She is both distinct and non-distinct from them, like moonlight from the moon;
she is manifested through those various distinct forms of knowledge and diverse scriptures.

44. He establishes, by means of the verse beginning with "pṛthagbhūtā" and "apṛthagbhūtā," exactly what was stated in the preceding verse regarding the abiding of Nārāyaṇī in the nature of Nārāyaṇa: when there is a desire to distinguish between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmī*), which are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), the property is designated separately; however, when no such distinction is intended...
By way of its substratum (*dharmitayā*), as in "white color" or "a white cloth.
This very same supreme Goddess is worshipped in many ways;
go for refuge to that illustrious one who is born from the lotus. (45)
Having propitiated the consort of Viṣṇu through various specific austerities and those same diverse, auspicious observances, stabilize your own prosperity.
With her face brightened by grace, this Goddess—who grants the desired objects even to those who possess desires—will lead you to her own abode. 47.
47. Attainment of liberation in the form of the supreme state through the grace of the Goddess, along with the secondary fruits of the three aims of life—
thus was Śakra himself instructed by his preceptor, Nārada.
Desiring to propitiate her, he went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
There, making his dwelling at the foot of a *bilva* tree, he performed divine austerities;
standing on one leg, observing silence, motionless as a piece of wood, and subsisting only on air.
With his eyes, arms, and face turned upwards, self-restrained and with a disciplined mind,
he performed most difficult penance for a thousand divine years.
At the concluding bath of that austerity, that goddess born from the lotus,
the consort of Viṣṇu, with a gracious countenance, appeared before his sight.
Beholding with his eyes that supreme Goddess, the mother of the worlds, standing before him, Śakra was struck with the utmost wonder.
Then, overwhelmed and with palms joined in reverence, Balarāma’s slayer, the subduer of Pāka,
prostrated himself and praised Śrī, the lotus-born goddess, with the Śrīsūkta.
Seeing him who had attained a state of solitude and was established in sincere devotion, the Mother of the Worlds spoke these words: (54)
Śrī said: "O child Śakra, O you of noble vows, I am pleased with your austerity.
Choose a boon, O illustrious one; what desired thing shall I do for you? (55)
Śakra said:
"O Goddess, today the fruit of my asceticism, self-restraint, and observance has been obtained immediately, since the Blessed One has been seen by me. (56)
Or if a boon is to be granted by you to me, O Supreme Goddess,
then tell me, O Queen of Gods, what kind of being you are who are departing.

O Goddess, what are her means of valid cognition, what is her support, and what are her methods? Who is she who is eternal, and by whom, or in what manner, is your connection with her established? || 58 ||
And whatever else is to be known by you, augmented by various scriptures—O Goddess, tell me all that; I am seated before you, please teach me. (59)
Thus consoled and gratified by him, like a milch-cow by her calf,
Padmā, with a heart full of affection, spoke to the subduer of Pāka (Indra).
Śrī said: Listen, O illustrious Śakra, to who I am and in what manner I exist.
O slayer of Vṛtra, whatever kind of relationship I have with him, or with whomsoever else, [is such].
Thus, in the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*, within the *Lakṣmītantra*,
[the chapter titled] "The Manifestation of All Supports" (or simply "The Introduction of the Scripture").
The First Chapter. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter. Śīrū said:
There exists the Supreme Self, whose characteristic is the experience of bliss free from suffering and devoid of cold; the wise behold that which is His supreme state. (1)

1. By the words "free from suffering" (*nirduḥkha*) and so forth, the nature of [Brahman] as being the opposite of all that is to be discarded and as a mine of infinite auspicious qualities is established. [Objection: Suppose someone were to say, "There might be some Self for some people, and some other [Self] for others; and for that one too, there might be yet another," and thus, in this manner, where this [series] continues—
It remains fixed. || 2 ||

2. *Ātmā*: the meaning is "the controller. Regarding the word *eṣa* ("this"): the word *vyavasthā* ("establishment") is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The connection with the preceding is: "He who establishes—that is, attains—the path, he is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). [The path] to the further shore of the paths.
They spoke of the Supreme Self:
"That object which is remembered as 'I' is declared to be the Self. (3)

3. Regarding the phrase "of the paths" (*adhvanām*): in comparison with the path pertaining to the three aims of life (*traivargika-adhvā*), there is the supreme path, which is the path to liberation (*mokṣādhvā*) beginning with the rays of light (*arcir-ādi*).

The meaning is that he reaches its further shore (*pāram*), as stated in the scriptural passage: "He attains the end of the path; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. The citation from the Śruti here is: "Of the paths, the Lord of the Path" (*adhvanām adhvapate*). Regarding the word "I" (*aham*): it refers to He who...

The meaning is that the object of the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is that Self. Being of an undivided nature, I am designated as the Supreme Self (paramātman). This entire world, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient, is embraced within it. || 4 ||

4. *Anavacchinna* (unconditioned): The meaning is that he who is perceived through the unlimited function of the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), by way of not being delimited by objects and the like, is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
By whom that state is remembered as "I," he is the eternal Supreme Self.
That Blessed One, Vāsudeva, is considered the supreme Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Viṣṇu is called Nārāyaṇa, Viśva, and Viśvarūpa;
this entire world is pervaded by his sense of "I-ness."
And it is said elsewhere in the *Śakranītisāra*: "O Mother, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by you and Viṣṇu;
there is no entity, whether real or unreal, that is not permeated by the sense of 'I' (*ahaṃtā*)."
That which is grasped as "this-ness" (idaṃtā) is overcome by "I-ness" (ahaṃtā). || 7 ||
7. "As this" (idaṃtayā): the meaning is that the entire world is perceived as the referent of the word "this.
He alone is entirely peaceful, changeless, and eternal;
he is infinite, being devoid of limitations such as space and time. 8.
It is called "Great Manifestation" (Mahāvibhūti) because that pervasiveness is great;
it is Brahman, the supreme abode, whose meditation is without support.
It is like a waveless ocean of nectar, the sixfold quality (ṣāḍguṇya) made radiant;
it is that one mass of consciousness, peaceful, and devoid of rising and setting.
10. By the verse beginning with "nirastaraṅga" (waveless), the state of the Lord as both quiescent and emergent is described. He states this very point:
"quiescent.
Because its powers are not separate [from it], that is called the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*).
His supreme power is like the moonlight of the cold-rayed moon.

11. Regarding "the non-duality of Brahman" (*brahmādvaitam*): the meaning is that because it is qualified by the egoity (*ahaṃtā*) which is a power (*śakti*) inseparable from itself, Brahman as thus qualified is the one and only reality. He states, by way of an illustration, that its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed inseparable from that [Brahman], using the words "like light" (*jyotsnā*).
The Goddess who exists in all states, inseparable from his own self, is the I-consciousness of that Brahman; I am she, the eternal one. (12)

12. By the phrase "she who does not depart from him in any state," the statement of the great seers is recalled: "Sītā was [his] in the state of Rāghava, Rukmiṇī in the birth of Kṛṣṇa; in other incarnations as well, she is the inseparable companion of Viṣṇu.
He is remembered as Hari, the Self of all beings, who has become the "I" (the inner self).
I am the eternal ego-consciousness of all beings. || 13 ||
By whatever nature the eternal Vāsudeva exists,
I am declared to be that very nature of that god, his companion.
Brahman consists of both existence and non-existence; therefore, that is the eternal state.
From it arises the Lord Nārāyaṇa as existence (bhava), and I, the supreme Lakṣmī, as non-existence (bhāva). 15.
Therefore, that eternal Brahman known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is [the ground];
for the object "I" (ahamartha) becomes manifest when it is pervaded by the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā). 16.
16. The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman is indeed endowed with Śrī (Prosperity), and not devoid of Śrī.

Although both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are the remnants of the sacrificial offering (*ātmahaviḥśeṣita*), the intention is that there is no contingency of having two separate remnants, because—as in the case of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* and other offerings—it is the "qualified" one alone who is the object of dedication (*uddeśya*), and because that [qualified entity] is a single unity.
And that sense of "I-ness" (sāhaṃtā) is proclaimed to arise from the object of the notion of "I" (ahamartha);
for they are inseparable from one another and are mutually concomitant. (17)
Know that the relationship between me and my Lord is one of identity;
for without the sense of "I," I, being indefinable, cannot be established.

18. "Indefinable" means devoid of specific distinctions. The sense is that in the world, every object is established only by way of a particular mode such as "this is thus," and not as something devoid of distinctions.
Without the referent of "I" (ahamartha), the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) cannot be established as it would be without a substratum.
Its form consists of both existence and non-existence, and it is the object of both the collective and the individual.
In the world, both the indirect and the direct are contemplated;
when there is no unfolding, that very "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is the unmanifest Supreme Goddess.
Having embraced the entire universe, it abides within Brahman;
its manifestation is like that of the ocean at the rising of the moon.
At that time, I was the power of Nārāyaṇa, characterized by the desire to create;
that which is called a "nimeṣa" (moment) of that Supreme Self pertains to his act of withdrawal.

22. It has been stated previously that the Goddess possesses the nature of Śakti; now, its divisions are described: namely, the power of the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā-śakti*) and the power of the desire to sleep (*suṣupsā-śakti*). By the first, creation (*sṛṣṭi*) arises, and by the second, dissolution (*saṃhāra*). In that regard, with respect to the eternal manifestation (*nitya-vibhūti*), only the first is active; as for the second, however—
Its utility lies solely within the realm of divine play (līlā-vibhūti).
For I am Nārāyaṇī, the power characterized by the desire to sleep; indeed, as my desire to create arises, she too awakens.
From the God himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī. || 23 ||
Unobstructed and uncontracted sovereignty unfolds;
that knowledge is the supreme Brahman, the teacher of all, the seer of all, and free from affliction.

24. Among the six qualities beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*), knowledge is the attribute that defines its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). The other qualities, however, serve as qualifiers for the nature already thus defined; this is the distinction. He will state this later:
"The remainder—sovereignty, heroism, and so forth—is an attribute of knowledge. It is the attribute of the essential nature known as knowledge.
This is the meaning.
Likewise, my egoity (ahaṃtā) consists of knowledge; it is all-knowing and all-seeing. The supreme form of both Brahmā and myself consists of knowledge. (25)
The remaining attributes, such as sovereignty, valor, and so forth, are the eternal qualities of knowledge;
the internal form "I" is proclaimed to be the very nature of knowledge.
The nature of light and so forth is characterized by qualities such as those found in crystal and the like;
therefore, the nature of consciousness belongs to both me and Nārāyaṇa. (27)
"That which is unimpeded by whatever it raises up is my supreme sovereignty;
that is called *icchā* (will) by the learned in the various treatises on the principles (*tattva-śāstra*). (28)

28. "Desire" (iccheti). That the power of the desire to create (sisṛkṣā-śakti) is of the nature of sovereignty (aiśvarya-rūpa) was described previously in the twenty-fourth verse; it should be recalled here. For the desire to create is the wish to emanate.
"That which is my state as the primordial material cause (prakṛti-bhāva) of the universe is called 'power' (śakti)."
That I experience no fatigue while creating is what I consider my strength. || 29 ||

29. The Goddess’s state of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the world is not by way of her own essential nature (*svarūpa*), for if it were so, the consequence would be that she is subject to modification (*vikāritva*). Rather, it should be understood as being through her self-nature consisting of both consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*). For this alone is the logical conclusion regarding Brahman’s status as the material cause of the universe.
And that which is the support of an effect is called its power (*bala*);
those who are skilled in the true nature of things declare that such support is brought about by a portion of capacity (*śakti*). (30)
Even though I am the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), I am always free from modification;
for water quickly abandons its own nature when it arises as curd. (31)

31. Because it is accepted—according to the manner previously stated—that transformation (*pariṇāma*) occurs in the aspect of the mode (*prakāra*) and not in the aspect of the substratum (*prakārin*), the attempt to maintain the absence of modification by accepting transformation in the very nature (*svarūpa*) which is the substratum, on the grounds of the power to accomplish the impossible, is not tenable. For this very reason, [the text speaks of] *māyā*.
Regarding the statement "one should know Prakṛti," some maintain that the meaning here is that Māyā, which serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the Lord, is what constitutes Prakṛti.
Even in the state of the world's manifestation, she is neither my Prakṛti nor my transformation (vikṛti) at any time.
The absence of modification is considered by the knowers of reality to be vigor. || 32 ||
Vikrama is said to be valor; it is traditionally held to be a portion of sovereignty (aiśvarya).
For my lack of dependence on auxiliary causes in the performance of all tasks is indeed [that valor]. (33)
Those who know the true nature of things declare that *tejas* (splendor) is the sixth quality;
some describe *tejas* as the capacity for overcoming others.
Some who are experts in the principles of that splendor employ it in sovereignty;
thus, these five qualities are the manifestations and the stainless streams of knowledge.
These six qualities, beginning with knowledge, constitute my sixfold nature (ṣāḍguṇya), which is my very body;
thus, this is the ten-thousandth part of my digit that has arisen from the desire to create.
36. "Rising" (udyatī) means having attained emergence.
The entire group, consisting of both pure and impure aspects, has been embraced by her.
Among those, O Lord of the Gods, I shall explain the path that consists of purity. 37. [Verse 37 follows as part of the commentary on the preceding verse.]

37. Creation is twofold: pure creation (*śuddha-sṛṣṭi*) and impure creation (*aśuddha-sṛṣṭi*). Among these, the pure [creation] is devoid of the three guṇas and consists of pure *sattva*. Some maintain that because it is self-luminous, it possesses non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*); others maintain that it is indeed inert (*jaḍatva*). This very [pure creation] is designated by the term "eternal realm" (*nityavibhūti*). As for impure creation, however—
The manifestation of divine play (*līlāvibhūti*) is composed of the three *guṇas* and is insentient in nature;
however, that form of the Supreme Lord is radiant, characterized by the sequential unfolding of the six *guṇas*—both manifest and unmanifest—and assumes four distinct forms. (38)

38. It should be understood that not only is the eternal glory (nityavibhūti) itself a pure creation, but the manifestations (vyūha)—namely Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—who shine forth therein, are likewise so. Among them, in the first, Vāsudeva, there is no clear manifestation of the sequence of the six attributes (ṣāḍguṇya). This is the case with the manifestations following that one as well.
It should be understood that this occurs gradually, little by little.
Superimposed through the conceptualization of qualities, it follows a sequence produced by the manifestation of those qualities.
And that which has its qualities personified; thus this wonderful path is threefold. || 39 ||

39. Among these, in some configuration (*vyūha*), because the qualities (*guṇa*) do not manifest properly, there is no knowledge [of them] as being of the nature of the qualities. In others, however, because they manifest sequentially, there is a gradual manifestation. In yet others, due to the extreme luminosity of the qualities, there is full comprehension of them as being of the nature of the qualities; such is the sequence.
The six [categories] have three pairs, which are indeed called "knowledge" and so forth;
their fourfold nature is analyzed both in brief and in detail. (40)
When that triad of those [qualities], through the distinction of being taken together or separately, is intended to be expressed by me, that is the fourfold nature of Śāntā. (41)
Even without considering specific forms, those who contemplate reality declare that this fourfold nature of the Śāntā belongs to the conceptualization of qualities. (42)
From the state of absolute peace and supreme tranquility, there arises my manifestation within the triad of form and the other [senses].
That primordial nature of mine, which is my fourfold self, is both sequentially manifest and formless.
Waveless, indescribable, devoid of being yet the very essence of being, imperishable—this unfolding called pure consciousness is my primordial, undeviating state of peace. (44)
Previously, within Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is known as the power of manifest knowledge,
every modification exists within me like a mole on the skin.

45. "Like a mole" (tilakālakavat): Just as on the body of living beings a particular small, dark-colored mark like a mole is seen in some very limited corner, so too the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) resides in one part of Me; this is the meaning. He is called Saṃkarṣaṇa because he draws [all things] together; thus his name is etymologically significant. Here—
The manifestation of knowledge and power:
therefore, the wise know me as Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose nature is knowledge and power;
thereafter, I myself assume agency as they emerge.
Ṅ, Ī: Parā || 46 ||
Then they called me Pradyumna, the illuminator of all objects;
for in that form, the power of sovereignty and valor was fully manifested.
47. One whose *dyumna*—meaning excellence, strength, or splendor—is preeminent; thus the name is etymologically appropriate.

Because he is the creator of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), there is here the full manifestation of power (*vīrya*) and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Then, through that power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), [they] attain possession (*āveśa*). [ā, B, c, ḍ:]
Through the desire to act, it has attained the state known as "engaged" and "unceased" by those skilled in reality. (48)

48. Regarding "Aniruddha": he is the one who performs protection (*pālana*). Herein lies the full manifestation (*samunmeṣa*) of power (*śakti*) and splendor (*tejas*). And so they have recorded: "Vāsudeva is supreme because of his sixfold qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*); you, O Blessed One, are the object of enjoyment for the liberated.
Because of your abundant strength and awakening, you are Saṃkarṣaṇa; through your sovereignty and heroism (*vīrya*), you take away [evil] and you spread the scripture."

"O Lord, as Pradyumna you lead forth the dharma of creation; as Aniruddha, maintaining the splendor of Śakti, you protect the quality of Sattva and likewise cause it to proceed, having thus manifested yourself, O Sovereign of the Stage.
These are my successive states: deep sleep, dreaming, and waking."
My three powers, known as my own nature, are consciousness, sovereignty, and potency. || 49 ||

49. Regarding the passage beginning with "suṣupti" (deep sleep): Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the presiding deities over deep sleep and the other states respectively; Vāsudeva, however, is the presiding deity over the fourth state (*turya*). This is the distinction.
This very division is indicated in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* by the names Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya.
Manifesting through the three distinct principles, they are proclaimed as the triad of qualities: strength, vigor, and likewise splendor. || 50 ||

[This state] is characterized by the absence of faults such as fatigue and ignorance; thus, for me, who experiences the distinction between the two states of the quiescent and the arisen, [there is no such thing]. (51)
51. Regarding "the tranquil and the arisen": the tranquil state is the state of Paravāsudeva; the arisen state is the state of Vyūha.

Even therein, the first Vyūha possesses both the tranquil and the arisen states, whereas the other three possess only the eternally arisen state—this is the distinction. The surging of the waves of its own attributes does not lead to differentiation, just as in the case of the ocean.
For it is by means of this *kṛtyā* that I generally abide in the performance of whatever qualities are to be accomplished.
In that regard, that pair of qualities is said to be my own form;
therefore, O Lord, the deity Saṃkarṣaṇa is proclaimed as the power of knowledge.

Pradyumna consists of sovereignty and heroism; Aniruddha consists of power and splendor; but the First One possesses the sixfold attributes indivisibly, existing non-separately from the reality of Brahman.
Just as a single actor assumes various distinctions of costume and gesture through qualities such as conciliation, generosity, cruelty, and heroism, so too does [the soul]. (55)
In the same way, although you are one, you alone am I through qualities such as the power of knowledge and sovereignty.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the world, I worship the true being of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
The purpose is, in due order, the favoring of living beings through dissolution, creation, and maintenance;
and furthermore, there is another purpose consisting of the scripture, the meaning of the scripture, and its fruits. (57)

57. Saṃkarṣaṇa is the agent of dissolution and the instructor of the scriptures; Pradyumna is the agent of creation and the promoter of the meaning of the scriptures; Aniruddha is the agent of preservation and the one who brings to fruition the results of the meaning of the scriptures—such is the division of their respective functions.
One should observe the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, even within the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha);
for the pervasive Lord, whose faces include Padmanābha and others, possesses infinite forms.

58. Having described the manifestations of others, the manifestation [of Viṣṇu] is now explained here. There are many incarnations of the manifestation, such as Padmanābha and others; even the Fish, Tortoise, and so forth are enumerated here as incarnations.
The expansion of Aniruddha is shown in the Sāttvata [Purāṇa].
Even that worship which is worldly belongs to those whose selves have been permeated by the Blessed One.
59. *Arcā* refers to specific images installed in temples;
through the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra and the Lord of Mantra, it too possesses a body of six attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
Within this [context], from the Supreme (*parā*) down to the *arcā*, in my [descent]—[variant: in the descent of the Supreme and other forms of worship]—...
The states beginning with the fourth (turya) are to be understood; this is the path of purity.
The distinction between the Vyūha and Vibhava [forms] is to be understood through slight differences.
Furthermore, O Śakra, listen to my [teaching on] the path that is both pure and otherwise. || 61 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Pure Path," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Pāñcarātra*). [Note: Some manuscripts omit the title; others refer to it as *śuddhasṛṣṭi*.]
Chapter Three.
Śrī said:
I am that supreme Vaiṣṇavī reality named Nārāyaṇī, who possesses eternal, faultless, and boundless auspicious qualities.
I do not recall any limitation by way of place, time, or form;
pure consciousness alone is my form, and qualities such as universal sovereignty are mine. (2)

2. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the attribute that defines its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). The meaning is that the other five attributes are also of a nature whose essence has been defined. In that context, the distinction exists solely by virtue of their respective independence.
That which is the differentiation consisting of the nature of the power of sovereignty over consciousness has been described.

Thus, he states that even this differentiation is produced solely by my will: "by its own sovereignty. Now, however, there is another [aspect], namely the unfolding of the powers of sovereignty over consciousness.
Always by my own impulsive rising, which is beyond reasoning and unfit for formal command.

4. "The other" means that previously, in the pure creation (*śuddhasṛṣṭi*), one unfolding (*unmeṣa*) was mentioned; now, in the creation consisting of the impure three qualities (*traiguṇya*), there is another unfolding—this is the meaning.
By [His] will, another form was produced in the triad beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*).
Just as the clear juice of sugarcane attains the state of molasses. || 5 ||
5. The meaning is that the triad consisting of knowledge and the rest was made otherwise by means of the triad consisting of *sattva* and the rest.
Likewise, knowledge, which is essentially pure, attains the state of *sattva*; sovereignty becomes *rajas*, and power (*śakti*) likewise becomes *tamas*. 6.
He says that very thing: "In the same way" (tadvat). The sense is that knowledge arises from *sattva*, sovereignty from *rajas*, and power from *tamas*.
These three qualities, O Śakra, are designated as the "triad of qualities" (*traiguṇya*).
In its creation, that triad of qualities (traiguṇya) revolves with rajas as the predominant factor.
7–8. The term *traiguṇyam* is formed with the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (svārthe), as in the word *cāturvarṇyam*.
In the state of maintenance (*sthiti*), that [nature] has *sattva* as its predominant quality, but in dissolution (*saṃhṛti*), it is headed by *tamas*.
O Purandara, I am the primordial consciousness (*saṃvinmayī*), all-pervasive (*vyāpinī*), yet [I appear as] the city [of the body].
Presiding over the qualities (guṇas), she brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
though herself devoid of qualities, she presides over these very qualities by her own will.

9. "Even though devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇāpi*): Since the sixfold set of qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) was mentioned previously, the term "devoid of qualities" here means being free from the mixed qualities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. By the phrase "by His own desire," it is stated that His sole motive in the creation of the world and so forth is divine play (*līlā*). As the Blessed One has said:
Bādarāyaṇa says: "But as in the world, it is mere sport.
[The Lord says: "I alone set in motion the wheel consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Śakra said:
Having established the two modes within the three ages beginning with the Age of Knowledge (the Kṛta Yuga), which correspond to the three qualities (guṇas). || 10 ||
For what purpose do you proceed by means of the distinction between the pure and the impure?
O Lotus, what is the mutual relationship between these two injunctions?
"Being asked this by me, speak; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! Śrī said:
"My sovereignty is not subject to command; my own will alone is its cause. (12)
Even the great are deluded in this matter; nevertheless, hear the truth from me.
For I always abide in the state of both the Lord and the one to be ruled.
I am always [thus]. || 13 ||
13. The relationship between the pure and the other [impure] creations is stated: "The Lord and the one to be ruled.
This means the relationship of protector and protected.
Nārāyaṇa is to be known as the Lord (īśa), and I am his lordship (īśatā).
But that which is to be ruled over, O Purandara, is to be known as both consciousness and unconsciousness.
The power of consciousness (cic-chakti), however, is supreme therein; it attains the state of the enjoyer (bhoktṛtā).
Its non-conscious aspect (acid-pada) consists of the objects of enjoyment, the instruments, and the locus. 15.
That power of consciousness (cicchakti), eternally pierced by beginningless ignorance (avidyā) set in motion by me, has attained the state of an enjoyer.
Indeed, due to the connection with the notions of "I" and "mine," the insentient is identified as one's own;
that is ignorance (avidyā), which truly passes away through knowledge (vidyā) when it is obscured.
Then the power of consciousness (cic-chakti), free from egoism, shall attain my own state;
she is that Vidyā established on the pure path, whose forms are the Supreme Assembly (paravyūha) and the rest. 18.
Out of compassion, I, who perceive the true nature of knowledge, set this forth;
for this relationship of the protected and the protector exists between two injunctions. (19)
The first category protects and the second category is protected;
this has been told to you, O Śakra. What more do you wish to hear?
Śakra said:
For what purpose do you proceed by way of the relationship between the lord and the subject?
Tell me: how many varieties are there of the subject, and what is its nature in that regard? (21)
Śrī said: This nature of mine and of Nārāyaṇa is not to be questioned.
I am the Lord, and he is the one to be ruled; I am not that eternal God. || 22 ||
That which is to be ruled is declared to be twofold, by way of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious.
Here, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is of the nature of the enjoyer, and she bears the form of consciousness—indeed, my own form.

The power of the insentient (acit-śakti) exists in three ways through the objects of enjoyment, the instruments, and the locations; and that third stage of my expanding [power] is known as a "knot" (parvan) by the wise.
Even though these two powers, consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness, are distinct, they are nonetheless my eternal forms by virtue of my own sovereign will.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) is stainless, pure, consisting of consciousness, and of the nature of bliss;
yet, pierced by beginningless ignorance, it thus certainly undergoes transmigratory existence.

Even though the power of consciousness (acicchakti) is insentient, impure, subject to transformation, and composed of the three qualities (triguṇa), this [universe] is merely the manifestation of my own sovereign freedom. || 27 ||
Just as a comet, though blazing, is itself joined with smoke,
so too do I— though my essential nature is pure consciousness— partake in the state of insentience.

28. Just as a comet, though its inherent nature is fire, assumes the form of dark smoke, so too do I, though my essential nature is knowledge, fall into the state of insentience (acidbhāva); this is the meaning.
[I am] unassailed by conceptual construction (vikalpa), and not tormented even by words (śabda).
In this way, I exist as one whose nature is insentient, even while conditioned by the substrate of meditative concentration.

29. "By means of the adjunct of meditation" (ādhyānopadhineti) means by means of the adjunct consisting of my own will; or, it means for the purpose of providing an object for meditation, as he will state: "The stages of rest for meditation" (4-24).
For, within external and internal objects, the nature of consciousness remains undivided.
Nevertheless, this [consciousness] is distinguished by the presence of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
"Sovereignty alone is my cause; I am not subject to any questioning whatsoever.
Knowing me as one of such power, you will become a Buddha. (31)
Śakra:
How indeed do you create the worlds endowed with both pleasure and pain?
Indeed, non-creation would be better, or else let creation be of the nature of happiness. (32)
32. Regarding "non-creation" (*asṛṣṭi*): here, one should recall the statement from the *Ślokavārttika*: "Impelled by compassion, he would create only happiness alone.
Śrī.
Observing the accumulated karma— composed of both the existent and the non-existent— of living beings pierced by beginningless ignorance, I bring about this mixed creation.
Śakra said:
O Goddess born from the Ocean of Milk, how can there be autonomy for you?
If you bestow happiness and suffering only after taking account of past action (karman). (34)
Śrī said:
"While I am performing my tasks, the act of performing them is traditionally held to belong to the agent;
moreover, the agent's dependence upon an instrument does not constitute a violation of his autonomy. (35)
I am faultless and independent, not situated within the sphere of questioning;
I divide myself manifoldly through the categories of agent, object, action, and so forth.
"No cause for this sport need be sought here; remain thus composed.
Śakra said: "Whether it be so or otherwise, O Goddess, such is your sovereignty."
Tell us the manner of creation; salutations to you, O lotus-born one!

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Three Qualities" (traiguṇyaprakāśa), in the Lakṣmītantra, which is the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. (Note: Variants include *śrīpañcarātrasāre*, *śrīpāñcarātre*, and *miśrasṛṣṭi* as the chapter title.)
Chapter Four: Śrī [B: Śrī said]— p. 14)
I am like the stainless sky, consisting of consciousness and peerless bliss;
I am named Nārāyaṇī, and my nature is such as that of Hari.
I am not quiescent, nor active, nor even intermediate; I am of the nature of consciousness, the very form of that Lord Hari Viṣṇu, the Self of all. || 2 ||

I, who am non-variegated and possess that same single form as he— who, though variegated, dwells upon the path of conceptual construction— have attained total equality with him by assuming his very form.
In those two, the very self of consciousness has arisen as a certain unfolding;
it is a fraction [of that] which is [as subtle as] ten million times ten million times ten million times ten million.
That which is called the desire to create is my very form; "I shall perform the desired creation.
With one portion, I truly exist in the form of the pure sacrifice.
Just as the radiance of a diamond-jewel flashes forth in every direction,
so does this path, consisting of purity, flash forth for me in every direction. (6)
From my form, which is like the cloudless sky and resembles a motionless ocean,
a pure creation proceeds from the mass of my gnosis.
The supreme knowledge, which is devoid of activity [or free from latent impressions], eternally blissful, pure, and the essence of all, first manifests; that is called Saṃkarṣaṇa.
That sovereignty which is independent of any other cause in the creation of the universe—that was my lordship; I was Pradyumna, the Supreme Person. (9)
That power of mine which, possessing variegated forms, is latent and omnipresent, and remains unimpeded, is proclaimed as Aniruddha. || 10 ||
These lotus-eyed gods, who are the agents of creation, preservation, and destruction, and who possess the powers of wisdom and sovereignty, are my very form. They are the Puruṣas. (11)
Vāsudeva is my primordial form, resembling a waveless ocean and comparable to the cloudless sky, as I desire to create.
[Consisting of the self] || 12 ||
When knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor manifest simultaneously and without exception, He is then called Vāsudeva.
Upon the manifestation of their power of knowledge, Saṃkarṣaṇa is proclaimed;
he sustains the entire universe from himself, like a sesame seed with its black spot.
Its name is indeed "Power" (bala), and from that it is designated as Vedānta;
when there is the manifestation of vigor and sovereignty, he is celebrated as Pradyumna.
Freedom from modification is vigor, and therefore he is unchanging;
for when power and splendor manifest, he is declared to be unobstructed.
Moreover, its luminosity is independent of anything else and is indeed unobstructed;
thus the scripture shines forth from Saṃkarṣaṇa alone,
like the sound of a thunderclap.
Since all that activity arises from the god Pradyumna,
they declare that the entire fruit of action proceeds from Aniruddha.
For here Aniruddha creates, Pradyumna protects what has been created,
and the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa devours that which was created and protected. (19)
19. Here, the creative agency of Aniruddha and the preservative agency of Pradyumna are stated;

however, previously in the second chapter, the preservative agency of Aniruddha and the creative agency of Pradyumna were mentioned. That [previous statement] should be understood as referring to another cycle of creation (kalpa).
These gods themselves always bestow grace through the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, as well as through the fruits of the teachings and dharma.
Even though each one manifests a single quality, nevertheless these six qualities are all neither less nor more than Vāsudeva, the eternal.
Their limbs, minor members, intellect, and so forth, are not considered to be composed of the elements;
rather, their divine and eternal body consists solely of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).

22. Here, "intellect" (buddhi) refers to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). By the statement "these are not composed of the elements," the passage from the Śāntiparvan—"the body of this Supreme Self is not a configuration of an aggregate of elements"—is recalled.
O Lord of Heaven, one should not contemplate a real distinction among these.
This [distinction] was made by virtue of conceptual construction for the sake of establishing various specific effects. || 23 ||
Sovereignty is not other than knowledge, and power is not other than that;
O Śakra, these have been conceived by me as grounds for resting in meditation. (24)

24. Regarding "meditation" (*dhyāna*): the meaning is that a conceptual differentiation is constructed therein in order to provide objects of focus according to the inclination of the lay practitioners (*upāsaka*).
First is the substance (*vastu*), then its existence (*bhāva*), then the object (*artha*), and finally the activity (*kriyā*).
This fourfold nature should be known as existing at all times within all entities. || 25 ||
Having divided myself fourfold by means of my own self in the forms of Vāsudeva and the others, I abide pervading all things through consciousness.
The gods, Vāsudeva and the others, each dividing their own body threefold by way of Keśava and the other forms. (27)
27. Thus, all twelve emanations (vyūha), beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara, are to be meditated upon as distinct manifestations.
This intermediate manifestation is designated in the Pañcarātra;
these twelve deities are established for the guidance of time (or action). 28.
For the benefit of the worlds, the expansion of the all-pervading and unceasing Hari is known as his manifestation (vibhava), such as Padmanābha and others. || 29 ||

That wherein the Lord of the World, entering again and again, effects the welfare of the world— consisting of gods, humans, and so forth— that should be known as another form of manifestation (vibhava).
30. By the phrase "gods, humans, and so forth," one should also contemplate that Dattātreya, Bādarāyaṇa, and others are likewise manifestations [of the Lord].
[He acts] for the welfare of the worlds, either through gods, sages, ancestors, perfected beings (siddhas), and so on, or by himself.
The image fashioned in the form of the Blessed One is pure consciousness itself.
31. By the word "itself" (*svayam*), the images situated in self-manifested fields (*svayambhūkṣetra*) are intended.
Thus, this pure path has been briefly demonstrated to you;
now listen as I describe the other path, which consists of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). 32.
That knowledge which was previously described to you manifests through sattva;
sovereignty through rajas, and power also through tamas.
In that state of creation, rajas predominates and revolves;
the two other qualities, sattva and tamas, remain present on all sides as its attendants.
That which was previously described by me as the ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth—by a portion that is the ten-millionth part of that, I emit the universe. (35)
I am Mahālakṣmī, the primordial source of all, the Great Sovereign composed of the three qualities;
presiding over the quality of Rajas, I perform the desired work of creation.
36. By this it is understood that during the state of being the creator of the three-fold world, she is designated as Mahālakṣmī. 37.
She, whose every limb is beautiful, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, bears the two divine states consisting of Agni and Soma, characterized as female and male.
Four-armed and large-eyed, resembling molten gold,
she bears a citron, a mace, a shield, and a vessel of nectar.
I am known as Mahālakṣmī, beautiful in every limb;
I am Mahāśrī, Mahālakṣmī, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍī, and Caṇḍikā. (39)
Bhadrakālī, as well as Bhadrā, Kālī, Durgā, Maheśvarī, the Goddess of the three qualities (Triguṇā), the Consort of the Blessed One, and likewise the supreme Bhagavatī.
These designations, as well as others, have been recorded by me there in many ways;
I shall now describe those various ones arising from different modifications in their entirety.
I perceive the entire world, with its merits and demerits, and its deeds done and left undone;
and she who is celebrated everywhere as Mahālakṣmī is truly great.
She is called Mahāśrī because she is to be resorted to by the great;
she is Caṇḍī as the beloved of Caṇḍa, and she is considered Caṇḍikā because of her fierce nature (caṇḍatva).
I am auspicious in form and am Bhadrā; I am Kālī because I am the reckoning (kalana) of the virtuous.
Furthermore, I am proclaimed as Kālī because I possess the form of Death (Kāla) for my enemies.
Because she simultaneously ordains both good and evil for friends and enemies alike, she is celebrated as Bhadrakālī, whose nature consists of the wondrous qualities of Māyā. (45)
45. Regarding the phrase "māyāścaryā" (the wonder of illusion): by this, it is stated that the meaning of the word *māyā* is that which is wonderful.
By this, the assumption that the word *māyā* signifies "falsehood" is refuted.
Furthermore, she is called *Mahāmāyā* because of her greatness, and she is considered *Mohinī* because of her power to delude.
And Durgā is so called because she is difficult to attain, as well as because of her method of protecting her devotees. (46)
Because of my connection (yojana), I am called Yoga and Yogamāyā;
I should be understood as Māyāyoga because of my connection with the knowledge of men. 47.

47. Regarding the phrase "by the application of knowledge" (*jñānayojanata*): by this, based on the statement of Yāska that "māyā is *vayuna*, which is knowledge," it is shown that the word *māyā* has the meaning of "knowledge. Furthermore, the interpretation of the passage "I manifest through my own *māyā*" (*saṃbhavāmyātmamāyayā*) as meaning "through my own volition" (*ātmasaṃkalpena*) is also rooted in this very principle.
Because I am the embodiment of the six perfections in their fullness, I am remembered as Bhagavatī;
because of my union with the sacrifice of the Blessed One, I am the consort of the Blessed One.
48. Regarding the phrase "due to connection with sacrifice" (*yajñasaṃyogāt*): the form *patyuḥ naḥ yajñasaṃyoge* is established by grammatical rule (Pāṇini 6.3.23).

Furthermore, the sacrifice of the Blessed One should be understood as consisting in the protection of those who have taken refuge in Him. In that context, her connection [to Him] occurs through her being His instrument of action (*puruṣakāra*) and so forth.
She is remembered as Vyoma because of her vastness, and she is remembered as Purī because she fills all things;
she is remembered as Parāvarā because she is the nature of both the transcendent and the immanent. 49.
I am called Śakti because of my power; I am called Rājñī because I always delight [the world];
and I am celebrated as Śāntā because I am eternally free from all modifications.
The universe is produced from me; I am proclaimed as that Prakṛti (Nature). Residing [in all], I am the one to be resorted to; I destroy the evil of the virtuous.

51. The verbal root *śri* is used in the sense of "resorting to," and the root *śṛ* in the sense of "injuring. I hear the compassionate word; I destroy the world with my qualities. (I lie within) all beings; I take delight.
Of those who perform meritorious deeds. || 52 ||
52. The verbal roots intended here are *śru* (in the sense of hearing), *śrī* (in the sense of pleasing), *śī* (in the sense of sleeping), and *ram* (in the sense of sporting).

Regarding the explanation of the letter *śa* in the name *Śrī*: "I lie within" (*śaye'ntar*). Regarding the explanation of the letter *ra*: "I sport" (*rame'ham*). Furthermore, I am always praised by the gods, and I am indeed the body of Viṣṇu.
Having observed these qualities in me, those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas [honored me]. || 53 ||
53. Explanation of the letter *ī*: “*Īḍitā*” (the praised). The verbal root is *īḍ*, meaning “to praise. The meaning is that she is the body or form of Viṣṇu.
Those who know the application of the connection of qualities call me Śrī.
I am indeed such as this: eternal, possessing all forms, and everlasting.
p.
17) She who presides over the three qualities (guṇa) is proclaimed as the "Threefold One" (Triguṇā).
For the sake of creation through the imbalance of the qualities— [ā, B, c, ḍ: by means of the qualities for the sake of the creation of imbalance—]
I have become active with the desire to create.
Having the luster of molten gold and adorned with ornaments of molten gold,
I fill this world, which was devoid of light, with my own splendor.
In the past, in order to fill that entire empty world with myself,
I assumed another form consisting solely of darkness.
Resembling crushed collyrium, with a beautiful face adorned by fangs,
that woman became large-eyed and slender-waisted. (58)
Her great arms were adorned with a sword, a skull-bowl, a head, and a shield;
she wore a necklace of headless trunks and bore a garland of serpent-heads upon her head.
Having been born, that most excellent woman spoke to me:
"O Mother, give me a name and a deed; salutations, salutations to you! (60) [Śānti].
Śrī said:
I spoke to that Tāmasī, the best of women with beautiful limbs:
"I shall give you names, and those shall be your deeds. (61)
Mahākālī, Mahāmāyā, Mahāmārī, Hunger,
Thirst, Sleep, and Blackness (or Craving) are each a solitary heroine.
The night of time is difficult to cross.
These names of yours are to be explained by means of [these] names;
he who studies them after having understood your deeds through these [names] attains happiness.
Considering this first creation to be insufficient,
I then bore a form resembling the moon, consisting of the manifestation of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Holding a rosary and a goad, and bearing a lute and a book, she became that excellent woman; for at that time, I gave her the name Karmā.
She is Mahāvidyā, Mahāvāṇī, Bhāratī, Vāk, Sarasvatī, Āryā, Brāhmī, the Great Cow, she whose womb is the Veda, Wisdom, and Speech. (66)
The action of this virtuous one shall be in accordance with her name; her deed is truly wonderful. We three have been proclaimed as mothers, the sustainers of the world.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Mahālakṣmī," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpāñcarātra*). Chapter 4.
Fifth Chapter. Śrī said:
She who is the primordial greatness of Hari, possessing all forms, eternal, whose nature is pure bliss and consciousness, and who has attained equanimity toward all things. || 1 ||

1. Herein is the state of tranquility (*śāntāvasthā*). In the second verse is the state of emergence (*uditāvasthā*). In the third verse is the state of the three qualities (*traiguṇyāvasthā*), known as Mahālakṣmī. In the fourth is the state dominated by *rajas*, which is Mahāśrī, another synonym for Mahālakṣmī. And [finally] there is Mahāmāyā, who was described in the preceding chapter as being dominated by *tamas*.
In the fifth [chapter], there is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) characterized by Sattva, as described in the preceding chapter.
Desiring to create, I, being endowed with even a very slight portion of my own Bindu,
performed a pure creation whose form consists of the fullness of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).
[The forms of the letters] || 2 ||
I am the Great Fortune (Mahālakṣmī), who revolves through the three qualities (guṇas), yet I am called such by my own tiny drop of form, though it is not my true nature. || 3 ||

Therein, I am the Great Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign, whose nature is predominantly *rajas*. That aspect of mine which is of the nature of *tamas* is known as Mahāmāyā; that aspect of mine which is of the nature of *sattva* is known as Mahāvidyā.
I and she are two lovers; thus we three are powerful.
He created three kinds of pairs of different forms;
that pair of mine was mental and of beautiful appearance.
Know that this beautiful lotus-seated Pradyumna, who grasps gold and has lotus-petals for ears, was born from my mind.
Dhātṛ, Vidhi, Viriñci, and Brahmā are remembered as Puruṣa;
Śrī, Padmā, Kamalā, and Lakṣmī are proclaimed there as Nārī.
From a portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, there arose a pair born of Mahāmāyā;
he who was the male being there had three eyes and beautiful limbs throughout his entire body, and was mind-born.
He is Rudra, Śaṅkara, Sthāṇu, Kapardin, and the Three-eyed One;
there also reside the three goddesses Trayī, Īśvarā, Bhāṣā, as well as Vidyā and Akṣarā.
She should be known as Kāmadhenu; she is both the woman and the cow, Sarasvatī.
She is born from a portion of Aniruddha and originates from Mahāvidyā.
That mental couple which exists there—Puruṣa is Keśava, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, and Janārdana. || 12 ||
Umā, Mahāgaurī, Satī, Caṇḍā, and the fortunate woman Satī—
by my command, she became the three wives of Brahmā. || 13 ||
Gaurī is the beloved of Rudra, and Ambujā is that of Vāsudeva;
she is the manifestation of rajas, tamas, and sattva.
This first section, consisting of that triad of couples, has been told to you;
I shall now speak of the middle section concerning the qualities—listen to this.

15. Regarding "the first mountain": from the portion of Pradyumna, the mental creation of the *rājasa* Lakṣmī is Viriñci and Śrī; from the portion of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the mental creation of the *tāmasa* Mahāmāyā is Rudra and the Trayī; and from the portion of Aniruddha, the mental creation of the *sāttvika* Mahāvidyā [is Brahmā and Sarasvatī].

—Viṣṇu and Gaurī. Thus, the meaning is that it takes the form of a conceptualization of couples: of the rājasa Viriñci with the tāmasī Trayī; of the tāmasa Rudra with the sāttvikī Gaurī; and of the sāttvika Viṣṇu with the rājasi Śrī. "The middle mountain" refers to the creation of the cosmic egg by the Creator (Dhātṛ).

Its piercing was performed by Rudra; therein, moreover, the primary creation within the egg was carried out by Dhātṛ, while its preservation was the function of Viṣṇu—this is the meaning. Having come together with Bhāṣā, Viriñca produced the egg.
At my command, that Śaṅkara divided this [world] together with Gaurī. || 16 ||
Keśava protected that very primary matter which was the effect of the Creator within the egg, together with Padmā. (17)
Thus has this middle section of the qualities been fully described;
I shall now speak of the third section, so listen to it here with a focused mind. (18)
18. Regarding the third mountain: from the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu, there is the manifestation of Hiraṇyagarbha together with the three Vedas.

That navel-lotus, its emergence, and the pair [of the Vedas]—this triad taken together is called the "Great" (mahat). From that, in the sequence beginning with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the meaning is that the creation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) takes place.
Within the egg is indeed the Pradhāna, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
it is the three qualities (traiguṇya), primordial nature (prakṛti), the ether (vyoman), inherent nature (svabhāva), the womb (yoni), and the imperishable (akṣara).
Having thus liquefied that reality known as the Unmanifest,
the Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, together with Padmā and Vidyā, [entered it].
Having entered into the yoga of sleep, he made his bed upon the waters;
she who was called Mahākālī became that very sleep of the nature of darkness (tāmasī). || 21 ||
O Purandara, as he was lying down, a lotus then emerged from his navel;
at that time, it was declared to be a "lotus" (paṅkaja) even though it was not born of mud (apaṅkaja).

[The vowels e and ī represent] time (kāla). Its names are the locus of water (jalādhikaraṇa), the lotus (padma), the support (ādhāra), the flower (puṣkara), the wheel (cakra), and the white lotus (puṇḍarīka). Thus are its names. (23)
Śakra said:

"The principle of consciousness and non-consciousness has been declared; consciousness is proclaimed as *cit* (the sentient), and non-consciousness is said to be the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). What other [principle] is remembered as Time (*kāla*)? (24)

Śrī said: "The insentient portion is the other [aspect], and time is remembered as the other; as for the power and so forth that were previously mentioned, they are declared to be the triad within the sixfold attributes. (25)
25. "The triad" means the nature of power (*bala*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and vigor (*vīrya*).
This very triad revolves within the process of creation in the form of time. While this triad of qualities (*traiguṇya*) is itself unchanging, it is subject to transformation.
This pair, consisting of Kālī and Kāla, is proclaimed to be the fire;
it belongs to my Goddess Mahāśrī, who creates manifold states of being.

27. Time consists of moments and so forth; "pertaining to time" (kālya) refers to that which possesses the three qualities and the entire collection of their transformations. This time, composed of mind (manmaya), always functions as an instrument.
From that lotus composed of time, which arose from the navel of Viṣṇu— 28. [From that lotus...]
Brahmā, consisting of the Veda, was born together with the triple knowledge (trayī),
he who is powerful and was previously called Hiraṇyagarbha, originating from Lakṣmī.
The woman who was born from Mahākālī is remembered as the Triad (Trayī);
this very couple was produced from the lotus of Viṣṇu’s navel.

The lotus, the pair born from the lotus [i.e., Brahmā and his consort], and likewise Dharma and the others— this triad together is declared by the ancient sages to be the great transformation characterized by tamas. (31)
31–32. The pair born from the lotus consists of Hiraṇyagarbha and the Triple Veda (Trayī).
There is a threefold division: Prāṇa, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Buddhi.
Because he rests upon the lotus, the male, and the female, his greatness is proclaimed.
32. Prāṇa, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Buddhi are the distinctions of Mahat. (p.
20) The quality of prāṇa is vibration, while that of buddhi is determination.
Dharma and so forth, as well as adharma and so forth—this pair is considered to be a quality (guṇa) of the person (puruṣa). || 33 ||
33. Regarding the word "puṃsaḥ" (of the person): it means of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are thus described.
Since virtue and the other qualities are proclaimed as the opposites of vice and the rest, [they are so named]. || 34 ||

34. Regarding the phrase "because": the meaning is that the opposites of dharma and the other qualities—namely, adharma, ignorance (ajñāna), lack of dispassion (avairāgya), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya)—are to be known.
These enter the Great One (Mahat) and impel him toward his own creation [with the desire to create].
From that [source], being impelled, the ego (ahaṃkāra) was born.
He who was previously called Śaṅkara, born from Mahāmāyā— Gaurī, who was his wife, was born here as Abhimati.
36. "The desire [to create] belongs to Ahaṃkāra alone"—this is its quality and another name for it.
"Having entered this Ahaṃkāra, I impel it toward creation;
it then became threefold at first due to the intermingling of the guṇas. 37.
Among those, the source of the elements (bhūtādi) is composed of tamas; hear from me how all this [unfolds] from it:
from the source of the elements comes the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), and from that subtle element arises sound.
38. It should be understood that *bhūtādi* is another name for the *tāmasa* ego, *vaikārika* for the *sāttvika* ego, and *taijasa* for the *rājasa* ego.
From the subtle element of sound, impelled by Me, the subtle element of touch indeed came into being.
But touch arose from the subtle element of touch, impelled by me from that subtle element.
Then there was the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra); and from that, impelled by me, the primordial form manifested, followed thereafter by the subtle element of taste (rasa-mātra).
From that *rasa*-tanmātra which was cast forth by me when it was agitated, *rasa* was born;
and from that, when impelled by me, the *gandha*-tanmātra also came into being.
"The pure fragrance has arisen"—this is the distinction regarding the derivative elements (bhautika).
Others [distinguish] between the subtle elements (mātrās) and the gross elements (sthūlabhūtas). (42)
Sound and the others are declared to be qualities; however, those sounds and others which constitute the emission of the gross elements are not other than the qualities of sound and the rest. (43)
Quiescence, ferocity, and delusion—these are its threefold nature;
they exist in subtle things as manifestations of the emergence of *sattva* and the other [guṇas]. (44)
Therefore, their state as mere [subtle elements] is proclaimed for those subtle ones;
however, in other cases, they possess grossness because they bestow pleasure, pain, and so forth. (45)
The threefold states of the gross elements alone are proclaimed,
according to their divisions as subtle, born of the father, and abundant. (46)
The various external objects, such as jars and the like, are called "abundant.
The specific qualities produced from semen and blood are known as those born of the father. (47)
The subtle forms of the five elements, which serve as the support for the subtle body, are thus described;
indeed, the creation born from Bhūtādi has been proclaimed in its proper sequence.

48. From the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), sound and the subtle element of touch (sparśatanmātra) were born. From the subtle element of touch, touch and the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra) were born. From the subtle element of form, form and the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra) were born.
From the subtle element of taste, taste and the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) were born. From the subtle element of smell, smell was born.

This is the process according to this [system]. The Sāṃkhyas, however, assert that all the *tanmātras* arise directly from *bhūtādi*. The Upaniṣadic process, on the other hand, is as follows: from *bhūtādi* arises the *tanmātra* of sound; from that, space (*ākāśa*); from that, the *tanmātra* of touch; from that, air (*vāyu*); from that...
From that [ahaṃkāra] arises the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra), from that fire, from that the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra), from that water,
from that the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra), and from that earth is born. Such are the two aspects of ahaṃkāra, which depend upon the qualities of rajas and sattva.
The Sāttvika portion of those two is declared to be the Vaikārika; the one which is the other is called Taijasa by the wise. Listen now to this creation of theirs:
from the Vaikārika-ahaṃkāra arose the organs of perception, such as the ear and the rest.
And the organs of action, beginning with speech, proceed from the taijasa [ego].
And from those two [the intellect and the organs], the mind arose as both an organ of cognition and an organ of action. || 51 ||

51. Here, a distinction is made regarding the origin of the organs of cognition from the *vaikārika* [sattva] and the organs of action from the *taijasa* [rajas]. However, the followers of the Upaniṣads declare that all the organs originate from the *vaikārika*. Likewise, according to the Sāṃkhya system, the mind possesses the nature of both types of organs.
But according to the Upaniṣadic view, they are indeed organs of cognition:
"The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these they call the five organs of cognition; this power is of my nature. (52)
Speech, hands, feet, as well as the generative organ and the anus—these they call the five organs of action; this power is of my own nature.
That power of consciousness which has come down to me through a succession of lineages, having presided over the faculties of perception, operates upon the objects of the senses. (54)
And that power of action which has come to me through the lineage of succession, having presided over the organs of action, operates toward what is to be done. (55)
Sound is considered the object of the ear, and hearing is considered its activity;
touch is considered the object of the skin, and touching is considered its activity. (56)
Form is considered the object of the eye, and seeing is considered its activity; taste is considered the object of the tongue, and tasting is considered its activity. || 57 ||
The object of the nose is odor, and its function is considered to be smelling;
the functions of the ear and the other senses with respect to their objects are hearing and so forth. (58)
The [five] observations are taught, and that consists of the apprehension of the mere substratum (dharmin):
namely, the directions, lightning, the sun, the moon, and likewise the earth. (59)

59. What is called *ālocana* (perceptual observation) is the grasping of the mere object itself, occurring between the clear apprehension of properties such as sound and so forth. That too is indeed indistinct. And they have said: "There exists an initial non-conceptual cognition of observation, resembling the consciousness of infants, the mute, and others, which has a simple object."
That which is proclaimed as *adhidaiva* (the divine) pertains, in order, to the pentad beginning with the ear;
that which is proclaimed as *adhibhūta* (the elemental) consists, in order, of the objects of perception beginning with sound.
This pentad beginning with the ear is proclaimed as internal;
however, the creation of the ear and the other senses from the *sāttvika* aspect occurs in relation to the elements beginning with space (*vyoman*).
Therefore, it is said that the pentad beginning with the ear is elemental (bhautika) in sequence;
the object of speech is sound, and its activity is considered to be speaking.
The taking of what is not to be taken is considered the function of the hand-faculty;
going to the place to be gone to is considered the function of the foot-faculty. || 63 ||
The bliss of the generative organ is considered its bliss, and its function is considered to be sexual pleasure;
that which is to be excreted is the object of the anus, and its function is considered to be evacuation.
The group of four beginning with the hand consists of the five sense objects;
likewise, Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the first Prajāpati [or Dyau]. || 65 ||
And Mitra—thus should the presiding deities be known in sequence by the discerning. Furthermore, sound and that which is the object of speech and the other [senses] consists of five elements. (66)
That is declared to be the *adhibhūta*, while speech and the rest are called *adhyātma*;
the mind, however, is the common factor in both of these pentads.
And by means of the group of cognitive faculties, this is conceptualization (vikalpa)—
conceptualization being a manifold construction— and that is declared to be the qualification.
The connection with a property (dharma) is said to belong to the property-bearer (dharmin);
that conceptual construction (vikalpa) is to be known as fivefold, according to substance, action, quality, and so forth. (69)
A person is designated as "staff-bearer" due to connection with a substance; as "white" due to association with a quality;
as "going" due to engagement in action; and as a "human being" due to the presence of a universal.
(22) "Ḍittha" exists in five ways through its association with words.
And through the groups of organs of action, the mind expands this volition.
That which is the departure from indifference is called "volition" and "exertion";
and by means of the ego (ahaṃkāra), there is a state of abiding in both of these categories within this [mind]. (72)

This very [self] functions within the group of the organs of knowledge through the sense of ego (abhimāna). The connection with space and time belonging to the knower is proclaimed as "ego" (abhimāna). || 73 ||
"Today this object appears before me"—in this way the thing is perceived;
yet it proceeds with such intensity within the group of the organs of action. (74)
Agitation is proclaimed to have volition as its precursor;
the intellect, established in the group of sensory organs, functions through determination. (75)
