Intellect (buddhi) is declared to be the determination of objects;
the ascertainment of objects is proclaimed to be certainty (niścaya). || 76 ||
The intellect operates with effort upon the group of organs of action;
this thirteenfold instrument is to be known by the wise as such. (77)
The external is to be known as tenfold, and the internal organ is remembered as threefold;
these twenty-three are proclaimed to be the transformations of Virāj.
The ten organs and the three subtle elements from which the gross body arises—this is proclaimed as the subtle body of Virāj. (79)
The individual manifestations and subtle bodies are established for each living being;
they, born from their own source, cease upon the liberation of those beings. (80)
These twenty-three principles, beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas, arise through mutual assistance; indeed, they produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
Then that golden egg came into being, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Prajāpati, the four-faced divine Virāj.
82. Here, the very sequence of creation previously described is stated again, summarized together with the creation of Manu and others:
"From Virāj, Manu was born; from Manu, the Mānavas are said to have arisen.
From them [were born] Marīci and the others, from whom this world of moving and unmoving beings [proceeded]. 83.
This mode of my arising has been shown to you only in brief;
for the power of consciousness (cicchakti), though inherently pure and clear, is obscured by beginningless ignorance (avidyā).
One situated therein experiences suffering arising from birth, old age, and so forth;
yet, through connection with pure consciousness and association with pure karma, when one shakes off that ignorance, then one enjoys infinite bliss. (85)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Primal Creation" (or "The Creation of the World by Brahmā and Others"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
p. 23) The Sixth Chapter. Śrī [B: Śrī said]:
I am the primordial Ahaṃtā of Hari, whose form is like a waveless ocean, a vast sea of the bliss of consciousness consisting of the six perfections in their fullness.
I am such a pure one, yet in some respects I have attained a state of swelling;
I am the Goddess characterized by the desire to emanate, autonomous, and whose essence is Being-Consciousness.
For seven days, the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti indeed entered into the state of the six sheaths—
she who is Māyā, the Source, and Nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities.

3. Among the six sheaths known as Śakti, Māyā, Prasūti, Prakṛti, Brahmāṇḍa, and Jīvadeha, the Śakti-sheath is that which initiates the path of purity. It is precisely therein that the manifestation of the triad beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa occurs.

The cosmic egg and the body of the living being—these are designated as the six sheaths. That supreme desire of Viṣṇu to create, which has arisen from his sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), [is the first]. || 4 ||
That power (śakti) is the first sheath (kośa), which sets the pure path in motion;
"sheath" is a synonym for "nest," possessing another name for the body. || 5 ||
In this first treasury, characterized by the first unfolding, there was indeed the supreme Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the possessor of the ego-sense. || 6 ||
There, a smooth transformation exists like a mole or a freckle;
that goddess who is his ego (ahaṃtā) is I myself, the supreme Saṃkarṣaṇī.
She who is endowed with the power of consciousness is celebrated as Śrī;
that manifestation of mine which is her [power] is proclaimed as Pradyumna.
8. Śrī is the queen of Saṃkarṣaṇa; Sarasvatī is [the queen] of Pradyumna; Rati is [the queen] of Aniruddha;
and Śānti is [the queen] of Vāsudeva. [These are] the powers (śaktis) of the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, who presides over the treasury of power (śaktikośa).
The god Pradyumna, the Supreme Person, abides in the state of intellect (buddhi).
The aggregate of the enjoyer and the enjoyed remains dissolved therein;
that which is known as the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) of that deity who has become the mind (manobhūta). || 10 ||
I am she named Sarasvatī, who manifests through power and sovereignty;
that which is my unfolding is proclaimed as Aniruddha.
I am established in the function of ego-consciousness for that Saṃkarṣaṇa;
these three ancient gods are Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others.
Those proclaimed by the names Jīva, Buddhi, and Ahaṃkāra are not deities composed of material nature (prākṛta), but rather consist of pure consciousness. || 13 ||
Of the primordial, manifested Lord Vāsudeva who sports, these [forms] are designated by various names according to their performance of specific tasks. (14)
All of them are said to possess the six qualities, and all of them are Supreme Persons;
[they arise] from the great ocean of eternal bliss, which is full and steady in its sixfold attributes.
The simultaneous manifestation of the six qualities by virtue of their functional activity—
that which arose is Vāsudeva, the first conceptualized manifestation (vyūha). || 16 ||
Her peace is indeed the state of non-ego (ahantā), and she is proclaimed as that Power (Śakti).
Therein, the gods residing within the treasury of Power are brought forth when they are meditated upon. || 17 ||
That which is the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) of Aniruddha, designated as "Delight" (rati), is that very goddess Mahālakṣmī; she is called the sheath of Māyā. || 18 ||

18. Impure Emanation Beginning with the Womb of Māyā. It was previously stated that Mahālakṣmī possesses the quality of *rajas* and is the causal basis for the emanation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
That manifestation of Mahālakṣmī which is designated as the qualities (guṇas) of Māyā is proclaimed as the pair of Mahākālī and Mahāvidyā. (19)
The third treasury of mine, named Prasūti, which consists of Mahālakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, and Mahāvidyā, is now recited.
20. The Prasūtikośa is the composite form of Rājasyā Mahālakṣmī, Tāmasī Mahāmāyā, and Sāttvikī Mahāvidyā.
Therein were three pairs, which have been previously mentioned by you.
Having turned primordial matter (pradhāna) into water, the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) lies upon it.
21. Three pairs are described in the fifth chapter by the seven verses beginning with the seventh.

Primordial matter (pradhāna) alone is called the "sheath of nature" (prakṛtikośa). In the Upaniṣads, these natures—the illusion (māyā), the birth (prasūti), and the primordial matter (prakṛti)—are designated by the names "darkness" (tamas), "the unmanifest" (avyakta), and "primordial matter" (prakṛti).
She is declared to be Nature (prakṛti), the womb (yoni), whose essential form is the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas).
It was indeed from her that Viriñca first generated the cosmic egg within his own self.

Regarding this, some who are experts in the treatises on the principles (tattva) declare that it is Primordial Matter (prakṛti), together with the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) which is constructed from the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with Earth. (23)
That is declared to be the "Cosmic Egg" (Brahmāṇḍa), wherein Brahmā became the Virāj;
it is the body endowed with limbs and minor members belonging to all living beings here.
This sixth method of the treasury has gradually become diminished;
these six descents of mine from the Full State have thus been proclaimed. (25)
In the first sheath, the Lord himself abides as the threefold "I-ness" (ahaṃtā);
in the other five sheaths, various kinds of individual souls (jīvas) abide. (26)
They experience various conditions arising from the distinction between the auspicious and the inauspicious;
among those, there are three divine ones, as well as the triads of their pairs.
The incarnations within the Egg that are remembered as belonging to them and to those [deities] were created by their own sovereign will; they do not follow the power of karma.
The bodies of both [groups] are proclaimed to be non-material (aprākṛta). Others, from the gods down to the stationary beings, reside within the five sheaths (pañcakośa). || 29 ||
Those living beings who, occupying various states, transmigrate through the power of their karmas—
these, by virtue of the ripening of merit, bring about the exhaustion of their office (adhikāra).
30. Regarding "office" (*adhikāra*): "The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office," is the sūtra of Bādarāyaṇa.
Having attained an abundance of knowledge, those whose impurities have been destroyed by yoga gradually ascend the sheaths; once ascended, they do not fall. 31.
From Satyaloka onwards, those who have ascended to whichever stage they reach do not return; they either remain there or proceed further upward.
Śakra said:
O Goddess born from the Ocean of Milk, O Consort of the Lotus-navelled One!
Who indeed is this so-called "life-force" (jīva)? Tell me that; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One.
Śrī said: "I am the primordial, perfect egoity of Hari; I am that supreme sovereign of all.
O bull among the gods, four states of mine are remembered as belonging to her [the True One]."
The knower (*pramātṛ*) is one [state], while the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) within it is another;
the external organ (*bahiḥkaraṇa*) is yet another, and the fourth is the ground of objective existence (*bhāvabhūmikā*). (35)

35. The knower is the individual soul (jīva). The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is threefold, consisting of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṃkāra). The external organs (bahiḥkaraṇa) are tenfold, consisting of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya) and the organs of action (karmendriya). The ground of states (bhāvabhūmikā) is the entire manifold of objects of knowledge (prameyaprapañca).
The cognizer is declared to be consciousness; that is said to be my contraction.
For I am indeed that which has attained indefiniteness with respect to space, time, and so forth. (36)
(25) Precisely because of her sovereignty, she assumes limitation without abandoning her own nature;
therein, that first limitation is proclaimed as the subject (pramātṛ). || 37 ||
Just as the universe remains dissolved within me, who am the conscious self,
so too does it abide within the cognizer, like mountains reflected in the interior of a mirror.
The subject attains a state of uniformity, duality, triplicity, fourfold division, and the form of seven pentads. (39)
39–40. There are four divisions: the states of waking and so forth.
For by means of its own light, the Self possesses a twofold nature through the relation of the grasped and the grasper;
it possesses a threefold nature by way of the forms of cognition and action.
The state of consisting of seven pentads is established in the abiding of each respective principle (*tattva*).
Śakra asked: "O lotus-eyed one, what are those principles, how many are there, and of what nature are they? (41)
"Tell me this which I have asked; salutations to you, O one born from the ocean! Śrī said:
"The ten elements, through their division into gross and subtle..."
And the cavities. || 42 ||
Through the distinction between knowledge and action, there are the three internal organs,
as well as Prakṛti, Prasūti, Māyā, and the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas.
Time, destiny, power, the person, and the supreme ether—these are the principles that the Sāttvatas study as the Blessed One. (44)
Śakra said:
"I have heard the truths from the lotus of your mouth;
explain these to me, O Goddess; salutations to you, O Sarasīruhā. (45)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Six Sheaths," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Chapter Seven: Śrī [B: Śrī said] — (p. 26)
Therefore, O Śakra, I shall explain to you in due order the sequence of the principles (*tattvapaddhati*).
This sequence of principles is said to be pure, impure, and mixed. (1)
Resembling a cloudless sky,
like a motionless ocean,
he is the great ocean of eternal bliss, characterized by pure and autonomous consciousness. || 2 ||

2. The thirty-five principles (*tattva*) mentioned in the preceding chapter are now described in reverse order. Among them, first is the description of the principle of the Lord (*bhagavat-tattva*). The principle of the Lord consists of Paravāsudeva in his state of tranquility (*śāntāvasthā*), the emanations (*vyūha*) in their state of manifestation (*uditāvasthā*), and the Goddess (*devī*) who is non-distinct from them (*apṛthaksiddhā*).
Free from distinctions of form, place, time, and so forth— [free from qualifications, according to versions ā, B, c, and F]—
the Lord is to be known as the eternal Supreme Self. || 3 ||
Her ego is supreme; such is her eternal lordliness—Nārāyaṇī, the highest, subtle, free from conceptual construction, and stainless.
He is a great ocean of knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor;
he is indeed the first manifestation of the six qualities occurring simultaneously.
He is designated as twofold by virtue of being both existence (*bhava*) and its essence (*bhāva*);
for here, Vāsudeva is "existence," while the state of being Vāsudeva (*vāsudevatā*) is the "essence" within him.
I am that eternal Goddess known by the name Śānti;
the manifestations (vyūhas) beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa, who are identical with me, have been described previously.

O Lord of the Gods, these three and the fourfold nature— these four are the reality that is beyond the principles (nistattva), yet is the supreme reality (tattva) which is the referent of the Blessed One.
8. *Nistattva* means that which has emerged from, or transcended, other principles (*tattva*); this is the meaning. He states this very point by saying "the supreme principle" (*tattvam uttamam*).
As for *nabhas*, it is the supreme void, designated as the *paramākāśa*.
Wherein the god, having divided himself by himself along with me, [remains].
The eternal Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, sports with Ramā;
that region, where the six divine attributes manifest, is the supreme ether.

10. By describing the Supreme Void (*paravyoman*) as having the nature of the manifestation of the six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), its non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) is intended; for others maintain the position that it is indeed inert. [The opponent says:
"The Puruṣa is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), immutable (*kuṭastha*), omniscient (*sarvajña*), and facing in all directions (*sarvatomukha*)."
From him, all eternal living beings emanate in part.

11. The Puruṣa Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the aggregate of individual souls (jīva-samaṣṭi) and the immutable enjoyer (bhoktṛ-kūṭastha), is the supreme person; even at the time of dissolution, those whose nature is karma enter into him.
This is that state of a mother of mine, which I previously described to you.
Mahālakṣmī is declared by the wise to be the principle of Śakti;
Niyati is Mahāvidyā, and Kāla is proclaimed as Kālī. (13)
The triad of qualities is declared to be sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Sattva is remembered as being of the nature of happiness, clear, a producer of knowledge, and light.
Rajas should be known as being of the nature of suffering, mobile, red, and impelling.
Tamas should be known as having the nature of delusion; it is heavy, black, and restrictive.
O Vāsava, Māyā, Prasūti, and Prakṛti—this triad of natures has already been explained to you previously. (16)
The elements are ten in number, and likewise the cavities are thirteen.
All these twenty-three were also clearly explained by me in the past.
Therefore, this contracted subject of mine, consisting of pure consciousness, always remains like a mirror, with the flood of all principles manifesting within itself. (18)

18. Having thus defined the thirty-five principles introduced by verses 42–44 in the sixth chapter, he now defines the four states of the self introduced in verse 35, beginning with the words "tadayam" and continuing until the end of the chapter.
Now listen with a one-pointed mind to that which is its fourfold nature here:
the first is proclaimed as the mother consisting of emptiness (*śūnya*) in states such as fainting. (19)
Then, the one consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya) is proclaimed as the mother in deep sleep;
for it is the vital breaths alone that expand within a person during deep sleep. 20.
In cases such as fainting or being struck by poison, even the vital breath (prāṇa) ceases;
only the existence of one's own self remains, and therefore at that time the person is void.
The third [state] is proclaimed as the mother in the dream [state], measuring eight cities;
it consists of the vital breaths, the elements, the actions, the organs, and the three qualities. || 22 ||
22. Consisting of the eight *puri*s. The word *mātra* signifies either "measure" or "exclusive.
The meaning is that [the soul] is devoid of external activity. The eight *puri*s will be described in the following verse:
"Prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the subtle body (*liṅga*) are remembered as the eight *puri*s."
For in a dream, one indeed wanders at will by means of the internal organ alone. || 23 ||
23. The *liṅga* is the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*).

The embodied soul, exerting itself with its own physical body, has entered the waking state. Listen to me regarding this fourfold nature of the person, as well as its threefold nature. 24. Listen to me regarding this fourfold nature of the person, as well as its threefold nature.
The contraction of those whose nature consists of knowledge and action is indeed threefold;
that very state of theirs possesses a threefold form—listen now to this explanation of it. (25)

Through *māyā*, there is the contraction of knowledge; due to the lack of sovereignty, there is the loss of action; and due to incapacity, there is atomicity (*aṇutā*). Thus, within the nature of the self, it is designated as threefold. (26)

26. *Kriyāvyaya* is the incapacity to perform the desired action. In the term *ānaiśvarya*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of "the state of one who is not a lord" (*anīśvarasya bhāvaḥ*), resulting in the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of both syllables.
By the statement that [the soul] is of the nature of an atom (*aṇu-rūpa*) due to the contraction of its own form, it is not [denied] that the soul's natural state is all-pervasive (*vibhu-rūpa*).

It must be understood that the nature of that [self] as being atomic (aṇu) is established by numerous means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Therefore, the specific description here of its atomic form should be understood as referring to its lack of omnipotence, lack of omniscience, and so forth.
That very point is explained by the phrase "due to incapacity" (aśakteḥ).
"He is minute, an agent of something, and a knower of something"—this has already been established previously regarding his dual nature as well as his single nature. (27)
Thus, O Śakra and others, the specific states of the mother have been proclaimed by me today; now listen to me regarding the state of the internal organ as well. 28.
28. In the previous chapter, the second state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) was indicated; it is explained here.

"I am consciousness itself, acting according to its own will, having attained self-awareness by its own nature. Having abandoned that awareness, I have likewise descended from there, step by step. 29.
The "shrinker of the shrine" (caityasaṃkocanī) is said to be the mind (citta), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
and that triad consists of the intellect (manas), the faculty of discernment (buddhi), and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). 30.

30. *Caitya* means the state of being accumulated (*cita*), that is to say, consciousness (*caitanya*). Furthermore, conceptualization (*vikalpa*), determination (*vyavasāya*), and self-conceit (*abhimāna*) [are its functions].
(Ā, Ī: *vikalpo vyavasāyaḥ*)—the mind (*manas*) conceptualizes the object, and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) conceives "I. 31.

31. *Vikalpa* is manifold conceptualization; it is knowledge that is non-conclusive in nature. It conceives [of objects] as its own and perceives them as such. And the intellect (*buddhi*), always presided over by consciousness (*cetanā*), determines [its objects].
The intellect is said to be the internal (adhyātma), while discernment is the elemental (adhibhūtaka).
32. It determines and ascertains. (p. 28) The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), reflected in the mirror of the intellect, is the presiding deity.
Likewise, the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) is the internal aspect, while self-conceit (abhimāna) is the elemental aspect. || 33 ||
Furthermore, Rudra is proclaimed as the presiding deity (adhidaiva) of the mind (manas), while the mind itself is declared as the internal self (adhyātma).
Likewise, conceptual construction (vikalpa) is the elemental sphere (adhibhūta), and the moon is its presiding deity (adhidaivata).
In the performance of their functions, the qualities consist of vital breath (*prāṇa*), impulsion (*saṃrambha*), and volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Vital breath is said to be effort (*prayatna*); impulsion is called pride (*garva*). (35)

The nature of pride (*garva*) is said to be the state of ownership over the fruit [of one's actions], while *saṃrambha* is so called. The wise declare that mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is the departure from indifference. (36)
This second state, belonging to the internal organ, has been explained by me;
for from that, the "I" which belongs to the internal organ falls away from its form.
Having gradually attained a state of torpor, she is designated as the "external instrument" (bahiṣkaraṇa);
indeed, the external instruments have already been explained by me previously. (38)
But when the cognitive faculties are active, the mind and the others proceed;
the eye perceives the object, and it is that mind which conceptualizes it. (39)
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), abiding in the conceptualization of perception, conceives [the object];
then the intellect (buddhi), having determined it, presents it to the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 40 ||
40. "Having determined" (*adhyavasya*), "having resolved" (*adhyavasāya*), meaning having performed the act of determination.

However, regarding the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the sequence is traditionally held to be reversed; for the acts of speaking and so forth follow upon volition (*saṃkalpa*) and the rest. 41.
41. "Parācīnā" means that which exists behind.
All the specific distinctions regarding the internal self (adhyātma) and so forth have been previously declared.
This third [state] is called "vidhā," and it resides in the external organs (bahiṣkaraṇa). 42.

Now listen to me regarding this fourth limit, which indeed has the nature of the object of knowledge (*meyarūpa*). That object of knowledge is twofold, according to its external and internal arrangement. (43)
43. "It is mine. This very [state] was previously designated as the stage of existence (*bhāvabhūmikā*).
But the external—blue, yellow, and so forth—and the internal—pleasure, pain, and so forth—I have fallen into a state of torpor through these four modes. 44.

By means of objects arising from the conceptual constructions of my own mind, even though I am directly perceived, I was forgotten; [now I am remembered] through the instruction of a true teacher, following sound reasoning. (45)
When I am clearly perceived by the discerning as being within the object of knowledge itself, then,
having dissolved all this state consisting of the form of the cognizable, I am likewise [the absolute]. || 46 ||
46–47. The object of thought is that which is to be measured.
Then, in the light [of consciousness], I myself am the independent, full form of consciousness;
being clear and clearer than clear, I am thereafter designated as the instruments [of perception].
Then, within the mother, I manifest as exceedingly pure and consisting of pure consciousness;
by contemplating both my ascent and descent, one whose mind is fixed on me and whose life-breath has gone unto me attains to my own state of being. (48)

Thus ends the [chapter titled] "The Illumination of the Knower and the Instruments" in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*. (Note: In some versions, the title is given as "The Determination of the Pure and Mixed Principles.")
The Seventh Chapter. || 7 ||
Chapter Eight. Śakra:
Salutations to you, O goddess born from the ocean; salutations to you, O goddess born from the lotus.
Salutations to you, whose abode is the lake-born flower; salutations to the consort of Nārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
O Lotus-born One, you ought to explain in detail to me, who asks, those incarnations of yours that have been mentioned in your five treasuries.

2. Since it is well known that the first sheath, the *śaktikośa*, is connected with the Lord in his supreme form (*pararūpa*) and with the fourfold manifestations (*caturvyūha*), we shall set it aside for now; here, a question is posed concerning the five sheaths beginning with *māyā*:
for what purpose are they, of what kind are they, how many are they, and what is their essential nature?
Tell me the truth, O Goddess, for you are indeed omniscient and eternal.
Śrī said: It is without waves, indefinable, unshakable, incomparable, formless,
without categories, indivisible, free from conceptual construction, and undisturbed.
Unchanging and undisturbed. || 4 ||

4. Incidentally, he describes the abiding of the Lord’s supreme form within the treasury of powers (śaktikośa) with the words beginning "waveless" (ataraṅgam). Here, one should keep in mind what was stated in the seventeenth verse of the sixth chapter:
"The one Brahman Nārāyaṇa is void, pure, and free from affliction."
Whatever is seen, heard, or inferred—
this is declared to be Nārāyaṇa,
the Nārāyaṇa who is to be realized through the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The world— consisting of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle and the gross, the sentient and the insentient— is characterized by both existence and non-existence.
6. The three means of valid cognition are perception, inference, and verbal testimony.
All this is the unsurpassed Brahman, Nārāyaṇa. [E, Ī: unsurpassed]
The dense mass of consciousness, which is pure, autonomous, and blissful, being entirely free from ignorance. || 7 ||
The divine, supreme end of the path,
consisting of both being and non-being, exists in two ways through the state of the possessor of power and power itself.
That Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, is the Possessor of Power, and I am that;
she is Nārāyaṇī, the Power, and I am the ego-sense (ahaṃtā) whose nature is existence.
9. I am the object of the cognition "I. There is no place that exists without me; nor is there any place of mine that exists without it. 10. [This is the same as verse 9.]
10. "Without that" means without that [specific] Brahman.
11. "In one way and indeed in two ways," we two, who are the cause of all things, are designated by those various scriptures that have crossed the ocean of reality.
In some cases creation is preceded by becoming (bhāva), in some it is preceded by being (bhavat), and in others it is preceded by both being and becoming;
the wise man is not deluded therein.
For when Nārāyaṇa alone descended due to the business of the gods, I was there with him, sharing in his very nature.
And when I alone descended out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, that Lord who is the referent of the term "I" became manifest within me as my ego-sense. (14)
When we both descended equally with the desire to accomplish the work of the gods,
we two remained as one another's counterparts, consisting of the nature of existence and non-existence.
Since the reality is established in this manner, hear now the account of the descent of the Lord:
Aniruddha, the all-pervading deity, the god of gods.
The eternal one. || 16 ||
Then, O Vāsava, having arisen from that Great Vidyā, I myself came into being as Mahālakṣmī, known by the name Kamalā, from me alone.
17. He speaks of the descent from the treasury of Māyā: "From me alone [came] Mahālakṣmī. Here, one should keep in mind what was stated in the eighteenth verse of the sixth chapter:
"These two divine parents are considered the progenitors of the worlds."
But in the descent as Padmanābha, these two were not born from a womb. || 18 ||
18. He describes the descent as Prasūtikośā with the words "the descent of Padmanābhā," and so forth.
The descent of Mahālakṣmī, Mahāvidyā, and Mahāmāyā was previously mentioned here in the twentieth verse of the sixth chapter.
He who is the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, known by the name Śaktīśa, has many forms; I am devoted to him in all of them. (19)
In one way, two ways, four ways, six ways, and likewise eight ways, and again twelve ways; hear from me the names therein. (20)
"I am Śrī, the one of excellent complexion, who dwells on the lap of the two-armed Lord.
O Vāsava, Śrī and Puṣṭi are the two forms on either side of his thighs."
In the four directions, Śrī, Kīrti, Jayā, and likewise Māyā— assuming these forms— I am enjoyed by that very Viṣṇu.
O Indra, hear now my sixfold name as it resides in the six corners of that very [mandala]:
Śuddhi (Purity), Nirañjanā (The Stainless One), Nityā (The Eternal), and Jñānaśakti (the Power of Knowledge).
Likewise, Aparājitā is the sixth supreme Prakṛti;
and she, as "I," am established in eight forms within the directions of that very [Prakṛti]. (24)
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, the bestower of all desires, the increaser of affection, the bringer of fame, the giver of peace, the giver of contentment, and Puṣṭi as the eighth. (25)
In the six corners of that very [triangle], I abide as twelvefold:
Śrī, Kāmeśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śakti, and Vibhūti.
Desire, joy, and delight, as well as illusion, intellect, and greatness—
thus I am established in six ways within the four-armed one in successive order.
O Vāsava, I am likewise the mistress of that very six-armed one and of the eight-armed one;
I am also the mistress of the twelve-armed one and of the fourteen-armed one.
Likewise, for one who is sixteen cubits tall and possesses eighteen arms, there are established these many varieties by dividing the self in various ways. (29)
Indeed, regarding that incarnation of Viṣṇu known as Sindhuśāyin,
I abide surrounding him, having assumed four forms.

30. He speaks of the descent into the Prakṛti-kośa (the sheath of primordial nature) with the words "sindhuśāyī" (lying in the ocean). Here, one should keep in mind what was stated in the twenty-first verse of the fifth chapter:
"Lakṣmī, Nidrā, Prīti, and Vidyā are the distinct [powers]."
For this incarnation of Viṣṇu is known by the name Śrīpati—or, according to another reading, Śaktīśa.
There, I stood to his left under the name of Śrī; for I am indeed an incarnation of Viṣṇu known by the name Pārijātacit.
Then she, whose hands rest upon his shoulders, stands on the left lap of Hari;
for she is the auspicious incarnation of Viṣṇu known by the name Mīnadhara.
33. He speaks of the descent of the vessel of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍakośa), beginning with "by the name Mīnadhara" and so forth: "I wander there and there, assuming the form of a boat."
The supreme incarnation of Viṣṇu is remembered as the manifestation of the three strides (Traivikramodaya). || 34 ||
I am Gaṅgā, the producer of delight, who originates from his foot;
I am that incarnation of Hari known as Anantaśayana.
Established in the four directions of that [Lord], she has assumed a fourfold nature,
being endowed with the names Lakṣmī, Cintā, Nidrā, and Puṣṭi. (36)
Thus, among these, I am the one who has descended together with the Siddhas from the center of the cosmic egg.
When the incarnations have become distinct from within the middle of the Brahmāṇḍa, [37]...
In that same manner, I too have descended individually as Anuvratā;
for that which is known as the descent of the Boar is indeed celebrated in the Vedas. (38)
Then I too, having become separate under the name Bhū, shall partake [of that state];
for whatever is called an incarnation is indeed the ancient Dharma-Viṣṇu.
Then I was proclaimed as the goddess Śrī, born of fame, known by the name Bhārgavī;
for he who was indeed the incarnation named Dattātreya, the son of Atri, [was my husband]. (40)
For at that time, I arose from the lake for his enjoyment;
indeed, that auspicious descent known as Vāmana belongs to Viṣṇu. || 41 ||
Born from a lotus, I was then renowned as Padmā;
when Viṣṇu descended as the one known as Rāma Bhārgava. || 42 ||
At that time, I was the power named Dharaṇī, born not from a womb;
for he who is known as the auspicious Rāma, son of Daśaratha, was indeed an incarnation. (43)
I was born at the sacrifice of Janaka from the furrow wounded by the tip of the plough;
I am renowned by the name Sītā, the destroyer of the Ten-faced one.
For just as the fourfold incarnation of Viṣṇu will come to pass,
so too shall I manifest myself in four forms in Mathurā.
Revatī, Rukmiṇī, and likewise she who is named Rati, as well as Uṣā;
and that other incarnation known as Buddha, which is the deluder. || 46 ||
There, I am indeed known by the name Tārā and also celebrated as Dhārā;
those who are the incarnations beginning with Dhruva are remembered as being exclusively Vaiṣṇava.
47. He speaks of the descent into the sheath of the living body: "The eternal ones and so forth.
I, having become those various bodies, am established as their object of enjoyment.
As for that form of mine which is delusive—
It is heard that it is the sustainer of immortality. || 48 ||
At that time, existence and non-existence were perceived equally there in that form,
by the gods in the form of men, in the form of women, and likewise by others.
"Born together and born separately—this birth of mine is wondrous!
It has been proclaimed by you, O Lord of Gods; now hear of my birth alone. (50)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Lakṣmī," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Note: The titles *Śrīpañcarātra* and *Śrīpañcarātre* are variants found in manuscripts E and ī respectively.)
Chapter Nine:

For me, there can be no separation from him, nor for him from me,
at any time or in any place.
And by virtue of those various tasks, we two shall assume other forms of wondrous appearance.

Brahmā and the others, compelled by the power of his asceticism and yoga,

Assuming such and such forms, we two, the eternal ones,

It should be understood,
O Lord of the Gods, as the origin, the prowess in battle, and the hymn of praise.
The Brahmins, who have mastered the Vedas, relate this in great detail.
By praising, meditating upon, or even bowing down to that goddess of such power,
one constantly obtains the fruit of eternal and imperishable sovereignty.
That goddess who is called Yoganidrā of Hari, she who is difficult to overcome—
know me to be that eternal goddess, possessing the body of Mahākālī. 15.
For at that time, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were deluded by her; consequently, they were slain by Viṣṇu, the God of gods, through the power of a boon he had received.
O Purandara, that hymn beginning with "Viśveśvarī" was always seen by Brahmā in the past for the purpose of praising me, the Goddess Yoganidrā.
17. And this narrative is recited in the first chapter of the Devīmāhātmya within the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:

Enchanted by praise, she brings everything moving and unmoving under the control of the one who praises her.

O Śakra, during that period characterized by darkness (tāmasa), there was indeed a supreme great vidyā born from the body of Gaurī; at that time, I was known as Kauśikī.

"The hymn named the Nārāyaṇī-stuti is most beautiful;
at that time, these praises were seen by me as they were uttered by the gods led by Agni. 25.
When worshipped with devotion, she bestows omniscience;
O Lord of all gods, I am Kauśikī, the granter of many desires. My origins, my martial prowess, and my praises have been extolled by the ancients.

Furthermore, during the Vaivasvata interval, these two, Sumbha and Niśumbha,
will be born again, intoxicated by their boons and causing affliction to the gods.
"I, Sunandā Vindhyavāsinī, shall destroy those two who were born in the family of the cowherd Nanda and originated from the womb of Yaśodā."
Furthermore, descending upon the surface of the earth in an exceedingly fierce form,
I shall slay the great Asuras of the Vaipracitta lineage.
And as she devours those fierce great Asuras, the sons of Vipracitti,

Then all the deities and the humans in the mortal world,
praising me, will constantly address me as Raktadantikā (the Red-toothed One).
In that very interval, O Śakra, during the fortieth yuga,

"Remembered by the sages, I shall be born upon the earth not from a womb;

O Śakra, men will proclaim me as "Śatākṣī" (the Hundred-eyed One);

"I shall nourish [them] with auspicious, gathered vegetables that sustain life;
therefore, O Vāsava, the gods will then praise me as Śāmbharī. (36)
And right there I shall slay the great asura named Durga;

O Śakra, by praising, meditating upon, worshipping, and bowing to Śākambharī,
one quickly attains inexhaustible food and drink.
[He attains] delight. || 38 ||
And at the fiftieth cycle of four ages, she was entreated by the sages on the Himalayas; having assumed both a beautiful and an exceedingly terrifying form, [she appeared]. (39)
"I shall devour the Rākṣasas for the sake of protecting the sages;

"O Bhīma goddess, be gracious!"—thus [he addressed] Bhīmā, the bestower of fearlessness.

She will cause great affliction to both men and sages; there,

"For the sake of the welfare of the three worlds, I shall slay the great asura;

50. And this narrative is seen in the first chapter of the Devīmāhātmya in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa,

Having shaken off all illusion, one attains perfect knowledge;
one obtains every prosperity and dispels all calamities.
"By my power, he shall enjoy good fortune and fame;
even if these [deities] alone, without Viṣṇu, should speak of me. (54)

Having thus known me as manifest and universally acknowledged in such a manner, || 58 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Exclusive Incarnations" (or "The Discourse on the Inseparability from the Lord"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Chapter Ten. Śakra:
Salutations to you, who are the very fruit of the labor of churning the Ocean of Milk; salutations to the enemy of Madhu’s sister, salutations to you, the source of nectar. || 1 ||
Those categories ending with "existence" have been heard by me from the lotus of your mouth;
now I wish to hear the categories that follow "existence. (2)
O Lotus-seated One, salutations to you! Being asked by me, please tell me: what are the forms of those Vaiṣṇava incarnations, and how many have they been described by the wise?
Śrī said: "Ah, O Śakra, I shall tell you the various ways in which you have been surpassed;
how many Vaiṣṇava incarnations there are, and of what nature they are."
The sixfold policy is the stainless Brahman—faultless, undecaying, and eternal;
it possesses all powers, is free from affliction, and is the object of supportless contemplation.
That indeed first unfolds through the relationship between the possessor of power and power;
the supreme deity Nārāyaṇa exists as the possessor of power.
"I am his firm power (śakti), O All-pervading One, performing all his works;
we two manifest in many forms for the sake of the world. (7)
Just as I have previously explained to you my abiding through various manifestations,
now hear from me the transformations of Viṣṇu, who is himself changeless.
Resorting to my own power, that most wonderful primordial nature, which is non-material, incomparable, and radiant with inconceivable majesty— (9)
For the welfare of the world, the Lord of the World arises in three forms:
first, in his supreme form, and then also in his manifested (vyūha) forms.
Likewise, the all-pervading Lord, desiring to bestow grace upon his devotees, assumes various states through the form of manifestation.
He possesses a supreme body that is incomparable and indescribable,
which nourishes the entire universe with a radiance equal to ten million full moons.
He has two arms, lotus-like eyes, and hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
in his two hands, he holds a discus and a conch shell made of lines.
It is marked [with signs], situated upon feet free from change, supremely beautiful,
and adorned with its own six qualities, neither deficient nor excessive.
With limbs perfectly proportioned and all parts beautiful,
he was adorned with white ornaments that resembled the surging waves of nectar.

This single divine form, known as the Supreme, belonging to Viṣṇu, is indeed the highest; it is imperishable, consisting of Acyuta and the other [forms], which are themselves formless and become rays of light.
Those perfected in yoga worship her, who resides in the heart as the state of the Fourth (turya).
Now, I shall describe to you her second form, the Vyūha.
Having divided himself fourfold according to the distinctions of the directions starting with the east,
the Lord abides on the path of deep sleep through the divisions of Vāsudeva and the others.
The configuration of the primordial form is indeed remembered as being common to all;
the first form possesses six qualities arising from the pairs beginning with knowledge. (19)
The other forms have been described by me previously;
[the supreme form] has the characteristic of bliss and vibration, shining like a thousand suns, moons, and fires.
Know that to be the seed of all actions and of their conceptualizations, the locus of them, the state of deep sleep, and the fourfold nature— O Vāsava, know that to be the first.
even in the state of dream, the Lord likewise divides himself by himself through his own power,
according to the distinctions of the directions such as the east, in the forms of Vāsudeva and the others.
Through the distinction of concise and detailed descriptions of the qualities, Puruṣottama [is described] with most wonderful [forms] resembling white, red, gold, and clouds. (23)
It abides in four forms equal to the primordial form,
bestowing the fruit of liberation and enjoyment, and bringing about the destruction of the seed of worldly existence.
The second is the fourfold nature (cāturātmya), which is beautiful with an abundance of nectar;
then, in the state of waking, O Lord, [the deity appears] through the distinctions of white, red, and so forth.
With four arms and noble limbs, marked with the conch, the discus, and other signs, their bodies variegated by various banners, they are designated as Vāsudeva and the others. || 26 ||
The All-pervading Lord, by means of his own divine play, remains there having divided himself into various manifestations;
among these, the first form of the Blessed One possesses the luster of snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Four-armed, with a gentle countenance and eyes resembling lotuses,

With his primary right hand he bestows fearlessness upon the terrified,
while with his left hand, likewise positioned, he holds an excellent conch shell.
With his other [left] hand he holds the Sudarśana discus,
and with his right hand a heavy mace resting upon the surface of the earth.
One should thus meditate upon Vāsudeva in the space before one:
having the form of a peak of vermilion, with a gentle face and four arms. (31)
Clad in garments resembling the color of flax flowers and marked with the palm-tree emblem,
he is equal to the first Lord by means of his two principal hands.
One should contemplate Saṃkarṣaṇa in this manner on the right side: he holds a plow in his hand and a mace in his other hand.
He possessed the luster of a multitude of fireflies appearing on a rainy night,
was clothed in garments of red silk, and was adorned with the dolphin-bannered god of love.
The third supreme lord has a gentle face and four arms;
O great-minded one, his two principal hands are identical to those described previously. (35)
In the left [hand] he holds a Śārṅga bow, and in the right, five arrows;
in the other portion, one should contemplate Pradyumna—thus it is proclaimed. (36)
Resembling the mountain of collyrium, clothed in beautiful yellow garments,
four-armed, large-eyed, and adorned with the mark of the deer. || 37 ||
One should contemplate his first pair of hands as being like the beginning;
then, in the sequence starting from the right, he holds a sword and a shield with two hands.
One should meditate on Aniruddha, holding [the conch], in the northern quarter;

Adorned on the chest with the Kaustubha, the king of jewels,

One should contemplate that divine [reality], which effects persistence, origination, and dissolution, and is endowed with all instruments; for him in whose teaching the universe abides,
there exists the threefold fourfold nature within the triad of states beginning with deep sleep.
Clearly manifest in that fourth state (turya) is the supreme reality, which is characterized by the qualities (guṇas).
This second form of Viṣṇu, known as the Vyūha, which desires to emanate the worlds through knowledge, action, and so forth, has been described by me.
Now behold the third form of Viṣṇu, called Vibhava, situated in the center of the universal temple, the performer of various forms and actions. (44)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Supreme Vyūha," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. || 10 ||
Chapter Eleven:
Śrī [B: Śrī said]
Faultless, without end, beyond all support, irreproachable, and eternal;
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Lord of Śrī, the supreme Self, the eternal;

Taking up the pure sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*),
she appropriately fashioned for him various forms, such as the military arrays (*vyūha*) and others, in a manner that was immediately suitable.
I shall reveal to you the nature of the God that transcends existence;
I am the activity of that God, of this there is no doubt.
"For whatever action was performed by me, it is said to have been performed by him. Indeed, I am remembered as the active agency of that god.

The four stages beginning with the Fourth (turya) and ending with the waking state (jāgrat), which have been described,

The marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth are clearly visible, somewhat visible, slightly visible, and not visible at all;

This division was fashioned by the Blessed One himself for the purpose of providing a support for meditation for yogins. And of this—

Thus, when the array of states of waking is manifested from the state of dreaming,
the great Taijasa is worshipped at the end of the waking state, arising from the state of dreaming.
The Blessed One Viśākhayūpa is that god, a treasury of splendors,
within the triad of Cāturātmya beginning with the fourth and ending with the dream state.
For [that which is taught] in the Cāturātmya and other [texts]... || 15 ||
In that [state] endowed with various sovereign powers, the sixfold policy is well-established;

Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktīśa, Madhusūdana, Kapila—the presiding deity of knowledge—Viśvarūpa, and Vihaga. || 19 ||

The one whose nature is wrath (*krodhātmā*) has the face of a mare (*baḍavāvaktro*).
Likewise, he is Dharma and Vāgīśvara;

The Boar and the Man-Lion, likewise the Stealer of the Nectar;
the Lord of Śrī with a divine body, and the Embodiment of Beauty who holds the nectar. (21)
The conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, and likewise the one who carried off the Pārijāta tree;
the Lord of the World with a tranquil soul, Dattātreya, the Great Lord. || 22 ||
The Blessed One reclining on a banyan tree, as well as he whose body has a single horn;
the god with a dwarfed form, the all-pervading Trivikrama. (23)
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as Hari and Kṛṣṇa;
Rāma bearing the flaming axe, and the other Rāma who is the wielder of the bow.
The Lord Kalkī, the knower of the Vedas, and the Master who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla)—

These manifestations of the omnipresent Viśākha-yūpa, appearing according to their respective functions, are known as his vibhavas; and their functions are indeed non-confounded.
Between the pure and impure paths, Padmanābha is established;
other gods, beginning with Dhruva, are manifested within the temple of the universe.
Their forms, weapons, powers, and various other modes are likewise present.
All that is established in the Sāttvata; it has been shown to be a mere matter of terminology. || 28 ||
The branches of the all-pervading Lord are proclaimed to be Vāsudeva and the others;

Then, from the four branches, three [manifestations] beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara have emerged; that is called another vyūha.

[the arising] || 31 ||
O Lord of the Thirty-three, the bodies of all the deities, beginning with Para and ending with Vibhava, consist of the nature of the pure sixfold qualities.
Whatever weapons of the gods there are, such as the discus and the conch, as well as various ornaments and diverse garments; || 33 ||
O Lord of the Gods, there are banners of various forms, splendors such as white and others, and diverse vehicles beginning with the Truth (Satya). 34.
The powers (śaktis), which bestow enjoyment and exist in various forms, as well as the entire group consisting of the internal organs and all their functions, [are that]. 35.
And whatever common instrument of assistance there may be shared with other men, know all that to be produced by the sixfold policy, O slayer of Bala. (36)
I am that very Self consisting of pure consciousness, fully endowed with the six attributes;
I manifest in whatever way corresponds to whatever is desired by each individual. (37)
Indeed, my existence does not occur without the God of gods;
nor indeed does the existence of the god Viṣṇu occur without me.
Thus we two have attained oneness, yet we remain established in a dual form;
we assume whichever particular mode is required in each respective case.
Śakra said:
O Daughter of the Ocean, salutations to you; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One!
What purpose does the Lord have in the distinctions of the supreme manifestation (paravyūha) and the others?
Śrī said:
For the sake of favoring living beings and out of compassion for my devotees...

Śakra said:

Śrī said:

the conceptualization of him as the Supreme (para), the Manifested (vyūha), and so forth, occurs in accordance with their respective functions.
It is performed by the God of gods, who presides over me as his power,
for the sake of the authority of those who have perfected the principles of yoga within the Supreme Self.

For those of middling capacity who are engaged in mixed practices, there is the cultivation of the military array (vyūha) in forms such as the Vaibhavīya and others, for those whose minds are devoid of discernment.
Having observed the disparity in the qualification of his devotees—who are afflicted by the notions of "I" and "mine" (or ignorance regarding "mine")—with respect to the Supreme Lord, he... (50)
It assumes various states designated as the "manifestation for others" (paravyūha) and so forth;
thus, O Śakra, these two-fold natures have been shown to you in brief.
The manifestations of myself and Nārāyaṇa, which consist of both existence and non-existence,
reside within the group of sheaths arising from me— both the pure and the impure.
Today you have shown us our station— both separate and together, and entirely so.
Having thus known me as manifest and universally acknowledged in this manner, [53]
Having constantly worshipped her, who possesses manifold natures, by means of various methods,

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Power" (*vibhavaprakāśa*), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*. 11.
Chapter Twelve. Śakra:

If the eternal living being (*jīva*) is indeed your pure power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), how can there be contact with afflictions, karma, and latent impressions (*kleśa-karma-āśaya*) for him within the lotus [of the heart]? (1)

What are the afflictions (kleśa), and how many are they said to be? What is action (karman) like, and of what kind is it? O Goddess, what is that which is called intention (āśaya), and what is its fruit remembered to be? || 2 ||
O Daughter of the Ocean, tell me this; salutations, salutations to you!
For indeed, O Omniscient One, no one other than you is able to speak of this.
Śrī said:
"I am the goddess Nārāyaṇī, consisting of pure and autonomous consciousness; I am the faultless, inseparable Śrī of Viṣṇu. (4)
I have fashioned my form in two ways through the distinction between the Lord and that which is to be ruled;
and that which is to be ruled is distinct from Him solely by virtue of His own absolute freedom (*svācchandyāt*).
Consciousness-power (*cicchakti*) is one, called the subject (*bhoktṛ*), while the other consists of the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and so forth.
She has been divided by me into two types, according to the distinction between Kālī and Akālī.
In that regard, the power consisting of time is both deluding and binding;
this very nature (prakṛti), along with its transformations, is the power of consciousness (cicchakti) by which [consciousness] is bound.
That form by which the power of consciousness, having attained the state of an enjoyer, becomes afflicted—know that affliction to be fivefold; hear from me its names as well. (8)
Darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhatāmisra)—this is the fivefold ignorance; it is the highest state of darkness.
Although the power of consciousness is unattached, pure, and immutable,
it bears its own form as if permeated by impurity due to its stainlessness.
Śakra said:
O Lotus-born One, I perceive as it were a contradiction in the power of consciousness—its attachment to afflictions. My mind seems to be bewildered today; dispel that delusion.
Śrī is independent, the cause of all accomplishments (siddhis) here, and most wonderful.
I am the eternal goddess, the power of Nārāyaṇa, who is ever-manifested.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, for me there are five eternal functions:
concealment, as well as creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
"Anugraha" is said to be my fivefold activity;
O Śakra, hear from me the sequential explanation of these actions.

In that regard, the concealment of one's own nature is proclaimed to be the manifestation of something else; for that pure power of consciousness belonging to me is indeed designated as the "experiencer. (15)
That power of mine by which [the soul] exists under the sway of Prakṛti is called my power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti), known as "concealment" (tirobhāva). || 16 ||
This is my divided form, created by me through my power of true resolve;
that descent of mine which was described to you previously was the first.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) is thus proclaimed by the wise as the individual soul (jīva);
the distinction between them is declared to arise solely from my own sovereign will.

And that form of my *caitya* which was fashioned by you through your power of true resolve—that very thing is now being unified with me, for I am performing the unification with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). (19)
That supreme power is ignorance (avidyā), known as concealment (tirobhāva).
It has five stages; learn from me what they are.

(41) Ignorance (avidyā), however, is the first stage; it is that cognition which the living being (jīva) possesses regarding what is not the self and what is not its own nature, namely, the conceptualized object (caitya). (21)

That which consists of "mineness" (svatā) and "I-ness" (ahantā) is traditionally known as darkness (tamas) and ignorance (avidyā). And when an object is grasped through "I-ness," the pride that arises therein [is also part of it]. || 22 ||
The great delusion called *asmitā* is the second stage of afflictions; it is the attainment of a state of oneness between the knower and the knowable through ignorance. (23)

That latent impression (vāsanā) which, being established through the sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), is the cause for the recollection of pleasure, is designated by the terms "delusion" (moha), "egoism" (asmitā), and "great delusion" (mahāmoha). (24)
That passion for the objects of attachment is the third stage of affliction;
it is the cause for the recollection of suffering, which is established by the latent impression of egoism. 25.
That hatred, directed toward its hateful object, is the fourth stage of affliction.
For one who seeks to abandon suffering through yogic means and likewise desires to attain happiness, [this arises]. (26)
The terror that arises in the midst of those obstacles, known as "blindness," is the attachment [to existence]; that is the fifth stage of affliction. (27)
Having perceived the body as the self, one then attains identification with it; consequently,
one desires to acquire what is pleasurable and likewise wishes to abandon its opposite.
Fearing obstacles to that [attainment], the conscious being (or embodied soul) practices its remedy for the sake of obtaining the desired and for the prevention of the undesired. (29)
Whatever threefold action, consisting of three types, this person performs—that action has been described by the virtuous who are experts in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (30)

The pleasure produced from that, as well as the pain, and that which consists of both pain and pleasure—the wise learned in the treatises on reality have declared this threefold ripening (vipāka). || 31 ||

Latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are said to be the underlying dispositions (*āśaya*), born from afflictions, karma, and their maturation; for they reside within the internal organ and extend everywhere. (32)
Latent impressions (vāsanās) are constantly produced by the five stages of the afflictions (kleśas),
and likewise, latent impressions are the cause for actions (karmas) to produce results similar to themselves.
The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of pleasure and so forth is produced in three ways by the results of maturation (*vipāka*);
it is thus characterized by four marks known as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the rest. (34)
This method, known as concealment, is the binding of the sheath of the individual soul;
by this very power, the souls bound to me are eternally held fast. (35)
My powers of creation and so forth operate in continuous succession.
That power of mine for creation is twofold, according to its purity or impurity, by my own will.
That [power] has been shown to you after being analyzed; it exists again in sevenfold form, yet one of them is incessantly exercised through the ritual action pertaining to Prajāpati.
But others arise from the six sheaths, appearing at their respective times;
furthermore, in the sequence of creation arising from primordial nature (prakṛti), creation is to be known as threefold. (38)
It is divided into three types: the real (bhāvikī), the inferential (laiṅgikī), and the elemental (bhautikī);
just as [the potentiality] exists within the seed of a nyagrodha tree, so it exists within the primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (traiguṇya). || 39 ||

That state of the Mahat-tattva and the rest is called the creation of objective existence (bhāva-sṛṣṭi); it is the subtle body (liṅga) which is created by me through the distinction between the collective and the individual.
And likewise, for other beings, that [creation] is born from a linga;
it consists of the twenty principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas, as well as the three [unmanifest principles]. (41)
The objects of experience residing within the subtle body (liṅgadeha) are proclaimed to be the Virāj;
likewise, so too are the collective totality of the elements (khāni) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Those various portions which are established for each individual soul among that which exists in three ways, and those subtle elements of gross beings which were previously described; ||| 43 ||

These eighteen individual manifestations— afflictions, actions, latent impressions, and vital breaths— are designated as the subtle body (liṅga), which serves as the substratum for the hosts of individual souls.
For the powers of consciousness (cic-chaktayaḥ) residing in the subtle body (liṅga) transmigrate in such a manner;
however, this occurs when pure divine knowledge has arisen for those who live by virtuous deeds. 45.
These signs of living beings cease at this time and not otherwise;
the Virāj is the gross body which has the other name of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 46 ||
Furthermore, there are four other kinds of bodies for embodied beings.
"This is my elemental creation"—such is the contemplation of creation. (47)
The third power of mine is called *sthiti* (stability), which was previously described to you;
I shall explain its essential nature—listen to that from me, O Śakra. (48)

That which is the first moment of creation and that which is the moment of the desire to withdraw— the interval between these two is what is called "the act of maintaining stability" for those who abide therein.
That supreme power of my own abiding nature manifests in various forms through Viṣṇu,
the god of gods, and likewise through me.
That state which has been described is declared by the contemplators of reality to be the first;
the second is proclaimed by the lords of the Manvantaras. || 51 ||
The third [power] consists of the sons of Manu and the Kṣudras; thus it is fourfold.
Now hear this division of the fourth, the power of withdrawal (saṃhṛtī-śakti). || 52 ||
That which is the constant destruction of beings such as those born from a womb is eternal; however, O Śakra, another dissolution is known as occasional (naimittikī).
That third [power], however, which has the three worlds as its object and is caused by the sleep of Brahmā,
is declared to be the primordial (prākṛtī),
depending upon the Great Principle (mahat) and the others.
The fourth, however, is *prāsūti*, and its object is the unmanifest (*avyakta*);
that which is called the fifth is *māyī*, and its object is indeed *prasūti*.
The sixth is to be known as Śāktī, which has Māyā as its object;
the seventh is declared to be Ātyantikī, the dissolution of yogins into me.
Then the subtle bodies of the virtuous cease to exist.
O Śakra, this sevenfold reabsorption has been described by me;
the fifth is called "grace."
"Listen to this power of mine for the sake of this exposition"—
thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Powers of Concealment and the Like," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*. 12.
Chapter Thirteen:
Śrī (Glorious Fortune)
O Śakra, my fifth power is known as being of the nature of grace; O child, I shall now describe this very power to you according to its true essence.
Pierced by ignorance and brought under the sway of egoism and the other afflictions,
they are concealed by my very power known as "concealment" (tirodhāna).
Falling from high to low, and eager to leap up from the low,
they are bound by three kinds of bonds and revolve through the three states of existence.
Standing in the midst of the embers of saṃsāra, being cooked by their own karma,
they imagine happiness while in constant suffering, overcome by ignorance.
Chasing after those wombs that distinguish between the moving and the unmoving,
they run through births ever-newer than before, variegated by their own respective causes.
Day and night, through the body, senses, mind, intellect, and sensations,
they bind themselves to births and likewise to deaths in various ways.
"Being afflicted" means being tormented by various afflictions arising from union and separation;
[he is so called] because the sin of those [afflictions] has been extinguished by the stream of his arising compassion. (7)
"I behold living beings freed from suffering by means of Śrī;
this is called grace (anugraha), which has another name, 'the descent of power' (śaktipāta)."
At that time, as they were being observed by me, these beings attained equality of karma;
that was the final body of those living beings as it was beheld by me. (9)
For I alone know that moment of the descent of power;
it is not brought about by human effort, nor by any other cause.
I look upon someone at some time solely by my own will;
from that moment on, that person’s inner self becomes perfectly pure.
Having attained equilibrium of the karmas and taking refuge in pure actions,
he is endowed with the knowledge of Vedānta and devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
By carrying forth true devotion toward Viṣṇu through the correct knowledge of the Sāttvatas,
the yogi, after a long time, shakes off the accumulation of afflictions.
Having shaken off various bonds and shining forth here and there,
he attains the supreme Brahman, whose essence is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
This, however, is my fifth power, consisting of grace;
my own freedom alone is the cause for acts such as concealment.
"O Śakra, understand it thus: therefore, nothing further should be asked.
Śakra said: "Homage to the one whose abode is the lotus; homage to the refuge of Nārāyaṇa! (16)
Homage to her who is eternally faultless and an ocean of auspicious qualities!
The great darkness within me has been washed away by the abundant nectar of your speech. (17)
[B: omits verses 18 and 19] "I desire to hear further about the supreme form of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). Śrī said:
Nārāyaṇa alone is the God, the eternal Supreme Self. || 18 ||
He is the eternal treasury of knowledge, power, sovereignty, valor, capability, and vigor;
he is beginningless and indefinable in terms of space, time, and essential nature.
I am his supreme goddess, radiant with the majesty of the six qualities; I am the eternal power named Ahaṃtā (the I-consciousness), the performer of all actions. (20)
Consciousness alone is my own nature, pure, autonomous,
and full; all the accomplishments of all living beings depend upon me.
Upon the wall of my own self, I manifest the entire universe by my own will;
these worlds flash forth within me like birds upon the surface of water.
Out of my own free will, I descend as the one who performs the fivefold act;
when I thus descend, I am indeed called the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
This contraction of mine is [actually] the pure, independent mass of consciousness;
even within this, the world appears like a mountain reflected in the interior of a mirror.
Like a diamond-jewel, this [self] is always transparent and radiant;
that which is its quality of consciousness is as stainless as the light of the sun. (25)
In that manner, this individual soul (jīva) vibrates by its own accord according to its corresponding form;
this very soul also perpetually performs the five functions.
The activity that occurs toward blue, yellow, and so forth— [or, as some read, "on a wall, blue, yellow, and so forth"]— is called *sṛṣṭi* (emission) by the wise.
That which is attachment to an object therein is *sthiti* (maintenance).
is proclaimed. || 27 ||
The withdrawal from an object already grasped due to the desire to grasp another is declared as "withdrawal" (saṃhṛti) by those expert in the treatises on reality. (28)
The obscuration of those latent impressions (vāsanās) is grace (anugraha), which is their dissolution;
this [consciousness], whose nature is to devour the object of perception, is always a consumer like fire. (29)
This individual soul (jīva) always nourishes my fuel by means of its own measure;
however, my true nature, which is beyond ignorance, was explained to you by me previously.
When he abandons contraction through union with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), then, shining forth, he is liberated from all bonds on every side. || 31 ||
Through the union of knowledge and action, one who is always all-knowing and all-doing, being without limitation and free from contraction, becomes fit for my own state of being.
As long as this [Self] is not perceived by me through compassion,
so long does it perceive the universe through its instruments with contracted knowledge.
Having perceived objects with the eye and having conceptualized them likewise with the mind,
one determines them through the intellect alone by means of self-identification arising from the ego-sense.
Then, during wakefulness or in a dream, it moves about by means of the internal organs; but having abandoned those in deep sleep, it abides in its own essential nature. || 35 ||
These three states are innate and do not belong to the individual soul at all;
yet the fourth state arises in the soul when it is established in samādhi.
That too is not for him; rather, this is the abiding state of a pure being (śuddhasattva), which is without fluctuation and untouched by all the qualities of nature (prākṛtaguṇa).
The nature of the individual soul (jīva), however, is composed of consciousness, unconditioned, and indestructible;
yet even though it is of such a nature, it is veiled by beginningless ignorance (avidyā). 38.
"Therefore, he does not see me, who am so clearly visible and have become his very self.
Śakra said: "O Goddess, how can you be so clearly visible while remaining beyond all measure? (39)
"Even the Vedantas do not know you in this manner, O Lotus-born One.
Śrī said: "But know me, O Śakra, to be perceptible to all embodied beings."
Having become composed in mind, listen to this my doctrine.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Nature of the Individual Soul," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Or: in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, the illumination of the types of individual souls. 13.
Chapter Fourteen:
Śrī [B, E: Śrī said]
The Lord Vāsudeva, whose nature is consciousness, is undivided by space, time, and other such factors; he is the Supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities and stainless. || 1 ||
Bliss is eternally of one form, yet it possesses the six attributes and is undecaying and immortal;
I am its supreme power, the eternal and constant egoity.
This power of my activity, characterized by the desire to emanate,
becomes manifest; through portions of tens of thousands, millions, and hundreds of billions, I— having attained a twofold division through my own sovereignty— create.
By virtue of being the object of consciousness and consciousness itself, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and the conscious one (cetana) are these two.
My own self is consciousness itself, which has attained both sentience and insentience;
for my very form is consciousness alone, entirely full of clarity and autonomy.
Yet, through its union with the "sugar-cane juice" of the object, it assumes a state of solidification, just as sugar-cane juice does.

Therefore, when that object of cognition is examined—and [according to versions ā, B, c, and ḍ: when it is presented]—it will attain the nature of consciousness, for it does not relinquish its status as consciousness. || 6 ||
For just as fuel licked by fire becomes identical with it, so too the object of thought, when thoroughly consumed by consciousness, attains the state of being composed of consciousness.
Whether in blue, yellow, pleasure, or pain, the nature of consciousness remains undivided;
it is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), through its manifold collection of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that differentiates it.
For even conceptual construction is my very form.
It is created solely through its own freedom;
by means of this, the object of thought is conceptualized according to the distinction between external and internal.
Neither outside nor indeed within, that supreme [and stainless] form of mine is of the nature of consciousness;
it is not divided by me through its own selfhood into the forms of the object of knowledge and the knower.

That form which is not assailed by conceptual constructions, which is not distorted by words, and which does not wither under limiting conditions— that alone has attained the state of being an object of cognition.
When one abides with a mind from which conceptual construction has been cast far away,
having adopted the middle way, then that which is to be cognized exists as pure awareness.
Just as form situated in the eye perceives its own form externally, so too form situated in cognition perceives its own form within the object of knowledge. 13.
Just as wood permeated by fire is perceived as having that [fire’s] form,
so too the object of cognition permeated by consciousness is perceived as being of the nature of consciousness.

When the object of knowledge, having been brought to the state of being known, is determined by the knower, then that "I," consisting of consciousness, becomes directly perceived and vividly manifest. || 15 ||
For the state of "I-ness" (ahantā) itself is the nature of consciousness, a specific characteristic distinct from the object of knowledge;
and that [consciousness] is indeed myself. Therefore, I am everywhere composed of pure consciousness.
I am the hand-hold for those sinking in the ocean of consciousness, where all objects of thought have been submerged and have reached a state of oneness upon this island of the word "this. 17.

Those whose entire latent impressions have been washed away by the flowing nectar of the Middle Way perceive within themselves only Me— the Consciousness that pacifies the flood of all objects of thought.
People perceive the state of being the object and the subject within my mind, which is of a single form.
In the past, they believed precisely because of ignorance, as it was fashioned by my own volition.
In my own nature, I am neither quiescent, nor emergent, nor even intermediate;
such is the case for those who possess discernment of me, even while they are awake in the light of day.
By means of a mind that is free from division and devoid of waves, I am known;
yet, when being conceptualized, even though I am directly perceived, I am forgotten.
Just as an object standing before one does not appear to a mind that desires something else,
so too do I not appear to those who are possessed by latent impressions (vāsanā).
Just as one who desires to know restrains the mental modifications with his mind and perceives an object directly, so too does he perceive me, the pure consciousness.
The body of mine, which is always unobstructed and indeed luminous,
is directly perceived even during the time when there is no movement of thought by those of pure self (or those who have realized the Self).
Just as a cloth that is white by nature, when dyed with some color, would not resort to another color without first returning to its own original hue. || 25 ||
If one who perceives blue and so forth in this manner does not rest within me—the pure conscious self in the midst of the yellow—how indeed could he know that yellow? (26)
In that very way, how could one proceed from one phoneme to the next while uttering the word, if one does not rest within me, the pure conscious Self, in the interval? (27)
Thus, although I am pure and independent, when I am colored by forms,
I wander in the middle state as something purely pure, having abandoned those [forms] and not moving toward others.
By the cessation of movement through the right and left channels, resting in the middle channel,
the state that has fire and moon as its fuel illumines my state.
That which one experiences within, without relying on the intellect for meditation and without touching external objects— that is my undisturbed form.
But that which persists correctly in both light and darkness,
and remains present in both existence and non-existence— that is my stainless body.
For one whose desire for sense objects has ceased and whose soul is radiant with devotion to me,
that internal, supportless "I-ness" is my very body.

For those who practice that very [meditation], the nature of the "I" (aham-rūpa), which is beyond the reach of the body, vital breath, and so forth, remains for the discerning ones in the state of being Me (mad-bhāva).
Just as light is manifested from the sun but not produced [by it], so too the nature of consciousness is manifested by mental states but is certainly not produced [by them]. (34)
Just as the sun rises in the expanse of the sky without [physical] objects,
so too my own form shines forth by itself, even without objects of cognition.
Just as a gem such as crystal, because its nature is absolutely transparent, does not appear in its own form when colored by objects such as a *japa* flower. (36)

Furthermore, though I am pure, I am not perceived as distinct by ordinary people due to the mental constructs (caityas) intensified by my own volition; yet, for all that, it is not the case that I do not exist.
Just as the state of gold is not perceived as distinct from earrings and the like,
and yet it cannot be pointed out [as separate], nevertheless, it certainly exists. (38)
Thus, my state, consisting of pure consciousness, is eternal, pure, undivided by pleasure, pain, and the like, and is to be known through self-awareness. (39)
Likewise, there is a commonality of the root *jñā* (to know) with respect to the knower, the act of knowing, and the object to be known;
this very commonality of mine is distinguished by the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). (40)
Place, time, action, and form are well-known causes of differentiation;
since consciousness differentiates them, how could there be any differentiation in it? (41)

For that time which is the differentiation of the object of thought, consisting of the triad of the past and so forth—that too is dissolved in the great ocean of consciousness and becomes identical with it. (42)
For when the past and the future are excluded from me while I am present, then this very state of being present would not exist at all. (43)
I am the substratum of all things without exception, yet I am not supported by anything;
even space is conceived as having a substratum, therefore no such thing exists for me.
There is no state whatsoever for me in which consciousness does not exist.
Therefore, they worship me as the one, dense with consciousness, who possesses all forms. || 45 ||
Time, place, as well as form, action, the agent, and the object; the instrument, the recipient, and whatever fruit arises from that. (46)
The object of enjoyment and the enjoyer—all that is dissolved within the self of consciousness.
So too are the gods, the Daityas, the Nāgas, the Gandharvas, and the hosts of Rākṣasas. (47)
The eight classes [of beings] are the Vidyādharas, Piśācas, and Bhūtas;
and humans are manifold in nature, differentiated by caste, karma, and so forth. (48)
Then there are domestic animals, wild beasts, birds,
reptiles, and likewise other stationary beings whose nature consists of base conduct. (49)
The worlds situated in heaven and those situated in hell, as well as the fourteen worlds, the rivers, islands, and oceans— indeed, the entire succession of cosmic eggs.
High and low principles, various collections of sounds, as well as that which is known as the object of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the place of enjoyment. (51)
The sheaths, as well as those born from the sheaths—these consist of both conscious and unconscious natures;
the states composed of pure and impure matter constitute the fourfold purpose of the person. || 52 ||
Everything is bound by the primordial natures (prakṛtis) and likewise measured by time;
thus, this entire reality consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
That which consists of the non-self and that which consists of the self are dissolved and abide within me;
for I am always, in every respect, composed of pure and free consciousness.
By the wise one, she who consists of bliss and is peaceful should be perceived within every state of being;
thus am I established, though designated by the name "concealment. (55)
