Bound by power (śakti), the power of consciousness (cicchakti) does not perceive Me at all by itself;
but when it becomes weary, it is awakened by the drop (bindu) of My grace.
Then, having propitiated me through various means, the individual soul— known as the power of consciousness—
diminishes all afflictions and shakes off the dust of latent impressions.
Having attained the true essence of knowledge, with his bonds destroyed by yoga, he attains me alone— Lakṣmī, who consists of supreme bliss.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Nature of Lakṣmī," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. 14.
Fifteenth Chapter. Śakra:
Salutations to you, O Padmasaṃbhūtā; salutations to you, O wearer of the lotus garland;
salutations to the dweller in the lotus, the garlanded one, the housewife of Govinda. || 1 ||
Salutations to you, O Goddess whose playful tresses are fashioned from the filaments of the lotus;
O Omniscient One, who dwells within all beings and is the witness of all.
All that has emerged from the lotus of your mouth has been understood;
therefore, it was created by you, protected by you, and shall return to dissolution in you alone.
The mother, the measure, and the object of measurement—these three are of your own nature;
by worshipping you alone, living beings cross the ocean of worldly existence.
"O Goddess, such things as these have been understood by me in their true essence;
yet, O Lotus-born One, a curiosity arises within me today. (5)
By what means, O Lotus-seated One, are you to be propitiated?
For that which is the supreme human goal is the attainment of your favor. (6)
6. Liberation (mokṣa) is the supreme goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). Devotion to You is its means. As they have said:

"For men, the highest good (śreyaḥ) is never possible through the paths of worldly existence, the imperishable [liberation], or Vaiṣṇavism, except through the grace of the beloved of the mind of the lotus-eyed One."
"What would be the means for your pleasure? Of what nature and of what kind is it remembered to be?
Tell me all of this; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One. (7)
Śrī said:
The Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, possesses a fourfold nature;
it is everything, transcending all, dwelling within all beings, and free from all affliction. || 8 ||

8. The definition of the essential nature (svarūpalakṣaṇa), as taught in such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth, is stated by the words "Being" (sat) and so on. It is called "all" (sarva) because it is the material cause of all and the self of all; nevertheless, he declares its distinction from everything else: "surpassing all" (sarvottara).
Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, the great one consisting of Nārāyaṇa— the refuge (ayana) of men (narāṇām).
I am His supreme power, consisting of the consciousness of "I-ness" and bliss.
9–10. "The suffix *mayaṭ* in the word *nārāyaṇamaya* is used in its own sense (i.e., denoting identity).
I exist both as distinct and non-distinct from Him, like moonlight from the cold-rayed moon.
Yet we two are one single reality; having become twofold, we remain established [in that state]."

10. Disagreeing with the view of some who hold that prosperity (*śrī*) is merely a distinct state (*avasthābheda*) of Brahman itself, like a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he says: "Bhinna..."—[that] by the knowledge of which alone a yogi may attain me, Nārāyaṇa, who am Brahman. [E, ī: vā]
There is no other path for the wise to reach higher knowledge than through wisdom. || 11 ||
11. An ascetic is one who possesses self-restraint. Here, the seeker of the fourth stage of life (the *parivrājaka*) is not intended.
Knowledge is that which arises from discernment (*viveka*), pure in every respect, flawless, having Vāsudeva as its sole object, and the cause of non-return [to rebirth]. 12.
12. Discrimination (*viveka*) is the knowledge that Brahman is distinct from everything else.
When that knowledge has arisen, [the seeker] enters Me immediately;
I, being pleased by those various means, [grant liberation] to those pure-souled living beings. 13.
I manifest that knowledge which reveals the light of the Self;
and those four means of mine increase my delight. (14)
14. Here, four yogas—namely those called karma, jñāna, bhakti, and nyāsa—are intended. (p.
49) Śakra says:
O Blessed One, who dwells within the lotus, O Lotus-eyed beloved!
What are those four means? Show them to me, O Lotus-born one. (15)
Śrī said:
O Śakra, listen to the four means that increase my pleasure, by which I shall attain supreme and enduring satisfaction. (16)
Action prescribed by one's own birth, as well as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the renunciation of everything—these have been declared by the wise to be the means [to liberation]. 17.
The Vedic ritual action is threefold, endowed with four characteristics, pertaining to one's own caste and stage of life, and consisting of the obligatory and occasional rites. (18)

18. The four characteristics will be explained in the twentieth verse. There is a threefold division based on the distinctions between obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and desire-driven (*kāmya*) [actions].
That action which is accomplished by one whose desires have not been destroyed is the aforementioned means.
In that regard, a wise person should practice the fourfold renunciation.

19. He states the distinction regarding optional rites (*kāmyakarman*)—beginning with the word "akāma": Rites performed with a desire for specific fruits are "optional" (*kāmya*), such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others; these are said to be "struck by desire" (*kāmahata*). Those performed without desire, solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord, are "not struck by desire" (*akāmahata*). By this, [it is shown that] even among optional rites...

The performance of actions without desire is permitted; however, this refers only to those whose focus is on other means [of liberation]. But for those established in the yoga of renunciation (*nyāsa-yoga*), there is an absolute abandonment of actions performed for specific desires even in their essential form, and not merely their performance without desire.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is to be understood as being either in the deity mentioned in the mantra, or in the primordial matter (prakṛti), or in the senses,
or in the supreme God of gods, Vāsudeva Janārdana. || 20 ||
20. It should be understood that for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), the renunciation of actions alone must be performed toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva;
however, the assignment [of actions] to mantras, deities, and so forth pertains to those seeking worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu).
Previously, it was stated: "The renunciation of agency over all [actions], as well as the renunciation of fruits."
Even the renunciation of karmas [is accomplished] in Janārdana, the God of gods.

21. The intended mode of contemplation is this: "The Blessed Lord Himself, with His own remaining essence as the sole flavor and by means of His own implements, personally causes me—whose sole purpose is His own propitiation—to perform this work which has become His own remnant."
By thus practicing the duties prescribed by the scriptures, consisting of both obligatory and occasional rites, a man who desires my propitiation constantly pleases me. (22)
Thus, this has been declared to you in brief, as demonstrated by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Now hear the second means, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
Indeed, three types of enumeration (saṃkhyā) are to be understood as demonstrated in the Sāṃkhya treatises:
the first is worldly enumeration, and the second consists of analytical reflection (carcanā). || 24 ||
24. An exposition of all three of these types of knowledge will be provided right here.
That which is correct cognition is recited as the third [type].
The collection of the three numbers is recited as Sāṃkhya. 25.
25. The "saṃkhyās" (enumerations) are the knowledges previously mentioned; their collection is called "sāṃkhya. This very thing is called "jñānayoga" (the yoga of knowledge).
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well—
The great ego-sense and likewise primordial nature (prakṛti) are supreme. || 26 ||

26. By this verse, worldly calculation pertaining to the world is stated; its detailed exposition is provided by the subsequent verses. These are the eight primary categories; hear this explanation of them.
Nature is said to be threefold: Māyā, Sūti, and that which consists of the Guṇas. || 27 ||

27. Māyā, Prasūti, and Traiguṇya are the divisions of Prakṛti. Although Prakṛti is indeed subtle, nevertheless, because it exists therein in three forms—subtle, subtler, and subtlest—there is this conventional designation. (p. 50)
That which is unattached, non-attached, non-dual, waveless, and imperishable—the supreme subtlety of insentient things—is sung as *māyā*. (28)
A slight swelling of that [Prakṛti] is proclaimed as its "procreation";
it is the supreme Prakṛti, the manifestation of the three qualities in a state of equilibrium. (29)

The Unmanifest (avyakta), the Imperishable (akṣara), the Source (yoni), Ignorance (avidyā), the Three Qualities (triguṇā), Stability (sthiti), Illusion (māyā), and Nature (svabhāva)—these and other such words are synonyms expressing the same meaning. (30)

30. Summarizing the synonyms for *prakṛti* along with their internal subdivisions, such as the *avyakta* (the unmanifest) and so forth: in the Upaniṣads, these three are conventionally treated as follows: "The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable (*akṣara*); the imperishable dissolves into darkness (*tamas*); and darkness becomes one with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)."
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are considered the three qualities (guṇas). Among them, sattva is to be known as light, consisting of happiness, and unshakable. (31)
That which is called illumination (prakāśa) is its function, consisting of the apprehension of consciousness;
and rajas should also be known as light, of the nature of suffering, and flickering. || 32 ||

32. The "seizing" (*udgrahaṇa*) of consciousness (*caitanya*), that is, of knowledge (*jñāna*), means its unfolding (*unmeṣa*); in other words, it is the nature of grasping the true reality of things.
What is called "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is its function, the imperishable cause of vibration (*spanda*).
Tamas is to be known as heavy, of the nature of delusion, and unsteady. || 33 ||
That which is called "restriction" (niyama) is its functioning in certain instances, characterized by inducing sleep;
that does not exist on earth, nor in heaven, nor in the sky, O Vāsava.
34. Restriction is bondage. When the being is liberated from these three qualities born of primordial nature (prakṛti), [it attains release].
These qualities, having presided over the mind, likewise reside in the senses. 35.
Pleasure, pain, and likewise delusion, which reside in the objects of the senses, are produced; having attained the state of body and senses,
the *guṇas* perform actions.
He whose mind is thus constant attains the transcendence of the qualities.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Methods of Means," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. 15.
Chapter Sixteen: Śrī (Glorious Fortune) — p. 51)
O Śakra, listen attentively to my explanation of that which is the first manifestation of the imbalance of the guṇas. || 1 ||

1. By this, it is stated that the designation "Prakṛti" applies when the three qualities (guṇas) are in a state of equilibrium, whereas the designation "Mahat" applies when they are in a state of disequilibrium.
That which is called Mahat also has its threefold divisions proclaimed.
The sattvic is said to be the intellect (buddhi), while the rajasic is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). || 2 ||
Time has been described as consisting of the quality of tamas; hear now this explanation concerning them:
intellect (buddhi) is the faculty of determination, and vital breath (prāṇa) is that of exertion. (3)
3. Here, the tamasic nature of time is stated. According to the Upaniṣadic method, they maintain that time is indeed non-material (aprākṛta).
Time is the cause of transformation in the form of measurement (kālana).
From the Great One (mahat), undergoing transformation, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born. [In some versions: from this, it is born. || 4 ||

4. *Kalanam* means transformation (*vipariṇati*). The meaning is that it refers to the transformation of an unripe mango and so forth into the nature of its fruit, and likewise the transformation of a young body into the nature of a wrinkled and aged body.
Furthermore, that [transformation] is to be known as threefold, arising from the imbalance of the *guṇas*.
From the tamasic [ego], however, arises the radiant group of subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with space.

From the *sattva*-predominant [state] is born the great group of the faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), and from the *rajas*-predominant [state] the group of the faculties of action (*karmendriya*); [from the state] consisting of both, [the internal organs arise]. (6)

6. The division of the organs of action as being *rājasa* and the mind (*manas*) as being both *sāttvika* and *rājasa* is according to the opinion of certain Tantric authorities. In reality, however, the view of many Pāñcarātrikas is that all eleven organs are indeed *sāttvika*. The ten deities are the *vaikārika* [forms].
And it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The eleventh is the mind.
This sequence of principles has arisen from both [Prakṛti and Puruṣa];
herein, Prakṛti alone is the eternal root cause. (7)

7. The Pathway of the Principles (*Tattvapaddhati*). This means the pathway of the non-conscious principle (*acittattva*). Herein is the division: the principle (*tattva*) is of two kinds, namely, the non-conscious principle (*acittattva*) and the conscious principle (*cittattva*). Among these, the non-conscious principle is twenty-fourfold:
the three—primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the intellect (*mahat*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*).
There are eleven organs. The principle of consciousness (cittattva) is twofold: the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). Altogether there are twenty-six principles.
Furthermore, the seven others beginning with Mahat consist of both cause and effect.
The specific elements, beginning with space, have arisen from the subtle elements (tanmātras). || 8 ||
The two groups of five—the organs of cognition and the organs of action—and the mind itself:
these sixteen are to be known as mere modifications by those who reflect. (9)
These twenty-four principles have been described to you; whatever further detail is to be stated here, and of whatever nature it may be, [is now to follow].
All of that was previously told to you, O slayer of Vṛtra;
it is endowed with twenty-three of its own transformations.
(52) This nature has been described to you as unmanifest, O Lord of the Gods;
it consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and is eternally characterized by productivity. || 12 ||
12. In its state as primordial nature (prakṛti), it is unmanifest; in its state of transformation (pariṇāma), it is manifest.
This statement is made because there is no difference between cause and effect.
That power of consciousness (cicchakti) should be known as distinct and imperishable.
That is declared to be the living soul (jīva) by the virtuous who are experts in the scriptures of reality. || 13 ||
This [Self] is by its own nature pure, devoid of transformation, immutable, a mass of consciousness, eternal, infinite, and non-transmigrating. (14)
14. "By their own nature" means by their very essence. "Infinite" means unlimited in number and in qualities such as knowledge.
These two, though naturally unattached, remain as if they were attached to the self [or: established as the essence of existence].
Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed greater than even the Mahat-tattvas. || 15 ||
Both are graspable by means of a logical mark (liṅga), and both are likewise eternal and without a logical mark; thus a wise person should infer their similarity and so forth.
O Śakra, understand from me the difference between these two:
Prakṛti is eternally composed of the three guṇas and is constantly subject to transformation. (17)
It is devoid of discrimination, impure, always equal toward all living beings, insentient in its nature, and the cause of pleasure, pain, and delusion. (18)
The Puruṣa is eternally neutral, active yet undisturbed;
he is the witness, the vision, and likewise the seer—pure, infinite, and composed of the qualities (guṇas). || 19 ||
This is the difference between these two; now hear their natures: that which is eternal, devoid of conceptual constructions such as "existent" and "non-existent," and so forth. (20)
20. "Vikalpavikalā" means she who possesses various transformations (pariṇati).
"I am Nārāyaṇī, the Śakti of Viṣṇu, Śrī, his inseparable consort—eternally risen, ever-blissful, and whose form consists of the six perfections in their fullness. 21.
For these two proceed from me and shall return to dissolution in me alone;
thus, I have attained such expansion through various states of being [or: through various objects].
Having established myself in Nārāyaṇa, I shall rise up from him once more;
Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the eternal one, is alone.
Because its powers are non-distinct from it, Brahman is partless and non-dual;
it is a great ocean of knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor.

24. Because of the relationship of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddha*) between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), there is oneness. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction with the state of being non-dual (*advitīyatva*).
This [Self] is always without waves, and this entire world of moving and unmoving things is that very same thing.
Thus, O Śakra, this knowledge of Sāṃkhya has been shown to you in brief.
25. This means that he, Nārāyaṇa himself, exists in the form of the world consisting of the moving and the unmoving.
First, the wise person should practice the enumeration—that is, the counting—of the categories of reality (tattvas);
thereafter, [he should study] their common and specific characteristics, their essential nature, their origin, and so forth. 26.
One should perform a deliberative enumeration arising from the instruction on the reality of the scriptures;
for when this deliberative enumeration has been accomplished within the stainless self— || 27 ||
27. *Carca* means repeated and thorough investigation.

That correct enumeration which arises within the scope of the true nature of reality (*sattattva*)—this is that supreme enumeration, born from my grace. 28. [This is the concluding verse of the previous section.]
This enumeration of the Sāṃkhya philosophy has been declared to you.
Indeed, having thus enumerated it, the followers of Sāṃkhya have attained my own state. (29)
The third means, which shall be described as "yoga," is to be known as twofold: namely, *samādhi* and *saṃyama*. (30)
The concentration arising from the limbs of *yama* is established in the Supreme,
in Brahman known as Śrīnivāsa, which is indeed devoid of emergence.
For that state of those who know the eternal Brahman consists of direct realization;
it abides in the non-differentiation of the meditator and the object of meditation, and arises from my grace. (32)

32. Regarding the phrase "as non-distinct": according to the principle stated in the passage, "They conceive of [it] as the Self and cause others to grasp it," what is intended here is the meditation upon the Supreme Brahman as non-distinct [from the self].
What is called *saṃyama* (restraint) is good action whose sole object is the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, that is said to be of two kinds: physical as well as mental.
Concentration (samādhi) and restraint (saṃyama) will be explained in detail;
that which was previously described as your first means is characterized by action (karmātmā).
One should generate pure perception through the purification of the internal organ;
for by that, and by the constant practice of right conduct, I am truly gratified.
I grant that yoga of the intellect which purifies the internal organ—that second means called Sāṃkhya which was described to you. 36.
This certainty, born of the scriptures and though beyond direct perception, has attained such firmness that it is as if it had become manifest; may it generate supreme love for me. (37)
For when I am reckoned by my own nature, qualities, and majesty,
I manifest that knowledge which is direct and born of discernment.
The third, however, consists of meditative absorption; it is direct perception, unerring, and firm.
For it is an excellence of clarity born from preeminent sattva. (39)
That third method which has been described as "restraint" (saṃyama) is for my extreme delight, arising from pure enjoyments produced in three ways.
For there, I am the Soul of the Universe, the supreme and inferior power of Viṣṇu;
I am the very God to be propitiated, or rather, Puruṣottama himself. (41)
Thus have these three powerful means been correctly explained to you;
now hear from me the fourth means, which is called the renunciation of everything.
There, having abandoned all dharmas—every variety of high and low limbs—one scorched by the fire of saṃsāra should go for refuge to me alone. (43)
For I have indeed sought refuge with the Man whose mind is focused on no other;
by my own self, I shall attain the Self from which all impurities have been shaken off. 44.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Methods of Means," in the Lakṣmītantra, which is the essence of the Śrī Pañcarātra. (Chapter 16)
Chapter Seventeen. Śakra:
Salutations to you, O abode of Kamalā, the mother of all embodied beings;
salutations to you, the consort of Padmanābha, O lotus-born one! 1.
Those three previous means have been explained and mastered;
now I shall expound that fourth, supreme means, O Lotus-like One.
Śrī said: "The one god Nārāyaṇa is Vāsudeva, the eternal;
he is the fourfold self, the supreme Brahman, being existence, consciousness, bliss, and without blemish. (3)
I alone am his supreme power, the eternal goddess;
following all states of being, I perform every action.
That which is the supreme, eternal Brahman— tranquil, infinite consciousness-bliss—
is the abode of great manifestation, having attained equanimity in all respects. || 5 ||

5. Mahāvibhūti (the Great Manifestation) is the eternal manifestation. Its status as the "Great Manifestation" is due to its greatness in comparison to the *līlāvibhūti* (the manifestation of divine play), according to the scriptural statement: "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven. My power (*śakti*) is that which is of the nature of Brahman—tranquil, blissful, and conscious.
Possessing great majesty and free from fault, she has attained equanimity toward all things.
That splendor which was personified for the consolation of living beings—
Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the divine delight to the eyes.
Then I, that supreme power Nārāyaṇī, became embodied— equal,
with limbs perfectly proportioned, and beautiful in every part.
For those two of us, there is the supreme void, the highest state free from suffering— [a state of] bliss—
where the divine expansion of the six qualities has attained the status of a region through its own spontaneity.
9. By my will, the very expansion of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) has attained the state of being a transcendent, divine realm; this is the meaning.

[It is inhabited] by Siddhas devoted to their own duties, who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas, and who have completely exhausted all impurities through a succession of many births. 10.

By the perfected ones (siddhas) who have transcended all obstacles through great effort, by the Sāṃkhyas who know the rules and methods of enumeration and have reached the further shore of calculation; || 11 ||
That which is attained with constant effort by practitioners of yoga who have withdrawn the collection of their senses, who possess concentration and meditation, and who are ever-composed.
Those who are flawless, who know the five times of the day, who are experts in the five sacrifices, and who are steadfast—
what they attain directly at the completion of a full hundred years, [others attain] easily.
13. *Acchidrāḥ* means free from the defect (*chidra*) consisting of the lack of experience of the Blessed One. As it has been said:

"That moment, or even that instant, during which Vāsudeva is not meditated upon—that is a loss, that is a great defect, that is delusion, and that is a distortion. There are five [limbs of worship] known as *abhigamana*, *upādāna*, *ijyā*, *svādhyāya*, and *yoga*.
The times: That which is the ancient ether, supreme to all and eternal;
that state reaching which the knowers of reality are liberated from all bonds. (14)
Resembling ten million suns and like unto ten thousand full moons, those liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra shine resplendent in that state. (15)
Devoid of the apertures of the senses, shining forth on all sides,
without outflows, without food, possessing bodies of six attributes, and stainless. (16)
(55) Where those exclusively devoted and highly fortunate ones always behold us two,
having exhausted their own offices over a long period of time. (17)

17. Regarding the word "having exhausted" (*kṣapayitvā*): here, one should keep in mind the *Śārīraka-sūtra*, "The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office," as well as the scriptural passages that corroborate it, such as:
"Wherein the Vedhas and the Śaṅkaras rejoice."
Together with Purandara, the wise ones are eternally perfected; they are always omniscient and all-seeing. || 18 ||
There, those who are solely devoted to the eight-syllabled mantra and whose souls delight in the six-syllabled mantra directly perceive the supreme form of Viṣṇu.

19. The eight-syllabled [mantra] is the Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara-mantra; the twelve-syllabled [mantra] is the Vāsudevadvādaśākṣara-mantra. For those devoted to the six-syllabled [mantra], whose minds are fixed upon the Praṇava...
For those whose minds are detached from worldly objects and who are devoted to the goal of crossing over [saṃsāra]. || 20 ||

20. The six-syllabled mantra of Śrī Viṣṇu consists of the six syllables. The mantra in the form of verses beginning with "jitaṃ te jitaṃ te puṇḍarīkākṣa" [and so forth] is also included. Its greatness and other qualities should be understood as they are described in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā. The Tārikā is the mantra "hrīṃ".
That state belonging to those of pure soul who are unattached to the unreal is attained by the stainless ones,
such as Ananta, Vihageśāna, Viṣvaksena, and others.
21. The *anutārā* is the *śrīṃ* mantra.
Where the lords of all rejoice as executors of my command, there dwells Janārdana, the glorious God of gods, possessing a divine form. 22.
Seated upon a couch of infinite enjoyments, he is exceedingly radiant with bliss;
he abides in the mastery, heroism, and sovereignty of consciousness, and is intense with power, splendor, and strength.
He was adorned with divine and wonderful weapons and ornaments,
and was attended by the fivefold Suparṇa, the king of birds.
24. By means of his fivefold self, in the form of the mantras of the five Upaniṣads; having attained a state of conformity, he was directly marked with the Śrīvatsa.
It was properly frequented by the commander-in-chief, the radiant Viṣvaksena. || 25 ||
25. *Sārūpya* (conformity) means conformity with the Blessed One by means of [bearing] the conch, the discus, and so forth. He states that very thing: "with the *śrīvatsa" and so on.
And these two qualifiers connect with the word *senānyā* (the commander of the army). [He is] for the welfare of all worlds and for the meditation of the wise.
For the liberation from all bonds and for the bestowing of form upon yogins. || 26 ||
There dwells the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Vāsudeva,
the youthful god, delicate of form, marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Four-armed and large-eyed, wearing a diadem and bearing the Kaustubha gem,
he shone with necklaces, anklets, armlets, a girdle, and yellow garments.
Wearing a divine forest garland consisting of the five supreme powers,
he is endowed with all limbs and beautiful in every part of his body.
29–30. Creation, maintenance, destruction, restraint, and grace are the five powers.
He is the king of kings of this entire universe, the Supreme Lord of all.
Such is that beloved god Viṣṇu, who is endowed with excellent qualities.
I am always the beloved goddess, supreme, consisting of the bliss of knowledge; blameless, with faultless limbs, I am eternally one whose nature conforms to His.
The sovereign of all beings, lotus-eyed and garlanded with lotuses,
she is the supreme one, eternally served by her powers such as those of creation, maintenance, and so forth.

32. *Īśvarī* (The Sovereign). The suffix *varaṭ* is added in the sense of "she rules" (*īṣṭe*) in the agentive case, according to the *uṇādi* rules. She is surrounded by thirty-two thousand powers of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-śakti*).
She is surrounded by twice that number of divine powers of stability.
And then, filled with powers of withdrawal that were twice as great, she became the mistress of all powers, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds. (34)
The queen of the God of gods, the all-yielding cow of the omnipresent Lord, was equal to Hari in virtue, age, and beauty, and she was the captivator of his heart. (35)
Through those various corresponding dispositions, I, ever following his nature, perform every duty for the divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
I was seated upon the lap of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
cherished by him exceedingly, I attained a state of perfect union (sāmarasya).
At one time, compassion for all-seeing ones arose within me spontaneously upon seeing living beings suffering in the belly of the fire of saṃsāra. (38)
"How indeed shall these beings cross over suffering and reach the heights of happiness?
How indeed shall they attain the further shore of saṃsāra and reach me?"
[Ā: "Yes," he said. || 39 ||
Filled with compassion within, I urged the God of gods:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, my beloved! (40)
O you who are everything, O beginning, middle, and end of all, O all, O supreme among all, O infallible one! O Govinda, O lotus-eyed one, O ancient one, O Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)! 41.
O cause of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is difficult to traverse and shoreless;
O you who have fashioned the fourfold categories known as the Manifest, the Unmanifest, the Knower, and Time! 42.
O Vāsudeva, Lord of the World; O Saṃkarṣaṇa, Master of the Universe;
O Pradyumna, the Auspicious One who pervades all; O Śrīman Aniruddha, the Unconquered!
The locus of various manifestations and various manifestations themselves,
whose form is the arising of the six qualities and the bliss of divine, peaceful emergence. || 44 ||
O Lord with a shimmering crown, armlets, necklace, anklets, and the Kaustubha gem;
O wearer of yellow garments, most noble one, whose eyes resemble white lotuses! 45.
O you of four forms, O fourfold manifestation, you who possess the luster of an autumnal blue lotus;
O Lord of the most beautiful body, O Nārāyaṇa, you who pervade the universe! 46.
For all these living beings are submerged in the ocean of afflictions; O Lord, how do you contemplate their deliverance from this? (47)
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods, smiling, spoke this:
"O Goddess seated upon the lotus, O you whose womb is a lotus, O you who dwell within the water-born flower! (48)
I have prescribed these means for their deliverance:
action, Sāṃkhya, and likewise Yoga, which are based upon the scriptures. (49)
Having spoken thus to Puruṣottama, I replied to the God:
"O God of gods, it is not possible for you to do these things as time passes."
For Time alone, being independent and consisting of existence itself, as it measures all things,
cuts away their knowledge, goodness, strength, and even their life-span. (51)
For the various latent impressions (vāsanās) residing within the internal organ drive embodied beings at the appropriate time, according to their respective conditions.

Remaining thus indifferent toward living beings performing their various actions, you bestow upon them the fruits corresponding to those deeds in accordance with their respective times [and conditions]. 53.
"O Janārdana, tell me, who am bowed before you, that means by which you, though agitated, will protect living beings."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One replied as if smiling:
"O Lotus-born One, you understand everything that has occurred regarding yourself."
"But since you wish to know me, O Goddess, listen nevertheless, O beautiful lady;
the means and the obstacles have been established according to the scriptures."
by me || 56 ||

56. Expedients (*upāya*) are those that accomplish merit (*puṇya*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others; missteps (*apāya*) are those that accomplish evil (*pāpa*), such as harming others and so forth. Those expedients which are prescribed are considered [right], while the others are considered prohibited.
The states of woe lead down that person who follows after them.
The skillful means lead upward him who follows them;
having abandoned both skillful means and their absence, he relies upon the middle way.
58. "The renouncer" (saṃtyāgī) means one who, having abandoned those optional and prohibited rites that produce merit and demerit, is devoted solely to the obligatory and occasional duties.
Having come to Me alone as his refuge, he attains Me alone at the end.
And hear from me, O Lotus-born one, that six-limbed means (upāya). || 59 ||

59. "Me alone" (mām ekam) means "me indeed. The word *eka* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and functions to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Here, this should be understood: whether or not there was recourse to a middle course prior to taking refuge, if such a middle course existed, [it is excluded] from the act of taking refuge.

It generates urgency. If there is no delay, then immediately after taking refuge, one must necessarily practice with the middle course of conduct for as long as life lasts; otherwise, the fruit will not arise due to procrastination.
Furthermore, previously committed karmas are destroyed by the very power of this entrustment (*nyāsa*), whereas those committed subsequently—

Actions committed through negligence do not adhere [to the soul], yet even those performed intentionally can be removed by expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Therefore, for the sake of avoiding expiations such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*, one should follow the middle course:
the resolve to act favorably and the avoidance of what is unfavorable.
There is trust that "He will protect," as well as the choosing of Him as one's protector.
In the wretchedness of surrendering one's self, there is a sixfold taking of refuge;
having thus come to me for refuge, one is freed from sorrow, fear, and fatigue. (61)
Free from undertakings, free from expectations, devoid of possessiveness, and without egoism—
one who has taken refuge in me alone may cross the ocean of saṃsāra. 62.
Those who are devoted to virtuous deeds, those who are pure, and likewise those who know Sāṃkhya and Yoga—
even all of them together do not equal even a ten-millionth part of one who has taken refuge.

63. "Those devoted to virtuous action are established in the yoga of action; those who know the Sāṃkhya are practitioners of the yoga of knowledge; and those who know Yoga are practitioners of the yoga of devotion. Having heard these words of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, [the sages spoke].
I was pleased, O Śakra; this which has been described to you [is for that purpose].
Śakra said:
O Mahādevī, beloved of the gods, salutations to you who sit upon the lotus! Explain to me in detail your disposition of favorability and so forth.
Śrī said:
"Favorability" is declared to be the state of being favorable toward all beings, based on the certainty that "I abide within all things. (66)
66. The resolve for conformity is not directed toward us alone; rather, it extends to all beings who are subordinate to us. Thus he says, "all":
"For one should practice conformity toward all beings just as toward Me."
In the same way, one should completely avoid hostility toward living beings. || 67 ||
The abandonment of pride born from learning, character, and other virtues; and the absence of miserliness even when there is an insufficiency of the necessary means or an incapacity for actions. (68)
Furthermore, because the requisite qualification is not established due to the exhaustion of merit over time and place, the means do not succeed at all; likewise, obstacles are numerous. (69)
Thus, the loss of pride is called wretchedness and meanness;
yet, because power is easily accessible and because of eternal compassion, [it is not so]. (70)

Even though this relationship between the Lord and those to be ruled has no beginning in time, that very firm conviction which holds "He will protect those who are favorable" [is what constitutes devotion]. (71)
O Śakra, that faith shall be the destroyer of all evil deeds;
it is clearly compassionate, capable, and the sovereign of embodied beings.
"One should not protect [the Lord] unless requested"—this thought constitutes the request;
"He shall indeed become my protector"—thus is the formal choice of a protector (goptṛtva-varaṇa) remembered.
For one who is thus protected by him, there is an inseparable ownership over the fruit;
indeed, the surrender of oneself is said to culminate in the offering to Keśava. (74)
Renunciation (*nyāsa*), which is synonymous with entrustment (*nikṣepa*), is endowed with five limbs;
it is called renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), abandonment (*tyāga*), and also taking refuge (*śaraṇāgati*). (75)
This fourth method has been declared to you, which bestows results swiftly; for those who abide in this rite practiced by the Brahmins, [it is effective]. 76.
The first three means may be unappealing; [the fourth] consists of turning away from danger through both compliance and its opposite. (77)
Even through wretchedness, the cessation of means is declared here;
yet, out of trust that "he will protect me," one devises the means for what is desired. (78)
The "request for protection" (goptṛtvavaraṇa) consists in the communication of one's own intention;
for even though the Lord of the Universe is omniscient and eternally compassionate, [he requires this request]. (79)

79. Anticipating the objection that the Protector, being omniscient and a source of compassion, will protect those in distress by himself, he says: "Even though he is omniscient. What is called "being subject to the course of saṃsāra" refers to the carrying out of his playful manifestation (*līlāvibhūti*). Regarding protection that does not depend on such a pretext, [it applies] to both the virtuous and the wicked alike.
If one were occupied with protecting everyone,
there would arise the confusion of right and wrong actions, what ought and ought not to be done, and justice and injustice. If, by one's own will,
one protects only some while not protecting others, how can it be said, "I am equal toward all beings"?
The sense is that for one who proclaims this, there would follow the consequence of partiality and cruelty.
Because [the Lord] follows the course of the mechanism of saṃsāra, He awaits the expectation of protection;
for the entrusting of the burden of "self" and "mine" is called "self-surrender. (80)
Violence, theft, and so forth have been shown by the scriptures to be means of ruin;
ritual action, Sāṃkhya, and so forth have been shown by the scriptures to be means [to liberation]. (81)

Having abandoned the means leading to the lower realms and having established himself in the middle way, he will protect [the world]; thus being certain, he has relinquished his own respective sphere of activity. (82)
One should awaken the Lord of the gods of gods, the protector, the Supreme Person.
Śakra said:
O Ambikā, what is the state between means and their failure?

Every ritual action relies solely upon the means for avoiding what is undesirable; this applies both to the acceptance [of injunctions] and the exclusion [of prohibitions] found in the scriptures of positive and negative injunctions.

84. There is misfortune in accepting what is prohibited and in rejecting what is prescribed; there is success in accepting what is prescribed and in rejecting what is prohibited. Thus, the nature of action as both misfortune and success is clearly perceived.
Śrī said: "O Lord of Gods, behold the threefold, profound course of action. (85)
Learn from me that twofold method from the treatises of prohibition and injunction:
one is the means for achieving what is harmful, and the other is the means for achieving what is beneficial.
86. Acts such as violence are means for achieving what is harmful; acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice are means for achieving goals such as heaven;
acts such as expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) are means for avoiding what is harmful;
and certain actions are taught for the purpose of avoiding what is harmful.
Even some dharmas [are included].
Thus, the threefold classification of actions should be understood by one whose eye is the scripture. (87)
One should abandon the two preceding heaps, which are characterized by the notions of misfortune and means;
the third is of two kinds.
The zodiac sign is the remover of misfortune. || 88 ||

88. The third [category], which averts misfortune, is twofold: penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* destroy misfortunes that have already arisen; whereas obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth avert future misfortunes.
Thus, a certain type consisting of penance is the destroyer of arisen misfortune.
A wise person should not make that portion [of the day] like the preceding heap. || 89 ||

89. Regarding the third [section], he states the first method: "Prāyaścitta... etc. One should perform that action which, while being performed, does not conduce to any purpose, and which, like non-action, leads to misfortune. 90.
90. In the third [verse], he states the second mode—beginning with "kriyamāṇa" and so forth.
The meaning is that it consists of the forms of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
This is that Vedic steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*).
This [state] is the means, the non-means, and the middle;
established in this, one should take refuge in Janārdana, the Lord of the World. 91.
For this meaning of the scripture, once accomplished, shall deliver a person;
yet it is lost through lack of steadfastness when one is beset by means and obstacles.
92. Following the maxim that "the purpose of a scripture is accomplished once," he says: "For indeed, by this alone.
"By this" means by the form of *prapatti* (surrender).
One should immediately perform the expiation when immersed in a flood of calamities.
The atonement for this is that one should once again take refuge [in the Buddha]. || 93 ||
93. "The inundation of calamities" means the possibility of errors occurring despite prior deliberation.
Indeed, even when one adopts various means as a strategy, this very [deliberation] is necessary for the non-disruption of the dharmas and for the protection of the lineage. 94.

94. Even if one accepts that the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices are means to liberation, there will certainly be a falling away from steadfastness. Therefore, one should not perform them. This is the distilled meaning here: for those established in the yoga of devotion, [the fruits of past actions are destroyed] by the very power of that yoga; likewise, for those established in the yoga of surrender (prapatti), they are destroyed by the very power of surrender. Thus, the former [actions]...

All actions that are contrary to liberation—whether performed intentionally or unintentionally—are destroyed along with their very roots. For those who have taken refuge, such actions generally do not even occur after the surrender; and even if they should occasionally arise, being unintentional, they do not adhere [to the soul].
[The sins] exist [as potentialities]. However, those committed intentionally are destroyed by means of *prapadana* (surrender).
For those who have not performed *prapadana*, their destruction occurs through the experience of the fruit of that [sin] after a small punishment.
Even *prārabdha-karma* (karma already set in motion) [is exhausted] for one who has surrendered, either immediately or at the end of that body, according to the degree of their distress.

They perish. This is the extraordinary greatness of the yoga of renunciation (*nyāsayoga*) as compared to the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*): the yoga of devotion is not capable of removing even commenced karmas (*prārabdhakarman*), whereas the yoga of renunciation is capable of removing even commenced karmas. This is so because, at the time of surrender (*prapatti*), due to the intensity of one's distress...

If their destruction is prayed for immediately, then they perish at once; if it is prayed for at the end of that body, then they perish precisely at the end of that body. However, unlike those established in the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), these do not bring about another body for the sake of experiencing [the results of karma]. Thus they say: "But that *sādhyabhakti* is the destroyer."

"Even regarding that which has already begun, it is for the most part [to be abandoned]. Furthermore, Vedic rites performed with a desire for results are permitted to be practiced as limbs of the yoga of devotion when performed without desire;
however, for those who have surrendered (prapanna), even performing them without desire is contrary to their essential nature.
For the sake of gathering the world together and for the establishment of moral boundaries,
and for the pleasure of me and Viṣṇu, the god of gods who wields the Śārṅga bow.
A wise man should not transgress Vedic conduct even in his mind,
just as a favorite of the king does not cross a river caused to flow by the king.
Even if one is indifferent toward it, one would ascend a stake to leap over a beautiful field that is useful to the world and increases its abundant harvest.
(60) Thus, a mortal who transgresses the boundaries established by the Veda is not dear to me, even if he is otherwise beloved, because he has overstepped my command. 98.

98. This is the meaning: obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites are not entirely devoid of fruit; rather, their fruit is the prevention of the arising of transgression (pratyavāya). For even though the attainment of worlds such as that of Prajāpati is a secondary (ānuṣaṅgika) result, those rites are still respected. And transgression is indeed the Lord’s punishment. And thus:
"O Blessed One, since those [actions] are performed for the sake of the arising and cessation of restraint, they are not entirely purposeless.
Therefore, there is no room for the objection that 'even a fool does not engage in activity without aiming at a purpose.
In this regard, one should avoid grasping at them as being the [ultimate] means."
The wise one, with his mind, thus resorted to this fourfold means which takes refuge as its support. (99)
Having transcended all afflictions, one enters the stainless state,
established in the middle way that is free from both misfortune and gain.
This supreme refuge is the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
This is the refuge for those who lack knowledge; this alone is [the refuge] for those who possess it. 101.
This is for those desiring to cross to the further shore, this is for those desiring infinity; yet, when the occasion for expiation arises from the emergence of all sins,
one should take refuge in me alone, the queen of the God of gods.
One should constantly avoid the lower realms and likewise go for refuge to me alone. || 103 ||
Having thinned out all his evil, the man gradually attains me;
then, intent upon the means, he enjoys healthy pleasures. (104) [Variant:
"human-like" (amānavān)]
Having first attained detachment, one enters the supreme state;
this means is easy to perform, yet in my opinion, it is difficult to accomplish.

105. Now, it may be objected that it is not logical for devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), which is accomplished over a long period of time, and surrender (*nyāsayoga*), which is accomplished in a moment, to have an equal fruit known as liberation (*mokṣa*); for there can be no option between two means that are so unequal in weight. If that were the case, all discerning people would engage only in the easy means and never in the difficult one.
To the objection that this injunction would be invalid because it lacks the characteristic of being practiced, he says: "The means is easy.

Although this yoga of renunciation is indeed easy to perform—since it must be undertaken for only a moment and does not require the auxiliary limbs of ritual action and so forth—it nevertheless depends upon such factors as supreme faith, which are exceedingly difficult to attain.

The sense is that [this practice] is indeed difficult because it relies upon a middle course that is hard to traverse. Although in this regard a systematic distinction among practitioners could easily be stated based on the presence or absence of the fullness of knowledge, power, and so forth,

nevertheless— since the performance of *nyāsa* and *yoga* is prescribed even for those possessing knowledge and such qualities by the passage beginning with "those who understand this very [teaching]" (*atra yadyapi...*)— that [distinction] remains [applicable].
This path is not disregarded;

it is practiced by the learned, by those whose consciousness is free from desire, and by both those without desires and those with desires. Therefore, for the sake of attaining perfection for oneself, one should follow it.
My body, consisting of mantra, should be constantly worshipped by men;
having entered the initiation according to rule and obtained the wealth of the goal from the guru.
One should worship my mantra-formed body with mantras consisting of *manas*.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Secret Means," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. || 17 ||
Chapter Eighteen. Śakra:
[This verse is omitted by F. Salutations to you, O abode of the lotus; salutations to you, O one born from the lotus!
That which is to be known has been known by me—even that which is difficult to attain even in the Vedāntas.
O beloved of Viṣṇu, tell me now the path consisting of mantra, by knowing which I may worship your divine body composed of mantra. (2)
From where does the origin of the mantra arise, and where is the mantra dissolved?
What is the fruit of the mantra in the lotus, and by what is it filled in the center? (3)
How many are its modes, what indeed is its measure, and of what nature is the supreme state of the field and the knower of the field within the lotus? (4)
By whom should the mantra be received, and what kind of person should be the instructor?
And what is the method of worship for this [mantra], O Lotus-born One? (5)

Whatever matter is useful for worship in the Lotus-seated One, as well as the yoga for accomplishing supernatural powers (siddhi) and the various types of meditative realizations (pratyaya), [are all explained].
Yoga, the yoga of self-study, and likewise the yoga of protection;
the procedure for expiation, and also the ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha). || 7 ||

The ritual procedure for initiation and consecration, as well as the ritual procedure for the yantra—all this, and whatever else is required that has not been seen [before], [is contained herein]. (8)
Explain that to me in its entirety; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One!
With my head bowed, I prostrate at your lotus-red feet.
"I have taken refuge in you, O Lotus-born One; please teach me.
Śrī said:
"O Purandara, this burden of questions you have proposed is incomparable."
Listen, O Vāsava; out of our bond of affection, I shall tell you everything without omission.
He who is the full Person (Puruṣa), the lotus-eyed one, is the very "I" (Aham);
he is the inherent nature of all things, both existent and non-existent.
This is that which has been licked by her—whatever exists in the world, both real and unreal.

12. "By this-ness" (*idaṃtayā*): the meaning is "by being the object of the cognition 'this'. That is to say, by way of extroversion (*parāktvena*). For they declare that being the sphere of the notions of "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "I" (*asmat*) is, respectively, the definition of extroversion and introversion (*pratyaktva*). Those things possessing those respective definitions dissolve into that [supreme] "I-ness" (*ahantva*).
This island of the word "this" having dissolved, the ocean of consciousness has attained oneness.

13. Regarding the passage beginning with *vilīna* (dissolved): the meaning is that all insentient (*acit*) objects, which constitute the referents of the word "this" (*idam*), are themselves the islands; having dissolved into Vāsudeva, who is the ocean of consciousness (*cidambudhi*), they have attained oneness with him.
Vāsudeva shines forth as infinite and free from waves.
I am His fullness, His singular ego, consisting of the power of lordship.

Perpetually risen, eternally blissful, and having attained equanimity toward all things, she is the source of the manifestation of all states of being and is acknowledged as the direct perception of everything. 15.
15. Regarding "eternally arisen" (*nityodita*): arising is of two kinds—arising as quiescence (*śāntodaya*) and eternal arising (*nityodaya*).
The former pertains to the state of descent (*avatārāvasthā*), while the latter pertains to the supreme state (*parāvasthā*).
For this very intuition (*pratibhā*), though colored by the sequence of various objects, is [inherently] luminous.
When the constituent elements have been extracted, she [Śakti] possesses a sequential order.
That reflective awareness of the inward Self, which is of the nature of awakening,
vibrating with great bliss, is celebrated as the Śabdabrahman. (17)

17–18. She is the inward-reflexive awareness, the object of the "I"-consciousness; her essence is light and bliss; she is the supreme "I," the progenitor of all mantras. She is the power (śakti) who gives birth to all sounds, and is devoid of rising and setting.
That which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, the stainless Nārāyaṇa—
that state known as Peace (śāntatā) is I, the source of all that is peaceful.
That slight exertion of mine, known as the desire to emit, which arose—being pacified through the differentiation of word and meaning—is called the "unfolding" (unmeṣa). || 20 ||
The emergence of meaning everywhere is traditionally held to be preceded by the emergence of the word;
for that [meaning] is the gross form of the word, consisting in the manifestation of the word and its referent. (21)

21. The emergence of sound occurs first, followed immediately by that of meaning; this is the established doctrine of the Tantras. In the Śruti as well, in the statement "I shall unfold name and form," it should be understood that the unfolding of name is mentioned first, and thereafter the unfolding of form.
The opening of consciousness is known as sound (śabda), and the opening of sound is said to be the object (artha).
The emergence of sound from the rising power is the first manifestation of the tranquil Self.
That is renowned as *nāda*, which at that time is unmanifest and subtle;
together with *nāda*, that *śakti* is celebrated as "the Subtle" (*sūkṣmā*).
23. Thus, *śabdabrahman*, *parāvāk*, and *nāda* are synonyms. Beyond *nāda* is the second unfolding (*unmeṣa*), which arises from *śakti*;
it is called *bindu*, and here it remains as the smooth (*masṛṇa*) signified (*vācya*). 24.
24. That which follows sound (*nāda*) and is the unfolding of power (*śakti*) is called the *bindu* and also *paśyantī*.
This state named *paśyantī* is my divine and greatly exalted condition.
Beyond that is the third unfolding, which arises from power (*śakti*). 25.

25. Following the Point (bindu), there is the state called the "Emergence of Power" (śaktyunmeṣa), which is the Middle (madhyamā). In that state, it refines the union [of subject and object]; at that time, the distinction between the signified and the signifier consists of the nature of that refinement.
26. At that time, the distinction between the signified and the signifier consists of the nature of that refinement.
But the fourth unfolding of power, which is beyond the Madhyamā, is the state called Vaikharī, in which phonemes and sentences arise clearly manifest. (27)

I possess a power whose nature is action, which follows after the form of consciousness [and is inseparable from it]. That power animates the succession of the unfolding of power, beginning with the subtle sound (nāda) and so forth.
Then there are Śāntarūpā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and likewise Vaikharī;
these four forms I declare to be the fourfold object of speech (vācya) created by myself. (29)
Vāsudeva and the others are to be understood as subtle, while Śānta and the others correspond to them in sequence;
I am to be known as the single-footed one, whose nature is light and bliss. (30)
Furthermore, she is traditionally known as "two-footed" (dvipadī) through the distinction between the signified and the signifier;
and I am "four-footed" (catuṣpadī) due to the distinctions among the sibilants, semivowels, vowels, and stops.
31. *Śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the sibilants (*ūṣman*). *Ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are the semivowels (*antaḥstha*). The vowels (*ac*) are the sounds. From *ka* to *ma* are the stops (*sparśa*).
Due to the division into eight groups, this is remembered as the "Eight-Footed" (*aṣṭapadī*) [alphabet].
The nine-word [mantra] is traditionally taught as being joined with another [syllable] that is unvoiced (aghoṣa) in form. || 32 ||

32. The eight groups (vargas): the group of vowels (svaravarga), the five groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *pa*, the group of sibilants (*ūṣmavarga*), and the group of semivowels (*antaḥsthavarga*). Furthermore, the voiceless [consonants] are: the *yamās*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *upadhmānīya*, and the *visarga*.
I am the divine one-footed supreme [state], consisting of the Śabdabrahman;
furthermore, I exist as two-footed through the nature of sound and phonemes. (33)

33. Another way of describing [the powers] beginning with "one" is stated: she is of one form as the nature of Śabdabrahman; she is of two forms as the essence of sound and phonemes. She fashions all water, as well as all substances, classes, qualities, and actions.
"Since I declare [the truth] in four ways, I am called 'Catuṣpadī' by the wise. (34)
34. *Takṣatī* means cutting, fashioning, or making thin. She fashions all the "water"—that is, the cause of transmigration consisting of attachment to the material world (*prakṛti*).
A specific type of satisfaction known as "water" (*salila*) is well-known in the Sāṃkhya tradition. Regarding this, it is said: "Gaurī has uttered [the hymn], fashioning the waters;
she is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, nine-footed, and she who has become thousand-syllabled."
The Vedic scripture is cited: "In the highest heaven" (Ṛgveda 1.164.41). It is four-footed, possessing four forms by way of the words denoting substance, genus, quality, and action.

Endowed with both name and existence, I am remembered as the eight-padded one (aṣṭapadī). Abiding in both the non-conceptual and the conceptual, I am remembered as the nine-padded one (navapadī). || 35 ||
35–36. Since each of these very [principles] is twofold by virtue of having both sound and meaning as its essence, they comprise eight forms in total.
In the supreme void, I am indeed the divine one, garlanded with infinite syllables;
expanded across this vast expanse, I am the primordial Fullness of Ego (Pūrṇāhaṃtā).
36. And this arrangement exists only in the ordinary world; however, in the extraordinary world, she consists of infinite syllables.
She should be known as the mother of mantras, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
From me alone, the ocean of consciousness, surge forth the waves of mantras. 37. [This is the continuation of verse 36.]
Depending on me alone, they revolve; again and again they go to their setting within me—those whose bodies are sound, beautiful with the abundance of consciousness and bliss. (38)

38. They evolve and transform. Here, the term *vivarta* (evolution) is not intended in the sense defined by others [as illusory appearance]; rather, because it has been stated that "the triad of qualities (*traiguṇya*) is transformative," sound is a transformation of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). For those consisting of *manas* are essentially mantras, full of potency and bestowers of fruits.
Phonemes, words, and sentences, together with the chapters and daily lessons. || 39 ||

Furthermore, there are chapters (adhyāyas), sections (paricchedas), creations (sargas), and breath-pauses (ucchvāsakas); as well as book-sections (paṭalas) and other divisions (avacchedas), questions (praśnas), sections (vākas), and recitations (anuvākas). || 40 ||
The Maṇḍalas and the Kāṇḍas, the various Saṃhitās, the Ṛks, Yajus, Sāmans, and the Sūktas together with the Khilas; || 41 ||
Words consisting of scriptures and tantras, as well as external and internal traditions, and those various languages—these are remembered as both articulate and inarticulate sounds. (42)
O Śakra, know this mantra-form to be my own form for those who understand my nature;
the distinction between the mantra and the mantrin is established by the degree of their meditative cultivation.
The sound which is embraced through yoga with the thought, "This one protects me," and which always has a hidden intention, protects the knower of mantra from fear. (44)

That mantra, when recollected, is the expansion of the ego through the sequential stages born of sound; for it is connected to pure consciousness, arising from the fullness of the Great Ego (pūrṇāhaṃtā). || 45 ||
All mantras belong to me for those who know their origin and dissolution;
they are mine or belong to others according to the degree of one's meditative realization.
My mantras, which follow the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti), shall be preeminent;
for they enter, by their own inherent power, into Brahman, whose essence consists of both existence and non-existence.
Mantras such as the Tārikā and Uttārikā, which are inherent by their very nature,
spontaneously attain that state which transcends worldly existence.
Those [deities] such as Tāra and Prāsādaka should be known as bestowers of liberation for those who resort to the state of existence that is either superior in being or equal to it. (49)
Mantras such as the Tārikā and others should be known as bestowers of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
some enter into the very state of being, while others simply go toward existence itself.

Bestowing both enjoyment and liberation, those two function according to their respective dispositions; such is the nature of those who follow the path of *prakṛti*. By the power of their intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), they extend all things within those two states. (51)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Mantras," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (In the Ā manuscript, it is titled *Śrīpañcarātra*; in the Ī manuscript, the title is omitted. 18.
Chapter Nineteen: Śrī [B, ī: Śrī said]— p. 64) Chapter Nineteen:
Śrī [B, ī: Śrī said]—
I am the primordial, full I-consciousness of Hari, characterized by the desire to create;
I am proclaimed as the supreme power whose form is creation. || 1 ||
In the state of desiring to create, she is celebrated by the name Ahaṃtā; in the state of creation, she is celebrated by the name Parā Śakti.
O delighter of the gods, my ten and five states are equal.
My eternal nature is consciousness, which is unsurpassed and self-cognized. || 2 ||

2. Regarding "ten" and so forth: it should be understood that there are fifteen states (*daśā*) beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the nasal bindu (*m*). Because the visarga is the source-nature (*prakṛti*) of these states, it is not included among the states themselves; this is how it should be understood. The principle of speech (*vāktattva*) is essentially the letter *a*, from which all verbal expression arises.
That very [sound], in the form of bliss, is intended as the second vowel. || 3 ||
The third is the self of will (icchātman), the fourth is the self of Īśāna;
the fifth is called Unmeṣa, and the sixth is said to be the form of Ūrjatā.
The middle group of four is the transformation of [the letters] beginning with *i*;
through its union with *anuttara* and *icchā*, that which is called the letter *e* is born. (5)
5. "The tetrad" means the form of the vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. Therefore, they have not been mentioned separately.
From the union of that very [tetrad] with bliss (*ānanda*), the source of the universe (*jagadyoni*) is proclaimed.
From the yoga of the unsurpassed unfolding, that which is called the syllable *O* arises.
6. The syllable *ai* is the source of the world (*jagadyoni*). From its very union with the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*), there arises Sadyojāta.
These expansions, which depend upon the object of knowledge (*vedya*), emerge from the Unsurpassed. 7.

7. Sadyojāta is the vowel *au*. There are thirteen [expansions], beginning with Ānanda, which are such-and-such manifestations (*samunmeṣāḥ*). These thirteen manifestations have resorted to the state of being residual to pure consciousness (*vedana*). 8.
8. "Remaining as sensation" means remaining in the form of pure consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*). This connects with the subsequent phrase, "his subtle state.
That fifteenth vowel, however, is the unsurpassed subtle state. [B: the fifteenth]
These fifteen states are the throbbing efforts of emission. 9.
9. The subtle stage is the *bindu*. It is the fifteenth when counting starting from the letter *a*. Thus, with these fifteen limbs, she is complete in her desire to create.
The divine power, consisting of creation, exerts its effort in every task.
10–11. "By the desire to emit"—the third case ending here expresses cause (*hetu*).
From that [desire], as she emits, the twenty-five principles arise from me:
beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *pṛthivī*, and [corresponding to them] those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
11. *Me* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a case-ending used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*), meaning "from me" (*mad*). It connects with the word *samudgatāḥ*.

The phrase *kādimāntāḥ* (those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*) is to be construed in reverse order. Through the manifestation of each respective syllable, each corresponding principle (*tattva*) has emerged.
The fourfold form for retention, beginning with *ya* and ending with *va*, is proclaimed.

12. Regarding *dhāraṇā*: it is designated as *dhāraṇā* because it sustains (*dhāraṇāt*) a person who is descending from the higher state (*paradaśā*) into the lower state (*aparadaśā*). For they sustain the person within [the body], therefore they are known as *dhāraṇās*.
The *kalā* is of the nature of slight activity; the letter *ya* is designated as wind (*vāta*). || 13 ||
Vidyā, whose nature is limited knowledge, is the letter *repha*, known as fire;
Māyā, whose nature is paralysis and delusion, is the letter *la*, considered to be earth.
The letter *va* is of the nature of passion (*rañjanātmā*), the power of attachment (*rāgaśakti*), and has Varuṇa as its essence;
it always sustains the individual soul (*nara*) in the midst of the states of the supreme and the non-supreme. (15)
These four dhāraṇās are to be known by those skilled in the principles;
indeed, that which begins with 'śa' and ends with 'kṣa' is to be understood as the pure fivefold Brahman.

O Lord of the Thirty-three, the letters śa, ṣa, sa, and ha, along with Aniruddha and the others, should be known as my wondrous form which, being agitated at the beginning of creation, brings forth [the universe]. (17)

17. The sequence of correspondence is as follows: "Aniruddha and the others. The letter Śa is of the nature of Aniruddha. Kṣobhikā is that Great Power (Mahāśakti), whose essence is Kṣa and who is called by the other name Satī.
[She consists of] the five divine powers beginning with Earth and ending with Space. 18.

18. He states that the letter *kṣa* has the nature of truth: "The divine ones named after me and the [beings] possessing sattva, whose essence consists of the fivefold powers such as *bala*, are the powers beginning with *śa*; they arise from my radiance and have the nature of gnosis. 19.
19. "Strength and so forth" means strength (*bala*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), heroism (*vīrya*), power (*śakti*), and splendor (*tejas*).
As for that which was previously called "emission" (*visarga*) and possessed fifteen limbs, I am that Śakti consisting of the Moon, crowded with ten thousand rays. 20.
Contraction and expansion—those two alone have been proclaimed;
that which was described by me as the fifteenth is said to be the final one of the limbs.

21. *Bindu* is contraction; *visarga* is expansion. "The last" means *bindu*. Know that the Sun, whose nature is grasping (*ādāna*), is truly the enjoyer. O Purandara, these two—the Sun and the Moon—are *bindu* and *visarga*. 22. [Continued: Know that the Sun, whose nature is grasping, is truly the enjoyer. O Purandara, these two—the Sun and the Moon—are *bindu* and *visarga*.

22. "The enjoyer" means the one who withdraws [the universe]. "Bindu" is the sun; "visarga" is the moon—this is the meaning. [B: omits three lines from here] "The rays of these two deities shall be seven each.
One should arrange the fourteen remaining vowels into seven pairs. 23.
O Purandara, among those seven pairs, the former seven are the rays of mine, who am known as the Enjoyer (Bhoktrī) and whose form is the Sun; they are the witherers (Śoṣakas).
24. "The seven in the east" means the seven vowels: a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, and o. The seven in the subsequent pairs are cool and refreshing;
they are my rays, nourishing and known as objects of enjoyment, belonging to her whose form is Soma. 25.
25. "The seven in the north" means: ā, ī, ū, ṛ, ḷ, ai, and au. These are the seven.
26. Illumination, sharpness, pervasion, grasping, casting, movement, and digestion—these are declared to be the rays originating from the Sun that were previously mentioned.
26. He describes the solar nature and the qualities of the seven pairs of letters beginning with *a* and ending with *u*: "Light," and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*:
"Light, sharpness, pervasion, grasping, destruction, movement, digestion, and attainment—these are the eight."
Established in the solar portion, within these short vowels beginning with 'a', there are in sequence: fluidity,
the state of coolness, tranquility, luster, and clarity.
Rasa, tāna, and ānanda—these seven are the lunar rays. || 27 ||

27. Thus, he describes the lunar nature and the qualities of the subsequent letters beginning with the word *dravatā* and so forth. And in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "Fluidity, the state of coolness, satisfaction, luster, clarity, sapidity, taste, and bliss—these eight are considered the lunar qualities" (6.15).
Thus, by joining the *visarga* here, its eightfold nature (*aṣṭatva*) is to be contemplated.
Resplendent with beauty through these rays, which consist of Agni and Soma, she qualifies the Person (*pumāṃs*), who is in the form of the *bindu*, by embracing him. (28)
Surpassing the form of the moon, adorned with the mandala of the ten million powers (śakti),
the Great Emanation, the Great Bliss, proceeds by means of the nature of the final vowel.
As that [power] proceeds, the pentad of Brahmā arises—
beginning with *kṣa* and ending in the tranquil state (*śānta*), O Lord of the Gods, distinguished by the unfolding of power (*śaktyunmeṣa*). (30)
The great agitation known as "kṣa" arose with the designation of "Reality" (satya); then, through the name Vāsudeva, there was the emergence of Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is associated with "ho. (31)
31. He states the names of the five Brahmans presiding over [the letters] beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *śa*, starting with the word "satya":
"Pradyumna is to be known by the name *pa*; Aniruddha, however, by the name *śa*.
These are the five supreme powers (*śakti*), whose nature consists of the five Brahmans. 32.
32–33. "Consisting of Brahman" means being composed of Brahman. These manifestations, which are non-different from me, are the causes of the world's origination;
they are my powers (śaktis), like the flames of a great fire, belonging to me, who am Brahman.
33. "Brahman is mine": the meaning is that "mine" is non-different from Brahman.

Four states of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) have arisen, beginning with *vāda* and ending with *yānta*; these are proclaimed as the stages beginning with the fourth (*turya*) and ending with the waking state (*jāgrat*). 34.
These sustain the male in the middle between two sets of ten;
this is called the "Brahma-daśā," as well as that which is natural (prākṛtī) and elemental (bhautikī).
35. "In the middle" means between the two states of the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā). Regarding "beginning with *bha*":
one should know that the principles beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with earth (*pṛthivī*) are the presiding deities for the letters starting from *bha* up to *ka*.
In the middle of those [letters], there is that which is called *ma*, due to the fourfold set of concentrations (*dhāraṇā*).
That person is said to be sustained [or: supported; or: acted upon], possessing the distinctions of waking and the other states.
(36) If he were not sustained by those [states], he would fall into one or another [of them];
whether into the state of Brahmā or into the primordial nature (prakṛti), there would be no cyclic existence (saṃsṛti) at all thereafter. (37)
For this purpose, O Dhāraṇā, you have emerged from me by my command;
from that [emergence], the Person (puruṣa), known as the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), is situated within the four sets of ten. || 38 ||

38. The *dhāraṇās* are the "intermediate" (*antaḥstha*) vowels. They are called "intermediate" because they reside between the state of Brahman and the state of Prakṛti. In the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, however, another etymological derivation is stated: "They are called 'intermediate' because they lie within the Person who dwells in the intermediate."
"From me was born 'Ma'—thus [is he] fit for both enjoyment and liberation.
For the sake of producing enjoyments for this Puruṣa, O Vāsava," (39)

39. By the phrase "I was born from *mat*," the etymological derivation of the word *mat*, which denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), is intended. Furthermore, its derivation from the root *man* is stated elsewhere:
"It is insentient, supreme, subtle, the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*), and non-manifest (*anulbaṇa*)."
The perception of the womb as having an inherent nature arose from me myself as "I am."

40. "Acaitanya" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its meaning is "insentient. It has been stated elsewhere: "It is insentient, for the sake of another, eternal, and constantly changing. "Anulvaṇa" means "unmanifest. Its name is also "Yoni," which signifies "inherent nature" (*svabhāva*). "Bha" means by virtue of being denoted by the syllable *bha*.

For the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of objects of experience and so forth, for the wise one (or, according to variant F, for the unwise one) who is experiencing them— (p. 67) [B: for the sake of the state of being an enjoyer of objects of experience and so forth].
O Purandara, from the entire collection of letters beginning with 'ba' and ending with 'ka', [arises the truth].
41. Following the sequence for the manifestation of reality (*tattva*), the letters have been presented out of their usual order, beginning with "Bā" and so forth:
"From me, twenty-three [letters] were produced clearly in succession."
Likewise, the creation of the intellect, ego, and mind proceeds from the first three [elements].
The emergence of the pentad beginning with the ear occurs within the letters from *nā* to *d*.
The emergence of the pentad beginning with speech (*vāk*) occurs within the letters from *ṇā* to *ṭ*. || 43 ||

The five subtle elements, beginning with sound and ending with the ether (vyoman), were born from the letters beginning with Ña and ending with Ca; the gross elements, beginning with space (viyat) and ending with earth, were born from the letters beginning with Ṅa and ending with Ka.
Cognition arises in the form of sound, and from that, sound [arises] in the form of meaning;
know, however, that cognition is my very nature, for all this manifestation proceeds from me.
O Lord of Gods, listen as I describe to you this middle path (madhyamā rīti) of the phonemic route (varṇādhvan), beginning with the first and ending with the last. (46)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Castes," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Chapter 19)
(p. 68) Chapter Twenty. Śakra said:
Salutations to her who possesses the power to create, protect, and withdraw the entire universe;
salutations to you, O embodiment of knowledge, who is the very nature of Hari. 1.
O Padmā, through your grace I have heard the supreme secret;
you ought to tell me once more the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) exactly as it is.
Śrī said:
Listen, O bull among the gods, to the primordial method of the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan),
by the thorough knowledge of which the practitioner attains my own nature.
That which is the supreme Brahman, free from the known and the knower, imperishable, whose nature is light that never sets, non-different from all, and the very state of the word "I. (4)

That power called "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is non-different from Him, eternally manifest, consisting of the nature of light that never sets, and devoid of the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower. || 5 ||
I am the essence of light and bliss, having attained equanimity in all respects;
yet, being stirred within a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part, I remain active.
Indeed, by my own power and in the form of Śabdabrahman,
I arise from the Supreme Lord myself for the liberation of all living beings.
Know that to be the unmanifest syllable, like an indistinct sound on a lute string; yet it proceeds in many ways for the sake of stability through the nature of distinct phonemes.
This [Self], whose nature is subtle color and sound, assumes the form of a continuous stream for the discerning one who is established in Me and liberated from the sheaths of the five paths.
9. The five paths (adhvan) are the path of worlds (bhuvana), the path of words (pada), the path of mantras, the path of principles (tattva), and the path of limited powers (kalā).
