The five sheaths (kośa) are known as Māyā, Prasūti, Prakṛti, the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), and the individual body (jīvadeha).
By his grace, one attains the state of direct experience (anubhūtipada).
The collection of my fourfold nature should indeed be understood as being of the same essence as that Supreme Self.
10. The fourfold nature consisting of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the others, exists through that [Supreme] Self in the form of the castes;
this will be explained immediately hereafter.
It is characterized by light, form, and sound, through the connection of its origin and dissolution.
It ends with the letter *s*, as well as with the letter *a* and the letter *h*. || 11 ||
11. In the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), it is characterized by sound; in the stage of dissolution (*apyayakrama*), which is the supreme form, it is characterized by consciousness (*citta*).
When counting from the letter *a* up to the letter *sa*, there are forty-eight phonemes (*varṇa*). For example:
sixteen vowels, twenty-five consonants (*sparśa*), four semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), and the letter *ha*.
"Beyond [these] are three heats. Thus it is also when counting starting from the letter *ha* up to the long *ā*.
"In the *prabhava* [phase], the letter *ha* is at the end of the twelve; but in the *apaya*, the letter *a* is there. Both of these ends of the twelve are equal. (12)

12. For the fourfold selves, such as Vāsudeva and the others, the letter *ha* becomes the twelfth [division] at the time of manifestation (*prabhava*), while at the time of dissolution (*apyaya*), it is the letter *a*. This is the intended meaning: when the previously mentioned forty-eight letters are divided twelvefold, four letters are obtained in each division. And these, in sequence—

They are presided over by the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva. At the end of the twelve divisions, the letter *ha* occurs at the time of manifestation (*prabhava*) and the letter *a* at the time of dissolution (*laya*).
Within this collection of manifestations (*vyūhasamūha*) consisting of phonemes, that which is to be known is to be understood through the meditative absorption of knowledge (*jñānasamādhi*).
Rest, arising, pervasion, and manifestation proceed from Vāsudeva. || 13 ||

13. Vāsudeva and the others, established in their respective divisions, should be understood as being, in sequence, the forms of repose (*viśrāma*), emergence (*udaya*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), and manifestation (*vyakti*).
In this regard, one should know that each individual form is indeed likewise joined with a group of four preceded by rest; thus it is in brief. (14)
One should contemplate the god Viśrāma, the eternal Vāsudeva;
the lotus-eyed Akāra, the primordial and eternal deity. (15)
15. He clarifies that very point with the verse beginning "viśrāmam" (rest):
"For here, in dissolution, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa find rest;
therefore, one should meditate upon the god Saṃkarṣaṇa as having the form of emergence. 16.
For he, the Self of all, has arisen; first, one should meditate upon that Lord Pradyumna, the creator of all, who is himself pervading, as the syllable *i*. (17)
By means of that which consists of the threefold karma, the world is obtained in its various forms;
one should meditate upon that Aniruddha, who is the manifest form, as the syllable *Ī*.
For here all powers, such as the creation of the world and so forth, are manifested;
indeed, they are situated exactly like this, arranged in the manner of a staff (daṇḍavat). 19.
Up to the letter *sa*, my fourfold nature is endowed with four forms;
during the contemplation of its manifestation, one should remember the letter *ha* at the limit of the twelve.
20. "Up to the letter *sa*" means up to the limit of the letter *sa*. One should contemplate the letter *ha* as Vāsudeva, the place of rest;
one should remember the letter *sa* as Saṃkarṣaṇa, its arising at the time of dissolution. 21.
21. He describes the establishment of the fourfold self within the sequence of the letters: "The letter *ha*," etc.
Thus, one should contemplate the divine fourfold self according to its form;
and the twelve-fold meditation on the internal characteristics consists of twelve *dhāraṇās*.
22. "By way of form" (ākārataḥ) means up to the limit of form.
That which serves as a staircase, having ascended which one enters the supreme city from the dvādaśānta—this is shown as the first method of the path of phonemes (varṇamārga). 23.
The subtle [speech] consists of those four aspects; it is of the nature of light, composed of mind, and supreme.
The intermediate [speech] has already been described; hear from me its specific distinction. (24)
The four dhāraṇās previously mentioned, which have my own nature, belong to Nīruruddha, who is designated by the syllable VA; his power is known as Rāga.
Māyā is Mahālakṣmī, whose other name is Lakārā; she who is known by the designation of the letter Ra is Vidyā, and she is remembered as Mahāvāṇī.
Vātasaṃjñā, Mahākālī, and Kriyāśakti Yakāriṇī;
the three forms beginning with Brahmā, and those wives beginning with Trayī—[these are the eight]. (27)
That entire object of knowledge is subtle within the first part of the letter A;
in the middle part, the Puruṣa, the immutable enjoyer, is established. (28)
Every transmigrating person abides in the final portion;
this middle path of the varṇa-way has been shown to you. (29)
Now, O slayer of Bala, I shall describe the final mode;
the final mode is Vaikharī, which distinguishes effort and place of articulation.
When articulated by those with distinct speech, she certainly becomes manifest;
she is the illuminator of the respective true paths for living beings bound to bodies. (31)
This Mātṛkā is born, nourished by the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu;
therein, fifty powers are proclaimed to be equal to Viṣṇu himself. || 32 ||
Vāsudeva and the other vyuhas, as well as the ten and two beginning with Keśava, preside over whichever *mātṛkā* consisting of the garland of letters [is recited]. (33)
The gods who preside over the vowels—listen to their powers:
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are declared to be the powers of the Vyūhas. (34)
Śrī, Vāgīśvarī, Kānti, Kriyā, Śānti, Vibhūti, Icchā, Prīti, Rati, Māyā, Dhī, and Mahimā. (35)
These powers of Keśava and the others are these very powers of the vowels;
listen as I describe the deities presiding over the consonants beginning with 'ka'.
The Viṣṇus named Padmanābha and others are the presiding deities of the letters beginning with *ka*.
They are Padmanābha, Dhruva, Ananta, Śaktīśa, and Madhusūdana. (37)
37. The various manifestations, such as Padmanābha and others, have already been recited and should be understood [as explained] previously in the eleventh chapter.
The presiding deity of knowledge (vidyādhideva), Kapila, Viśvarūpa, Vihangama, Kroḍātman, Dharmātman, Baḍabāmukha, Dharma, and likewise Vāgīśvara. || 38 ||
The Lord who lay upon the single ocean, the Tortoise who supports the netherworld, the Boar, the Man-lion, and likewise the one who carried away the nectar; || 39 ||
The Lord of Śrī, possessing a divine body, the soul of beauty, the bearer of nectar;
the conqueror of Rāhu, the slayer of Kālanemi, the great one who seized the Pārijāta tree.
Then there is the Lord of the World, the tranquil-souled Dattātreya, the great master;
thereafter is the Blessed One who sleeps beneath the banyan tree, whose body has but a single horn.
The god Vāmanadeha, the all-pervading Trivikrama, as well as Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa. || 42 ||
Rāma, who wields a flaming axe; another Rāma, the wielder of the bow;
the Lord Kalki, the knower of the Vedas; and the Lord who reclines upon the netherworld (Pātāla). || 43 ||
Among these last four, the four deities beginning with Rāma reside; they likewise reside in the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya sounds.
44. The nasal (anunāsika) is the color. The *yamās* are specific phonemes well-known in the *Prātiśākhyas*.
[The goddesses are] Dhīḥ, Tārā, Vāruṇī, Śakti, Padmā, and likewise Vidyā;
Saṃkhyā, Viśvā, Khagā, Bhūḥ, Gauḥ, Lakṣmī, and likewise Vāgīśvarī. 45.
Amṛtā, Dharaṇī, Chāyā, Nārāyaṇī, Sudhā, Śrī, Kīrti, Viśvakāmā, Mā, Satyā, Kānti, and Saroruhā. (46)
Māyā, Padmāsanā, Kharvā, Vikrānti born of Nara, Nārāyaṇī, Hariprīti, Gāndhārī, and likewise Kāśyapī. || 47 ||
Vaidehī, Vedavidyā, Padminī, and Nāgaśāyinī (or Padmavāsinī)—
these goddesses, who are my own portions, are to be known as the powers beginning with *Ka*. || 48 ||
And this [world] is presided over by the Mothers, who are the instruments of existence, along with the gods beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, Ānanda, and Sūkṣma, and the powers beginning with Lambodarī.
And by the Vināyakas, the Durgās, the Kṣetrapālas, and likewise the Mātṛs; and by those established in the Samaya, as well as by the Buddhists and others who follow the Ārhata path. || 50 ||
Just as hungry children attend upon their mother, so do all the gods attend upon the Goddess Mātṛkā. || 51 ||
For this is the source of mantras and the birthplace of vidyās;
it is the place of origin for the principles (tattvas) and for authentic knowledges.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Mātṛkās," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (20)
Chapter Twenty-One. Śakra:

Salutations to you, O beloved of Hari, who take the form of the manifestation of word and meaning, who revolve through the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and who are known as the awakening that transcends those paths. || 1 ||
1. Regarding the "six paths" (ṣaḍadhvan): the six paths are known as phoneme (varṇa), portion (kalā), principle (tattva), mantra, word (pada), and world (bhuvana).
O Goddess, the phonemes have been explained by me exactly as they are, being the causes of all things.

Now, you should speak to me correctly regarding the path of mantra. 2. O Goddess, the phonemes have been explained by me exactly as they are, being the causes of all things. Now, you should speak to me correctly regarding the path of mantra.
2. "All" means both words and their referents. Śrī said: "The Supreme Lord alone is the illustrious and most excellent of persons."
The divine ocean of the sixfold policy, the self of all, facing every direction. || 3 ||
I am his supreme power, the ego, the inseparable Śrī;
the support of all, possessing all powers, all-knowing, and facing in every direction.
The entire universe shines within me, like reflections on the surface of a mirror;
pure consciousness alone is my own nature, characterized by stainless bliss. (5)
Subject to my own will, revolving within a portion of the Awakener,
and becoming composed of the Śabdabrahman, I evolve through the path of the Kalās.
6. "Dependent on will" means acting according to one's own desire (*svacchanda*). "Manifestation" (*vivarta*) means transformation (*pariṇāma*). Regarding "the path of *kalā*":
it means consisting of qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*).
The *kalās* are said to be the six supreme qualities of the Lord, beginning with knowledge.
Through the separation of three and two of these, one revolves upon the path of reality.
7–8. "By the union of three and two" means by the conjunction of three pairs.
O best of gods, the deities beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa are the principles (tattvas);
they are further manifested through the permutations of the phonemes (varṇavyatikara) by way of the path of mantra.
Listen as I describe the manifestation of that path of mantra:
this is an expansion of the Śabdabrahman, crowded with ten thousand rays.
The characteristic of the mind consists of six qualities, and its division is fourfold:
in some cases it is the seed (bīja), in some the mass (piṇḍa), in some the name (saṃjñā), and in some the word (pada).

The fourth state (turya), deep sleep (suṣupti), dream (svapna), and waking (jāgrat), along with their seeds and so forth, correspond respectively to a single vowel, a double vowel, or a pair consisting of both a vowel and a consonant. (11)

11. The meaning is that the seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), designations (*saṃjñā*), and words (*pada*) mantras should be understood as being associated respectively with the four states beginning with the fourth (*turya*) and ending with the waking state (*jāgrat*).
O Lord of the Wise, the seed-syllable should also be known as having many vowels.
In between, there were horses—[in some versions: *antarāhurayaḥ*, *antarāhalayaḥ*, *antarākulayaḥ*, or *anantarāvilaṃ*]—and in some places, balls of food mixed with their own juices. || 12 ||
12. The *haras* situated within, in the middle, are the *vyañjanas*; the meaning is that they constitute the *piṇḍamantra*.
He states an exception to this with the words "in some cases":
"The designation for each respective object of expression, joined with *namaḥ* and the *praṇava*."
It is characterized by action, the agent, conjunction, praise, and awakening. || 13 ||
13. He states the essential nature of the *padamantra* with the words "action" (*kriyā*), etc. *Saṃbodha* means awakening.
The *mantra* whose essence is the word (*pada*) is said to be endowed with various superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
These four constitute the complete *mantra* within the self of the deity. 14.
14. The designation "abhijñā" (higher knowledge).
It is connected with the fourfold [set] and bestows the desired accomplishment.
And [I shall explain] the nature of the field and the knower of the field regarding mantras, O Lord of the Thirty-three.
15. That deity. Having understood the mantras according to their true nature, the wise one should employ them.
Śakra said:
O Lotus-born One, tell me the true nature of the field and the knower of the field with respect to the mantras.
Having understood this, they do not become deluded and shall attain accomplishment before long.
Śrī said:
The seed is the life-force of those possessing seeds, and the remainder is proclaimed as the field. || 17 ||

17. For mantras possessing seed-syllables (*bīja*), the seed-syllable is the "life" (*jīva*); this is the meaning. For those without seed-syllables, the initial [syllable] is the life, while the remainder is the field (*kṣetra*).

And for both seed-syllables and clusters (*piṇḍa*), that which remains is called the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). 18. [As stated above. (Note: Verse 18 is identical in content to the second half of verse 17.)
18. *Ādi* means the first letter; that is to say, the letter *a*. "Let it be so," [it is said]; the meaning is "let it be the letter *a*.

But the remainder is declared to be the field (*kṣetra*) when devoid of the letter *a*; the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is declared to be the vowel (*svara*), and furthermore, when the vowel is alone. 19. [The verse continues: "But the remainder is declared to be the field when devoid of the letter *a*; the knower of the field is declared to be the vowel, and furthermore, when the vowel is alone."

19. "Furthermore, [the syllable] devoid of the letter 'a'..."—this connects with what follows. "A vowel" means any vowel whatsoever. "And in a solitary vowel"—this also connects with what follows. "The Jīva would be the first mātrā; the second and so forth would be the Tanu (or Manu)."
But when there is only one [element], there would be a living being characterized by latent impressions (saṃskāra)—[in another reading: characterized by the awakening of latent impressions]. || 20 ||
20. Regarding the term *saṃskāra*: it means the "intermediate speech" (*madhyamā vāk*). In this regard, the twenty-sixth verse of the eighteenth chapter should be noted:
"That which is being uttered would be the field (*kṣetra*); furthermore, in the soundless *piṇḍaka*..."
The first is designated as the living being (jīva); the remainder is called the field (kṣetra) [or, it is said to be the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)].
21. "Being uttered" means in the form of *vaikharī* speech.

This true nature of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) has been fully demonstrated to you—either at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, or in all three, or in any one of them. 22.
The aggregate of these, or their seed-syllables, are those mantras that are effective at all times;
however, in the absence of seed-syllables for the mantras, one should take the first letter as the seed.
23. Where there is no seed-syllable (*bīja*) in a mantra, the meaning is that the first syllable joined with the *anusvāra* is the seed-syllable.
For example, in "Gaṇapataye namaḥ," the seed-mantra is "gaṃ.
Thereafter, the entire mantra is said to be joined with the *anusvāra*.
The mantras sport with the person who has been colored by passion.
In the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) belonging to Prakṛti, which consists of fourteen divisions;
and in the path of categories (*padādhvan*) belonging to Prakṛti, beginning with deep sleep (*suṣupti*), excluding the fourth state (*turya*). || 25 ||
Having rescued from the path of the worlds that person who stands within the gaze of the Teacher, whose senses are restrained, the mantras—possessing faces gracious with serenity—elevate him. (26)
Producing dispassion at every step toward the path of the word,
they gradually lead him through the stages of the principles (tattva), the digits (kalā), the phonemes (varṇa), and the words (pada). (27)
Having reached the temple of the mantra, with all bonds completely shaken off, he enters that eternal Brahman known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. || 28 ||
Śakra:
O Goddess, what kind of teacher is he, and what kind of disciple does he have?
Among mantras, which mantra is capable of leading to the supreme attainment? (29)
How should he be instructed? Tell me this; salutations be unto you! Śrī said:
A Brāhmaṇa endowed with all the auspicious marks, who has mastered the Vedas... (30)

Devoted to the six duties, tranquil, intent upon the five times, and pure; a knower of the meaning of the Pañcarātra, observant of silence, and one who has exerted himself in the syllables of the mantra. (31)
Neither stout nor lean, neither short nor one-eyed, nor indeed afflicted by disease;
neither blind, nor deaf, nor dull-witted, nor bald, nor lame. (32)
Neither deficient in limb nor having an extra limb, neither afflicted with vitiligo nor hypocritical;
neither prone to anger nor having diseased skin, nor one whose consciousness is destroyed by greed. (33)
One should avoid one who is of low birth, of evil conduct, deceitful, and crooked; rather, one should accept one who is endowed with compassion, self-restraint, and tranquility,
who possesses firm devotion, and is intent on ritual action.
One who is truthful in speech and endowed with virtuous conduct, skilled in the arts of drawing lines, having conquered the senses, well-contented, and whose mind is filled with compassion. || 35 ||
One should know the Guru as one who is endowed with the characteristics of a teacher, upright, possessing a beautiful smile,
and thus filled with a multitude of virtues.
The Vaiṣṇava [alone]. || 36 ||
And such a disciple should be known as one endowed with all the required characteristics:
patient, virtuous, pure, and free from anger and greed. (37)
Constantly devoted to bathing and worship, ever intent on serving his guru, he was faithful toward Brahmins, the sacred fire, the gods, and the ancestors, and habitually practiced libations.
Likewise, one who is of noble birth, wise, and always devoted to the meaning of the scriptures—whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra—who is solely intent upon the Blessed Lord. (39)
A disciple endowed with such characteristics and possessed of sincerity, or a woman endowed with the performance of her caste-duties and possessing sound discernment— (40)

The husband should give his wife, who is devoted to him and considers him her sole lord, to the one who has given his consent. An ācārya who is identical with the Blessed One should, according to the rule and with the gaze of a guru, cause such a disciple— possessing these characteristics— to know the mantras.
But having observed... || 41 ||
41. By this, the eligibility of women and Śūdras for receiving Tantric mantras is ordained. However, specific details regarding the Tārā-mantra should be understood from other texts.
Thus ends [the section on] the Śrīpāñcarātrasāra [A: Śrīpañcarātra; B, Ḍ: in the Śrīpāñcarātra].
In the Lakṣmītantra, the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Guru and the Disciple. || 21 ||
Chapter Twenty-Two. Śakra:
O Goddess, who are without beginning or end, omniscient, and beloved of Hari, how indeed should one understand the mantras, and what is their form? (1)
Are these [means] of equal importance, or is there a distinction of seniority and juniority?
Having been asked this by me, please speak; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One!
Śrī said: Listen, O Pākaśāsana, to everything from me in its entirety—
how I am the embodiment of mantra and how I cause them to know.
3. "I make known" means that I cause [you] to understand by way of being the Teacher (ācārya).
The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, consisting of the six attributes, stainless and radiant, unconditioned by space or time, formless, and incomparable. 4.
4. "Incomparable" (anūpama) means "without comparison.
That Brahman is indeed "I"—the self-realization of one's own nature, devoid of attributes, without beginning or end, divine, the Great Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. 5.

5. It is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), being free from the material qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest; it is the divine essence of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandarasam*), indivisible, undecaying, and immortal;
its state of phenomenal existence does not manifest, and it is devoid of the subject-object duality (*grāhyagrāhakavarjita*). 6.
6. "Unblinking," and so forth: the meaning is that in the supreme state of peace (*śāntaparāvasthā*), there is an absence of the emergence (*unmeṣa*) of the nature of becoming or existing entities.
Likewise, the phrase "graspable" and so on should also be understood in this way.
That supreme Brahman is "stilled" (*stimita*); I am its state of being stilled.
Then, at one time, the Supreme Brahman, by means of the established state of becoming and being...
Sometimes, by her own will, she unfolds while not abandoning her essential nature;
I am that "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), whose essence is the state of "I," who is to be fully worshipped as the Supreme Self.
8. "Unmiṣati" means "it shines forth. Regarding "not abandoning," etc.: the meaning is "not abandoning its natural state of changelessness.
"I arise from you, O Lord, solely by your will, like the sun [established in its course]."
Having gathered the entire collection of requisites created by his own will, solely through his desire.
9. From Vivasvat— that is, from the Lord consisting of light—
having taken what was written upon my own wall, I manifest through the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
The phonetic, the consisting of parts, the essential, and likewise the mantric.
The six paths are proclaimed as the Pādika and the Bhauvana;
that which is supreme, called Ahaṃtā (I-consciousness), is the stainless form of consciousness [or the nature of being and consciousness].
Of that, the first unfolding is proclaimed as the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan).
O Pākaśāsana, his prediction was shown by you previously.
That very same great form of mine, consisting of pure consciousness,
unfolds as the path through the nature of knowledge and the other [powers], such as *kalā*.
The qualities of the supreme self—the digits such as knowledge and the rest—have already been described to you; how many they are and what they are like has been well explained.
Depending upon the two time-periods, that form of mine, consisting of consciousness, exists by way of the path of reality in the form of Vāsudeva and others. (15)
15. The two paths refer to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) and the path of ritual energies (*kalādhvan*).
75) Furthermore, there are the manifestations (*vyūha*), the emanations (*vibhava*), and whatever else consists of the Blessed One.
That manifestation of the supreme self is proclaimed as the path of reality (tattvādhvan).

16. "Other" means other arrays (*vyūha*) and other manifestations (*vibhava*). Taking up the two preceding paths, that very form of mine, consisting of consciousness, perpetually unfolds through the supreme path of mantra. 17.
For the deliverance of living beings submerged in the ocean of existence, for the enjoyment of those dwelling in worldly life, and for the generation of dispassion; (18)
18. He states the purpose of the path of mantra (mantrādhvan) with the words beginning "for the sake of deliverance" (uttāraṇāya):
for the sake of accomplishing propitiation (ārādhanaprasiddhyartham), and for the sake of a mental support (mānasālambanāya).
The path of mantra is supremely vast, characterized by my own nature of consciousness. || 19 ||

19. "For the sake of providing a mental object" means that by displaying forms of beautiful substrates, it provides a meditative object for the minds of yogins. This has been explained in detail in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"It assumes the form of deities such as Vāsudeva."
All mantras are of the nature of consciousness, all-pervading, and the accomplishers of all things. || 20 ||
20. Now he describes the majesty of the mantra under discussion, beginning with the words "The mantras": "The mantras protect the reciter and are hidden in form according to the scriptures;
for they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, belonging to Śārṅgin, the God of gods. (21)

21. By way of describing his greatness, he states the etymological meaning of the word *mantra*: "And [the root] *trai*... The intention is that it is derived from the roots *mandhāti* and *traidhāti*. He states another derivation: "Protected (*gupta*)...
The verbal root is *matri* in the sense of "speaking secretly."
O Blessed One, my mantras are to be understood as stainless forms:
the fourfold states consisting of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya). || 22 ||
The nature of the path of the knowable (jñeya) is the waking state, which proceeds through the external senses;
this occurs when the power of the external senses has been overcome by darkness (tamas). || 23 ||

23. He defines the state of dream with the words beginning "bāhya" (external) and so forth: "That modification of the internal organ which has residual impressions as its only remainder is to be known as dream; in the absence of that, it is the state of deep sleep. 24.

24. In the absence of that, there is the absence of mental formations (saṃskāra). When the fluctuations (vṛtti) residing in the external and internal organs have ceased for the wise man who abides in purity (sattva) and is not overwhelmed by darkness (tamas), [then the mind becomes one-pointed]. 25.
The continuum of the pure being’s clarity is designated as the fourth state.
Thus, these fourfold paths have been explained in this discourse on the stages.
Excluding the fourth state, [the individual soul] resorts to impure states such as deep sleep and the like;
the sequence of worlds (bhuvanapaddhati) is said to extend from Māyā down to the earth (kṣiti). || 27 ||
27. He defines the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*)—beginning with *māyā*—as follows:
"That path of the worlds is to be known as impure, mired in the mud of *mala*.
Those mantras sport eternally with the man who is dominated by passion. 28.
Displaying various nets of illusory enjoyments, he was utterly deluded;
yet he was properly beheld with a compassionate gaze by the Guru, who looked upon him with pity. (29)
They cause [beings] to cross over, engendering detachment at every step;
then, they gradually lead them along paths consisting of purity. (30)
30. At every step, [they lead one] through the states of waking and so forth; this is the meaning. They cause one to attain the supreme glory in the Śabdabrahman.
Such are the great-souled mantras, supremely purifying. 31.
31. "In the Śabdabrahman" means in the mantras.
They are to be known as threefold: the inferior, the middling, and the superior—those who have attained the form of deities as the instruments for worldly existence (bhava). 32.
32. "The others" means the supreme ones. They are the instruments of existence (*bhava*), serving as the means for creation.
Those mantras which yield finite results should be known by the wise as inferior.

The mantras of the *Vibhava* deities, however, are their very forms (*mūrti*) along with their powers (*śakti*). 33. [Continuation of verse 33: ...[The mantras] of the *Vibhava* deities are indeed their embodied manifestations together with their powers.
p.
76) Those who immerse themselves in Brahman, which consists of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, should be known as the middle mantras, the supreme forms of the cosmic array (vyūha). || 34 ||
Those mantras established through existence and non-existence are the most excellent of the excellent;
thus should the seniority and juniority among them be understood by those skilled in mantras. (35)
Those established in the Pañcarātra are the highest; those consisting of the Trayī (the three Vedas) are middling;
and those established in other tantras are to be known as the lowest by one whose eye is the scripture. (36)

36. Regarding the phrase "established in the Pañcarātra": because they are engaged in the exposition of the Bhāgavata doctrine, which is exclusively devoted to the Sāttvika aspect, they are considered supreme. Regarding the phrase "consisting of the Trayī": because they have the three guṇas as their object, they are considered middling. It is said: "Those with the Kalās as their limbs are to be known as superior; those with other [elements] as their limbs are remembered as middling."
The mantras without the syllable Anaṅga are inferior; listen further, O Lord of the Gods. (37)
37. The *kalās* are those beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*). Those joined with seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and so forth, are proclaimed as the highest (*uttama*).
Mantras that have any one of the seed-syllables and so on situated within them are designated as middling (*madhyama*). 38.
Mantras that lack the seed-syllable (bīja) and other such elements are to be known as those designated as inferior.
Having thus understood the various types of mantras, the preceptor, whose vision is the scripture,
should, when requested, instruct the disciples according to their respective natures.
The Manus. || 39 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Mantras of the Six Paths," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra [or: in the Śrīpañcarātra; or: in the Śrīpāñcarātra]. || 22 ||
The Twenty-third Chapter: Śrī (Goddess of Fortune) — page 77.
That which is the all-pervading, supreme, and great Brahman is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
I am indeed Nārāyaṇī, his supreme power in the form of ego (ahaṃtā).
For the sake of favoring the worlds, I have assumed the role of a teacher;
in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa, I illuminate the scripture.
Furthermore, abiding in the form of the Guru and endowed with perfect knowledge,
she [should look] with her own gaze consisting of power, filled with compassion and mantra.
"Being a guru, I protect the disciples who approach me;
therefore, that teacher should always be known by the disciples as being of my own nature."
One should instruct the disciple in the mantras; listen as it is:
first, in a place that is pure, level, smooth, and free from defects of the ground. || 5 ||
5. Defects of the site include those arising from contact with hair, nails, or bones, as well as salinity and the like.
[The ground should be] smeared with cow dung, enriched with colors matching its own hue, fumigated, free of thorns or obstacles, and adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. 6.

6. "Corresponding to the [social] classes" (*varṇānurūpa*), and so forth. This means [the ground] is endowed with colors such as white, which are appropriate for the *varṇas* beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.

Thus it is stated in the *Paramasaṃhitā*: "The ground of a Brāhmaṇa is white; that of a Kṣatriya should be reddish; that of a Vaiśya is yellow in color; and that of a Śūdra is declared to be black. (7.5)
"Thorns" refers to thorns and the like.
When sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and anointed with sandalwood paste and other substances.
And one should fashion a small clay vessel using only auspicious flowers.
7. With *kevalaiḥ*, meaning loose and unstrung;
one should worship with one's own mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Then, one should recite the previous *vyāhṛti*.
[She is] preceded by the syllable Om. || 8 ||
8. "With the previous one" means with the *vyāhṛti* mantra.
Then, having spread earth upon the ground, it should be consecrated with perfumes and incense [or flowers].
It should be either square or circular, measuring two cubits or even one cubit.
Having made the seat of the Mātṛkās perfectly level, one should spread it out;
she is the single Goddess of fifteen syllables who exists within the divided classes [of consonants].
10. "Bhinnavargā" means that she is differentiated by way of the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) and the others.
She is the manifest mother of mantras, my very body composed of sound.
The practitioner of mantra should spread [the syllables] either in the form of a lotus or in the form of a wheel. 11.
In the *puruṣa* [cakra], one should follow the form of the discus and the lotus-born Lakṣmī.
The power consisting of Agni and Soma is called *visṛṣṭi*; it is sixteenfold [the Vidyā is called *sṛṣṭi*, being sixteenfold]. || 12 ||
One should write that which is called "Svara" (the vowels) on the leaf or the spoke situated in the eastern direction.
As for the five groups beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', they consist of the elements starting from Earth and ending with Puruṣa. || 13 ||
13. The letter *ka* is the Earth; the letter *ma* is the Male (*pumān*).
One should write that [Earth] like a leaf from a tree, extending from Fire up to Wind.
The four letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *va* are the form of the internal support (*dhāraṇā*). 14.
The wise one should write [the syllables] in an upward direction on a leaf or a petal as before:
beginning with *śa* and ending with *kṣa*, up to the end of the fourth [vowel], which is the aforementioned group of five Brahmās. (15)
One should write [the syllable] situated in the ten directions upon a lotus or even on a leaf;
that which is called Sound is the Supreme Brahman, consisting of light and free from all affliction.
One should meditate on the form of light at the periphery of the wheel and the lotus,
using those syllables known as the *tattvas*, beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*.
The wise one should worship Prakṛti there, who is my very form as the Tattva;
then, in the center of its pericarp, he should contemplate the Mantra-mātṛkā.
I bow to the Goddess who is without beginning or end, the Great One, the Supreme Puruṣa;
the Goddess who holds the noose and the goad, the Lotus-Born One adorned with a garland of lotuses.

The woman of Puruṣottama is Puruṣottamī. She is gracious, possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds, her limbs fashioned with perfect color, and adorned with ornaments of various hues.
One should know that the body is Śabdabrahman and should remember the Praṇava as the head;
one should know "a" and "ā" as the eyebrows, and "i" and "ī" as the eyes.
U and ū are the two ears; ṛ and ṝ are the two nostrils; e and ai are to be known as the two cheeks; e and o are the two lips; and o and au are the two rows of teeth. (22)
22. "The other two" means the vowels *ḷ* and *ḹ*. Because these two are neuter, they are not designated by masculine nouns. 23.

A wise person should contemplate the anus (*aṃ*) and the visarga (*aḥ*) as the tongue; the *ka*-group and *ca*-group as the hands; the *ṭa*-group and *ta*-group as the feet; and one should contemplate the *pa*-group and *pha*-group as the sides.
One should contemplate the syllable *maṃ* as the regions of the back and the front;
one should know that *ya* and *ra* are the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and heat (*uṣman*), and one should contemplate *laṃ* as the necklace (*hāra*).
One should contemplate the letter *va* as the waist-thread (*kaṭisūtra*), and *śa* and *ṣa* as the two earrings;
one should know the letter *sa* to be the heart, and one should contemplate *ha* as residing within the heart.
One should know the spreading radiance to be the syllable *kṣa*, blazing like lightning;
one should know the *raṅga* located at the tip of the nose,
and one should remember that which is called *yama* in the heart.
26. One should know that the nasal [consonants] have their place in the nose; the *jihvāmūlīya* should be known as being at the root of the tongue immediately thereafter;
and likewise, one should know the *upadhmānīya* to be at the lips in due order. 27.
She wore a forest garland made of auspicious, radiant lotuses consisting of fire and moon, which hung from her neck down to her feet.
The wise one should contemplate the crown of the Supreme Lord, which has the luster of ten million fires, moons, and suns, and is adorned with shimmering jewels; it is the letter *Ha* (or *Ma*).

Having thus recollected that Goddess Mātṛkā, the mother of mantras, one should worship her with water for the guest-offering (arghya), flowers, and other offerings, reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Mother of Mantras."
"Accept this arghya," saying thus, he should offer the ritual enjoyments in due order;
then, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, he should prostrate himself on the ground with the eight limbs.

O Goddess who dwells in the lotus, whose abode is the lotus, who are the lotus itself, beloved of the lotus-eyed one; O Sovereign Mother of all mantras, the support established by all principles! || 32 ||
"Reveal to me your supreme, divine form consisting of Lakṣmī.
Having thus prayed with self-restraint, the practitioner himself becomes composed of Lakṣmī. (33)
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the Mātṛkā, being himself composed of the true Mātṛkā,
he should extract the desired mantra and then instruct it to the disciple.

34. "Mātṛkā," and so forth. He is one by whom the arrangement—that is, the placement—of the lotus and the wheel has been performed with the phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. The mantras consisting of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*) have attained preeminence among mantras.
In that regard, O Lord of Serīsā, the seeds are superior even to the clusters.
(79) Among the seeds, O Vāsava, there are seven seeds that are like jewels:
*tāraka* is the first seed, and *tārikā* is remembered as the second. (36)
36. The sequence for extracting the mantras beginning with Tārā will be explained in the following chapter.
Of those two, the third, Anutārikā, is equal to their splendor;
the fourth, however, is called the supreme seed-syllable (bīja), the womb of the universe. 37.
The fifth seed-syllable is that of Prādyumna; the sixth is considered to be that of Sarasvatī;
and the seventh is proclaimed to consist of Mahālakṣmī. (38)
The gross, subtle, and supreme states have been proclaimed for each [seed-syllable] individually;
O Śakra, being attentive, listen to the seed-syllables in their proper sequence. (39)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Mātṛkās," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (p.
The Twenty-fourth Chapter. Śrī said:
"The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the incomparable supreme light."
The Brahman that is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is free from defects and untainted.
This entire universe is pervaded by that one supreme light;
I am the supreme *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness) of that Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Arising by her own will for the benefit of all living beings,
she becomes composed of the Śabdabrahman, having the Mātṛkā-mantra as her very form.
I exist in the form of mantra, imitating each respective object of expression;
first, in the form of the *tāra* (the syllable Om), one should extract me exactly as I am.
First, taking hold of the *dhruva* (the central point), one should then extract the *karṇa* (the diagonal);
thereafter, one should extract the *nābhi* (the center), and join these three together as one.
This syllable "Om," which has arisen as the first Tāraka Brahman,
should subsequently be adorned with the Bindu, and after that, with the Nāda.
One should meditate with a continuous sound, like an unbroken stream of oil;
this indeed is that Vaiṣṇava form, the three-syllabled eternal Brahman.
Aniruddha is the letter *a* here, Pradyumna is the fifth vowel (*u*), Saṃkarṣaṇa is the letter *ma*, and Vāsudeva is the bindu (the nasal dot). || 8 ||
O Lord of the Gods, there is no division of the four [states] within that sound;
that which is the supreme limit of sound is I-consciousness, the Supreme Goddess.
That power is supreme and subtle, called the sky at the end of sound;
consisting of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), subtle, and all-pervading, she is I.

10. "At the end of the sound," and so forth. The meaning is that she has the nature of the space within the end of the aforementioned sound, which is the *daharākāśa* (the internal ether). Since the Goddess has the nature of the *daharākāśa*, it is heard in scripture that the Supreme Brahman has its fixed residence therein: "In that [ether] is the small space, free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon."
And in the *Śrīsāttvata*: "The Lord Ananta is united with the space at the end of the *nāda*; when the *nāda* has ceased, he who becomes manifest by himself."
That supreme light is Brahman, known by the names Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus has been described to you this supreme, personal abode of Viṣṇu;
now listen to the true nature of its peaceful form.
Having first taken up the emission, one should join it with the sun at the end;
when the supreme proximity has arisen, that is the great light uttered as "Om."

13. *Visṛṣṭi* is emission. The Sun is the syllable *aṃ*. When *aḥ* + *aṃ* occurs, by the rule *ato roḥ*, the *u*-vowel substitution (*utva*), the *guṇa* strengthening, and the *pūrvarūpa* coalescence, it becomes *oṃ*. This is that supreme abode, characterized by the withdrawal of power (*śakti*).
That which, when being remembered, certainly reveals the supreme reality.
14. Because it consists of the union of the *visarga* and the *bindu*, its meaning is that it is characterized by emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Having withdrawn the entire collection arising from the pure and impure paths... (p. 81)
The power intent upon creation resides in the eternal Sun, the Puruṣa. || 15 ||

15. In the Sun, which is masculine and of the nature of the *bindu*, she—having performed the process of reabsorption into that supreme subject—emerges from that gross state consisting of fire and moon. 16.
The Śakti, eternally resting upon the middle couple consisting of Bindu and Nāda,
rests upon the divine, tranquil, and subtle couple;
she is established in the divine, all-pervading Supreme Self.
Its measure has been declared by those who know the ritual rules to be three and a half [mātrās]. || 18 ||
There are three sacrificial fires, three worlds, three Vedas,
three qualities (guṇas), three deities, three manifestations (vyūhas), three social classes (varṇas), and three vowels. || 19 ||
O Śakra, whatever triad exists within the world, that should be known as the primordial triad; the half-measure (ardhamātrā) is stainless (nirañjana).
20. "The first triad" means the triad beginning with the letter *a*. The half-mora is the *bindu*. All sounds arise from *a*; from *u* comes the triad of fires;
O Purandara, everything from earth up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*) arises from *m*. 21.

21. The triad of splendors consists of the forms of the sun, the moon, and fire. That half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is composed of light; it is the supreme digit (*kalā*) consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī*).
[It is formed] by the vowels together with the *bindu*, belonging to the two groups of six vowels at the beginning and the end. 22.

22. The supreme digit is *nāda*. The first group of six vowels consists of those beginning with *a* and ending with *ū*; the final group of six vowels consists of those beginning with *ḷ* and ending with *au*.

Among these, the even vowels are *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ḹ*, *ai*, and *au*. With these, together with the nasal bindu (*m*), one performs the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*). The ritual placement of the subsidiary limbs (*upāṅganyāsa*), however, is performed with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth, accompanied by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
The arrangement of his limbs, however, is defined by the six qualities beginning with knowledge (jñāna) and ending with dispassion (vairāgya);
[these are placed] at the navel, the back, as well as the two arms, the two thighs, the two knees, and the feet.
O Pākaśāsana, one should further place the qualities preceded by the syllable *tāra*;
having thus placed that mantra together with its limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*).
The Guru should meditate upon Puruṣottama residing within his own self;
listen to me as I explain correctly how this occurs, preceded by the dissolution of the universe and its elements. (25)
The universe, which is the locus of the waking state, the impeller of all the senses, and the enjoyer of the five objects of sense beginning with sound—[is this]. (26)
26. "Viśva" refers to the names of the self abiding in the waking state. One should contemplate that [self], which consists of Aniruddha, as the first syllable.
Having dissolved that god, together with his implements, into the letter A; || 27 ||

27. Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Lakṣmī, and Nārāyaṇa are the deities presiding over the states of waking and so forth, designated as Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turya, and Turyātīta. One should place the letter *A* within the deity Taijasa, Pradyumna, who abides in the state of dreaming.
One should dissolve [the mind] into that which impels the functions of the internal organ.
One should dissolve that [universe], along with its implements, into the god Ukāra;
and Ukāra into Īśvara, who resides in the body of Saṃkarṣaṇa as Prājña.

Having dissolved that Lord of Gods— who is eternally situated in the state of deep sleep, the pervasive impeller of the vital breaths and so forth— into the half-measure established in the fourth state (turya).
One should dissolve [the mind] into the god Vāsudeva, who consists of knowledge and bliss;
and that fourth state (turya) into the one beyond the fourth (turyātīta), whose self is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having dissolved his own divine Vaiṣṇava ego, he should take refuge in that [state];
becoming absorbed in that, he then gradually attains such a place of dissolution.
32. Consisting of that, consisting of the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā)—having descended from the waking state and having placed the initiated disciple before him—(p. 82). [Note: ā, c read "uditaṃ"].
The true guru, having become one with the Self (manmaya), should himself teach the Tāra-mantra.
33. He speaks of the contemplation on descending from the place of dissolution to the place of emanation—beginning with "jāgarām":
[The teacher] should constantly and in detail explain the sequence including the limbs and sub-limbs, along with the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
And he should give his own self as a fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru, together with wealth. 34.
Having then obtained permission, performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa),
he should go to the bank of a great river or to a sanctuary of the Siddhas and others.

35. Regarding that which is called *puraścaraṇa*: "The attainment of greater potency for a mantra received from a guru, consisting of japa, homa, tarpaṇa, abhiṣeka, and the feeding of Brahmins—this fivefold worship is called *puraścaraṇa* in the world. Thus it is said.
Or else, having thoroughly cleared a forest of *pālāśa* trees until the ground is visible on all sides,
he should bathe three times a day, remaining celibate and with his senses subdued. (36)
Eating any one of these— milk, barley-gruel, or alms-food— only once a day,
he sat upon a heap of *kuśa* grass, clothed in *kāśa* grass and *kuśa* lotuses.
Clad in a black antelope skin, he should carry a staff made of *pālāśa* wood;
with his mind fixed on me and becoming absorbed in me, he should proceed by the path instructed by the guru.
Constantly devoted to yoga,
possessing right knowledge and meditative absorption,
one should remain silent and recite the Tāra mantra ten hundred thousand times, for it delivers one from the cycle of existence.
One should offer oblations ten times [the number of recitations] with leaves, fuel-sticks, or even clarified butter;
thus pleased, my supreme Vaiṣṇava egoity shall manifest itself to him. (40)
40. "A tenth part" means one hundred thousand times.
Then, for the practitioner whose mind is perfectly endowed with right discernment, that state of aesthetic identity known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa shines forth. 41.
Even while living, he becomes liberated and purifies the world with his very glance;
all mantras, whether worldly or Vedic, become perfected for him.
He becomes one who has bathed in all the Vedas, in all branches of knowledge,
in all established doctrines, and in all sacred fords.
Whatever applications there are for all mantras, however many and of whatever kind they may be—it is the settled conclusion that his applications are of that same extent and of that same nature. (44)
Its three *vyāhṛtis* have arisen from the three social classes (*varṇa*), and from its feet has arisen the *Sāvitrī*, the purifier of all. (45)
From her feet emerged the three Vedas, characterized as Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman;
indeed, all worldly and Vedic speech consists of these alone. (46)
Just as a great tree is contained within the seed of a banyan, so too this entire universe consisting of speech is always situated within this [Self]. 47.
47. An illustration is given regarding how *tāra* (the sacred syllable Om) is the embodiment of all speech—beginning with the word "just as" (*yathā*).

*Dhānā* refers to a minute seed. Here, the statement that the great tree exists in a subtle state within the seed is made in accordance with the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). However, according to the Upaniṣadic view, [the relationship is] between the seed and the great tree.

The distinction [between the two views] is that the former maintains the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) because the substrate and the appropriation are one, while the latter maintains the conventional designation of cause and effect due to the difference in states.
This first [view] is the great seed, the supreme source of all words.
The Brahman of Sound is the supreme abode, the most sacred and the greatest.
He is Oṃkāra, Praṇava, Tāra, Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa, and Dhruva;
he is the soul of the Vedas, the source of all Vedas, Āditya, and the purifier of all. || 49 ||
The giver of liberation, the path to liberation, and capable of sustaining all—
such are the names [of this supreme support] found by the wise in every scripture. (50)
The great merits of the high-souled Oṃkāra have been recited [or:
proclaimed]. This is the refuge for the ignorant, and this alone is for those who possess knowledge. (51)
This [mantra], consisting of the conjunction of the letters *ha* and *au*, is known as the *Prāsāda*; it is a boat for those seeking heaven and for those desiring to cross to the further shore. (52)
This is the *piṇḍa* of all principles (*tattvas*), the eternal one who has become the very essence;
it consists of the means of attainment (*sādhana*), the practice (*pratipatti*), the application (*viniyoga*), and the retention (*dhāraṇā*).
O Lord of the Suras, know that this [mantra] is like the seed of this very temple;
this great mantra named Haṃsa is the name-mantra (saṃjñāmantra) of this very [temple]. 54.
Know the enjoyer to be the first letter and the object of enjoyment to be the second; the former consists of Nārāyaṇa, while the latter consists of Śrī. 55.
55. "The first letter" means the letter *ha*. "The second" means the letter *sa*. Know these two letters to be the eternal essence of Agni and Soma.
Between them, O Śakra, the nature of the *bindu* is established. 56.
56. The emission and withdrawal are the phenomena of the *bindu*. One should lead the phoneme of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) from the base up to the crown of the head.
One should emit from the mouth the second phoneme, which is designated as the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). 57.
57. Beginning from the location of the support (the base of the spine) and proceeding with the wind that reaches as far as the crown of the head, one should utter the syllable *ha*;
one should emit the syllable *sa* through the mouth. By means of this application of the utterance of *haṃsa*, the entire creation is accomplished.
This Vidyā, beautiful in all its parts, is declared to be the Ajapeya. || 58 ||
58. This mantra of the Haṃsa is known by the name Ajapā-mantra.
Within the eighty-four million and four hundred thousand species of birth, as well as in their various divisions, this mantra constantly recites itself. 59. [This is the continuation of verse 58.]
Along with the exhalation, the innerly radiant Vidyā arises;
the states of rising and setting are equal to inhalation and exhalation.
Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* are considered one *nāḍikā*.
Sixty *nāḍikās* make up a day and night; such is the movement of the process of time.
O Lord of Gods, according to this rule, when twenty-one thousand and six hundred sunrises have occurred, that many recitations shall have been performed.

62. The meaning is that when the *haṃsa* mantra is recited once, it becomes as if twenty-one thousand six hundred recitations have been performed; however, at the beginning of the day and so forth, one should form a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the intention:
"I shall perform this many recitations."
The intelligent one. || 63 ||
63. "Of such a number" means having this many counts. One should place the five limbs; learn their form from me:
Sūrya and Soma, ending in the dative case, joined with *namaḥ* and *svāhā*. 64.
64–65. The Sun and Moon are the letters *ha* and *sa*.
They are stainless (*nirañjana*) and without appearance (*nirābhāsa*), ending with *vauṣaṭ* and *huṃ phaṭ*.
The root mantra itself, ending with *phaṭ*, is the weapon (*astra*); these are its five limbs (*aṅga*).
This very same mantra of the supreme self is known as inverted;
having remembered the Śakti together with her equipment, one should unite her with the Sun, the enjoyer.

66. Regarding the term "inverted" (*viparyasta*): the meaning is that the mantra is *so'ham*. The sense is that one should take the letter *sa*, which represents *śakti*, and join it with the letter *ha*, which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The remaining portion is to be contemplated as being like the *praṇava*; such is the rule for the *saṃjñā-mantra*.
In the Pāñcarātrika ritual procedure, he should have three [types of] mantras: the foot-mantra, the principal mantra, and the weapon-mantra.
67. Regarding the phrase "three": although four mantras will be mentioned, nevertheless, by taking a certain distinction among them, a separate designation of three is made:
"Salutation to Viṣṇu" and likewise "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa."
Homage to the Blessed One, and likewise to Vāsudeva of the past.

68. He states the essential forms of the mantras, beginning with "To Viṣṇu" and so forth. At the beginning is "Obeisance to the Blessed One" (*namo bhagavate*), and at the end is "to Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāya*). The meaning is that the mantra is "Obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva" (*namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*).
Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One. (69)
This fourth is the *padamantra*, the destroyer of cities (*puraṃdara*) of the *praṇava*; it is proclaimed as such.
Those who know the ancient tradition recognize these mantras as being accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*. (70)

The arrangement of the limbs (aṅga) should be performed with syllables such as the Praṇava, which are endowed with qualities like knowledge and end with "namas"; likewise, the arrangement of the subsidiary limbs (upāṅga) should be done in the same manner.
For a mantra that has fewer syllables, the arrangement of the subsidiary limbs (upāṅgas) should be performed by means of its final syllable, joined with words expressing their respective qualities.
Regarding the phrase "of a mantra with fewer syllables": this refers to the deficiency in syllables found in mantras of six or eight syllables. In that case—

The meaning is that the completion should be performed with the final syllable. In the same way, one should fashion the final subsidiary limb (upāṅga) together with the "Tejas" [syllable], using all the remaining twelve additional expanded phonemes.
73. Regarding "sphītavarṇasya": the meaning is "of that which has an additional syllable," as in the mantra *jitaṃ te*.
Furthermore: "The solitary Tāraka and the four beginning with that (Tadādi)—these five are proclaimed in the Pāñcarātra as the all-pervading mantras. 74.
There is nothing here that cannot be accomplished by these mantras of the Great-Souled Ones;
this five-stepped ladder is for ascending to the Supreme Brahman. (75)
This divine Great Being is indeed the fifth mantra, consisting of the nature of Man (Manmaya).
By properly taking refuge in her through worship, recitation, meditation, and so forth,
one attains one's own Vaiṣṇava essence and reaches the Supreme Brahman.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Savior" (*tāraprakāśa*), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (24, p.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter. Śrī said:
"O Śakra, thus has this detailed account of Tāraka been told to you."
Listen to the sequence of my Tārikā, who delivers one across the ocean of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
First, learn the technical designations for the sake of accomplishing the ritual rules of the phonemes;
for when these have been heard according to rule, the ritual application of the mantras follows.
it proceeds. || 2 ||
The letter A is immeasurable and is remembered as the first all-pervading one;
likewise, the letter Ā is the primordial deity, bliss, and is remembered as the protector. || 3 ||
The letter *i*, known as Rāma, is proclaimed as kindled (*iddha*) and desired (*iṣṭa*);
the letter *ī* is indeed Pañcabindu, Viṣṇu, Māyā, and Purandara. || 4 ||
The letter *u* is called Bhuvana, as well as Uddama and Udaya;
the letter *ū* is the Lord of the World in the realm of *ūrj*, and is indeed named Prajñādhārā. (5)
Satya and Ṛtadhāmā are the syllable Ṛ, which is indeed the goad (aṅkuśa);
the syllable Ṛ is called Viṣṭara, and it is also the flame and the expansion.
The Lord is declared to be the self of the *liṅga*, and the syllable *ḷ* is remembered as the Savior (*tāraka*).
The syllable *ḷ* is Dīrghaghoṇa, as well as Devadatta, Sthira,
and Virāṭ.
The triangle is known as Eka (the One), the source of the world, and formless;
it is sovereignty, the creator of yoga, and the giver—Ai, Sa, and Airāvaṇa are thus remembered. || 8 ||
Okāra is Otadeha (or Deva), Odana, and Vikramī; Aurva, Bhūdhara, and Au are remembered as being of the nature of medicinal herbs.
The pervasive Aṃkāra is the bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds and the Lord of Space;
the Visarga is known as the creator of emanation, while the syllable Hyakāra is the Supreme Lord.
Kamala and Karāla are the letter Ka, the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti);
Khakāra is Kharvadeha, the soul of the Vedas, the creator of the universe. || 11 ||
The letter *ga* is the destroyer of disease (*gadadhvaṃsī*), Govinda, and the wielder of the mace (*gadādhara*).
The letter *gha*, moreover, is the sun (*gharmāṃśu*), as well as the radiant and luminous one.
The letter *ṅa* is known as Ekadaṃṣṭra, the soul of beings and the creator of beings; the letter *ca* is Cañcala and Cakī, and he is said to be like a ray of the moon.
Chandaḥpati, the destroyer of deceit (or strength), the letter *cha*, and indeed Chanda himself;
Janmahantṛ, the unconquered, and the eternal letter *ja*. || 14 ||
The letter Jha is known as Jhaṣa; he is a singer of the Sāmans and a reciter of the Sāman hymns.
The letter Ña is called Īśvara and Uttama, and he is the upholder of the principles (tattvas).
The letter *ṭa* is Candra, the delight that nourishes the universe;
the letter *ṭha* is Dhārādharas, and Nemi is called Kaustubha. (16)
Daṇḍadhāra, Ḍakāra, Mausala, Akhaṇḍavikrama, Ḍhakāra, Viśvarūpa, Vṛṣakarmā, and Pratardana. (17)
The letter *ṇa* is the teacher who bestows fearlessness, celebrated as Vaikuṇṭha.
The letter *ta* is marked by the *tāla* rhythm, and is Vairāja, the wearer of garlands (*sragdhara*).
Thus it is remembered. || 18 ||
The letter *tha* is the archer Bhuvanapāla and the restrainer of all;
the letter *da* is known as Datta-avakāśa, Damana, and the bestower of peace.
The letter *dha* is proclaimed as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Sustainer, and Mādhava;
the letter *na* is declared to be Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the Path. || 20 ||
The letter *pa* is Padmanābha, the pure one whose seat is in the west;
the letter *pha* is Phullanayana, the wielder of the plow, known as Śveta.
[Named thus] || 21 ||
The letter *va* is Vāmana; he is described as short yet possessing complete limbs.
The letter *bha* is known as Bhallātaka, which certainly bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The syllable *ma* is proclaimed as the crusher, time, and the primary principle;
the syllable *ya*, which consists of the four states of existence, is called the subtle conch. (23)
The letter *ra* is the support of all worlds without exception, the fire that is the conflagration of time;
the letter *la* is known as Vibudha, the Lord of the Earth, and the Sovereign of Puruṣa. (24)
The syllable *va* is known as Varāha, the support of nectar; the syllable *va* is remembered as Varuṇa; the syllable *śa* is proclaimed to be Śaṅkara, the peaceful Puṇḍarīka.
The letter *ṣa* is Nṛsiṃha, the form of fire,
and likewise the Sun;
the letter *sa* is proclaimed to be the nectar of immortality, satisfaction, and the Moon.
The letter *ha* is the sun and is proclaimed to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The letter *kṣa* is Ananteśa; it is the end of the classes of consonants and is likewise remembered as Garuḍa. (27)
These names of all the letters have been proclaimed by me;
indeed, they are to be described again according to the forward and reverse order of the letters.

28. This means that it is in accordance with the order of the names (*saṃjñā*) and in reverse order of the numbers (*saṃkhyā*). It is well known that the movement of digits is from left to right. O Śakra, that which is common to both the names and the numbers—
O Mahāmati, all these phonemes are indeed portions of consciousness, possessing radiant forms. || 29 ||
They are the cause of all mantras, augmented by the power of Lakṣmī;
these phonemes (varṇas), praised, fully worshipped, and meditated upon with devotion according to their designations, [are so called] by means of their names. 30.
They bestow supreme prosperity and cultivate higher knowledge;
furthermore, they enter into a state of mutual subordination within the arising of the mantra.
In this world of moving and unmoving beings, there is nothing that has not been permeated by these [deities];
for although those divine forms of the mantras are supreme and eternal. (32)
Nevertheless, through such meditations on these syllables, mantras become fully empowered according to the teachings of the scriptures. (33)
In this way, O Mahāmati, objects of perception indeed come to exist for cognitions; even though space is partless, a portion is conceptually constructed by the mind.
For the sake of ease, a portion of the letters within the mantra is thus meditated upon;
having performed the pervasive absorption (vyāpti) of the letters into the states of being, the worship of the letters is performed in three ways.
One should extract the mantras from the earth, from the lotus, and likewise from the body of the Goddess;
having taken up the Supreme Self, one should join it with the fire of time.
36. He extracts the *tārikā* mantra: "The Supreme Self," and so forth. The Supreme Self is the letter *ha*.
The Fire of Time is the letter *ra*. Māyā is the letter *ī*. The Bestower of Sovereignty over the Three Worlds is the *anusvāra*. Through the conjunction of these, *hrīṃ* is the *tārikā* mantra.
One should employ this Māyā, endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds, in this [rite];
for she is that supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti who grants all desires. (37)
Existence is full, consisting of consciousness and bliss; it is my uninterrupted form.
This is that supreme goal, which is eternal for those who know Brahman. 38.
Having reached this certainty, those who know reality enter into the Brahman that consists of me;
this very [truth] is contemplated in every scripture by the foremost among the knowers of reality. (39)

This world, which constitutes the very meaning of the word "universe," is indeed woven warp and woof within me; by means of this very [power], I, the eternal one, am always reckoned by the Sāṃkhyas. (40)
By this very [state] I am concentrated by those established in concentration through that concentration;
by this very [state] I am designated as the final of the thirty-six [principles] by the followers of Śiva. (41)
In the same way, I am the Great Queen; by this very [truth], I am the supreme Triad within the collection of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and within the solar mandala that is to be meditated upon.
The experts in Lokāyata philosophy determine that a young woman, endowed with beauty and lovely in all her limbs, is the very essence of this world.
To those who know the doctrine of momentary flux, the intellect is considered objectless;
and by this very name, I am always proclaimed as Yakṣī by the Ārhata followers.
I am the supreme power that delivers, the savior, appearing in the form of a savior.
Lakṣmī, Padmā, Mahālakṣmī, Tārā, Gaurī, and Nirañjanā. || 45 ||
Hṛllekhā, who resides in the Supreme Self, is the power Bhuvaneśvarī;
she is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the form of peace (śāntirūpā), the resonant one (ghoṣaṇī), and born from resonance (ghoṣasaṃbhavā). || 46 ||
"Kāmadhenu, Mahādhenū, Jagadyoni, Vibhāvarī"—such names as these have been declared by the learned in various scriptures. (47)
The etymologies of *tārikā* have been explained by scholars in each Veda;
however, *anutārikā* should be understood as another form of this very [goddess]. (48)
One should establish Śānti in the place of the former Supreme Self; the rest is the same. For this is my other body, which leads others across.
49. The letter *śa* is silent; "the rest is the same" means it is the same as the *tārikā*. The meaning is that *rīṃ* should be joined [to it].
*Śrīṃ* is the *anutārikā* mantra.
One should understand that its great majesty is to be known just like that of the *tārikā*.
O Purandara, these two supreme, divine powers are my own bodies.
Whatever is to be accomplished by this one must be accomplished by the other;
these two proceed in a sequence of prior and subsequent through their mutual desire.
And it fulfills the desired object of the practitioners who practice correctly. || 51 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Tārā and Anutārā," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Variants: *Śrīpañcarātra*; *Śrīpāñcarātre*; *Tārakānutāraprakāśaḥ*). Chapter 25.
(p. 88) Chapter Twenty-Six. Śakra:
O Supreme Brahman, O Supreme Abode, O Thou who dwellest in the lotus, O Wearer of the Lotus Garland!
Salutations to You, O Lotus-born One, O Padmā, O Consort of Govinda. || 1 ||
"O Goddess Śrī, these two eternal bodies of yours have been described; is there any distinction between them in their subtle form?"
In the beginning, there was one supreme reality consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa,
in whom the six divine attributes were perfectly quiescent, and who was a mass of pure, autonomous consciousness.
I am His supreme power, following Him in all states; that Goddess is the supreme, divine I-consciousness, known by the names gross, subtle, and transcendent.
O Purandara, these two powers of mine, Tārikā and Anutārikā, together fulfill all desires.
Both these divine doctrines are considered supreme and ultimate;
both are regarded as the final resting places, and both are dear to Viṣṇu.
Having reflected upon both of these, people then attain the highest goal.
But listen as I declare to you that supreme and most subtle reality.
The sequence is as follows: from that comes the Supreme Brahman, then the Tranquil, and then the Sound (nāda).
Pervading all things, I am she who exists in the form of both closing and opening the eyes.
The first is that supreme Brahman, subtle and possessing latent power;
having established itself there, the Tāra extends its vast course.
This unfolding of the Supreme Self, the Lord Brahmā,
which consists of the states of "being" (bhava) and "becoming" (bhāva), is that upon which Tārikā is firmly established.
The descent of Brahmā, which takes a peaceful form due to his desire to create, rests upon that [power] called Śānti, which abounds in the state of being (bhāva). || 11 ||
But the second is the descent, which is the powerful state called Śakti;
O Vāsava, the seed-syllables beginning with Vāgbhava reside therein.
This much of the distinction between these two has been declared to you by me, who am possessed of subtle intelligence;
now listen as I speak of the seed-syllables beginning with Vāgbhava.
One should extract the syllable *ai* (aiśvarya), which is endowed with the sovereignty over the three worlds;
this seed-syllable, known as Vāgbhava, is declared to be the source of the universe. (14)
14. He states the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbhava-bīja*) with the words beginning "trailokya" and so forth. *Aiśvarya* is the syllable *ai*.
When this is joined with the nasal bindu (*anusvāra*), the seed-mantra is *aiṃ*. Its nature as the womb of the universe will be explained immediately hereafter.
This is that very Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, within whom the universe is coiled (*kuṇḍalita*).
Understand that [knowledge] according to its nature as the power of sound. || 15 ||
15. The etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*) of the word *kuṇḍalinī* intended here is: "in whom the world is coiled" (*kuṇḍalitaṃ jagat*).
16. She is *Ī*, Māyā, the supreme power, the womb of the world, and the stainless one.
For she is the Fortune (*Śrī*) of the immeasurable, the housewife of the householder.

16–18. He explains that the vowel *ai* consists of a combination of four phonemes: "ī is Māyā. The sense is that by joining the phoneme *i*, called *Iṣṭā*, which precedes it; then the phoneme *ā*, called *Ānanda*, which precedes that;
and then the phoneme *a*, called *Aprameya*, which precedes that—once the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) is performed, the form *ai* arises.
One should first join the vowel *i* to this [syllable] with a subtle eye;
in this way, whatever is desired, whatever substance, and whatever [is sought],
that is established therein.
First, one should contemplate his bliss with the subtle eye;
then, one should first join the immeasurable with the subtle eye (or: with the subtle vision).
This power is the womb of the universe, radiant with the sovereignty over the three worlds;
it arises from the Supreme Self, which is immeasurable, without beginning or end, and all-pervading. (19)
Gopanī is the power that conceals all beings, filled with bliss,
and endowed with the forms of will, knowledge, and action arising from the syllable *I*.

"The Goddess who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds, the consort of Viṣṇu, the mother of the universe"—thus she should be addressed; one should meditate upon her as the lotus-born source of the seed of the world. (21)
In the world, *rati* is designated as play (*krīḍā*), and for me, play is action (*kriyā*).
Fuel, illumination, knowledge, and desire are indicated by the letter *i*.
[This has been] shown. || 22 ||

22–24. He explains the meaning of the long *ī* (īkāra), which constitutes the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), with the words "Rati" and so forth. *Rati* is the letter *ī*. Fuel and the like are its meanings. He etymologizes "bestower of sovereignty over the three worlds" (*trailokyaiśvaryadā*) with the words "the three worlds" (*trailokya*).
"Living beings are threefold" means bound, liberated, and eternal. "In the Lord of Space" (*vyomeśe*) refers to the *bindu*.
The three worlds are indeed the *triloka*; they consist of living beings who exist in a threefold manner. By bestowing sovereignty upon them, she is called *Trailokyaiśvaryadāmbikā*.
Having expanded the worlds through the path of the universe by means of the immeasurable and so forth,
[he dissolves them] once again into that very supreme Ātman, the Lord of Space.
Thus, my rising and setting are established as being beyond [the world].
Such is this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the source of the universe and the progenitor of all speech. (25)
The fifth is Kāmasū, also known as Kāmabījā; she is Prādyumnī, the supreme Śakti. Learn from me her form. (26)
That which is declared to be the western face among the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva) is the Madhyama;
it is the "colorer" (rañjana), colored by a slight experience of both sattva and tamas.
That supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), known as Kā, ordaining the arrangement of the world,
prepares itself for creation through its union with the Lord of Puruṣa.

28–29. Taking the letter *ka* as *prakṛti*, one should join with it the letter *la* as the Lord Puruṣa, the letter *i* as Māyā, and the Bindu as Vyomeśa. Thus arises *klīṃ*, the seed-syllable of Kāma, which manifests the three forms known as the Unmanifest, Puruṣa, and Īśa.
That goddess Māyā Śrī, moreover, is established in Vyomeśa. || 29 ||
Thus have I shown you the power and influence of form as the seed of desire; now listen to me as I declare the sixth vidyā, that of Sarasvatī. (30)

30–34. He states the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Sarasvatī with the words beginning "the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhīm*). The support of wisdom (*prajñādhāra*) is the letter *ū*. Prior to that is the letter *u*, which is the arising (*udaya*). Prior to that is the letter *ā*, which is bliss (*ānanda*). Prior to that is the letter *a*, which is the immeasurable (*aprameya*).
At the end is the Lord of Space (*vyomeśa*), the bindu; followed again by the visarga. Through the conjunction of these, *auḥ* is produced.
He states the meaning of the individual words, beginning with "arisen from the immeasurable" (*aprameyodita*):
"O Śakra, I am indeed the support of wisdom (*prajñā*), the birthplace of supreme knowledge;
as such, I am the mother of wisdom, endowed with the arising of Viṣṇu. (31)
One should join Ānanda before her with a subtle gaze;
first, one should meditate upon the Immeasurable (Aprameya) with a subtle gaze.
I am that immeasurably arisen one, auspicious and consisting of great bliss; I am the foundation of wisdom, established once more within the Mistress of Space (Vyomeśī).
(90) Furthermore, the sixth Vidyā, which had returned to the Supreme Lord for the sake of re-emergence, has been extracted by you both in its verbal form and in its meaning. 34.
This triad of seed-syllables is declared to be the Vidyā named Tripurā;
for through both reverse and direct order, she bestows identity with the Self.
And also from the detailed [account]. || 35 ||
This knowledge is declared to be the granter of all desires when accomplished through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites;
through the combination of consonants and vowels, they know its many divisions (or, as some read, its many parts). || 36 ||
Having analyzed and synthesized the causes of the four aims of human life,
this seventh [Vidyā] is Mahālakṣmī, the knowledge that accomplishes everything.
Having taken up the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), one should join it there with the sun;
having joined it through churning, one should then unite it with the fire of time (kālavahni).

38–39. He explains the extraction of the seed-syllable of Mahālakṣmī with the words beginning "parām" and so forth. Taking the *prakṛti*, which is the letter *ka*; by means of that, one should join the *bhāskara*, which is the letter *ṣa*; the *mardana*, which is the letter *ma*; the *kālavahni*, which is the letter *ra*; the *māyā*, which is the letter *ī*; and the *vyāpin*, which is the *bindu*. Thus, the mantra is *kṣmrīṃ*. And so it is said:

In the *Tantrarāja*: "The mantra of Kaulinī consists of the 'devourer' (grāsa), space (nabhas), the fire of burning (dāhavahni), and one's own (sva). In this context, the 'devourer' is the syllable *kṣa*, 'space' is the syllable *ma*, the 'fire of burning' is the letter *r*, and 'one's own' refers to the vowel *ī* and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
One should adorn the cluster (*piṇḍa*) with *māyā* (the letter *h*), and at the end, one should bring in the Pervasive One (*vyāpin*).
O Purandara, this seed-syllable of Mahālakṣmī has been declared to you.
For, by my own splendor, I draw forth the state of manifestation,
having entered the primary stage as the one who manifests the three forms.
"Having emanated every state of existence, she is firmly established in the Lord of Space (Vyomeśa);
thus should this seed-syllable be meditated upon by the practitioner while reciting it. (41)
Thus these rays are to be known as belonging to the Vidyā whose form is Tārikā;
that [group] beginning with Anuttārā is the Vidyā, and this [entirety] consists of Tārikā. (42)
One who worships this Tārikā vidyā according to the prescribed rule attains inexhaustible enjoyments in this world and the next, as well as the [higher] worlds. || 43 ||
43. The seven Vidyās: Tāra, Tārikā, Anutārikā, Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, Sārasvatabīja, and Mahālakṣmībīja. Thus ends [the section on] the Śrīpāñcarātrasāra [A: Śrīpañcarātra; B, F: Śrīpāñcarātre].
The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Seven Vidyās," in the Lakṣmītantra. || 26 ||
91) Chapter Twenty-Seven. Śakra:
Salutations to you, O Mistress of the World, beloved of the Lotus-eyed One;
O Sovereign of the entire universe, omniscient, and the source of all that exists.
I have correctly heard this supreme reality of the sciences;
furthermore, you should explain to me the ritual procedure for the Tārikā.
Śrī said: The primordial, singular, supreme Brahman, omniscient and consisting of existence-consciousness-bliss,
is the divine Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, manifested through His own power.
The Great One. || 3 ||
I am that supreme power called Ahaṃtā, eternal;
possessing its attributes, I am constant and stainless like the radiance of the sun.
O son of Āditi, those five functions are always performed by me alone,
who am of the nature of His very unfolding.
My supreme divine power is eternally possessed of my own nature;
she is Hṛllekhā, the supreme Vidyā, whose very form is mine.
O Purandara!
6. *Hṛllekhā* is the mantra *hrīṃ*, which is another name for the *tārikā* specified in the twenty-fifth chapter;
its nature will be described immediately hereafter.
