One should constantly contemplate this explanation with a mind that is fully attentive.
Full of faith, having sought refuge and approached me, accept this from me.
They declare that Self to be the supreme cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of all that moves and is stationary, known by the name of the Sun.
Know that the first syllable, the letter *ha*, is the eternal, primordial Puruṣottama, who is the constant impeller known as Prāṇa. || 9 ||
His first unfolding, which embraces the three worlds, is the support of all realms; it is of blazing form, immeasurable, and distinct from anything else.
Know that the letter *repha* (ra) to be beyond that, eternal and of the nature of splendor;
it is indeed the full unfolding (*unmeṣa*) which pervades every state of existence. || 11 ||
He sustains five functions characterized by creation and so forth,
and he consists of wondrous knowledge through the continuous succession of the closing and opening of his eyes.
Bearing the forms of will, knowledge, and action, and transcending the expansion of time through its sequence, this is the eternal state of the pair whose forms are *i* and *ī*.
Thus, I am that very Supreme Expansion (paramonmeṣa), whose nature is "I," whose arising is all-pervasive,
and who, in the form of will, knowledge, and action, performs the fivefold cosmic function of the All-pervasive Lord.
Consisting of various wonders, dense with consciousness, and of the nature of bliss, she is to be known as abiding in the Supreme Self, all-pervading, and the beloved of Viṣṇu. 15.
Having performed her entire duty, she who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds [merged] once again into that very god, Vyomeśa, the Supreme Self.
Having taken up all the requisites, I abide as the partless one.
Those who know the reality declare that her forms here consist of five. (17)
O Lord of Gods, listen as I describe those forms;
this single form which is proclaimed extends as far as Vyomeśa. (18)
18. "Up to Vyomeśa" means up to the point of the Bindu (the nasal drop). Regarding this, some desire the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) to be beyond Vyomeśa;
others, however, having set aside Vyomeśa, apply the Pradhāna [therein]. 19.
19. The Supreme Lord is the Visarga; the letter *ma* is the Pradhāna. They desire the Bindu and Nāda at its end, which is like the Praṇava.

At the very end, some wise ones declare that there is only the Pradhāna alone. 20. [This verse is part of the preceding continuity. (Note: Verse 20 as provided in the source text appears to be a continuation of the thought in verse 19 regarding the sequence of phonemes and their philosophical correspondences.)
In the end, other Vedic scholars study [her] as the creator of the universe;
thus the wise know the five forms of Tārikā. (21)
21. Visarga is the creator of emanation. O Sureśāna, such are the forms of Śāntisthā as well;
likewise [they exist] at the end of Pradhāna, at the end of Visṛṣṭi, and similarly at the end of Vyomeśa. 22.

22. He states the gradation of the fruits of these mantras with the words beginning "at the end of Pradhāna" and so forth. Within the fourfold form ending with the upward emission of Vyomeśa, there is the supreme accomplishment pertaining to this world, as well as that which pertains to each respective other world.
The other. || 23 ||
At the end of the primary *bindu* and *nāda*, there is only the glory of liberation (*mokṣaśrī*).
Having thus contemplated the supreme state of the *Tārikā*, [one attains it]. (24)
The teacher should impart the knowledge whose nature is the Supreme Brahman to a disciple of virtuous conduct who seeks the welfare of his guru and the Supreme Brahman.
Having first performed the placement of the hands and limbs upon oneself,
and then having placed them upon the body of the disciple, one should then instruct him in the mantra.
One should first place the supreme mantra within the heart of the disciple with devotion;
then, one should again place that most excellent mantra within one's own heart.
A wise disciple, having received the Vidyā from the Ācārya, should perform all of this preceded by initiation and consecration. (28)
Having given oneself, one's own wealth, or a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—whether it be the whole, half, or a portion—by which the teacher is satisfied. (29)
And while Vedic and worldly customs are firmly established,
one should never be negligent toward good conduct, teachers, elders, and Brahmins.
Constantly practicing non-malice toward the fourfold collection of living beings, always endowed with his own virtues, he is a follower of the characteristics of Dharma. || 31 ||
Refined by pure purificatory rites, he performed the rituals for the gods, the ancestors, and guests;
he studied the divine scriptures as well as the Vedic collections.
With a mind free from greed, moving through the various philosophical systems and taking from here and there only as much knowledge as is necessary for his purpose, (33)

Without finding fault with the scriptures, proceeding in accordance with the means of valid knowledge, and performing his daily rites according to rule, he realized the meaning of the scriptures through the sequence of his actions. (34)
Day and night, beginning with the day and ending with the night, he should constantly make them fruitful by performing the sequences of actions as they have been enjoined. (35)
Constantly devoted to the five times (pañcakāla), dedicated to the five sacrifices (pañcayajña), he was adorned with self-restraint and charity, as well as truthfulness and non-violence.
Having diligently accomplished this vidyā according to the prescribed sequence, one should remain endowed with a serene mind, ever devoted to one's own welfare and that of others. (37)
Desiring only supreme prosperity, one should avoid misfortune;
one should purify all beings with mind, eye, and speech. (38)
Cultivating the four goddesses who clarify the mind— loving-kindness and the others— one who seeks peace should be devoted to the sacrifice of recitation. (39)
Remaining vigilant while engaged in his own duties, even if negligence occurs through fate,
he should perform the appropriate expiation correctly for whatever act was committed by deed, mind, or speech, [worshipping] Janārdana, the God of gods.
He has constantly taken refuge in me and in her who possesses that dharma. || 41 ||
Having beheld an excellent man and a woman, one should constantly remember me; one should always honor a married couple and never cause a breach in the bond of matrimony.
Whether residing in sound or manifesting as meaning, know that the various forms of masculinity and femininity are of that same nature; remember Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. (43)
Having seen me— excellent, endowed with virtues, and graced with beauty and youth— with a mind free from desire, he thought only of me.
44. "Without longing" means being free from excessive attachment. Always patient-minded toward women, never speaking what is unpleasant, and avoiding any transgression that has arisen—always.
And they did not deliberate [or, according to manuscript B: they did not proclaim]. || 45 ||
45. Transgression is negligence.

While washing away the offense being committed against women by means of purifying rites, [one must avoid it even] toward a hunchbacked woman, or one who is deformed, or a woman in any state whatsoever. 46.
46. "By purifying acts" means by rites of purification. "Transgression" refers to negligence.
"One who moves about without censuring women, doing what is pleasing [to them] in accordance with the scriptures—a man of such conduct, following the path of the virtuous, is freed from sin. 47.
My devotee, who acts for my pleasure, who worships me, and who has me as his supreme goal, attains the highest abode, that supreme station of Viṣṇu. 48.
Thus, O Śakra, I have described to you the supreme state of Tārikā, as well as that of other vidyās. What more do you wish to hear? 49.
49. Regarding the term "of the Tārikā": this means of her who has Hṛllekhā as another name.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of Right Conduct," in the Lakṣmītantra, which is the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. (27)
Chapter Twenty-Eight. Śakra:
Salutations to you, O abode of Kamalā; salutations to you, who dwell within the three Vedas.
By your grace, this mantra has been heard according to rule through meditative absorption.
You should now explain the entirety of spiritual practice, its true nature as it exists, and the conduct pertaining to day and night.
Śrī said: Nārāyaṇa alone is glorious, beginningless, and lotus-eyed;
he is a great ocean of knowledge, sovereignty, great power, heroism, and splendor. (3)
He is the Self of all beings, the Swan, Nārāyaṇa, the Subduer [Hari]. I alone am His form of power (sāmarthya), possessing His attributes as my own.
Thus, repeatedly bringing about states such as creation and the rest,
when I am propitiated, I deliver all beings from the ocean of worldly existence.
Satisfied by righteousness, I bestow various enjoyments; my body, beginning with sentient beings, is established in the supreme state of the True Dharma.

6. Regarding the word *vividhān* (various): the meaning is that I grant manifold enjoyments—both those pertaining to this world and the next, as well as incidental ones—that bestow liberation (*apavarga*). The term *saddharmapareṣu saṃsthāna* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that in which there is a firm establishment among those devoted to the True Dharma.
This Dharma consists of right conduct (*ācāra*); it is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—or, according to manuscript *c*, the protection (*rakṣaṇa*)—of that conduct.
I shall proclaim that conduct which is observed by the virtuous.
Having abandoned the sleep born of yoga and having risen during the latter part of the night, one should take refuge in Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of Śrī, who is the worthy protector.

8. Regarding the phrase "consisting of yoga" (*yogamayīm*): among the duties such as *abhigamana* and so forth, the fifth duty, called "yoga," is to be practiced starting from the night of the preceding day until the *brāhma-muhūrta* of the following day.
Furthermore, O Lord of the Gods, the essential nature of *prapatti* has already been explained to you.
Listen further, and I shall tell you how she may become firmly established within you.

Having sipped water and become purified, and having remembered the weapon-mantra (astra) which has the form of blazing fire, he entered it; having emerged from it, he became sanctified by the splendor of that weapon.
One should employ that surrender (prapatti), endowed with its five constituent limbs:
hostility having been abandoned and favor having been resorted to; || 11 ||
By me, toward all beings, according to my power and according to my understanding—as one who is lazy, of little strength, and lacking full knowledge—[this has been done] exactly as it is. (12)
Those means being employed would not at all be my deliverers;
therefore, I am miserable, wretched, untainted, and possessing nothing.
Hṛṣīkeśa, together with Lakṣmī, who is the embodiment of compassion,
is celebrated as the protector of all beings in all the Siddhāntas and in the Vedānta as well.

14. What is intended here is "great trust" (*mahāviśvāsa*) in all established doctrines (*sarvasiddhānta*), in all divine scriptures (*divyaśāstra*), in Vedānta, and in the Upaniṣads: "Whatever I possess that is difficult to relinquish—be it sons, wife, ritual acts, and so forth—"
O Lord of Śrī, everything has been offered by me at your feet. || 15 ||
15. He speaks of the surrender of self and what belongs to the self with the words "That which is mine," etc. [The phrase] "with the self" (ātmanā) means together with the self.
(p. 95) "Be my refuge, O Lord of Gods, O Protector, O Lord of Lakṣmī!"
For one who has thus surrendered once, no other duty is prescribed.

16. He speaks of the choice for protection with the words beginning "refuge" (śaraṇam): "For a person who has abandoned both means and obstacles and is situated in the middle, another means is sought due to the weakness of his intellect. (17)
17. For one who abides in the middle [path], there is no other duty to be performed; this connects with what was stated previously.

"Due to weakness of intellect" (*buddhidaurbalyāt*): the sense is that engaging in difficult action without considering one's own capacity is indeed prompted by a weakness of intellect. The alternative means here is *bhaktiyoga*. By this—

One should not think that the path of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) is being censured, or that for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the path of devotion is contrary to its true nature. When it is said, "A man, due to the weakness of his intellect, desires to grasp the reflection of the moon," no discerning person would say that this statement is censuring the moon itself. Furthermore, by means of devotion...
"Or even by supreme surrender, O Mahāmati"—this statement that devotion is a means involving conceptualization would be contradicted [if it were otherwise].
If you argue that this is contrary to the nature of one who is incapable yet desires liberation, there is no disagreement on this point from anyone.
Beyond this, learn from me as I describe the conduct of the virtuous.
One should rise up, aspiring for the arising of happiness for all living beings.
May all beings abide on the pure path of goodness;
may they eternally worship the Lord of Śrī and enter the supreme state. 19.
Having thus properly offered auspicious wishes for all beings with both mind and speech,
and having performed the purification of the body according to the injunctions of the Dharmaśāstra, he who is learned [in these matters]— || 20 ||
Having performed purification according to the rules, he should chew the tooth-stick;
then, having sipped water according to the prescribed rite with purifying substances enjoined by the scriptures. || 21 ||
Having performed the ritual ablution, one should worship the Twilight (Sandhyā), the purifier of the three worlds;
she is my own threefold power, manifesting in the forms of the Sun, Moon, and Fire.
For the purification of all beings, the Goddess Sandhyā proceeds;

having approached Vivasvat, who dwells within as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). [23] 23. "Vivasvat" means possessing distinguished radiance; this is an epithet of the Supreme Person. He dwells within.
The visualization intended here is as follows: "situated within the solar disc," "standing in the center of the orb of the sun," "possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns," and so forth.
One should properly perform the ritual of fire and then carry out the taking up [of the materials].
One should practice [this]; however, when wealth exists, a wise person should not engage in the act of taking up [more]. || 24 ||

24. *Upādāna* means the acquisition of materials suitable for the propitiation of the Blessed One. And that [acquisition] for one who is destitute consists of accepting rice and other items obtained unasked from the best of Bhāgavatas who are devoted to the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) and the five times (*pañcakāla*). There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, labor, lending at interest, and seizure by force. Among these, the righteous ones are inheritance, gain, and purchase. For one who has no property, the righteous way is to accept what is offered unasked by those devoted to the five sacrifices and the five times. This is called *upādāna*. Furthermore, there is the following verse: "Inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, labor, lending at interest, and seizure by force—these are the seven ways of acquiring wealth. Application, the yoga of action, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous as well. || 25 ||
Having performed the threefold bath according to the prescribed rules as enjoined by the scriptures,
and having then performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should carry out the subsequent sacrifice.
One should worship me, Viṣṇu, or both of us, according to the scriptures, with enjoyments produced by oneself, increased, obtained, or likewise acquired from disciples and others. || 27 ||
In the afternoon, the wise practitioner should properly perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) according to the eightfold ritual procedure, concluding with the secondary offerings (anuyāga).

28. The eightfold sacrifice (*aṣṭāṅgayajana*) is as described in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), sacrifice of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), sacrifice of honey and so forth (*madhvādiyāga*), sacrifice of food (*annayāga*), the formal gift (*saṃpradāna*), the satiation of the fire (*vahnisaṃtarpaṇa*), sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyāga*), and the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) (Chapter 22, verses 75–80).
One should study the divine scriptures and the Vedic collections;
one should thoroughly follow all established doctrines for the sake of self-realization.
29. "The established doctrines" (siddhāntān) means the various divisions of the established doctrines, such as the Mantras and Āgamas.
With a mind free from greed, one who is devoid of passion and hatred— (p. 96)
One should not, in thought or speech, disparage any scriptures, whether they be high or low.
One should take only so much as is necessary for one's own purpose; for all the scriptures expound everything solely for the welfare of all living beings. (31)
Having reached each respective stage, those [teachings] extend the highest good—at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end of all scriptures. (32)
The glorious Nārāyaṇa was proclaimed by that very ordinance;
and I, though situated within Nārāyaṇa, am all-knowing and all-seeing.

33. Intending to show that all scriptures have the welfare of living beings as their aim—both by revealing the supreme reality and by teaching the means of propitiating it—the author says, "The Glorious One.
She who knows the root cause, resembling a physician, appears in the form of various gurus and others.
I set forth various treatises in their respective ways.
According to one's specific qualification, the authoritative means of knowledge are likewise [determined];
there is no scripture whatsoever that is to be rejected absolutely under any circumstances. (35)
In every situation, the good is easily obtained, whether it be small or great;
therefore, one should not harbor malice, but should resort to whatever is necessary for one's purpose.
One should never enter there for the *samaya* nor undergo initiation at any time;
thereafter, one should perform the evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) when half of the sun remains.
Having performed the duties pertaining to the sacred fires, one should then indeed practice yoga in a well-secluded, pure place that is free from thorns and is delightful. (38)
On a seat strewn with soft coverings, topped with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass, purified both inside and out, and cleansed by the restraints (yamas) and other practices; || 39 ||
Having assumed a posture such as the *cakra*, the *padma*, or the *svastika*,
or whichever one the intellect finds pleasant, one should press upon the pathways of the channels (*nāḍīs*).

Having conquered the village of the breaths and subdued his senses through withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and having exerted himself in the meditative fixations (dhāraṇās), he should meditate upon me with perfect concentration. || 41 ||
Incomparable, indescribable, non-conceptual, and stainless;
a fortune easily accessible everywhere, which has attained the state of being the object of all cognition. 42.

Or else the yogi [should visualize] the supreme Padmā, who possesses form, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who resembles the interior of a lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, and who is endowed with auspicious marks. (43)

Or else, [one should meditate on] the Goddess, who consists of consciousness and bliss, seated upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa and having attained a state of aesthetic union (sāmarasya), and likewise the Lord of Śrī in that same form. 44.
O Lord of the Gods, those paths of yoga should be understood to be manifold;
among them, you should adhere to that single dharma in which you possess devotion and faith.
Having generated correct contemplation, one should rely upon meditative concentration;
therein, the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation—this triad—is dissolved.
46. The supreme pinnacle of yoga is described by the words beginning with "dhyāta" (meditated upon). Regarding the word "yatra":
it means in that state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"At that time, I alone shine as the eternal, perfect I-ness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*)."
When I, the great ocean of consciousness, had attained a state of oneness. || 47 ||

47. When the state of oneness (*aikadhyam*) has been attained by the yogin as a single nature (*ekabhāva*), nothing else whatsoever manifests. Rather, the connection with the subsequent [verse] is: "I alone am the manifestation.
Nothing else manifests at all; at that time, I alone am the Supreme (*parā*).
When weary from yoga, one should perform recitation; when weary from that, one should practice yoga.
I quickly become pleased with that wise person who is devoted to the practice of recitation and yoga;
having thus spent the first watch of the night in such practices as recitation and yoga, [he should proceed].

49. He explains *yoganidrā* (yoga-sleep) with the words "having thus led [the mind]": "Remaining established in yoga, that wise one should sleep for two watches (*yāma*) thereafter; having risen during the latter part of the night, he should practice what was previously described. 50.

50. Yoga is defined as the contemplation of the multitude of attributes of the Supreme Self, preceded by the surrender of the individual self into the Supreme Self. The meaning is that while performing that very practice, one should experience sleep.
Thus, O slayer of Bala, that mixed duty has been declared to you.
One should pass the five times flawlessly through the performance of the rites dedicated to the Blessed One.

51. "Mixed" (*vyāmiśrā*) means the worship of the Blessed One accompanied by a multitude of various types of ritual actions. Regarding the phrase "without flaw" (*acchidrān*): "That moment or even that instant during which Vāsudeva is not meditated upon—that is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is a distortion. (Garuḍa Purāṇa, Pūrvakhaṇḍa 222).

(97) O Slayer of Bala, there is no difference whatsoever between these two in their steadfastness: the initiated one who knows the five times of worship and the one who is devoted to the Lakṣmī-mantra. 52.
Both of these are considered devoted; they enter into me at the dissolution of the body.
One who bears the discus and the lotus shall eternally be devoted to Lakṣmī.
One should be devoted to one's own wife and always remain a celibate student;
one should constantly practice my mantra, with mind fixed on me and intent upon me alone. (54)
One should contemplate all sounds, whether high or low, as being of that nature;
one who knows the division between fire and moon, and understands the distinction between action and manifestation.
He is the knower of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme according to reality;
he is an expert in the tantras of the primary and secondary limbs, and he knows the rules for the various types of mudrās.

Skilled in internal sacrifice, external sacrifice, recitation, and fire-offerings; knowing the various types of preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*); and understanding the true nature of the means for attaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
He was an expert in the formation of names and forms, knowledgeable in the methods for accomplishing them,
a knower of the reality of the body as a substratum, and proficient in the principles of yoga.
A man of this kind—one who knows the meaning of the scriptures, is steadfast and discerning, non-violent, and established in self-restraint and charity—shall worship me and attain prosperity. (59)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Right Conduct," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpañcarātra*). || 28 ||
Chapter Twenty-nine: Śakra— (p. 98)
Salutations to Śrīvatsabhāminī, the wondrous wall for the manifestation of the sixfold path—both pure and impure—and the pacifier of the torments of worldly existence. || 1 ||
O Lotus-born One, tell me truly of the division between Agni and Soma, as well as the rules for the manifestation of ritual actions, for the sake of the *tārikā* of the Vidyā.
Śrī said:
That which is the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, who indeed is the power Nārāyaṇī—through transformation, I become that very one in the form of the Praṇava. (3)
O delighter of the gods, listen to me regarding the division of Agni and Soma in the Tārikā, as well as the proper performance of the ritual for the manifestation of the elements.
The supreme opening of Viṣṇu’s eyes, consisting of the primordial sixfold qualities, is I myself;
I am that Power (Śakti) whose equipment has been gathered, as was declared by you of old.
Since I have created the entire universe, my form manifests in two ways as I strive for its protection: through the mouth of sovereignty and through the mouth of splendor. (6)
6. "By way of the face" means primarily. [Note: Ācārya omits this line. "The sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) itself is my form; it is considered by some to have splendor as its face.
The sixfold policy itself is my form, which is oriented toward supreme sovereignty. 7. [End of verse 7]
That form which has light as its face is called the power of action (kriyā-śakti);
that very power is called fire (agni), because it burns away all afflictions.
The form manifesting as sovereignty is called Bhūti and Lakṣmī;
that power, abounding in sovereignty, is my body consisting of the moon.
The power of fire, consisting of action, is that which dries up all defects;
the other, which nourishes the world, is called *bhūti* (prosperity) or *soma* here.
These [manifestations] of mine are born from my expansion (vyūha) and consist of will, knowledge, and action;
I am that Supreme Goddess, Vyūhinī, whose very body is the sixfold attributes (ṣāḍguṇya).
That power of mine known as Action (kriyā), which is the sixfold quality blazing with splendor—of that there were three manifestations (vyūhas): the powers of the Sun, the Moon, and Fire. || 12 ||
Among them, the first is the supreme, divine, and radiant power called Sūryā;
she revolves incessantly, carrying out the activities of the world.

O Lord of the Gods, know that the form of her who is named Sūryā is threefold: pertaining to the self (adhyātma), pertaining to the divine (adhidaiva), and likewise pertaining to the elemental (adhibhautika). 14.
But the power called Sūryā, abiding within the self and moving along the path of Piṅgalā, proceeds as the solar energy situated in the objective world through its light. 15.
That other power, which is of a divine nature, has the form of the solar disc;
it is those rays that are proclaimed to have the form of the solar disc. (16)

16. To explain that the deity residing within the solar disc possesses the nature of the three Vedas (*trayī*), his nature as the *Ṛgveda* is first stated in the second half of the verse, beginning with "Sūrya":
"Know those [rays], O Lord of Gods, to be the *Ṛks*, which are burning and whose essence is heat."
Know from me that those splendors which reside within them are the Sāman chants.

17. He states its nature as the *Yajus* with the words "situated within" (*antaḥstha*). By this, the Taittirīya Śruti—"The sun indeed shines as this orb; therein are those *Ṛks*; that is the orb of the *Ṛks*"—is further corroborated. And it is also stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (2.11...):
Know that supreme power which abides within, having assumed a human form— that is the divine Puruṣa, the delightful one, who consists of the Yajus. (18)

[He meditated on] the Lord of Śrī, who bears the conch and the discus, whose four arms are full and noble, whose face is gracious, who has a lotus for his seat, and whose eyes are like lotuses. || 19 ||
O Lord of the Gods, the ten-hotṛ is said to be the head of this Puruṣa,
and the four-hotṛ is his feet and hands.

20. For this Person who dwells within, the Daśahotṛ becomes the head. By the terms "Daśahotṛ" and so forth, the mantras bearing those respective names are intended. The Daśahotṛ is the mantra beginning with "cittiḥ sruc," found in the first section of the third book of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. In that very same [text]:
O Lord of the Gods, beginning with "Pṛthivī hotā," the Caturhotṛ is recited in the second Anuvāka;
"pāda-pāṇi" is treated as a singular compound;
and "loma-māṃsa-asthi-majjā-asṛk" constitutes the Pañcahotṛ.
The two breasts, the testicles, virility, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ priest, and the drinking vessel. || 21 ||
The Pañcahotṛ is recited in the third Anuvāka, beginning with "Agni is the Hotṛ. The Ṣaḍḍhotṛ is recited in the fourth Anuvāka, beginning with "The sun is your eye.
The Saptahotṛ is declared to be the seven vital breaths located in the head.
Its splendor is its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and its joints are known as the ritual requisites (saṃbhāra). || 22 ||

22. The *saptahotṛ* [formula] is recited in the fifth section, beginning with "mahāhavir hotā. The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are recited in the tenth section, beginning with "devasya tvā. The ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*) are recited in the eighth section, beginning with "agnir yajurbhiḥ."
The channels (nāḍīs) are his wives of the gods; the heart is the mind of the Hotṛ priests.
The *puruṣasūkta* is consciousness, and the *śrīsūkta* is said to be power.

23. The wives of the gods are those recited in the ninth Anuvāka, beginning with *senendrasya*. The *Hotṛ-hṛdaya* is that recited in the eleventh Anuvāka, beginning with *suvarṇaṃ gharmam*. The mantras of the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Śrīsūkta* are well known.
Oṃkāra, Praṇava, Tāra, and Guhya are his eternal names;
likewise, the Yajus, the Rudras, the Śukras, and the Sāmans are his gross names.

24. The Rudriyas are those recited beginning with "namaste rudra manyave. Likewise, the Śukriyas are specific types of mantras. In this regard, the fifty-eighth and fifty-ninth chapters of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā* should be consulted.
A person practicing the divine mantra consisting of the Yajus attains the Supreme Person.
One is also liberated from the sins of malevolent incantations and curses. || 25 ||
25. "Consisting of the Yajus" refers to the Sāvitrī. It follows after the Anuvyāhṛtis and the Vyāhṛtis. The phrase "practicing this" connects with what precedes it.
Thus, the supreme power, the triple Veda, shines in the sky under the name of the Sun.
This supreme power, known by the name of Sūrya, is celebrated as being threefold.

26. Regarding the word "trayī" (the triad): the Vedic scripture should be recalled which states, "The sun moves along, not devoid of the three Vedas. The one named Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, revolves; she is supported by the three-syllabled *praṇava*, has the three worlds (*bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*) as her three channels, and consists of the three phonemes.
27. [She is] the support for the three-fold *praṇava* and possesses the three channels of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.

With the wind of the first letter of that [syllable] as her breath, with the head-syllable fashioned as her crest-jewel, she has the letters beginning with earth and ending with puruṣa as her body, consisting of light and bliss. (28)
28. "Tadādi" means the phonemes beginning with *tat*. "Śiras" refers to the Gāyatrī-śiras mantra. "Kṣityādi" refers to the phonemes beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *ma*.
Having arisen from Brahman, one becomes firmly established in Brahman once again.
She is the mother of the Vedas and the supreme progenitor of the phonemes.
(100) Through both direct and reverse order, she is declared to be the lunar and the fiery;
she is this divine Sāvitrī, whose form is the Sun, a digit composed of my own essence.
That which is named Gāyatrī protects one who sings it from great fear;
it takes up the life-force produced by cows, the earth, rivers, and living beings.
31. Regarding the word "having taken" (ādāya): here, the Vedic scripture should be kept in mind which states, "By those rays with which the sun shines, Parjanya rains.
He releases again what was held for nine months by his rays into the clouds.
The power consisting of the sun has been described; now hear about the supreme power consisting of fire.
O Śakra, this power of mine consisting of fire is also threefold:
one has divine things as its fuel, while another has the earth as its fuel upon the ground.
33. Celestial lightning is without fuel; terrestrial [lightning] has wood as its fuel. It should be known that the digestive fire resides in the stomach.
Likewise, the power consisting of fire within the stomach, which has food for its fuel, is threefold.
She consists of all the gods; she is said to be the mouth of the gods.

Praised by those established in the three goals of life, this very [meter] is called *triṣṭubh* by the wise; it enables a man devoted to his own spiritual liberation to cross over all difficulties. 35.
But there is another power consisting of Soma, which is also said to be threefold:
one exists in the sky as the form of the celestial orb, and likewise another in the form of medicinal herbs. (36)

36. Even the moon-natured [element] is threefold: as the solar disc in the sky, as the medicinal herb on the earth, and as the *iḍā* [vital energy] within the bodies of living beings. It moves within living beings as the single essence of nectar through the *iḍā*.
Being praised with *anuṣṭubh* verses, she is thus proclaimed as the *Anuṣṭubh*. || 37 ||
That knowledge which destroys death is called Mṛtyuñjayā;
O Purandara, it consists of the forms of the Sun, the Moon, and Fire. 38.
Manifested from the sun as the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), she consists of the oblation and has the form of Soma;
likewise, under the name of Agni, she consumes the oblation through her nature as the fire and the mouth of the Brahmin.
By means of these three, the entire system of the world proceeds day and night;
thus, that Vyūhinī, whose essence is action, is endowed with a threefold array.
My power, supremely profound, has emerged from the mouth of my splendor;
it blazes with the brilliance of ten million, a hundred thousand, and a billion suns, moons, and fires.
The discus named Sudarśana becomes her destroyer of enemies;
the weapon named Āgneya is indeed the most fiercely radiant Vaiṣṇava weapon.

That supreme vitality of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, which is the very nature of the parodāma-form [because it is its essential nature], from that all weapons and all powers arise. || 43 ||
The instrument (karaṇa) is that which is most effective in the performance of the fivefold acts of Hari;
there is no such act of the high-souled Viṣṇu that could exist without it.
In the creation [of the world], she proceeds as Viṣṇu’s own nature consisting of volition and the like;
likewise, in protection and in withdrawal, she assumes a body composed of the discus.
Born from my own portion, the Vaiṣṇavī power of action (kriyāśakti) is indeed to be known as Parāgneyī;
she stands pervading the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, in six ways.
46. "Sixfold" means by means of the wheels (cakras) known as Kalā, Tattva, Varṇa, Pada, Mantra, and Bhuvana.
Among these, first hear, O Vāsava, the wheel consisting of phonemes (varṇa):
the pair of the Savior (Tāra) and the Savior (Tāraka), which is the supreme lordly [mantra] residing in the axle. 47.

47. *Tārikā* is the *hrīṃ* mantra; *tāraka* is the *praṇava*. In the navel, one should take recourse to the form of the sun and moon, the *svāra* [the syllable *ā*, according to B and C; *śriyāstāraṃ* according to Ī; *śritadvāraṃ* according to I], which consists of twice eight [sixteen].
The letters from *ka* to *bha* are on the three sets of eight spokes, while those from *ma* to *ha* are situated on the rim.

48. *Svāra* is a collection of vowels. "Twice eight" means sixteen. "Three times eight-spoked" refers to the form of twenty-four spokes. The *pradhi* (rim) is the nature of the fire at the periphery; it is like a mass at the end of the classes [of consonants].
This divine wheel of phonemes, resembling a mass, revolves by way of the path of phonemes. 49.
(101) O Śakra, this wheel of the arts (kalācakra) has gnosis as its axle, power as its hub, sovereignty as its spokes, and strength and the rest as its rim; it is composed of the three qualities.
But the reality is this: Vāsudeva is the axle, Saṃkarṣaṇa is the brilliant nave, O Śakra, Pradyumna is the spokes, and Aniruddha is the form of the rim.

The wheel of the [mantra] syllables is established by means of the axle, the nave, and the rim, beginning with the fourth [syllable], and by means of the mantras consisting of seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and words (*pada*). || 52 ||
The unmanifest, which has Time as its eye, consists of the cage of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest;
it is a sphere composed of the transformations of the mind, the sense of hearing, their objects, and so forth.
Bearing in her hands the final wheel, the world-system extending as far as the Lokāloka mountain, she has assumed a human form consisting of six wheels.
Sudarśana is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), belonging to Viṣṇu, and residing in the center of the discus.
Listen now to its fourfold nature: as seed-syllable (bīja), as body (piṇḍa), as word (pada), and as name (saṃjñā). || 55 ||
Having first taken the *soma*, one should join it with the *prāṇa* at the end;
then, having taken the *amṛta*, one should join it with the fire of time (*kālapāvaka*).

56–57. *Soma* is the letter *sa*; *prāṇa* is the letter *ha*. *Amṛta* is the letter *sa*; *Kālapāvaka* is the letter *ra*. *Anala* is the letter *ra*; *māyā* and *vyāpin* are the letter *ī*. *Sahasrāra* is the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*) *īṃ*.
One should place *anala* within that, and finally place *māyā* and *vyāpin*.
This is the seed-syllable of the Sudarśana, manifested through my power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 57 ||
This divine seed-syllable, consisting of seven phonemes, bestows great supernatural power (*maharddhi*);
it is itself the great mass (*piṇḍa*), free from the pervasive influence of *māyā*. (58)

58. "Consisting of seven phonemes" means: *soma-prāṇa-amṛta-kāla-pāvaka-anala-māyā-vyāpī-sahasrāra*. This is the *piṇḍa-mantra*. It has the form of ten thousand suns and fires of time; it is the sound of a vajra-cloud.
A great mass of five colors, difficult for even gods and dānavas to restrain. || 59 ||
But by one who is pure, it should be remembered once—that which is difficult to remember for those with uncontrolled senses;
having remembered it, it is to be remembered for the sake of peace within my seed-syllables, beginning with the Tārikā.

60. "Smarye" means that which is to be remembered. That syllable situated in the upper part of the *piṇḍa*, known as Kālānala, by it the lords of the Daityas and the worlds themselves are consumed at the end of the age (*yugakṣaye*). 61.
By the fire established within the second power (śakti), the fire is kindled;
the vital breath (prāṇa) animates that power, being itself filled with the splendor of nectar.
Thus, O bull among gods, the nature of the *piṇḍa* has been described to you;
the *piṇḍa* is fashioned by the five pervasive [syllables] at various internal points.
Beginning with the *dhruva* mantra and ending with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras, it attains the status of a designation-mantra (*saṃjñāmantra*).
One should join the two pervasive [mantras] at the end of the *piṇḍa* and the others, representing the Moon and the Sun.

64. He clarifies exactly what was stated previously with the words "the two pervaders" (vyāpakau): "At the end, one should bring in a single pervader for the peak of Soma and Agni; likewise, the two pervaders of the first and last letters are traditionally taught. 65.
He is armor, the vital breath, victory, and the sky; he is the crusher of wicked afflictions.
He who is Saṃkarṣaṇa is the dissolution at the end of the eon, pervading all things.
66. *Varma* is armor. For the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and victory (*ojas*), the mantra is *huṃ* in the ether.
That is followed by *phaṭ*, and at its end is joy (*āhlāda*), which brings about peace.
[Ā, C, Ḍ, F: insert here lines 2 to 14 (beginning with *tasyā vyāptim*...)]
Thus, the mantra of Soma and Agni is remembered as being of the nature of drawing out the *piṇḍa* (the sacrificial ball). || 67 ||
67. *Vikarṣa* is the continuous thread (*anusyūti*).
This mantra of the Sudarśana, possessing its own phonemes and limbs, is the fold (*valī*). (p. 102)
It is the means for attaining the enjoyments of the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms.

68. Regarding the phrase "with their own syllables" (*svavarṇaiḥ*): the meaning is that one should perform the ritual assignment of the six limbs, beginning with the heart, using those six syllables of the previously mentioned six-syllable mantra. He describes the majesty of the mantra with the words beginning "divya" (*divya*), etc.
O Purandara, this Manu is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who depend upon him;
having arisen from Nārāyaṇa, he is ever intent on the welfare of the world.
69. In the phrase "for the welfare of the world" (*jagaddhite*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "for the sake of the welfare of the world.

70. O Slayer of Vṛtra, the division between Agni and Soma has been described, as well as the distinction between action and its manifestation, and also the differentiation of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
And the power of the energy of action [is manifested] through the distinctions of seed-syllables, clusters, and so forth.
Furthermore, O Śakra, hear of such vast supernatural power (ṛddhi) belonging to the energy of action.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Division of Agni and Soma," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Chapter 29)
Chapter Thirty: Śrī (Goddess Lakṣmī) — p. 103)
O Śakra, this power consisting of action has been described to you by me;
I have explained its pervasion to you as it is differentiated into the sun, the moon, and fire.
I have also told you about Vyūhinī by way of her designation as a "seed-cluster" (bījapiṇḍa); O Śakra, learn from me now the nature of her word-mantra.
The first *piṇḍa* is the conjunction of the creations of Ajita and Anala;
the second *piṇḍa* is the union of the creations of Kamala and Anala. (3)
3. Ajita is the letter *ja*; Anala is the letter *ra*; Sarga is the *visarga*. *Jraḥ* [is formed]. Kamala is the letter *ka*; *kraḥ* [is formed].
The third *piṇḍa* is said to be the conjunction of Śvetā, Ādyā, and Āhlādi.
The fourth *piṇḍa* belongs to those pervaded by the vigor of the Sun; therefore, it is in the middle. 4.
4. The letter *pha* is white; the letter *ṭa* is delightful. *Phaṭ*. The sun is the letter *ha*; vigor is the letter *u*; the pervasive is the bindu. *Huṃ*.
Then there are the three weapons, followed by *kālacakrāya hutabhukpriyā*.
This king of mantras, Cakra, is preceded by the syllable TĀRAKA (OM). || 5 ||
5. In the middle are three *phaṭ* mantras; then *svāhā*. *Oṃ jraḥ kraḥ phaṭ hūṃ phaṭ 3 kālacakrāya svāhā*.
Indeed, O Vāsava, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by this mantra.
One whose mind is devoted to this does not suffer defeat.
O Vāsava, I shall further explain the entire power of that supreme Manu, Tṛyugārṇa, who was previously described to you.
7. The six-syllable mantra consists of the three *yugas* and the syllables *sahasrāra huṃ phaṭ*.

Meditating upon the wheel, which is like that which has neither name nor form and is radiant with the majesty of the six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), and reciting the mantra together with its seed-syllable (*sabīja*), one is liberated from bondage. 8.
The body of my power of action (kriyā-śakti) is the Great Mantra (mahā-manu), consisting of six syllables; it is established at the end of the Atharvaveda and is augmented by the Cakra.
9. Regarding "Atharva": here, the statements from the twenty-first to the twenty-fourth verses of the twentieth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā* should be considered:
"The supreme Sudarśana discus consists of the six paths and is full of vigor."
One should meditate upon [the deity] as radiant, with its parts clearly distinguished, beginning from the eyes and the navel.
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra, beginning with *amṛta*, upon the limbs starting from the axle;
likewise, one should contemplate them on the nave, the spokes, the rim, and the two ends of the axle.
11. The syllable *sa* is the nectar (*amṛta*). By the phrase "beginning with primordial nature" (*prakṛtyādi*) and so forth, the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is indicated.
The rim (*pradhi*) is woven together by the principles (*tattva*) beginning with primordial nature and ending with the specific elements (*viśeṣa*).
In the Sudarśana [cakra], Māyā, procreation, and the three qualities (*triguṇa*) constitute the felly (*nemi*). 12.
The mantras consist of a thousand spokes arranged at the ends of the paths;
the end of the spoke is situated on the path of the array, and there the nave consists of the kalās.
13. He speaks of the path of mantra (mantrādhvan): "The mantras," etc.
Indeed, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) extends as far as the individual letters; in its midst, I am the supreme Śakti.
Within me is the Supreme Brahman, which is devoid of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper. 14.
In the center, one should contemplate Tāra; outside of that, one should remember Tārikā;
outside of that, the seed-syllable of action (kriyā-bīja); and outside of that, the first letter. (15)
Thus, the four seed-syllables are to be known in sequence within the cavity of the eyes;
however, one should first worship the Sun and the other deities according to the direction previously stated. (16)
That which is the very nature of the short form possesses a thousandfold lineage,
distinguished by the pairs of the Sun, Time, and Fire, beginning with the immeasurable.
17. "Sūrya" and so forth; the meaning is: by means of *hraṃ hraṃ* and the like.
And by pairs of nectar and fire, likewise in that same number, one should pierce the letters beginning with *ka* by combining them with the vowels consisting of fire and moon. 18.
18. "Amṛta," etc. The meaning is: by means of *sraṃ*, *srāṃ*, and so forth.
Having excluded the sun, moon, and wind [syllables], as well as thirty-one, those syllables would directly amount to one thousand minus eight (nine hundred ninety-two). 19.
19. "Sūrya," etc. This means excluding the letters *ha*, *sa*, and *ya*. Regarding "eight less":
one should know that there are 992 syllables (calculated as 31 × 16 × 2).
Furthermore, the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*) beginning with *tāra* (*oṃ*) should then be joined with short vowels.
The pervasion of fire is said to extend from Īśa and the others up to the region of Vāyu. || 20 ||

20. Together with the 992 syllables previously mentioned, when joined with the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*), there are one thousand syllables. However, regarding Ahirbudhnya, the state of having one thousand syllables is stated in another manner (23a, verses 82–83):
"Having placed the pair of threads and the *cārī* [or: the pair of weapons (*astra*) and the *cārī*], in four ways..."
One should divide the ground;
one should make fifty spokes for each floor.
The movement is the animal realm (tiryaggati). Multiplied by five, it is fifty (50); [multiplied again] by twenty-five, these spokes (arā) would be one thousand (1,000).
Upon them, one should place a thousand syllables from the east (prāk) to the moon (soma), and then indeed upon the diagonal lines (koṇasūtra).
One should place the four [deities] abiding in the path of mantra, possessing the qualities of fire, in sequence:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā. (23)
23. "Vartinyaḥ" means those that revolve. This connects with the following word, "mantradevatāḥ" (the deities of the mantras).
The mantra-deities are situated along the lines starting from Agni and ending with Īśāna.
Filling the spokes, that rim of the Sudarśana [disc] stands firm. 24.
O Vāsava, all the weapons are situated within its hub;
O Purandara, all the weapons are positioned at the front as the initiators.
One should meditate on both sides equally upon those who turn back with their heads marked by weapons, their hands joined in reverence, yet still arrogant.
In the Nemi-kṣetra, Mahālakṣmī is situated in the eastern direction;
Mahāmāyā is in the south, and Sarasvatī is in the west. || 27 ||
In the northern direction, she who is the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura is to be known;
outside of that, all around, are the gods, the threefold forms beginning with Brahmā.
Beyond that are the incarnations joined with the powers beginning with Turyā;
then follows the twenty-fourfold [principles] starting from Prakṛti and ending with Viśeṣa. (29)
29. "Turyādi" means the states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. "Avatārāḥ" refers to the Vyūhas.
30. In the [upper] portion situated before the *pradhi*, the collection of principles (*tattvajāta*) stands in sequence;
the gods who are the instruments of worldly existence (*bhava-upakaraṇa*) are established in the middle portion.

The worlds of the Bhuvanas, beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Suvaḥ, which are situated separately in the final portion and are grown within the interior of the cosmic egg, exist together with their respective worlds.

All the mountains such as Meru and others, likewise the rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others, the oceans such as the Ocean of Milk and others, and the islands known by names beginning with Jambū; || 32 ||
All the hosts of celestial beings dwelling in mansions (vaimānika-gaṇas), as well as the planets beginning with the Sun,
the lunar mansions, the stars, the Tārās, and likewise the bhūtas, pretas, and so forth— 33.
O Purandara, the thirty-three crores of gods who have taken refuge in its rim are like bees upon honey.
34. "Tisra" and so forth; the meaning is "thirty-three. *Saraghāḥ* means honey-bees. *Sāragham* means honey.
O Lord of the Gods, two tens of thousands (twenty thousand) fires revolve on both sides of the Pradhipa, acting as the initiators and the terminators. (35)

There, the fires that set things in motion and consume the Daityas and Dānavas possess the brilliance of a thousand fires of cosmic destruction (Kālānala) and are agitated by flickering, blazing flames.
The wise ones— tranquil, profound, serene, and possessing sharp splendor—
turn me away from my desires and pacify those impulses that lead me forward.
At the end of the Sudarśana-mantra is that which arises from Saṃkarṣaṇa,
the most terrible plough-weapon (lāṅgalāstra) that effects the destruction of all.

38. The mantra for the plow-weapon (lāṅgalāstra) is *phaṭ*. Of that [wheel] which stands crosswise, those arising from its eastern half are the initiators; however, those arising from the portion above it are the terminators. 39.
These [two] are of the nature of Agni and Soma, acting as the initiator and the terminator;
the lineage of weapons arises from that which originates from Agni and Soma. (40)
Listen to these two tens of thousands of forms of the fires of diverse natures, by remembering which a person may cross over the terrible ocean of calamity. (41)

41. "Two tens of thousands" (*dve ayute*) is the word division; the *sandhi* (euphonic junction) is archaic (*ārṣa*). This aggregate (*piṇḍa*), which is the support of all worlds, possesses the vital essence (*ūrjabindu*) of the four states of existence, and is the savior (*tāraka*), is said to be the body of the fires mentioned previously.
[Up to the word "vāyu" for fire. || 42 ||
42. The letter *repha* is the support of all worlds without exception; the letter *ya* is the fourfold course of existence; the letter *ū* is vigor (*ūrja*).

43. Preceded by the *Tāra*, and possessing the drop (*bindu*) of vigor from the fire that carries the support of nectar—this is declared to be the divine body of the *Piṇḍa* [mantra] of Nivartaka and the others.
43. The syllable *va* is the support of immortality (*amṛtādhāra*).

Having divided the rim (*pradhi*) tenfold—by way of the forms of time, the person (*puruṣa*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the manifest (*vyakta*)—preceded by the respective colors corresponding to those forms; 44.

In the sequence beginning with the eastern quarter and so forth, by means of the eight seed-syllable leaders beginning with *ka*, preceded and followed by vowels, and numbering twelve (two times six), [the mandala is formed]. || 45 ||
One should write the bodies of the *pravartaka* [mantras] joined with *tāra* (om) at the end;
likewise, the bodies of the *nivartaka* [mantras] with *amṛta* (som), *agni* (ram), and *yuga* (hūm). // 46 //
One should meditate upon the seven terrible and seven peaceful flames of each fire,
beginning from the first, as pairs starting with the first vowel, sequentially interspersed with the vowels.
Born from the pair of the Sun and Fire, arisen from the pair of the Nectar and Fire;
the end of the classes (kṣa), the Pradhāna, and likewise Vāmana, the bestower of perfection. 48.
48. The pair of Sun and Fire is *hra*. The pair of Nectar and Fire is *sra*. The end of the class is the letter *ha*.
The principal is the letter *ma*. The bestower of success is the letter *bha*. Vāmana is the letter *ba*. And Śveta, Tattvadhāra, Jhaṣa, and Śāśvata as well.
Likewise, the Lord of the Veda (Oṃ), the Discus-bearer (Hūṃ), and the letters beginning with Kāla (Ka) along with the bindu. || 49 ||

49. Śveta is the letter *pha*; Tattvadhara is the letter *ña*; Jhaṣa is the letter *jha*; Śāśvata is the letter *ja*; Chandaḥpati is the letter *cha*; Cakrī is the letter *ca*; and Kāla is the letter *ma*.
These four, whose forms reside within the central line of the navel-wheel, belong to Īśvara.
The gods, Keśava and the others, are stationed all around the spokes. || 50 ||

All [the forms] beginning with Padmanābha and ending with Dāmodara are to be meditated upon according to their respective marks, such as the lotus and so forth, situated upon the spokes and the rim of the wheel.
All the gods are endowed with their respective consorts and powers;
in the eastern quarter is the goddess Kamalā, and in the south is the radiant Kīrti.
52. The powers (śaktis), such as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and others, are mentioned in this very work in the twentieth chapter.
Jayā resides in the western quarter, while Māyā is in the northern quarter;
each is surrounded by powers numbering ten million. 53.
They constantly preside over the thousand-spoked Sudarśana, the wheel of time which is without beginning or end; its splendor is proclaimed to be immeasurable.
(106) It is fashioned with five divisions, designated as year, season, month, fortnight, day-and-night, axle, nave, and rim. || 55 ||
55–56. *Vibhakti* means division.
Five and five [beings], beginning with the male (*pums*), are supported by the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*)—by means of a thousand-spoked wheel adorned with a rim, spokes, and a felly.
56. Five, five, and twenty-five: beginning with the male principle (*pumān*) and extending to the earth, there are the deities of the letters from *A* to *KṢ*.
Furthermore, the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), such as the letters (*varṇa*), the principles (*tattva*), and the kalās, are maintained [or: exist].
The body of the Supreme Person, the devotee of Viṣṇu, consists of all reality.
This supreme [self] is held and indeed made to revolve, mounted upon the machine by means of the thousand-spoked rim situated at the bulb of the navel. 58.
By this wheel, which consists of various mantras and is firmly established within him, the Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas are slain.
This thousand-spoked [wheel], when practiced incessantly by men, destroys enemies immediately upon being merely remembered. (60)
One should destroy in an instant all defects—the afflictions, karma, and latent impressions—along with this fourfold set: the seed, the aggregate, the designation, and the form. (61)
This thousand-spoked wheel, devoid of beginning or end,
nourishes this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings by pervading it with the sun, moon, and fire.
The first form is the fiery one, the divine power called Kriyā;
in the form of the thousand-spoked wheel, she creates, protects, and destroys.
O Lord of the Gods, this ritual procedure, which is indeed arrayed with the manifestations of the sun, moon, and fire, has been declared to you; now hear it from me once again.
Thus has been described the manifestation (vyūha) consisting of the forms of the sun, moon, and fire;
now learn from me this same manifestation as the power of action (kriyāśakti). || 65 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Power of Action," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. || 30 ||
Chapter Thirty-One: Śrī (Fortune) — p. 107)
That power of action, which was manifested as the abode of the splendor of the sixfold policy, having assumed a fiery form, now bears a human body. || 1 ||

1. The meaning is that it is established as the primary element even among the six measures of statecraft (*ṣāḍguṇya*), specifically within *tejas* (martial splendor). It is interwoven with all missiles and weapons, and has the sun, moon, and fire as its root.
It is great, named Sudarśana, adorned with various forms [or various arrays]. || 2 ||
2. The density of all weapons and missiles (*sarva-śastrāstra-nibiḍatva*) of Sudarśana is stated in the twentieth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*.
The statement regarding its being rooted in the Sun, Moon, and Fire is made with reference to the essential nature of the syllable "Sahasrāra.
Situated in its center is the Power of Action (*kriyā-śakti*), which has assumed a human-like form (*pauruṣīṃ tanum āsthitā*).
[She is] dependent [upon them],
by way of her own gentle and fiery natures, according to the arrangement of their respective times. || 3 ||

3–4. With reference to the function consisting of protecting devotees and disciplining the wicked, the statement regarding his nature as being both gentle (saumya) and fiery (āgneya) has been shown previously; the designator of that [nature] is fourfold.
Among these, the mantra consisting of names (*saṃjñāmaya*) is by far the most powerful.
4. There is a fourfold nature consisting of seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), names (*saṃjñā*), and forms (*rūpa*). O Śakra, listen as I explain this to you.
That power which consists of the essence of the Moon is the first unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of Hara. 5.
I am the primordial power, Śrī; she is established in the first syllable.
She is the immortal one, whose form is satisfaction, the essence of the moon, and the sovereign of all.
6. The first syllable is *sa*. He describes its nature as being composed of nectar and so forth with the words beginning "amṛta" (*amṛta* etc.).
*Tṛpti* and *soma* also follow the syllable *sa*.
One should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), which resides in the digit of the moon (*indukalā*) of emission (*sarga*).
Likewise, the mantras beginning with Śiraḥpadma and the others are joined with the Supreme Lord.
By means of this emission (sṛti), one should effect both satisfaction and perfect accomplishment;
for this is the eternal power of life (jīvaśakti) conjoined with the creative force (sṛṣṭikṛt). || 8 ||
Endowed with the sovereignty of the three worlds, situated in the imperishable wind-dwelling,
she should be visualized in the form of a star upon the head of the enemy for the sake of achieving his destruction.
She is embraced by the immeasurable and partakes of the nature of both fire and moon.
From this power has arisen the brilliant and well-spoken Pauruṣa hymn.

10. "Of this" means of her who consists of the first syllable. The meaning is that from the letter *sa* the Pauruṣa Sūkta emerged. And so says the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā: "From the first syllable of this [Goddess], the Pauruṣa Sūkta arose; [the second part] was produced from the second syllable."
"O Sage, that which is called the Śrīsūkta... (18.33). Thus it is said: "The seers know a thousand such hymns;
this very mantra is eternally nourished by me, who am fond of Agni. (11)
There is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished by this [Goddess], who partakes in various effects and possesses the triad of powers inherent in each respective phoneme.
12. The triad of powers consists of the powers of the Sun, Moon, and Fire.
On the page (p.
108), it is said that she [the Supreme Power] authorizes all those powers within the Son; furthermore—
Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti that "she withdraws these again. Therefore, [this is so]. || 13 ||
Presiding over his own unfolding, that eternal Lord of Weapons, the sovereign of power and the Supreme Self, has arisen for the sake of the world.
14. Hetideva is Sudarśana; and Sūrya, having attained the state of the enjoyer and sustaining life, is desired as the vital breath (prāṇa). This one reveals the Self.
Endowed with the bestowal of sovereignty over the three worlds. || 15 ||
15. The letter *ha* is the sun; it is also the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Yogins investigate that which resides in the center of the heart-lotus;
for one who meditates correctly, the target is pierced by the force of the released arrow. 16.
16. "Of the liberated," and so forth; the meaning is "with extreme velocity.
Because he leads the vital breaths (prāṇas) upward with excellence, he is designated by this word "Prāṇa.
Enveloped by the lunar orb, he possesses pervasiveness and immeasurability. 17.

17. The pervasive anusvāra, when meditated upon while situated at the root of the tongue, restrains the flow of speech. When that very same [anusvāra] is meditated upon while situated in the circle of the letter *aṃ*, it indeed flows with nectar (*sudhā*). 18.
18. "At the root of the tongue" refers to the location of the throat. The *amaṇḍala* is the anusvāra.
When meditated upon, it renders even the worlds free from poison.
Indeed, from this [syllable] embraced by Rāma, the *Śrīsūkta* has emerged. 19.

19. "From *rāmopagūḍha*" means "together with the letter *i*. The seers know a thousand such hymns (*sūkta*s), which are enjoyed at their respective times by those who partake in the threefold power of the respective phonemes. 20.
By this, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished within the three worlds;
it destroys the entire world and leads one to the stainless state. || 21 ||

21. By the words "is slain" (*hanyate*) and so forth, the etymological derivation of the letter *ha* is performed. With the intention of the meaning of the verbal root *han*, namely "to strike" or "to go," he says: "it causes [one] to go.
It causes one to abandon all affliction (*kleśa*), and it is reached by those who contemplate yoga.
Thus it is described by the virtuous who abide by such etymological definitions. || 22 ||
That very power of the Supreme Self, which is the support of all worlds without exception and is made manifest through volition, is recognized [as such]. (23)

23. The letter *repha* (the sound *ra*) is the support of all worlds without exception. Everything that moves within it is always destroyed by all [beings]. This very earth, established upon it, is bound to the pillar by means of movement (*sṛti*).

24. [The letter *ra*] is the foundation of the entire universe; everything moving within it is perpetually consumed by all [beings]. This earth, situated thereon, is joined to the pillar through its course.
24. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *srā*: "it moves" (*sarati*). The meaning is that it goes.
It is "sriyate," which means it is gone to or attained. From "movement" (*sṛtyāḥ*), there is "stiffness" (*stambhe*), which is to say, a state of immobility.
The meaning is that having been turned back from movement, it is restrained by being made rigid.
That which is named "Saha" is power; therein he delights, and that [power] is manifold in a thousand ways.
He is the thousandfold one, the possessor of a thousand, who is my very self as Agni and Soma. 25.

25. He provides another etymological derivation and explanation for the collective term *sahasra* with the words beginning "saha": From the word *saha*, which signifies strength (*bala*), when the suffix *ra*—derived from the verbal root *ram*—is added above it, the form *sahasra* is produced by joining them together.
That power of mine consists of Agni and Soma; it performs all actions.
Kindled by right resolve, it is a formidable mass of splendors.

26. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the syllable *ra* with the words beginning "Agni" and so forth. "The state of being the fire of time" refers to its form as the letter *ra*.
"Kevalī" is a qualifier for Śakti. Having attained the very nature of fire, she has become the fire of time.
Having thus become solitary, she blazes with incessant rising compassion.
She is the Supreme Lord, the cause of supreme wonder;
she is the Great Power known as "Ra," my primordial energy called Kriyā.
(109) An infinity of thousands is called *arānantya*.
O Purandara, the essential nature of the armor (*varma*) and the weapon (*astra*) has thus been shown to you. 29.
29. He states another etymological derivation with the words beginning "saṃkhyā" (number). The compound means "that which has infinite thousands as its spokes.
Furthermore, that the *dhruva* is the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) as its starting point has already been established previously.
In this very way, the great mantra is the essence arisen from the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
30. The Praṇava is eternal. The great power (Mahāśakti) of the Atharvaṇas is the beloved, great body of the power of action (Kriyāśakti).
Indeed, the great Veda known as the Atharva is the essence of the three Vedas and consists of five sections. 31.

31. Regarding the term *pañcaparvā*: it is produced by means of the five-fold [sections] consisting of the *nakṣatra*, *vidhāna*, *vidhi*, *saṃhitā*, and *śānti*—just as a tree is produced from its essence through its mantra. Those who know the rules for its ancillaries declare that it has six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*). 32. [The six ancillaries are: *nakṣatra*, *vidhāna*, *vidhi*, *saṃhitā*, *śānti*, and *upaniṣad*. These are the six ancillaries of this [Veda]. Just as a tree is produced from its essence, so too is this [Veda] produced from these five sections. Those who know the rules for its limbs declare that it possesses six limbs.
32. The meaning is that he has grown like a tree by means of its essence. The six limbs are the six limbs beginning with the heart.
One should also [visualize] the Gāyatrī, known as the wheel, and the enclosure wall designated as fire.
Because of its concealment, because of the rising of Varuṇa, and likewise because it is with interest and is nectar. || 33 ||
33. *Gopana* is the letter *ā*; *Varuṇa* is the letter *va*; *Udaya* is the letter *u*; *Amṛta* is the letter *sa*. The mantra is *vāṃ suṃ*.
From the heart up to the crest (*śikhā*), it is for the upward wheel (*ūrdhva-cakra*) with *svāhā*.
And above the word *sūryajvālā*, from the well-joined *sudarśana*: || 34 ||
34. "Beginning with the heart" means consisting of the forms of the heart, the head, and the crest. "Joined with *mama*" is intended to mean "to Mahāsudarśana.
"And *svāhā* to the upward-facing discus (*ūrdhva-cakra*)," and so forth, is the ritual procedure beginning with the armor (*varma*) and ending with the weapon (*astra*).
Salutation to the Discus; at its end we know that [discus] which consists of the four ages. || 35 ||
35. "The armor and so forth" refers to the armor, the eye, and the weapons. The four-yuga [mantra] consists of eight syllables: *namaścakrāya vidmahe*.
The nine-syllable [mantra] is: *jvālāya ca sahasrānte dhīmahi*.
"tannaḥ pracodayāt madhye cakre"—this is the eight-syllable mantra. || 36 ||
36. "We meditate upon the one with a thousand flames; may that Discus impel us"—this is the mantra.
Having formed a fist and extended the index finger, with the index finger positioned as if threatening, one should whirl it around while meditating on the Fire situated within the rampart. 37.
With the palms facing each other, right over left, the tips of the little fingers and thumbs are joined, and the remaining fingers are likewise extended. (38)
One should thus rotate it all around; this is declared to be the Cakra-mudrā.
The Aṅga-mudrās will now be described; listen to the mantra for the absorption of Śakti.
The purifier mounted upon fire, extending even to the left from beyond the Praṇava—thus [he worships] the King of Discuses, Mahāsudarśana, the great traveler. (40)

40–43. *Pavitram* and so forth: *Oṃ praṃ mahāsudarśana cakrarāja mahādhvaja asta-sarvaduṣṭabhayaṃkara chindhi chindhi bhindhi bhindhi vidāraya vidāraya paramantrān grasa grasa bhakṣaya bhakṣaya bhūtāni trāsaya trāsaya*. Immediately following this—
Having joined the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should join the word *svāhā* at the end.
This is the *śaktigrāsa-mantra*. Then, from the [mantra] beginning with *astagatate*, [the phrase] *sarvaduṣṭabhayaṅkara* [is added].
After that, one should proclaim: "Chindhī chindhī! Bhindhi bhindhi! (Cut, cut! Pierce, pierce! || 41 ||
"Then, one should utter twice: 'Tear asunder! Tear asunder! followed by 'Swallow the mantras of others! Swallow! Then one should utter twice: 'Devour the spirits! Terrify them! (42)
The armor (*varma*), the weapon (*astra*), and the fire-born wife (*vahnijāyā*) constitute the mantra for swallowing the *śakti*.
Having himself become Sudarśana, he should recite this mantra. (43)
One should mentally suck the power from the mouth, heart, and other parts of the Supreme;
O Purandara, hear now the meditation upon the six-syllabled mantra. (44)
Having placed the limbs with the *cakra-mudrās*, one stands within a rampart of fire,
amidst a great thousand-spoked wheel as fierce as a mass of ten-thousand fires.

45–51. He describes the meditation on Sudarśana with the words "nyastāṅga" (one whose limbs are placed). This means one who has performed the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*) of the limbs. The *cakramudrā* is explained in this very chapter, in verse thirty-eight; the "enclosure of fire" (*vahniprākāra*) is in verse thirty-seven; and the description of Sudarśana begins with the words "sahasrāra" (thousand-spoked), and so forth.

He begins the meditation on the Supreme Self in the form of a wheel within the center of the wheel with the words "Akṣastham" and so forth. He describes the weapons held in the right hands with the words "Cakram" and so forth.
He describes the weapons situated in the left hands with the words "Śaṅkham" and so forth. [The right...]

The meaning is "capable. The meditation on the eight-armed Sudarśana is to be understood as it is set forth in detail in the forty-fourth chapter of the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*. By the phrase "with upraised knee," the stance known as *pratyālīḍha*, a posture of readiness for battle, is intended.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self, the flawless Nārāyaṇa, who resides within the senses, who is composed of the six paths, who is deluded, and who is manifested by my power. 46.
One should meditate upon the Lord in the form of a discus, resembling saffron in color, wearing divine yellow garments, and adorned with ornaments of pearls. (47)
One should meditate upon him as eight-armed amidst a flood of great calamities—standing, most beautiful, with knees raised and holding many weapons. (48)
In the four right hands, he holds a discus, a pestle, a fierce goad, and a lotus; and in the four left arms, likewise. (49)
Holding a conch, an arrow, a bow, a noose,
and a heavy mace in his divine right hands, his face was radiant with prominent fangs.
Then one should meditate upon the god Sudarśana, who has tawny eyes, is adorned with tawny hair, is encircled by garlands of flames, and possesses sixteen arms. (51)
When an insult from others has been received for which there is no remedy, and even when one’s own standing is precarious, having nonetheless conquered the enemies; 52.
When great danger has arisen from thieves, tigers, elephants, and the like,
one should visualize the Lord standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, facing the direction of the enemy host.

53–60. The stance known as *pratyālīḍha* was previously indicated by the words "with one knee slightly bent" (*idyajjānu*). Regarding the sixteen arms, he describes the weapons of the eight right arms with the words beginning with "with the spear" (*śaktyā*), and the weapons of the eight left arms with the words beginning with "with the conch" (*śaṅkhena*). [He also mentions] "with the interwoven principles" (*saṃsyūtatattvayā*).

The meaning is "consisting of the twenty-four principles. This is a description of the nature of the *vanamālā* (forest-garland). For this very reason, it is also conventionally referred to as the *bhūtamālā*. The "sixfold path" (*adhvaṣaṭka*) refers to the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*) and so forth.
It is adorned with uplifted, thick arms that are ready for the exertion of striking.
With his spear, with his blazing sword, and with fire of a hundred flames.
Then, with his right lower hands, he holds in sequence a goad, a staff, a spear of blazing luster, an axe, and a discus.
With the conch and the preeminent bow, then with the noose and the plow,
with the thunderbolt, the mace-weapon, the club, and then from the trident.
It was filled with blazing weapons held aloft or directed downwards,
and agitated by the tumultuous roar of the terrible flames of fire spat out from his fangs.
He was adorned with a divine forest garland woven from the very essence of reality,
while the lords of the Daityas and Dānavas fled in terror at the sound of his formidable, loud laughter.
In that fire, thick with the fat of Daityas blazing amidst a mass of flames,
the abode of tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of fires, and radiant with splendor; || 59 ||
In times of great danger, a person should meditate upon the Lord, the wielder of the wheel, as being of such a nature within the supreme wheel consisting of the six paths.
Having meditated thus, one should further meditate upon the four-armed Sudarśana;
otherwise, there can be no peace, for such is the fiery splendor of Hari. (61)
61. Through meditation on this [deity], the pacification of all calamities (*ariṣṭa*) is to be seen as described in the forty-seventh chapter of the *Ahibudhnya-saṃhitā*.
Pauruṣa meditation is proclaimed through the distinction between the terrible (*ghora*) and the peaceful (*śānta*).
Thus, O tiger among gods, I have described this meditation; now hear from me another.
Whatever modes of human effort have been described in this meditation,
one should remember all of them as being composed of me alone, for the sake of swift accomplishment. (63)
O Śakra, this most wonderful secret has been proclaimed to you;
O bull among the gods, hear yet another secret from me.
That which was previously proclaimed as my own Āgneyī power is resplendent like ten billion suns and comparable to ten billion fires.
My body, consisting of vibration, shines with the luster of ten million billion moons;
it is the nectar, the Supreme Self, the support of all worlds.

66. She consists of vibration and consists of action. The letter *sa* is nectar; the letter *ha* is the Supreme Self; the letter *ra* is the support of all worlds. Having taken her stand as the essence of the five points (*pañcabindu*), she touches the all-pervading Supreme.
It arises from the Supreme Lord for the welfare of all beings. || 67 ||
67. The five dots are the vowel *ī*; the pervasive one is the *anusvāra*.
One should conceive that power (*śakti*) as the axle, and its radiance as the navel-mandala.
The spokes are the syllables of the six mantras; [the two] are the Sun and the Uddāma.
Both [are] accompanied by the bindu. || 68 ||

68–69. "Six spokes"—this refers to the intended six-spoked wheel. One should meditate on the two [deities] *Huṃ* and *Sūryoddāra* situated well upon the rim (*nemi*). The remainder, however, is the circle of the hub (*pradhimaṇḍala*).
One should meditate on oneself in the center as one's own *māyā* within the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
69. "The remainder" means the syllable *phaṭ*.
The yogi, devoted to meditation, should constantly contemplate this while emitting [the breath] situated between the sun and the fire, thus remaining intent on his meditation. 70.
Having shaken off all worldly defects entirely and having attained supreme devotion to me, one attains me alone at the end.
Standing between the Supreme Self and the Immortal,
the wise one should constantly recite [the mantra] and mentally contemplate the nourishment of the nectar.
For he is being bathed with nectar flowing from the cavity of the Śakti,
and his defects are burnt away by the brilliance of the fire as he is vitalized by the Prāṇa.
73. By means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the letter *ha*, the fire is the letter *ra*.
Through the attainment of the activity of the five points (*pañcabindu*), he has established himself in supreme sovereignty;
through the yoga of continuous practice, he is self-controlled, disciplined, and has conquered his senses. 74.
Having abandoned all affliction and having assumed my own garb,
the yogi becomes proud, endowed with power, and through his practice, he gains mastery over everything.
Having become the supreme Lord, abiding as the embodiment of all-pervasiveness,
one attains me alone, my own abode, through my grace.
That which is action is called consciousness (cit), and that which is consciousness is the supreme action (kriyā).
These three, together with supreme bliss (paramānanda), are proclaimed to be the [four] powers. || 77 ||
77. He states that one's own essential nature consists of action, consciousness, and bliss—beginning with the word "yet" (which).
The indivisible, unique, supreme Śakti has the form of consciousness, action, and bliss;
she is the Vaiṣṇavī power, the supreme I-consciousness, and I am she who fulfills all objects. 78.
(112) By my own free will, my creative resolve unfolds in this twofold manner.
One power is called Kriyā, and another is Mahābhūti. || 79 ||
79. "In two ways" means by way of the distinction between action (*kriyā*) and power (*vibhūti*). In general, O Śakra, I, the Supreme Goddess, abide as these two.
This entire power of yours, consisting of the form of action, has been demonstrated. 80.
Listen to the description of the Tārikā according to her gross, subtle, and supreme forms:
she whose creative activity is withdrawn, yet whose nature is manifest sovereignty. (81)

81. He introduces the description of the power of manifestation (*bhūti-śakti*), which is the subject matter of the immediately following chapter, with the words "nimīlita" (closed): the meaning is that within the form of the power of manifestation, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) remains closed or latent. With the word "spaṣṭa" (clear): the meaning is that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) becomes manifest.
