My subtle form consists of the sixfold attributes (ṣāḍguṇya), and that prosperity of mine is called Tārikā. Listen properly, O Lord of Gods, as I describe its gross and other forms with an attentive mind. (82)
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Illumination of Sudarśana," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (31)
Chapter Thirty-Two:
Śrī (The Goddess of Fortune)
For this which is the supreme knowledge is the deliverer that brings about liberation;
hear now of its three forms: the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. || 1 ||
1. "Vidyā" means that whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). By the term "the one who causes one to cross over" (*bhavatāriṇī*), he states the etymological significance of *Tārikā*.
2. "The five-syllabled and the four-syllabled" refers to my gross form;
the three-syllabled, known as the subtle, is my supreme (*parā*) state, which consists of Viṣṇu.

2. Having joined the resonance (*nāda*)—heard like the sound of a bell above the *bindu*—expressed as *hrīṃ*, one should abandon its fivefold nature and establish it in a fourfold nature. "Threefold" means having the form of *īṃ*. He states the ultimate form: "consisting of Viṣṇu," which means having the form of the solitary letter *e*.
These three states of mine are each indeed threefold;
however, that which is the supreme state within the gross is that which rests upon the Supreme Self.

3. "Each one is threefold. The meaning is that there is a threefold division: in the gross form (*sthūla-rūpa*), there are the gross, subtle, and supreme forms; in the subtle form (*sūkṣma-rūpa*), there are the gross, subtle, and supreme forms; and in the supreme form (*para-rūpa*) as well, there are the gross, subtle, and supreme forms.
Regarding the supreme form within the gross, he says: "In the gross, however... The Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the letter *Ha*.
This [nature], which is the support of all worlds without exception, the pervasive refuge of Viṣṇu,
and consists of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed— learn from me its form.
4. *Repha* is the support of all worlds; *īkāra* is Viṣṇu; the *anusvāra* is the pervasive one. Striking them together, it becomes *hrīṃ*.
[It is called] "by that which is born as the pervasive abode and support of all worlds."
By means of the Supreme Self and so forth, [the breath] reaches the surface of the forehead. || 5 ||
5. Regarding the phrase "having reached the surface of the forehead," the word "by means of her form" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Having ascended the Vaiṣṇava form, she establishes herself once again in her own [form].
Shining with the sound that is the cause of liberation, she is the beloved of Hari. 6.
6–7. By the word "having stepped upon" (ākramya), the non-manifestation of the Vaiṣṇava form is expressed.
Sustaining with her intellect the entire world, including all enjoyers and objects of enjoyment, the Goddess rests upon the all-pervading Supreme Self.
Remaining as such, she is Viṣṇu’s form, the gross, supreme state;
she is the power that performs the fivefold acts, augmented by the three kinds of sovereignty.

8. "By her as such" means in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. Now, he describes the subtle within the gross with the words beginning "fivefold activity" (*pañcakṛtya*). The five activities are creation and so forth.
She sustains the Lord with her splendor.
Resorting to a state that is like a blazing fire, this subtle movement is considered to possess the radiance of the surging ocean.
Having then performed the creation and other acts,
the Goddess, who causes all wonders and is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and end [of the world], remained established in the supreme ether.

10. Regarding the gross [form], he states its gross nature: "the creation and so forth," and "all wonders," etc. It should be understood that previously the intention for the creation of the world was mentioned in relation to the subtle [state], whereas here its actual creation is being described.
She rests upon the Sun and impels Viṣṇu.
The maintenance of the world, which is gross, composed of gross elements, and wonderful, [is sustained] by the fiery splendors of the fire of time. || 11 ||
O Vāsava, the three courses of my gross form have been described;
now hear, O slayer of Vṛtra, the three courses of my subtle form.
This very subtle Power of Time, O Supreme Goddess,
exists as the eternal one, resting upon the all-pervading Supreme Self. (13)
13. He states the common nature of the subtle form: "not of time" (*akāla*). By this, it is intended that the previously mentioned gross form is subject to being consumed by time (*kālakālya*).
The pure and the impure—thus the object of creation is said to be twofold.
The gross [power] is established in that which is other than pure; the subtle is established in the pure. || 14 ||
14. He states another distinction: "Pure," etc.
One should correctly perceive all three of these courses as being like that of the gross [body].
O Śakra, behold the form of that which is my supreme body. 15.

15. Regarding the threefold subtle form under discussion, he extends by analogy the previously mentioned gross movements with the words "the three. The only difference is this: while the previously mentioned gross movement has impure objects as its domain, this one has pure objects as its domain.
It is all-pervasive, divine, partless, and stainless.
That supreme power consisting of me is designated by the name Viṣṇu.
16. Now he describes the common form of Parā: "Pervading all," and so forth.
This is indeed that Vaiṣṇava existence; this is considered by Hari to be the I-consciousness (ahaṃtā).
This is the final goal of the yogins; this is the destination of those whose nature is Sāṃkhya. 17.
17. [This refers to] those who are Sāṃkhyas, meaning those who possess knowledge such as the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
"This is that supreme form; this is that supreme goal.
She is the primordial power, Kuṇḍalinī, the female bee (*bhramarī*) who bestows yoga. 18.
18. He states her different names, beginning with "Śakti": "For she is the Unstruck (Anāhatā), the Soundless (Aghoṣā), the Boundless (Nirmaryādā), and the Arisen from the River (Nadodgatā);
likewise she is the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahma), Śakti, and the Supreme Source of the Mothers (Mātṛkāyoni). 19.
19–20. Nada, Nāda;
Gāyatrī, Kalā, Gaurī, Śacī, the goddess Sarasvatī, Vṛṣākapāyī, Satyā, Prāṇapatnī, and Yaśasvinī.
She is the wife of Indra, the great milch-cow, Aditi, the delighter of the gods;
she is the goddess who is the mother of the Rudras and likewise the benefactress of the Vasus.
The sister of the Ādityas, the navel, the sustainer of immortality, the supreme;
she is Iḍā, delight, the one of lovely form, the great nourisher, most exalted. (22)
She is the Earth, Renown, and the Veda-triad; she is the Cow who is affectionate toward living beings, the Power, and Primordial Nature; she is the Great Queen who yields the milk of wisdom.
Tārā, Sītā, as well as Śrī, Kāmavatsā, Priyavratā, Taruṇī, Varārohā, Nīrūpā, and Rūpaśālinī. || 24 ||
Ambikā, Sundarī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, Ghorā, Manomayī, Siddhā, Siddhāntikā, Yogā, Yoginī, and Yogabhāvinī. || 25 ||
Such names as these have been declared in various scriptures by the wise who have reached the further shore of established doctrine—the secrets of Śakti. (26)

This very supreme, divine Śakti exists in three forms; she is manifested in a threefold manner through the states of gross, subtle, and supreme. Her essential nature has been declared, and she abides in these three ways.
Listen to this exposition of her in terms of the immeasurable and other such forms. || 28 ||
28. The letter *ī* signifies this meaning:

when that which is the sixfold quality (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, the imperishable in which all distinctions have been withdrawn, exists as one alone; at that time— 29. [The letter *ī*].

29. He states the supreme form of Parā: "The sixfold attributes" (*ṣāḍguṇya*), etc. "Withdrawn" (*saṃhṛta*): *bheda* refers to the differentiated phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This expression is used because, during the reabsorption (*pratisaṃcara*), the entire phenomenal world is dissolved into Brahman.
"Only one" (*ekam eva*): the meaning is that Brahman, characterized by the subtle state of both the conscious and the unconscious, became the single reality (*tattva*).
Then that deity, known as Aprameya, is meditated upon by yogins;
whether as the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader, or as the act of creation and the created.
At that time, there is no other object of cognition for it; nothing at all exists for it.
Then it was as if empty of forms, as if entirely asleep. || 31 ||

31. *Prameyatva* is the state of being an object of valid cognition (*pramā*). "As if empty" means that because all activity has ceased, it is like a non-entity; the word "as if" (*iva*) is used to refute the reality of that which is designated as "emptiness" by those who favor external [objects]. The sixfold quality (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is Brahman, and therein this [power] is established under the name of Viṣṇu.
The movement of power and the possessor of power is like that of a waveless ocean. || 32 ||

32. Now he describes the subtle form of Parā—beginning with the word "śakti. The phrase "when" (*yadā*), which occurs later in the sentence, is to be understood here at the beginning. The connection is as follows: "when there is the manifest movement—that is, the cognition—of both Power (*śakti*) and the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*).
Then, at that time when Brahman, known as Vāsudeva, is again without wound (*avraṇa*).
When it unfolds from its own volition, that is called the first [state]. || 33 ||
33. "The first" means "volition" (saṃkalpa), as is understood from the context.
For when Brahman expands itself through the paths known as pure and impure, that which is called Māyā then appears, having the nature of Brahman’s volition. 34.
34. This means that she is the supreme power (*parā śakti*).
From Saṃkarṣaṇa down to the earth, all are situated within her womb—as if in an embryo.
Furthermore, when the Supreme Brahman, having accomplished its own will, becomes distinct [from her]... 35.

35. He describes the gross form of Parā: "Saṃkarṣaṇa... etc. At that time, the Goddess, who performs the fivefold cosmic act (*pañcakṛtya*), exists as having a second [entity] through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader; she consists of five *bindus*. 36.
36. The five dots (pañcabindu) are the vowel *ī*. Thus, these three have been declared by me to be the path of Parā, my own body.

Dividing form after form, she is the differentiator of each respective category of phonemes (*tattvārṇa*). 37. [She is] the one who, having divided every single form, distinguishes each corresponding element and syllable.
37. The meaning is that the triple Veda (trayī) is threefold by way of its gross, subtle, and supreme forms.

Having been brought to the state of denoting those respective [entities], the body of the world, consisting of its own [divine] will, indeed abides as its very self within each and every one of those principles (tattva). 38.
That portion of mine which is subtle in form, like fire latent within wood,
having attained those various forms, is the eternal one called Sevanī.

39. *Sevanī* refers to the configuration of the bodily parts suitable for the articulation of phonemes and so forth in locations such as the tongue; [it is] the body of that particular individual through the coloring of the respective phonemes.
40. Within that, the portion which is of the nature of the Supreme Self exists by way of being the presiding deity (*adhidaivatabhāvena*).
40. "This which is a part..."—this connects with the phrase "this is hers" found in the subsequent verse.
"The Vaiṣṇava [power], whose nature is Śakti, remains restraining [me].
This very Goddess, who is imperishable, attains the state of being the designator of each respective [aspect]. 41.
The supreme sovereign Yoginī is the support of all worlds without exception;
yet the mere phoneme of her essence has attained the sovereignty over the three worlds. (42)
My eternal Śakti expresses each respective gross element as a reality through the naming of its various states, thereby manifesting her role as their controller.

43. Even the entire gross reality becomes eternal through my power; by this, the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) is intended. This very Goddess Īśvarā abides as two-fold power (śakti).
The peaceful fivefold Brahman, beginning with the letter *kṣa*, which was previously shown to you; || 44 ||
44. "Attached" (*sakta*) means being joined with attachment (*āsanga*). He explains that very point with the words "beginning with *kṣa*" (*kṣādi*):
by way of the essential nature of *kṣa* and so forth, she has attained the bestowal of sovereignty over the three worlds.
This [power] exists in two ways: in its essential nature and in its regulation. || 45 ||
45. "In two ways" means that she exists in a twofold manner, demonstrating both the essential nature and the regulation of all [the elements].
As for the group of four *dhāraṇās* beginning with *ya* and ending with *ya*, they have been proclaimed.
In that regard, when the state of the subtle and the supreme has been established, this [meditation] is likewise twofold, as before.
46. The meaning is that the four ending in *vādi* are said to be the four *dhāraṇās*.
This letter *ma* is threefold (or, according to B and C, exists in three states).
And it has been declared that [the letter 'A'] denotes consciousness;
therein also, this twofold division applies to the two states of the subtle (*sūkṣma*) and the supreme (*parā*). || 47 ||
47. That which exists in three states is "traiyavastha. It is called *bhāva*, whose nature consists of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) born of *māyā*.
The goddess named *Ī* is there as before, also in those two stages. 48.

Regarding the three forms of intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas) which begin with the letter *ba*, this Goddess is likewise twofold in each of those two groups, as previously described. (49)
49–50. In Bādika and Baphapa, and likewise in Nādika and Ṇādika, as well as in the two groups of sense-faculties,
this [energy] exists in two ways within the ten subtle and supreme [elements].
50. The dental class [consonants] begins with *na*; the retroflex class begins with *ṇa*.

In the fivefold manifestations (*vibhūti*), which consist of both gross and subtle forms, the Goddess resides as before in the two sets of ten, beginning with *ña* and *ṅa*. 51. [The Goddess resides] in the fivefold manifestations, which consist of both gross and subtle forms; in the two sets of ten, she is situated as previously described.

51–52. The five classes beginning with *ca* and the five classes beginning with *ka* have been described as having the nature of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*sthūlabhūta*).
On the path consisting of both the pure and the impure, this Power (*Śakti*), like an actress, herself assumes many forms through seventy divisions.
52. Regarding "seventy": since there are thirty-five divisions each for the pure and impure paths, there are seventy divisions in total. *Ī* means the power (*śakti*) whose form is the vowel *ī*;
it refers to this *īm* which has attained such an extent.
Having meditated upon the Supreme Goddess, one attains the supreme, eternal abode of Viṣṇu. || 53 ||
Wherever she has gone, whether on the pure or impure path, she remains there never abandoning her connection with Viṣṇu. (54)
Combined with one, two, three, and so forth, adorned with vowels and consonants, situated within the categories of the pure and impure paths, it is established through various divisions. (55)
Furthermore, of this very [Śakti] when devoid of the "tawny" (jaṭā) coloring, thinkers of reality should know that there is a threefold division according to her gross and other forms. (56)

56. Regarding "jaṭā": this means [the letters] beginning with *ja* and *ṭa*. This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes the coloring by other phonemes as well. "She is joined with the Creator (*sṛṣṭikṛt*), she is gross (*sthūlā*), she is subtle (*sūkṣmā*), she is joined with the Lord of Space (*vyomeśa*); she is the stainless (*nirañjanā*) Supreme (*parā*), and she is thus enamored with the letter *ī*. 57. [She is] joined with the Creator, she is gross, she is subtle, she is joined with the Lord of Space;
she is the stainless Supreme, and she is thus enamored with the letter *ī*.
57. He describes the divisions of this form, such as the gross and so forth, beginning with the words "sṛṣṭi" and so on. *Sṛṣṭikṛt* is the *visarga*.
*Vyomeśa* is the *anusvāra*.
This supreme consort of Viṣṇu is unwavering, like the flame of a lamp.
She remains perfectly motionless within all the foundational lotuses.
Extending from the region of the navel to the crown of the head, this one path of Brahman is devoted to its vow;
it is radiant, blazing, purifying, and glorious. (59)
59. The *basti* is the region below the navel.
Emerging from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and reaching the Great Lotus (*mahāpadma*), it is woven like warp and woof upon the path of supreme bliss. 60.
60. "Pervaded lengthwise and crosswise" (otaprota) means permeated throughout everything.
Having dissolved the mortal form, one should immerse the person in the immortal, together with the mantras consisting of Viṣṇu, along with the mantras composed of the Self. 61.

61. "This [body] is mortal," meaning it is subject to death; "that [knowledge] of mine is surely of undiminished splendor" refers to that which is the supreme Sāṃkhya. And those dual-less Sāṃkhya mantras bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through their recitation. 62. [The verse continues: "That [knowledge] of mine is surely of undiminished splendor"—this is the supreme Sāṃkhya. And those dual-less Sāṃkhya mantras bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through their recitation.
62. Anūnaśrī (500). This means that they are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpin*), being non-dual in number.
117) These very [energies] of the Supreme (*parā*)—or rather, of the Dense One (*ghanā*)—are proclaimed to be her droplets (*vipruṣ*).
For just as a mass of rays remains pervading the nature of light, || 63 ||
63. Radiance (*tejas*) is the quality of luminosity.
For just as stability is established pervading all earthly entities, it exists in various manifestations and forms, arranged in diverse structures. 64.
Pervading equally all external and internal existence consisting of sound,
the illustrious Goddess, the consort of Viṣṇu, remains thus established.
65. The grammatical connection is that the goddess Īrūpiṇī is present.
O Śakra, this distinction between the gross, the subtle, and so forth has been shown by me as it truly is;
now hear from me the limbs and other parts of Tārikā. 66.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Gross and Other [Levels]," in the Śrīlakṣmītantra, which is the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. || 32 ||
Chapter Thirty-Three. Śrī said:
Listen, O child Sureśāna, to my [exposition of] the ancillaries and sub-ancillaries of the mantra, consisting of various mantras, for the sake of the Tārikā-vidyā. (1)
Gopana, Pañcabindu, Ūrja, Airāvaṇa,
and Aurva— these five are each accompanied by Vyāpin.
2. Gopana is the letter Ā; Pañcabindu is the letter Ī; Ūrja is the letter Ū; Airāvaṇa is the letter AI;
Aurva is the letter AU; Vyāpin is the Anusvāra. Having thus placed this pentad of syllables above the fire of the vital breath (prāṇānala):
One should contemplate this seed-syllable of the limbs, beginning from the heart and ending with the eyes.

3. *Prāṇa* is the letter *ha*; *anala* is the letter *ra*. The "five clusters" (*piṇḍapañcaka*) are the fivefold mantra: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ*. "The heart and so forth" means the heart, head, crest, armor, and eyes.
[In place of these and the following two lines, B reads as follows:
"One should place the word *paraṃ* with the two seed-syllables of *praṇava*, and the word *jñānāya*;
likewise, *hṛdayāya namaḥ*—thus the mantra consists of eleven syllables. ]
After the seed-syllable of the heart, the word "jñānāya" should be joined, and then "hṛdayāya namaḥ"; this mantra bestows the power of concentration (dhāraṇā). || 4 ||
4. He indicates the mantra, beginning with "hṛt": *Oṃ hrāṃ jñānāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
This eleven-syllable mantra begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ*.
Furthermore, one should place the word for sovereignty (*aiśvaryāya*) between the two seed-syllables of the *praṇava*. 5.
5–10. Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head for sovereignty; oṃ hrūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the tuft of hair for power;
oṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor for strength; oṃ hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two eyes for splendor; oṃ hraḥ, phaṭ to the weapon for valor.
And likewise, "Śirase Svāhā"— this consists of eleven syllables.
One should then place the word "Śaktaye" preceded by the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava.
"Śikhāyai vauṣaṭ"—this ten-syllabled mantra is indeed the Śikha;
one should then place the word "balāya" between the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava.
The mantra for the armor is "kavacāya hūṃ," consisting of ten syllables;
one should then place the word "tejase" preceded by the two seed-syllables of the Praṇava.
With "Vauṣaṭ" for the two eyes, this ten-syllable mantra is for the eyes;
one should then place the Supreme Lord situated above the fire of the vital breath.
Therefore, preceded by the Praṇava, one should place the word for "prowess" (vīryāya) and then "phaṭ" for the weapon (astra); this mantra consists of ten syllables.
This group of six limbs has been declared; now hear of the triad of sub-limbs.
At the end of the *tārikā*, one should sequentially assign the sixfold word as before.
11–12. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to knowledge for the belly; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to power for the back; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to strength for the two arms.
One should install [these mantras] in sequence from knowledge up to splendor (tejas), and at the end of that as well.
And for the belly, the back, and the two arms—this indeed is the sequence of the words.
p.

119) "To the two thighs, then to the two knees, and to the two feet"—in this sequence, the word *namaḥ* (homage) should be applied thereafter; this is the rule for the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*). || 13 ||

13. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the thighs for sovereignty; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the knees for heroism; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the feet for splendor. Thus, the twelve mantras for the limbs and sub-limbs are proclaimed.
Now listen as I recite the mantras for my ornaments and weapons.
The Kaustubha gem is merged with space, and beyond that is the Supreme Self;
it is permeated by fire above and below, and is likewise endowed with the upward-moving vital energy (ūrg).
15–17. Oṃ ṭhaṃ rhrūḥ ṭhaṃ, obeisance to the Kaustubha gem, which is the soul of light; svāhā!
The Kaustubha is joined with the creator [syllable] at the head and joined with the pervasive [syllable];
after that comes the obeisance, and after that, "to the soul of light. (16)
Then, "Kaustubhāya Svāhā"—this sixteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the Praṇava, is the Kaustubha mantra that accomplishes all rites. || 17 ||
One should first extract Tāra; then one should extract Dhareśa.
Below that, one should place the one known as Tṛpti, and below that, Varāha.

18–20. Oṃ lsvīṃ namaḥ sthalajalodbhūtabhūṣite vanamāle svāhā. One should subsequently adorn [the deity] with Māyā (the syllable hrīṃ) and then mark it with Vyāpin (the syllable hskṣmlvryūṃ). This is the fivefold aggregate of phonemes (varṇapiṇḍa); after that follows the salutation (namaskāra). 19.
Then one should utter the word "sthalajalodbhūtabhūṣitapada," followed by "vanamāle" and then "svāhā"; this mantra accomplishes all aims. || 20 ||
This great mantra, consisting of a garland of forest flowers, comprises nineteen syllables;
at the conclusion of the word "tāraka," one should extract the syllable "vāmana."
21–23. Oṃ bsuṃ namaḥ śrīnivāsapadmāya svāhā. [The term] *tryadhikā daśākṣarāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has thirteen syllables.
Having applied *tṛptimā* beneath that, one should adorn it with the *udaya*.
The body, marked by the pervasive [syllable], consists of four syllables and is most wonderful.

After that, "namaskāraḥ," then "śrīnivāsapadam," and then "padmāya" followed by the wife of fire (svāhā); this is the twelve-syllable mantra known as Pādma. (Note: Some versions read it as thirteen syllables.)
First, one should take the syllable *vaikuṇṭha* (the letter *v*) and place the letter *ra* above it;
thereafter, one should mark it with *ānanda* (the vowel *ā*) and then with *vyāpin* (the vowel *ī*).
24–25. Oṃ rṇāṃ kastha kastha ṭhaṭha varapāśāya svāhā. One should utter the word *kasthakastha*, followed by the pair of *nemi* syllables.
Svāhā indeed to Varapāśa; the King of Nooses is preceded by the Praṇava.
This fifteen-syllable mantra brings swift accomplishment for those who possess desire;
it is joined at the end with the Praṇava, and the one named Virāṭ is conjoined with Vyāpin upon the head. (26)
26–28. Oṃ ḷ ṛkṛṃ niśitaghoṇāya aṅkuśāya svāhā.
These two [syllables] should be joined as a single cluster (piṇḍa): the letter *ra*, the lotus, and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
This third syllable is joined with the pervasive [vowel *u*] at its head. 27.

The word *pada* [is assigned] to the sharp-trunked one (*niśitaghoṇa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*); this fifteen-syllable mantra, beloved of Śikhin (Agni), is the Aṅkuśa, which bestows swift accomplishment. (28)
This pentad has been declared as that of the ornaments and the weapon-mantras;
now hear the form of the mantras for the support and the seat, O Purandara. (29)
29–31. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti (the Foundation Power).
Without whom the fulfillment of the Tārikā does not occur; situated between two fires, the vital breath (prāṇa) is possessed of Māyā and endowed with the Bindu. 30.
Then, beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namaḥ" for Ādhāraśakti, this nine-syllabled mantra of Ādhāraśakti is to be known. || 31 ||
Situated between the two anal regions, ending with the *bindu* and joined with *ūrja*, followed by "namas" at the end and preceded by the *praṇava*, [it is addressed] to Kālāgnikūrma. (32)
32. "Situated between two fires": the word *prāṇa* is to be supplied [to this phrase]. Oṃ rhrūṃ, obeisance to Kālāgnikūrma.
This ten-syllabled mantra of Kālāgnikūrma should be known;
it marks the vital breath with concealment and is joined with the Pervasive One at the crown of the head.

33-34. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta. Having extracted [the mantra] ending with the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by "salutation to Ananta," this eight-syllabled mantra of the Naga king is thus proclaimed. 34.
Having condensed into a single unit the fourfold—the lotus, the form of fire, Pradhāna, and Puruṣeśvara—along with Gopanavyāpin; 35.
35–36. Oṃ kṣmlāṃ, obeisance to Vasudhā.
After "obeisance to Vasudhā," this mantra beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) is to be known as belonging to Viśvaṃbharā; she is conceived as the foundational support. 36.
One should extract the two syllables "amṛta" and "varuṇa" together as a single cluster,
joined with the pervasive "gopana," at the end of the Praṇava.
37. Oṃ svāṃ, salutation to the Ocean of Milk.
This nine-syllable mantra for the Ocean of Milk consists of the syllables *kṣīrārṇavāya* and *nabhaḥ*;
it is pure, joined with the *udaya-vyāpin*, and ends with the *praṇava*. 38.
38. Oṃ puṃ, obeisance to the Foundation Lotus (ādhārapadma).
"Obeisance to the Foundation Lotus"—this ten-syllable [mantra] belongs to the Lotus.
Thus, the six mantras for the six foundations have been proclaimed. 39.
O Purandara, O Vāsava, listen to the ritual procedure for the mantras known as Ādhāra and Īśa: Dharta, Ajita, Amṛtādhāra, and Vibudha.

40–43. *Dhartā* (the Sustainer) is the letter *dha*. *Ajita* (the Unconquered) is the letter *ja*. *Amṛtādhāra* (the Support of Nectar) is the letter *va*. *Vibudha* (the Awakened) is the letter *la*. *Satya* (Truth) is the letter *ṛ*. *Oṃ dhṛṃ*, *oṃ dhṝṃ*, *oṃ dhḷṃ*, *oṃ dhḹṃ*:
these are, in order, the seed-mantras (*bījamantra*) of the Lords of the Supports (*dhāreśa*), known as Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya. *Oṃ jṛṃ*, *oṃ*... [text continues]

*jṝṃ oṃ*, *jḷṃ oṃ*, and *jḹṃ oṃ* are, in order, the seed-mantras of the Lords of the Supports (dhāreśabījamantra) known as Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya. Then: *oṃ vṛṃ*, *oṃ vṝṃ*, *oṃ vḷṃ*, and *oṃ vḹṃ*.

The seed-mantras of the presiding lords of the supports known as the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, *Sāman*, and *Atharva* Vedas are: *oṃ ḷṃ*, *oṃ ḹṃ*, *oṃ lḷṃ*, and *oṃ lḹṃ*. These are the seed-mantras of the presiding lords of the supports known as the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas.
Having extracted these four syllables, [one should place them] upon these.
The best of practitioners should place the four castes, beginning with Satya, [in their respective positions]. || 41 ||
O Vāsava, one should bestow these four seed-syllables, beginning with the Praṇava, which grant sovereignty over the three worlds, for the sixteen-fold Self beginning with Dharma.
Dharma and the rest, adharma and the rest, the deer and the rest, and the Kṛta age and the rest—
these four groups of four are established [or well-known] in the world.
One should arrange sixteen designations in groups of four;
with the seed-syllable at the beginning and "namaḥ" at the end, these are known as the sixteen mantras. || 44 ||
44. Now, the name-mantras of the sixteen [deities] beginning with Dharma are stated, starting with the words "catuḥ" and so forth:
*Oṃ dhṛṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ dhṝṃ jñānāya namaḥ*. They are to be understood in this sequence and so on.
One should place this short [syllable], together with the *soda* and *amṛta*, above the *praṇava*.
"Salutation to the Unmanifest Lotus"—this is the mantra known as the Unmanifest Lotus (*avyaktapadmaka*). || 45 ||
45. The letter *ba* is short. *Oṃ bsuṃ vyaktapadmāya namaḥ*.

To each of the positions of the sun, moon, and fire, and to their respective mandalas, there is the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and the word *namaḥ* at the end; these are the mantras for the three mandalas. 46.
46. Oṃ, homage to the solar mandala. Oṃ, homage to the lunar mandala. Oṃ, homage to the fiery mandala. These are the mantras for the three mandalas.
The word *soma*, which refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is possessed of emanation;
this three-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as "the Illumination of Consciousness" (*cidbhāsanā*).
47. "I am that"—this is the mantra of the manifestation of consciousness (*cidbhāsana*).
Thus, twenty-one mantras known as the *āsanas* have been declared.
This collection of mantras, ending with the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭhapūjā*), has been proclaimed by me. 48.

48. Regarding the "twenty-one": it should be understood that there are sixteen mantras for the lords of the foundations (*ādhāra*), one mantra for the unmanifest lotus (*avyaktapadma*), three mantras for the mandalas, and one mantra for the manifestation of consciousness (*cidbhāsana*).
Now listen to this supreme secret, the most profound mystery.
This collection of mantras, beginning with Kṣetreśa, is capable of crushing all obstacles. || 49 ||
Then, having condensed Garuḍa, Kāla, and Anala into a single form, one should mark it;
[with the mantra]: "Salutation indeed to Kṣetrapāla, together with Savyāpin and Ādideva. (50)

50. Oṃ kṣmrāṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. This nine-syllable mantra of the Lord of the Field begins with the Praṇava (Oṃ). For Śrī, the Tārā (Oṃ) follows "anutā" (anu tā), and the Tāraka (Oṃ) is at the beginning. 51.

51. Oṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī. This is the six-syllabled mantra of Śrī. Now hear of others, beginning with Caṇḍā; the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ) alone should be placed at the beginning, followed by *Sacañcalānalas*. 52. [The mantra is: Oṃ Sacañcalānalas Tāraḥ. (Note: *Sacañcalānalas* refers to the syllables *Sa-cañcala-anala*, which together form *Sacañcalānalas*). Thus, the mantra becomes: Oṃ Sacañcalānalas Oṃ. This is the six-syllabled mantra of Śrī. Now hear of others, beginning with Caṇḍā. The syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ) alone should be at the beginning.
52. Oṃ croṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa. "Obeisance to Caṇḍa" is indeed the supreme mantra of seven syllables.
With the sacred thread (pavitra) and fire (anala), it becomes the *tāra* (Oṃ); however, at the beginning, it should be used alone. 53.
53. Oṃ proṃ, obeisance to Pracaṇḍa.

The mantra "obeisance to Pracaṇḍa" consists of four yugas; it is preceded by the eternal fire (*saśāśvatānala*) and the *tāra* (Oṃ), and should be used in its entirety from the beginning. 54. [The mantra is: Oṃ proṃ pracaṇḍāya namaḥ. This Pracaṇḍa mantra consists of four yugas; it is preceded by the eternal fire and the *tāra*, and should be employed as a whole from the start.
54. Oṃ jroṃ, obeisance to Jayā.
"Obeisance to Jayā"—this is the description of the sage (ṛṣi) of Jayā.
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), conjoined with Varāha and Anala, is likewise pure and directed toward the quarters. 55.
55. Oṃ Vroṃ, obeisance to Vijaya.
Obeisance to Vijaya; he is this four-yuga form of Vijaya.
He is Govinda, possessed of fire, the wielder of Māyā, the all-pervading one, who reaches the end of the Praṇava. 56.
56. Oṃ grīṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā. Thus, "obeisance to Gaṅgā" is the description of the sage of Gaṅgā;
it is balanced, with fire, subtle, all-pervading, and ending with the Praṇava (Oṃ). 57.
57. Oṃ yrīṃ, salutation to Yamunā.
[C omits four lines from here] This [mantra] "Salutation to Yamunā" belongs to Yamunā; it is of the Yamunā-lineage and pertains to the four ages.
Śaṃkara, together with Agni and Soma, is all-pervading and resides at the end of the Praṇava.
58. Oṃ śrūṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi.
And thus, "Obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi" is this nine-syllabled mantra;
it is pure, accompanied by fire and the moon, all-pervading, and ending with the Praṇava (Oṃ). 59.
59. Oṃ prūṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi.
Thus, "obeisance to Padmanidhi" is this nine-syllable mantra.
This is the group of ten mantras, beginning with Kṣetreśa and ending with Padmanidhi. 60.
Now hear the established doctrine beginning with Gaṇeśa and the collection of mantras:
Govinda, joined with the pervasive *ūrja* syllable, ending with the *praṇava*. (61)
61–62. *Gaṇeśādīti*: This means the mantras beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Ādisiddha. *Oṃ gūṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*.
Then [follow] Govinda, Vaikuṇṭha, Pavitra, and likewise Sragdhara.
Śaṅkha is situated in the source of the world; he is Nara, Time, and possesses the power of emission.
This nine-syllable mantra is indeed proclaimed as belonging to Gaṇapati; having joined Govinda six times with the pairs beginning with Gopa and Nanda. (63)
63. *Oṃ gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*—thus it should be understood, and so forth.
The ritual arrangement of its limbs (*aṅgakalpti*) shall be joined with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and the rest.
It is conjoined with fire at the beginning and end, and endowed with the pervasive *māyā*. 64.
64–68. Oṃ kṣrīṃ hrīṃ sryāṃ stryāṃ a-kṣa (the letters from the vowel *a* to the consonant *kṣa*) vāgīśvaryai namaḥ. (p. 122)
At the end of Tāraka, one should contemplate Garuḍa, and at the end of that, Tārikā;
[one should contemplate] Soma, endowed with the pervasive [syllable], enriched by the letters Ra, Śaṅkha, and the other deities.
O Slayer of Bala, one should remember this fourth seed-syllable, which is enriched by Vairāja, Anala, and Śaṅkha, and joined with Gopana and Vyāpin. (66)
O Śakra, one should remember the fifth [letter], which is of the color of the moon, supremely wonderful,
beginning with the immeasurable primordial deity, and ending with the color of Garuḍa.
Having recited according to the text, then "namo vāgīśvaryai":
this mantra of sixty-one syllables is known as the mantra of Vāgīśvarī. (68)

The wise practitioner should correctly perform the arrangement of the limbs, conjoined with the internal seed-syllable, by means of the fourth seed-syllable which is distinguished by its concealment and other qualities.

69. *Oṃ sryāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth are the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*). "Jāti" is said to be the limb. One should place [the mantra] at the beginning and end of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which is distinguished by concealment and so on. One should then arrange the *praṇava*, the word *namaḥ*, and the *jāti*. 70.
One should then arrange the *praṇava*, the word *namaḥ*, and the *jāti*.
The three *praṇavas* joined with the pervasive [syllable], followed by *ga* together with its vowel, and then "namo gurave"—this is renowned for the worship of the Guru. (71)
71–73. Oṃ oṃ oṃ guṃ, obeisance to the Guru. Oṃ oṃ oṃ paṃ, obeisance to the Paramaguru.
Oṃ oṃ oṃ pāṃ, obeisance to the Parameṣṭhin. At the end of the triad of Praṇavas, [the syllable] pavitra is joined with vyāpin.
Salutation to the supreme teacher; he is indeed renowned as the teacher of teachers. || 72 ||
At the end of the triad of *praṇavas*, the syllable *pa* joined with bliss (*ānanda*), followed by "to the Parameṣṭhin" and then "namas"—this is the mantra of the Guru of the Guru of Gurus. (73)
One should place the five *tāras*, which are the delight (*āhlāda*), in the ether (*vyoma*) above the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
and the two *kālānalas* below that, above the Lord of All Worlds (*sarvalokeśvara*).
74–75. Oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ ṭhmrūṃ svadhā pitṛbhyo namaḥ.
Having formed the *piṇḍa* with the syllables uttered in their proper sequence, followed by *svadhā*, then *pitṛbhyaḥ*, and finally *namaḥ*—this is the king of mantras for the assembly of ancestors.
Ṣaṭtāra, Ādideva, then Vyomavān, then he who is Kevala;
Rāmavān, Damana, and then salutation to the Siddhas. (76)

76-77. Oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ oṃ āṃ, salutation to the primordial Siddhas (Ādisiddhas). This mantra belongs to the Ādisiddhas whose souls are permeated by the Blessed Lord; it is capable of crushing obstacles and [bestows] the Kṣetreśa and other [attainments] up to the status of an Ādisiddha.
The practitioner of mantras should perform worship even before the time of propitiation. Now, O Vāsava, hear the characteristics of the mantras of Lokeśvara. (78)

Having condensed the vital breath (prāṇa), the Lord of the Earth (dhareśa), and bliss (ānanda) as they abide in their sequential order, and having placed them together with the ether (vyoman) at the crown of the head, one should then offer salutation to Indra. || 79 ||
79. Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to Indra.
This mantra dedicated to Indra has been declared; now learn from me those beginning with Agni (Pāvaka).
One should form the *piṇḍa* [mantra] by means of Prāṇa, Anala, Ānanda, and Vyāpin as well. 80.
80–81. Oṃ hrāṃ agnaye namaḥ; Oṃ hyāṃ yamāya namaḥ.
Together with the deities such as Prāṇa and Kāla, and also with Vyāpin, one forms the *piṇḍaka* [mantra] as "Oṃ agnaye namaḥ" and likewise "Oṃ yamāya namaḥ."
That pervasive Lord Nara is the Piṇḍa; salutation to Nirṛti.
This is the mantra for the Lord of Yātudhānas; now learn that of the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa). || 82 ||
82. Oṃ nḷṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti. The wise one should unify the breath, Varuṇa, bliss, and the pervasive [element].
"Obeisance to Varuṇa" follows; this is the supreme mantra of Varuṇa. 83.
83. Oṃ hvāṃ, salutation to Varuṇa.
The wise one should concentrate upon the subtle vital breath, as well as bliss and the pervasive [self]. "Salutation to Vāyu"—this is the supreme mantra of the Vāyava [tattva]. 84.
84. Āṃ hyāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. (p.
123) One should merge Gharma, Aṃśu, Varuṇa, and Ānanda together with Vyāpin.
"Salutation to Soma"—thus the Saumya Mantra has been proclaimed. || 85 ||
85. Oṃ ghvāṃ, obeisance to Soma. One should then sequentially condense the Sun, Vitality (ūrj), Space, and the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrin).
Following this, "obeisance to Īśāna" is the supreme mantra of Īśāna. 86.
86. Oṃ hCūṃ, obeisance to Īśāna.
One should sequentially merge the vital breath (prāṇa), Vaikuṇṭha, and Bliss with the Pervasive One (Vyāpin).
Then, "obeisance to Ananta"—this is the mantra of the King of Nagas. 87.
87. Oṃ hṇāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. One should sequentially merge Prāṇa, Kharva, and Ānanda with Vyāpin.
"Obeisance to Brahmā"—this is the supreme mantra of Brahmā. 88.
88. Oṃ hravāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. First, hear [the mantra] for all weapons: the Praṇava (Oṃ) comes first; then, [the mantras] for Anala, Janmahantṛ, Pradhāna, Anala, and Urjaka.
89. [Oṃ hravāṃ] to Anala, [Oṃ hravāṃ] to Janmahantṛ, [Oṃ hravāṃ] to Pradhāna, [Oṃ hravāṃ] to Anala, and [Oṃ hravāṃ] to Urjaka.
89. Oṃ rjmrūḥ, homage to the Vajra.
By means of emission (sarga), one should condense the designation; "Homage to the King of Mantras, the Vajra.
Having removed *ūrja*, that position is adorned with *māyā*. 90.

91. Oṃ ḍmūḥ, obeisance to Daṇḍa. Having then condensed [the mantra], this is the name-mantra for Daṇḍa: *namo daṇḍamanu*.
The nourisher of the universe, Time, the Lord of the world, the Supreme Lord. || 92 ||
92. Oṃ ṭmrūḥ, salutation to the sword (khaḍga).
Having then condensed [the syllables], this is the mantra of the sword, with the name "Salutation.
These condensed [syllables]—Candra, Īśa, Anta, and the others—are the deities who perform creation. 93.
93. Oṃ ṭśāḥ, obeisance to the noose (pāśa). This wondrous mantra of the noose is "obeisance to the noose. These [syllables]—Ajita, Varuṇa, Ānanda, Sṛṣṭikṛt, and Piṇḍita—are thus combined. 94.
94. Oṃ jvāḥ, obeisance to the Banner (dhvaja). Thus the mantra of the Banner has been proclaimed: "Obeisance to the Banner.
One should merge [the elements] with the fierce fire of the Supreme Self, joined with the creative power. 95.

95. Oṃ hrūḥ, obeisance to Musala. After "obeisance to Musala," this Manu is the excellent Mausala; he is the fire, the destroyer of birth, the rising sun, and the one endowed with the power of creation. 96.

96. Oṃ rjuḥ, obeisance to the trident (śūla). Having then condensed [the mantra], this is the name-mantra for the trident: "Obeisance" (namaḥ), followed by the trident-mantra itself, joined with Karāla, mounted upon fire, accompanied by odana, and conjoined with Sṛṣṭikṛt. 97.
97. Oṃ kroḥ, salutation to Sīra. Having then condensed [the mantra], this is the name for Sīra: *namaḥ sīramanu*. [Then follow] Varuṇa, Nara, and Gopana.
The creator of emanation is joined with light. || 98 ||
98. Oṃ vnāḥ, homage to the lotus. [c: omits five lines from here] Having then condensed [the mantra], this is the name-mantra of the lotus: *namaḥ padmamanu*.
The Praṇava precedes all [mantras]; now listen to the mantra of Viṣvaksena. || 99 ||
One should sequentially merge Anala, Prāṇa, and Lokeśa with Vyāpin; likewise, one should sequentially merge Varuṇa and Bhūdhara with Vyāpin.
100. Oṃ rhūṃ vauṃ, salutation to Jñānada. This *piṇḍa* [mantra] is the giver of knowledge; thereafter follows the king of mantras of Viṣvaksena.
This mantra, beginning with the *praṇava*, is declared to be the accomplisher of all aims. 101.
But that which was previously devoid of vitality shall have its limbs fashioned by that [deity] who is joined with bliss and the rest, and it shall be endowed with caste and mudrā. 102.
102. *Oṃ rhrāṃ*, salutation to the heart, and so forth. (p.
124) One should sequentially condense Soma, Varuṇa, and the vowel *ī* with the Pervasive One (*vyāpin*).
"Salutation to Surabhī"—this mantra is preceded by the syllable *Tāra*. (103)
103. Oṃ svīṃ, salutation to Surabhī.
This [mantra] of Surabhī is declared for the purpose of fulfilling all enjoyments.
At the end of the two *praṇavas*, one should extract the two *tārikās*. 104.

104–106. Oṃ oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, you who abide in the supreme abode, who are intent upon the application of grace toward me, descend here, O bestower of desired accomplishments, O you whose body is mantra! Oṃ hrīṃ, salutations, salutations! This is the invocation mantra (āvāhanamantra).
Thereafter, by my grace, Paramadhāmā remains here;
and when she is intent upon her spiritual practice, she likewise descends here.
In this case, there are three [elements]: the desired word, "siddhide," and "iti"; then, within the body of the mantra, there is "tāra," "tārā," "namo," and "namaḥ. (106)
The forty-five-syllable mantra is for the purpose of invocation;
it consists of the Praṇava, the Tārikā, and the three vital breaths (prāṇas), followed by the three Vyāpina mantras.
107–108. *Oṃ hnīṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ hnīṃ hnīṃ hnīṃ, accept this, this, this, this arghya, svāhā*, and so forth.
After the three *tārikās*, one should utter the word "this" (*idam*) three times.
Take the wife of Vahni (the fire-god), and let this mantra for the granting of enjoyment be recited by you.
First, one should extract the syllable Oṃ; then Viṣṇu conjoined with Vyoma (Ha);
thereafter, one should extract Tārikā (Hrīṃ); and again, Viṣṇu in that same manner. 109.
109–110. *Oṃ īṃ hnīṃ īṃ haṃsapare parameśe prasīda oṃ hnīṃ namaḥ*.
This is the mantra for propitiation (*prasādana*).
Then, [one should recite] the *prāṇa* (the letter *ha*) joined with *vyoma* (the letter *kṣa*) and accompanied by the name of Soma (the letter *sa*).
Then, recite "Obeisance to Para and Parameshvara," followed by the Praṇava. || 110 ||
The *tārikā* and the word "namaḥ" at the end constitute this mantra for propitiation: first the *praṇava*, then the *tārikā*, and then the word "bhagavatī. (111)
111–112. Oṃ hnīṃ, O Blessed One, embodiment of the mantra, attain your own place, attain it!
Forgive me, forgive me! Oṃ hnīṃ, obeisance, obeisance! This is the mantra for dismissal (*visarjana*).
O embodiment of the mantra, now attain your own place; that is the pair [of mantras].
Having uttered "Forgive me" twice, [one should say] "Tārā, Tārā, homage, homage. (112)
"Vaisarjana-manuḥ," "so 'yam"—these are the leaders of the mantras, O tiger among gods, which have been declared as the removers of all sins and impurities. (113)
And these are not to be given at all to those who are non-devotees, to those of cruel deeds, to atheists, to the wicked, to rogues, or to those who delight in deception. (114)
Especially for my devotees who are believers, who practice faith and self-restraint,
who are intent upon my path (or my ritual action), who are refined, who have approached me in truth, and who rely upon firm faith.
This should be spoken to Vaiṣṇavas, but it must not be spoken to others.
He who speaks otherwise out of delusion, greed, or passion,
or even out of ignorance or childishness, goes to many hells in succession.
Therefore, having observed the entire collection of qualities as they have been described,
one should explain them according to dharma and in accordance with justice to a person who has approached for instruction.
He who speaks unrighteously, or he who asks unrighteously— both of them go to a terrible hell for an inexhaustible time. (119)
119. "In this regard, he who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two perishes or incurs enmity. Thus the word of Manu is to be noted.
Even if one were to give the earth filled with jewels, O Vāsava...
Indeed, it must not be given to one who is not a devotee, nor to one whose character has not been tested.
"Thus, O Śakra, your devotion toward me is exceedingly great;
and because you have approached me here in truth, I am well-pleased with you. (121)
The treasury of mantras for the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga) and so forth has been revealed;
now, listen as I speak to you concerning the treasury of mudrās. 122.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Mantras of the Limbs and Sub-limbs," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (33)
Chapter Thirty-Four:
Śrī (Glorious Fortune)
O Vāsava, I shall now proclaim the treasury of mudrās belonging to the treasury of mantras, by the mere knowledge of which the highest accomplishment of mantras is attained. (1)
The mantra-practitioner should indeed bind the mudrā at the time of bathing in the midst of water,

at the time of performing the self-assignment (nyāsa), at the conclusion of worship, during the ritual of the maṇḍala, during the act of adoration, during the arrangement of mantras, over the arghya vessels, and during the meal.
And at the conclusion of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), while the mantra remains within [the disciple]. || 3 ||
For the destruction of those who cause harm and for the pacification of all obstacles,
one should place the two hands facing each other, well-joined and fully extended.
Facing each other, with the middle fingers joined and the others extended,
they are formed by the group of arms directed toward one another.
Renowned as Mahāśrī, she bestows all auspicious fortune;
she is the liberator from all defects and the granter of swift accomplishment.
For a being who has become insentient, there is the awakening characterized by spiritual emergence;
having extended the left hand upward with the fingers spread apart and held steady. (7)
The fingers should be made with their tips slightly contracted; the thumb should be like a bridge, joined face-to-face with the middle finger among the other fingers.
One should bind the Śakti-mudrā, which bestows happiness, facing the heart.
O highly fortunate one, these mudrās are praised by the multitude of yogins. (9)
But as for me, who bestows affection upon you while you abide in the supreme subtle state, behold my Yonimudrā, which abides in the gross state. (10)
Having placed the two hands facing each other, well-joined and well-stretched out,
the two ring fingers should be reversed at the middle and at the base on the back.

Having placed [the hands] at the roots of the two index fingers, one should conceal them with those [fingers]; the tips of the two middle fingers and the tips of the remaining [two] [are joined], with the pair of little fingers in front.
With the backs of the hands joined together, the middle of the palms should be raised;
one should place the tips of both thumbs upon the first joints of the two middle fingers.
This mudrā, known as the Great Source (Mahāyoni), brings all under control;
this mudrā of mine has been demonstrated in three ways for the sake of the threefold [practice]. || 14 ||
The mudrā of Śakti, known as Sūkṣmā and so forth, is described therein as a modification:
starting from the forefinger, each finger is placed one by one like a bridge against the thumb. (15)
O Purandara, these four mudrās are to be known as being formed by placing [the fingers] upon the fingers [of the hands], belonging to my Śaktis, such as Lakṣmī and the others. || 16 ||
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā—these goddesses are indeed my powers (śaktis).
One should form a fist with the right hand. (17)
O best of gods, having placed the left thumb raised within [the palm] facing toward the heart—this is the Hārda-mudrā, which increases the intellect. (18)
With all the fingers extended, one should touch them with the thumb;
this shall be the Śairasī mudrā, which brings about the presence of the mantra. || 19 ||
Forming a fist with the index finger extended upward is known as the Śikhā-mudrā; it strikes fear into all malevolent beings.
Indeed, for the sake of destroying defects and obstacles, one should always display this;
therefore, at the outset, one should diligently display it within the sacrificial chamber. (21)
When joined with the mantra, it effects the destruction of all obstacles;
the branches should be positioned at the tips of both hands.
By joining those two [hands] together at the middle from the wrist-binding upwards, this *vārmaṇī* mudrā is formed; with it, one should touch both shoulders. (23)
It is indestructible by the assembly of the wicked, by spirits, vetālas, or yogins;
and at the time of performing the rite, this [mudrā] must be diligently bound by the mantra-practitioner.
The fingers of both hands are interlaced and closed, with the backs of the hands turned inward;
the two index fingers are joined at their tips, hollowed out, and raised. || 25 ||
With the two thumbs joined at their bases and crossed with one another,
this Cākṣuṣyā mudrā should be formed near the eyes.
One should snap the threatening gesture (tarjanī) with the thumb in the ten directions;
then, with both hands, one should quickly gaze intently with the eyes.
Known as the Astramudrā, it terrifies the enemies of the gods;
this is designated as the Ṣaṇmudrī of the limbs, which accomplishes all aims.
Now, observe these mudrās of the three pairs of Upāṅgas:
one should join all four fingers situated on the right side together. (29)
One should place the thumb across at the base of those [fingers];
this is the mudrā for the secondary limbs (upāṅgas), and with it, one should touch each respective station.
Now, observe the mudrās for the ornaments and weapon-mantras:
the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger are held in the center of the hand like a fist.
Then, with both hands behind, the wise one should join those two fists together;
having extended the pair of index fingers, he should then join their tips in front.
Having reversed the tips of the thumbs, one should place them between the two index fingers;
this mudrā is named Kaustubhī. Now hear of this Mālā-mudrā.
Rotating from the neck down to the feet along both shoulders with the two index fingers,
one should simultaneously perform this auspicious gesture consisting of a forest garland (vanamālā).
One should interlace the eight fingers, excluding the thumbs, with their tips joined together; one should let the two arms hang down—this is the *vanamālikā* (forest-garland) mudrā.
With the two thumbs joined at the sides and the fingers remaining spaced apart,
this is the Pāṅkeruhī mudrā, which increases nourishment and good fortune.
With the right hand turned upward, one should join the tips of the thumb and the little finger like a bridge; the remaining three fingers should be closely joined together like a triple creeper.
This mudrā, with the fingers formed in the shape of contracted hoods, is the Pāśa (noose). First, one should form two fists with the thumbs positioned at the back of the hands.
One should place the left hand face down and likewise the right hand upon its back;
this is the mudrā born of the tortoise and fire, beginning from the support-power (ādhāra-śakti).
Having bent both the ring finger and the index finger of the downward-facing left hand,
one should place them well-positioned upon the back of the middle finger.
One should make the middle finger straight and facing downwards;
then, one should firmly extend the little finger and the thumb.
This is the Anantāsana-mudrā; just as this Ananta has arisen, so too is this proclaimed as the foremost among all āsana-mudrās. (42)
The supreme power is undivided, designated as both the support and the supported;
it is the Kūrma-mudrā, and its unfolding is the Ananta-mudrā, whose essence is Nāda.
This should be constantly cultivated in this manner during the practice of sitting:
one should clasp two fists together in front with both hands. (44)
With just three fingers— the two index fingers and the two thumbs— one should join the tips together and then bring that pair together once more. (45)
This is that earth-mudrā (pārthivī mudrā), which sustains all beings;
the wrists are joined together, with the tips of the nails of both hands touching.
The ritual actions should be performed with the fingers interlaced, facing one another; then, one should move them rapidly between the tips of the thumbs when they are unsupported.
One should make a deep cavity between the two hands,
resembling a hollow;
this is the Padmī mudrā of the Ocean of Milk, as previously demonstrated.
Having first kept the two hands unjoined, one should then join them:
the mouth to the mouth, and likewise the two index fingers and the two middle fingers in succession. (49)
Then, after that, one should place face to face at the mouth with the two ring fingers, and place the pair of thumbs upon the tips of those respective fingers.
This set of four mudrās corresponds to the fourfold [set] beginning with Dharma;
likewise, there is a set of four mudrās for the fourfold [sets] beginning with Adharma.
The *pādmī* mudrā for the lotus situated above that has been previously described;
however, for the right hand, it consists of the joining of the index finger and the thumb. (52)
Having performed that binding, one should then gradually expand it and again make each individual cluster of branches fully upright. (53)
This is the mudrā of the three abodes; now hear that which pertains to the manifestation of consciousness:
one should make the two hands clearly extended, forming the shape of an añjali.
This supreme seal, consisting of pure being (*śuddhasattva*), is the manifestation of consciousness;
it is the thirty-second among the seals, which destroys all defects. (55)
O Śakra, the ornaments, weapons, postures, and so forth have been shown to you;
now hear the ten mudrās of the Kṣetreśvara and others. || 56 ||
Having grasped the collection of fingers with both hands, one should forcefully press them together while keeping the two thumbs raised. (57)
O Purandara, this is the mudrā of Kṣetrapāla, which destroys all that is evil; it is formed by placing both hands flat and close together.
Having placed the entire group of fingers slightly bent and positioned at the middle,
one should gradually bring the two thumbs to a state of clarity.
This mudrā of the seed-syllable of Śrī has first been described to you;
having raised the index finger from the left hand, which is born from the seed-syllable of Caṇḍa.
One should display that very same [mudrā] from the right hand for Pracaṇḍa;
by raising the middle finger from the left hand, it belongs to Jaya.
It is proclaimed to be from the seed-syllable called Vijaya on the right;
know that the Gāṅga [mudrā] is formed by placing the ring finger from the left as before. (62)
O Indra, the mudrā of the seed-syllable of Āmuṇa is said to begin with the right [hand];
the mudrā of Śaṅkhanidhi is said to be the little finger of the left hand.
Likewise, from the right hand of Padmanidhi,
that little finger [is to be grasped] with the right hand in a fist together with the thumb.
One should press the ring finger and the little finger of the left hand;
then, the middle finger should be joined to the back of those fingers whose tips have been exerted with effort. 65.
And just as it is seen, it has the form of a hanging hand, with the little finger of the left hand positioned not too close to the fist. (66)
One should contemplate it as being like fangs with the side of the right thumb;
the left thumb and the other [the index finger] are slightly oblique in their movement and clearly defined.
Just as those two auspicious [tusks] of Gaṇeśvara are seen, resembling the ears of an elephant, this is his seal which brings about the destruction of all obstacles. (68)
First, having joined the wrists of both hands together,
the pair of middle fingers should be raised from the front part so that they meet.
Likewise, one should bend the pair of ring fingers and similarly the pair of middle fingers;
having doubled the thumbs, one should incline them downward.
One should touch [the body] very gradually until [the hands reach] the surface of each respective pair of palms.
One should clearly and very widely separate the two thumbs in that manner, facing toward oneself.
With both little fingers held level on the ground,
this is the Vāgīśvarī mudrā, which bestows the power of eloquence.
Having joined the two hands together in front and extended them,
they should be placed against the forehead while the head is bowed.
This mudrā, which clarifies the mind, belongs to the triad beginning with the Guru;
having placed the right hand face upwards, one should then [arrange] the group of fingers.
Having slightly contracted the joined thumb and then extended it, one should then gradually and slightly turn it sideways and subsequently face it downwards. (75)
This mudrā is remembered as that which brings eternal satisfaction to the host of ancestors;
it always brings greater pleasure to the ancestors than a thousand śrāddha rites.
One should always strive to make [the hands] beautiful during the worship of the ancestors;
one should place both palms turned upwards at the region of the navel.
Placing the right hand on the back of the left, this is the mudrā of the assembly of the Siddhas;
it consists of the right hand being well-touched while turned away from one's own body.
One should form the left hand turned away and hanging down;
these two mudrās, granting the boon and fearlessness, are known as those of the World-Protectors.
With each individual mantra, one should sequentially display the vajra and other [weapons], joined with the power (śakti) called Astra, as previously described. (80)
Now, regarding the weapons of the World-Guardians (lokapāla) when worshipped here in sequence:
the three fingers beginning with the little finger of the left hand are placed in the middle of one's own palm. (81)
Of those [fingers], the index finger should be raised from behind the thumb;
then, with the right hand, it should be placed at the region of the bridge of the nose. (82)
Having formed a fist with only three fingers as before, one should double the index finger and place it upon the tip of the thumb. (83)
The right arm of Viṣvaksena is raised like a wheel being cast;
this is the mudrā that severs all bonds.
One should slightly contract the right hand and bring it toward the heart;
with the two thumbs separated and clearly visible, this is known as the mudrā for invocation.
Both [hands], with fingers slightly apart, should be shaped like the edge of a sword; having made the two thumbs straight like a staff, one should gradually form the fist-bind. (86)
One should perform this mudrā with the little fingers and so forth during the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
Having made the two hands open and joined together, facing downwards— || 87 ||
Likewise, having joined the two little fingers and the two thumbs so that they are well-locked together,
the pair of middle fingers should be placed on the backs of each other's hands.
Having placed the pair of ring fingers and likewise the pair of index fingers [into the palms], this mudrā named Kāmadhenu fulfills all desires. (89)
Know, O Vāsava, that the application of mudrās is of two kinds:
the internal, which has the form of consciousness, and the external, which is born of speech, action, and mind. (90)
Whoever, knowing the ritual procedure, binds the mudrā according to this method,
by him all this is sealed for the sake of achieving the state beyond rebirth.
Thus, O Purandara, the entire host of mudrās has been taught to you in this hymn;
now hear the supreme procedure for bathing, which pertains to the section on propitiation.
Misfortune, accompanied by internal and external impurities, takes possession of one;
for the purpose of warding it off, bathing is prescribed in all cases. (93)
Furthermore, that bathing is threefold—by means of water, mantra, and the sequence of recollection; O Puruhūta, this is remembered as being a hundred times superior in each successive stage.

The bath performed at sacred fords such as Puṣkara is considered to be "water-born"; however, the bath prescribed by the scriptures of the Blessed One is a hundred times more efficacious than that. 95.
Therefore, the power of mantra, arising from the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of mantra, is a hundred times greater than that;
and supreme meditation, consisting of pure consciousness, is a hundred times greater than that.
At the outset, one should perform the water-bath according to the general rule; thereafter, according to the specific rule. This, indeed, is the procedure for the specific [bath]. (97)
Having first bathed with earth and water, one should afterwards apply fragrant unguents and the like;
that constitutes bathing, which removes impurity, and one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should first perform the filling with twelve repetitions using the *tāra* [syllable];
one should hold it for sixteen repetitions and then release it with twelve.
By means of the sequences of exhalation through the left and right nostrils,
he destroys the impurities previously accumulated within the channels of the vital breath.

Then, having become composed of reality, one should purify the impure aggregate of elements— which consists of six sheaths and is devoid of essence— by means of the power of meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
One should lead all the principles, beginning with earth, into their respective causes— indeed, up to the Unmanifest— gradually by means of the concentrations (dhāraṇās). 102.
Then, one should merge oneself into me like milk into milk;
having subsequently become composed of Lakṣmī, one becomes identical with Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained the bond of concentration with a mind of pure essence,
that which is the state of being the Supreme Self is considered the supreme power.
Remaining in that very state, one should burn one's own body with the fire of dhāraṇā—
the mass of radiance of the flame of consciousness, which is the abode of sparks of light.
Then, one should meditate on a blazing mass [of light] falling upon the head;
thereafter, the true essence (sattva) residing within becomes tranquil, while rajas and tamas are reduced to ashes.
Having dispelled the ashes consisting of rajas and tamas by the wind of awakening,
[one emerges] from the great ocean of consciousness-bliss, which is a mine of qualities free from waves.
One should contemplate the nectar-water spreading forth by way of creation;
nourished by that, one should bring that internal essence to the state of a body.
That pure [soul] assumes a physical body through the path of its own creation;
this is declared to be internal purity. Now, hear about external purity.
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) using the limbs according to the sequence to be described.
When external purification has thus been accomplished, one should then perform the ritual bath (snāna).
Holding a portion of earth consecrated by mantras in his hand,
he should place it three times upon the tips of his left hand— at the base, the middle, and the tip.
First, one should perform the purification of the sacred sites (tīrtha) by means of the nature of the power of consciousness;
that sacred site is said to be threefold, consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme self.
It satisfies the entire gross world in its gross form;
however, through its subtle essence consisting of the quality of goodness (sattva), it satisfies the ancestors along with the gods.
One should lead [the disciple] to fitness for my ritual through the supreme form of bliss;
therefore, purification must first be performed by oneself at a sacred site (tīrtha) according to the vision of the scriptures.
Having drawn forth the Vaiṣṇava essence of the sacred sites by means of the retention of knowledge,
and having brought it to dissolution within me, who am Śakti;
In the great abode of consciousness and bliss. || 115 ||
Having burned away the gross [body] with the fire of knowledge, one should fill it with the bliss of Brahman;
then, having projected the Vaiṣṇava essence into the sacred bathing place by means of the power of knowledge.
The wise practitioner should, in due order, recollect the weapon-mantra, the root-mantra, and the limb-mantras within the sections of the earth at the beginning, middle, and end.
One should cast the weapon-mantra in the ten directions for the pacification of all obstacles;
one should cast a portion accompanied by the root mantra into the middle of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
By that, may there be the immediate presence of my mantra-body;
with that portion of earth which is the mantra of the limbs, one should smear the limbs. 119.
Having entered the midst of the water, one should indeed submerge and emerge again;
then, with both hands, one should first sprinkle upon the head the water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited.
The second [offering] is with the root mantra (mūlamantra), and the third with the limb mantras (aṅgamantra).
Then, having reached the bank and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly, one should proceed.
One should perform the ritual bath with mantras according to the rules through the rite of nyāsa;
thereafter, one should perform the meditative bath (dhyānasnāna) with a mind that is fully attentive.
Having meditated upon the supreme Lakṣmīdhara, who is self-abiding and lotus-eyed,
one should recollect the stream of water born from his feet as it falls upon one’s head. (123)
With that [water], one who is composed should flood the entire body, both internally and externally, either one by one, two by two, or three by three. 124.
According to one's capacity and at the appropriate time, one should perform the threefold bath;
with the names of the deities who consist of me, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, having gratified the sages, one should gratify the ancestors at the end of the *svadhā* offering.
Having thus performed the bath, one should [worship] the Lord of Mantras situated at the sacred ford.
Then, having drawn [the breath] in by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should meditate within the heart;
and having mentally drawn in the weapon (astra) that was previously stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having gathered the requisites for the sacrifice, one should proceed to the sacrificial hall—whether it be self-established, composed by a seer, or prepared by perfected beings (siddhas). || 128 ||

Or else, a celestial chariot (vimāna) according to the Pāñcarātra system, complete with all auspicious characteristics, fashioned by humans or conceived within the minds of those whose inner selves are purified by me. || 129 ||
A beautiful lotus bank, a secluded and enchanting place, or a solitary garden adorned with sacred trees. || 130 ||
Or a delightful sandy bank, spread out upon the sand, free from wind and the touch of water, and devoid of nearby defects. (131)
Or rather, wherever the mind finds pleasure, there one should go by the power of the mind—
to the supreme mantra residing in the center of the heart, whose form is awakened bliss.
Not looking toward the horizon, observing silence, and restraining the vital breaths, he should reach a favorable position there and exhale through the tip of the nose. (133)
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the mantra of the Self, who is the Supreme Soul and whose form is like a blazing fire,
as well as the external weapon-mantra, one should strike the earth with the foot.
Meditating upon me, the one supreme goddess Lakṣmī who consists of mantra,
one should reach a solitary place and assume a beautiful posture.
On *darbha* grass, on a hide, on a cloth, or on a plank made of sacrificial wood, having saluted Hari, me, and the lineage of gurus with devotion alone; || 136 ||
Having received their mental command, bowing his head to them,
he should perform all mental rites through the meditative absorption of gnosis (jñānasamādhi).
Whatever action is performed with wisdom through the meditative absorption of Brahman,
that becomes composed of pure being, imperishable, and eternal.
Since the defects characterized by passion and darkness are dependent upon external objects,
therefore their purification must also be performed through action, mind, and speech.
Therefore, having firmly established that pure knowledge which arises from consciousness and is thus uniquely free from defects and permeated by meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). || 140 ||
"One should indeed perform actions that are ultimate through the cultivation of knowledge.
Thus, O Lord of the Gods, the procedure for bathing has been correctly proclaimed to you.
Hereafter, I shall describe to you the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and other matters. 141.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rules for Bathing," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The Thirty-Fifth Chapter. Śrī said:
Listen to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) for the sake of accomplishing the internal sacrifice and other rites.
O Śakra, listen with an attentive mind as it is being told by me. || 1 ||

1. *Bhūtaśuddhi* (Purification of the Elements) consists of the practitioner’s offering of the constituent parts of the natural body—flesh, fat, bone, and so forth—to the Lord after contemplating their dissolution; and subsequently, the maintenance of a body commenced from Him, preceded by the manifestation of a non-natural being composed of the Lord, arising from His presence.
It is seen to be set forth in the various independent treatises (*svatantra*) as extending from *prakṛti* down to earth (*pṛthvī*),
and also as beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*.
The purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is here said to be the process of making [the self] one with the Divine through the intellect.
2. Regarding the phrase "beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*": by the letter *ka*, the earth (*pṛthivī*) is grasped, and by the letter *bha*, primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The wise know that within this group of eight principles, beginning with earth and ending with primordial nature, there are two forms distinguished as gross and subtle. 3.
That which exists within the range of the eye as a spatial configuration is described as gross form (sthūlarūpa); that wherein the nature of its cause resides is called a subtle element (tanmātra).
This reality consists of sixteen principles, divided into gross and subtle;
one should assign the objects, the senses, and their functions to their respective places therein.

One should bring to rest the triad beginning with the nose (the sense organs), the triad beginning with the anus and genitals (the organs of action), and the triad beginning with smell (the objects of the senses),
by means of the reverse order within the group of subtle elements starting with earth.
Just as waves in the ocean subside due to the wind,
so do the surges of the sense objects and senses subside within the great ocean of the primary elements.

7. He describes the previously mentioned dissolution by way of illustration: "Like waves... [ṅ: omits this line]. With a perfectly composed intellect, the wise man should cause that [mind] to set in the same manner; he should bring both the mind and the ego-sense (abhimāna) to rest within the ego (ahaṃkāra). 8.
One should suppress the vital breath, the mental resolve, and the intellect within the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva);
one should then lead the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—into primordial nature (prakṛti).
That which is the unmanifest cause consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth—
that triad of qualities, as well as its manifestation and Māyā, is indeed threefold.
10. Regarding "the three qualities" (traiguṇya): their sequential designations as *pradhāna*, *avyakta*, and *tamas* constitute the conventional usage of the Upaniṣads.
Thus, these ten should be understood by the knowers of reality (*tattvavid*) as the primary natures (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, through the distinction between gross and subtle, they are traditionally recorded as being twenty in number. || 11 ||
For the gross primordial natures (prakṛtis), these ten mantras are traditionally taught;
they consist of their respective names, ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, preceded by the *Tārikā* and beginning with the *Dhruva*.

12. Regarding "those respective designations": first the *praṇava* (oṃ), then the *tārikā* (hrīṃ), then the designations of the elements (*bhūtasaṃjñā*), and then *huṃ phaṭ*. Altogether, the mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ pṛthivyai huṃ phaṭ*. However, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* (10##–p.

Having recollected *māṃsa*, *medas*, and likewise *rasa*, the syllable of space (*vyomākṣara*), and again the three syllables, as well as the two "beyond the supreme" (*parāt paradvaya*) adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*. || 13 ||
Of the ten subtle forms, those nine beginning with Śakti are traditionally taught;
they are the powers known as "Supreme" (parā) which constitute the living principle within bodies.
Thereafter, one should meditate upon these—Śakti and the others—along with Māyā and Vyoman;
likewise, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti. (15)
15. He states the names of the powers of the individual soul (jīva-śakti): "Nivṛtti," and so forth.
16. "Śāntyatītābhimānā," "Prāṇā," "Guṇavatī," as well as "Guṇasūkṣmā" and "Nirguṇā"—these are recorded as their names in successive order.
Having joined these mantras— consisting of the ten seed-syllables along with Fire, Viṣṇu, and the Half-moon— to that [group], one should know them as residing within the presiding deities.
17. "Vahni," and so forth; the meaning is that one should join [the syllable] *rīṃ*.
Fragrance-gloriousness (*gandhaśrī*), taste-gloriousness (*rasaśrī*), form-gloriousness (*rūpaśrī*), preceded by touch-gloriousness (*sparśapūrvikā*);
sound-gloriousness (*śabdaśrī*), conceit-gloriousness (*abhimānaśrī*), and breath-gloriousness (*prāṇaśrī*), preceded by the qualities (*guṇapūrvikā*). 18.
18–19. Gandhaśrī and the others are names of the Śaktis;
likewise, by the designations Guṇasūkṣmaśrī and Māyāśrī, there are also presiding Śaktis within my group of ten.
Having thus understood the preparatory ritual (parikara), one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
First, one should perform the purification of the site (sthānaśuddhi); listen now as to how that is done.
20. "Before" means prior to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

Having meditated upon me as possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns at the time of universal dissolution and resembling smokeless embers, one should burn the earth with the fire issuing from my mouth. 21.
Then, one should sprinkle water produced from one's own mouth, which has the luster of ten million moons;
in this way, the purification of the site is accomplished. Now, listen to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
22. Thus, he describes the reanimation of the place that has been thus consumed by fire, beginning with "Soma":

"Having drawn forth the Earth—square, level, yellow, and marked with the thunderbolt sign—from within the body using the mantra, one should cause her, who resides in her own place, to enter into dissolution. (23)
23. "With the mantra": here, the mantra is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* (10.17) as *ślāṃ*.

Then, one should cause that [substance] consisting of mere fragrance to dissolve by means of its own seed-syllable; having established it within myself as the locus of empowerment, one should cast me into the external water. 24.
Having dissolved that deity—which resembles a half-moon and is marked with a lotus—into its own place by means of its own mantra within the mere essence (rasa), [one should proceed]. (25)
Having established that [deity] by means of the mantra, one should cause it to dissolve into me;
and having cast me into the external fire, this is the sequence for the rite of *āmāya*.
26. Regarding "by means of the mantra": in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, the mantra is stated as *ṣvāṃ*. Regarding "*āmāyam*":
the meaning is "up to *māyā*.
Everywhere, the wise one should not perceive [the mantra] as singular; rather, he should perceive it as the dissolution of my power (*macchakti*).
For just as one might pour clarified butter into milk that has been produced by churning it; || 27 ||
