27. "Not one" means that one would not perceive dissolution as being of a single kind everywhere; this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
He states that very point by way of an illustration: "Just as," and so forth. The phrase "produced from the churning of that" is an epithet of the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
Furthermore, there is clarified butter elsewhere in milk, and in that clarified butter there is also something else.
In this way, the wise man should remember that the power of primordial nature (prakṛti) is the presiding controller.
Thus, meditate upon me as that supreme power, endowed with the nine powers,
who extends to the end of the qualityless state,
and who acts as the substratum of Māyā.
Having led that [power] beyond the tenth, he established the eleventh power,
which consists of great agitation, is the embodiment of prosperity, and takes the form of the manifestation of the cosmic array (vyūha).
Having passed that eleventh day, one should cast that twelfth day— which is of the nature of the Supreme Self, indefinable, and beyond comparison— into me. (31)
Thus, having drawn up that supreme power, which consists of all twelve and extends to the end of the *dvādaśānta*, one should remember it within me, who am composed of phonemes.
32. Regarding "the end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*): the traditional convention is that the place situated twelve finger-breadths above the head, beyond *māyā*, is called the "end of the twelve.
It has the luster of ten million fires, moons, and suns, and its eyes, head, and mouth face in all directions.
My subtle body, consisting of color, takes the form of a continuous stream of rays. || 33 ||
33. He enters the body consisting of color—beginning with "Agni" and so forth. "In a continuous stream of flows" means having the form of a continuous stream of nectar.
It is fully equipped with all requisites for the benefit of all living beings.
In ancient times, she arose from Viṣṇu, blazing like lightning from a cloud.
Śakra said:
"In this body, in which locations should the dissolution be performed in sequence? And what are the forms of the earth and the other elements within the lotus? Please tell me. (35)
Śrī said:
The place of the earth is remembered as extending from the knees; that of water is up to the waist; the place of fire is up to the navel; and the place of air is at the heart. (36)

The station of the ether extends as far as the ears; that of the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) extends as far as the navel; the station of the Great Principle (mahat) extends as far as the eyebrows; but that which is beyond the ether is remembered as the supreme.
Then, at a distance of one span from the tip and four finger-breadths from the crown,
in that place of Prakṛti, the remainder of the fingers is twice eight (sixteen).
38. He states the location of *prakṛti* in space with the words "thence" (*tataḥ*).
The abiding place of *prakṛti* is four finger-breadths above the head. Above that, at a distance of sixteen finger-breadths, is the abiding place of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
On the eleventh day of the twelfth fortnight, there is the abode of the glory of the syllable of reality;
the great earthly form should be square and marked with a vajra. (39)

39. Beyond that, at a distance of eleven finger-breadths, is the locus of Māyā; beyond that, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, is the locus of Śabdabrahman—this is the distinction. This very place is called the "End of the Twelve" (dvādaśānta).
It is remembered as being like a half-moon, white, marked with a lotus, and consisting of water.
A triangle marked with a svastika and red in color is said to be fiery (taijasa). || 40 ||
Smoke-colored and joined with six dots, circular, is said to be the wind element;
likewise, the space element is like the color of collyrium, remembered as the supreme, consisting of a mere disc.
41. "The mere image" means that there is only the mere image of Pradhāna and the other principles, not their colors and so forth.

Thus, when the withdrawal of the principles has been performed, [the breath] has emerged from the cavity of the heart, is supported by the rope of knowledge, and follows the middle channel, Suṣumnā. 42.
Having raised [the breath] upward as far as the knees by means of a series of steps of power (śakti),
one should cast it into me, who abide in the center, within the row of the Dvādaśānta.

43. "One should cast it into me": when there arises the possibility of conceiving the burning of the living being (jīva) residing within the body upon the contemplation of the burning of the body, the casting of that living being into the Goddess is taught in order to prevent that. And at the end of that [is] a great lotus endowed with a thousand petals.
It possesses the radiance of ten billion suns and the splendor of ten million koṭis of moons.
44. At its end, in the *dvādaśānta*, there is the "Great Lotus" (*mahāpadma*). The word "exists" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
45. Abiding within the nature of both fire and moon, that body of mine is composed of great bliss; it is beyond description or comparison, consisting of pure consciousness, and is supreme.
From this [source], the excellent river of Jīvānanda flows forth in its various branches;
having brought this [individual] bliss, it leads one to the state consisting of Great Bliss (mahānanda). (46)
46. Then, one should burn this body of mine—which resembles a heap of salt—with great, high-velocity, and purely conscious flames issuing from my mouth on all sides. 47.

47. When the *jīva* has been led out from the body and brought to the *dvādaśānta*, the contemplation of the burning of the body is described by the words beginning with "tataḥ. The phrase "resembling a heap of salt" is a description of the body from which the *jīva* has departed.
The fire that burns is joined with the sixth vowel (*u*), is accompanied by the nasal drop (*bindu*), and is moist.
One situated between the *tārikā* and the *nati* should be understood by means of the eye of the scriptures. || 48 ||
48. The mantra for the fire that burns [impurities] is stated: *hrīṃ rthūṃ namaḥ*.
Thereafter, one should flood [the body] with nectars arising from my mouth, which consists of the Moon.
The subtle Moon, together with space, is traditionally taught as the means for the nourishment of the *piṇḍa*. 49.

49. Furthermore, he speaks of the contemplation of the attainment of a non-ordinary body with the words "consisting of the moon" (*somamayyā*). Regarding that, the mantra is *ṭyaṃ*. However, in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, it is stated as *vsaṃ* (10.78):
"By me, who am desirous of creating, consciousness (*saṃvit*) has been raised up and embraced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
One should remember those empowered Śaktis residing within me, who consist of the phonemes. || 50 ||
Then, one should sequentially recollect how that which begins with Māyā and ends with Earth was emanated by those Śaktis, preceded by the impulsion and the gateway.

51. That which is the extremely subtle state of Pradhāna when Māyā predominates, the followers of the Upaniṣads call "Tamas. From that, the formation of the body (piṇḍa) occurs, radiant with the manifestation of the instruments [of perception]. Having thus produced the great body consisting of pure Śrī, 52. [He] produced the great body consisting of pure Śrī.
Then, by means of the previously mentioned path, one should bring the heart and the life-force (jīva) [back].
The three phonemes, having become a single mass, are fire, moon, and the lunar orb.
53. He states the *jīvamant*ra: "become a body" (*piṇḍabhūtāḥ*). [The seed-syllable] *rṭsaḥ* is thus produced. It is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* as well:
"The *tārikā* situated between *na* and *ti* is declared to be the *jīvamant*ra.
One whose form is purified should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra in this manner. 54.
For the sake of qualification in worship, for the joy of the worshippers, for the eradication of Daityas and other obstacles, and for the sake of victory; || 55 ||
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate five times that wooden plank or similar object which was previously placed upon the ground, according to its respective mantra,
in the form of the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), the Earth (Urvī), the Ocean of Milk (Dugdhābdhi), and the Lotus (Ambuja).
One should meditate on Tārkṣya situated there, established in the nature of the seed-syllable Kharva.
57. "The seed-syllable *kha*": the meaning is that it has the form of the letter *kha*.
Having sat there and meditated upon the form of Lakṣmīśa as his own self, and having bound the directions with the *astra-mantra*, he should do so again and again in this manner. 58.

58. According to the principle stated as "one's own form" (svarūpa) means "the self" (ātman), the meaning is "consisting of one's own nature. Having fashioned a rampart resembling a thicket of reeds outside the seat, one should enclose that place, together with the rampart, with the armor-mantra (kavaca).

59. With the *astra-mantra*, "phaṭ" for the sake of power and for the weapon; likewise with the *kavaca-mantra*, "hūṃ" for the sake of strength and for the armor. One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in such a way that one becomes invisible to those stationed in the sky.
Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa), one should then perform the ritual placement on the body (deha-nyāsa).
One should place the Tārikā on the thumb, and its Śaktis on the fingers;
one should then place Lakṣmī on the index finger and Kīrti on the middle finger.
One should then place Jaya on the ring finger (anāmā), Māyā on the middle finger (madhyamā), and [the remaining syllables] on the little finger (kaniṣṭhā).
This is the sequence of that mantra, known as Satāra and Tārikā, which is the ultimate reality. (62)
62. "With six stars," and so forth; the meaning is: in the manner beginning with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī with the two index fingers," and so on.
63. Then, having assigned the five limbs in sequence starting from the little finger and proceeding to the heart and the rest, one should contemplate the eye-mantra upon the limbs.

One should place the Kaustubha gem on the right surface, and likewise the forest garland (vanamālā) on the other; one should also place a lotus in the middle of the right side and on the left surface as well.
64. Now, the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*)—beginning with "the Kaustubha," etc.—is as follows: "In the center" means on the palm.
One should place the goad on the right [hand] and likewise the noose on the left palm.
By this procedure, one should first perform the ritual placement on the hands. 65.
Now, listen to how one should perform the placement of the limbs (vigrahanyāsa):
from the head down to the feet, and from the feet up to the head.
66. He describes the placement of the body (dehanyāsa) starting from the head down to the feet, and starting from the feet up to the head—beginning with the words "ā mūrdhnaḥ.
[The *tāraka*... [Note: B omits five lines from here; C omits four lines from here. The *tāraka*.
Then he should place Tārikā upon his left shoulder, and both Lakṣmī and Kīrti, who resemble moonlight, upon his right.
One should place Jayā in the right hand and Māyā in the left hand;
the heart-mantra between the nostrils and the head-mantra on the crown of the head.
Then, having placed the *śikhā* at the site of the crest and the *kavaca* on the two shoulders,
one should place the *netra* in the two eyes and the *astra* on the palms of both hands.
The best of mantra-knowers should properly place the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) and the three ages (triyuga) on the navel, the back, both hands, the thighs, the knees, and the feet.
Placing the Kaustubha gem upon his chest in the center and the forest garland (vanamālā) on his shoulders,
and placing lotuses in his two hands, he should repeat the mantra in two ways.
Then, [one should place] the noose in the left hand and the goad in the right hand;
the gross and subtle Tārikā [should be placed] at the feet and in the joints.

She is indeed the leader of the mantras, residing at the *brahmarandhra* at the end; with each placement during the ritual installation (*nyāsa*), one should meditate upon the mantra which resembles moonlight and sunlight. (73)
The practitioner should mentally contemplate the mudrās in each respective place;
he should recollect that everything is pervaded by the supreme goddess Tārikā. (74)
When all the mantras have been arranged everywhere like one who has emerged from a flood, and when this synthesis of mantras following diverse paths has thus been performed; (75)
Just as the waters of the ocean become one in form,
so too, when the ritual placement (nyāsa) has been performed in this manner, the practitioner of mantra becomes manifestly identical with Lakṣmī.
Relying on the power born of meditation, one shall partake in all offices of authority;
and for the meditator, the manifestation of all supernatural accomplishments arises. (77)
With his limbs thus placed, he may remain fearless even in a region crowded with the wicked;
he shall conquer untimely deaths and all calamitous afflictions.
Having placed his limbs according to the rule with a mind conforming to the scripture, the mantra-practitioner should meditate upon me, the Supreme Goddess, as that very body composed of mantra. (79)
"I am that Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; I am the eternal Lakṣmī"—a yogi who possesses such a state of being is never born again. (80)

Thus, O Śakra, this purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) has been described by me according to the truth; now I shall speak of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga); listen to that in its true essence.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Purification of the Elements," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The Thirty-sixth Chapter: Śrī— O Śakra, that which consists of the bliss of Brahman is [attained] through ultimate enjoyments.
This sacrifice, which resides within the heart, is known as the "internal sacrifice" (antaryāga). || 1 ||
Having assumed either the lotus posture, the svastika posture, or the yoni posture,
one should meditate upon the Śakti in the form of the Ādhāra between the navel and the genitals.
2. The locus of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) is described by the passage beginning with "in the navel" and so forth:
"The Goddess, who cannot be established by anything else, formless, and consisting of light;
above that, however, is Kālakūrma, stainless and of radiant form. 3.
3. "Above that" means in the upper portion of the *ādhāraśakti*.
[One should meditate on] the Supreme Lord in the form of a tortoise, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
and above him, O King of Nagas, [one whose] face resembles the full moon. 4.

4. "Of him" means upon the tortoise. [He saw] Him who is higher than the highest, possessing a thousand hoods, whose eyes were rolling with intoxication, and whose hands held the discus and the plow. 5.
Above that is the goddess Vasudhā, resembling powdered saffron,
her body variegated with gold and jewels, and her face and eyes serene.
6. "Above that" means above the seat of the Lord of Nagas (Nāgendrāsana).
One should meditate upon her as being at the level of the head with palms joined in *añjali*, contemplating the All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*).
[This is done] in a field divided into four parts situated between the navel and the genitals. 7.

7. "Recalling" (saṃsmarantīm) means meditating upon. In this way, one should recall these deities, beginning with the Power of the Foundation (ādhāraśakti). [Variant reading: "One should recall these deities, beginning with the Power."]
One should meditate on the Ocean of Milk at the navel, having a form as white as the kunda flower and the moon.
One should meditate upon Him who is filled with rays like streams, whose face resembles the full moon, whose form is profound, who possesses all forms yet is formless.
Then, one should meditate upon a lotus arisen from the interior of the Ocean of Milk,
having the appearance of a tranquil fire and the brilliance of the rising sun.
He has a protruding belly, is smiling, possesses white teeth and an auspicious face;
he has two arms and is perpetually encircled by various beautiful six-legged insects.
Endowed with a thousand petals, surrounded by a thousand rays,
and resembling a thousand sunbeams— one should place the seat upon its back. || 12 ||
12. "On its back" means on the back of the lotus. "One should place" means one should meditate upon what has been placed.
13. One should remember these feet of the seat—dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya—in their respective order, situated in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneyī).

13. The legs of the seat, beginning with Dharmajñāna, are to be known as being in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneyī). All of these have the form of Puruṣas; they are white and lion-faced.
Possessing great enthusiasm and great heroism, they exerted themselves in upholding me.
The opposites of dharma and the other [qualities] are to be known as situated in the directions starting from the east:
namely, adharma, ignorance (ajñāna), non-detachment (avairāgya), and lack of mastery (anaiśvarya). || 15 ||
15–16. The opposites—unrighteousness, ignorance, and so forth—are located in the directions starting from the east.
These have human forms and resemble the *bandhūka* flower.
They are situated between the east and the northeast, in the interval between the eastern and southeastern directions.
Between Vāta and Vāruṇī, in the intermediate direction of Pāśi and Vāyu,
there is the tetrad beginning with the Ṛgveda, which is yellow.
Having the form of a human being. || 17 ||
17. Yātavī is in the direction of Nirṛti; Pāśī Varuṇa is [there].
Between the directions of Īśāna and Soma, and between the directions of Vahni and Antaka;
between the directions of Rākṣasa and Antaka, and between the directions of Vāyu and Soma. 18.
The multitude of ages beginning with Kṛta, however, is dark in color and has the form of a bull-man;
all of these have four arms, and likewise hold their seats with two.
With their two hands joined in the añjali gesture, they bow to her as she sits upon her seat;
one should contemplate above them a supreme throne consisting of pure intelligence.
20. "By two" means by the two arms; this is the ellipsis. "With palms joined" means with hands folded in *añjali*. One should visualize an unmanifest white lotus above that, having eight petals.
Above that is the solar disc, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that is the lunar orb, with a radiance equal to ten million moons;
above that is the fiery orb, with a radiance of ten million times ten thousand fires.
One should remember these qualities—tamas, rajas, and sattva—in their respective order; for the *praṇava* and the *namas*, those specific designations are placed in the middle. (23)
23. One should know that the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire consist respectively of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*. "Oṃ, obeisance to the orb of the sun," and so forth, are the mantras.
These are remembered as the collection of mantras for the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with *sattva*.
Then one should offer the seat of consciousness (cidāsana), which has the nature of supreme egoity (parāhaṃtā).
When the space from the navel to the heart is divided into five parts,
one should arrange the sequence beginning with the oceans and ending with the seats using four of those parts.

25. Having divided the portion from the navel up to the heart into five parts, one should first meditate upon the sequence beginning with the Ocean of Milk and ending with the seat (*āsana*) within the first four parts;
by means of the fifth part alone, one should perform the visualization of the lotus-seat (*padmāsana*) and so forth.
But the elements [are placed] in the Ādhāra-śakti, while the group of subtle elements (tanmātraka) is in the Kūrma.

26. In the fifth part, however, one should meditate upon the unmanifest lotus. Regarding the location of the constituent elements (padārtha) in the aforementioned places, he says: "The elements," etc. This means the five gross elements.
Likewise, speech and so forth [are located] in Ananta, and the pentad beginning with the ear is in the earth.
One should meditate on the mind in the Ocean of Milk, and then on the ego-sense in the lotus.
Twice eight [sixteen] are the qualities beginning with dharma; the seat is also known as the intellect (dhī).
Above that is the unmanifest (avyakta), which is a pure lotus.
28–29. "The white lotus" means the unmanifested lotus (*avyaktapadma*).
For the qualities beginning with *tamas* have been said to consist of the three lotuses (*abjatraya*).
Some declare this [unmanifest] to be Time (*kāla*), consisting of the triad beginning with the primary elements (*bhūtādi*).
29. This is the meaning of "the unmanifest lotus. In the *Pārameśvara*, it is conventionally referred to as the "Wheel of Time" (*kālacakra*).
Others have declared that the seat of consciousness, called the Infinite (*ananta*), is the Person (*puruṣa*). [In some versions, it is called the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*)].
Some declare that above the seat of consciousness (cidāsanam) is Garuḍa. || 30 ||
O Lord of the Gods, the wise declare that mantra to be the ninth, consisting of *kha-rva-vyoma-anvita*, followed by *khagāsana* (or *khagānana*) and *moyuta*. 31.
31. "Khaṃ! Salutation to Kha-gānanā.
When the seat has been thus prepared in due order with these various mantras, [one should worship] Viṣṇu, the god who is the soul of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, the stainless one. 32.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
four-armed, clad in yellow garments, with eyes like the white lotus.
33. Herein is the expansion of the meaning of the Śruti text: "His eyes are like a lotus with petals as yellow as a young monkey's [bottom].
One should remember the risen Lord, who is of the nature of the vibration of one's own power (*svaśakti*).
Listen further from me as to how that which is to be properly meditated upon is exactly so. 34.
With the limbs [of the body] properly adorned with mantras, having well-arranged the internal seat,
and having displayed all the mudrās, one should contemplate the majesty of the mantra. (35)
The Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, which stands beyond darkness—
that splendor consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa through the state of possessor of power and power itself.
He is everything, yet transcends all; he is established in all things and is the sustainer of all.
He is a mass of consciousness and bliss, the embodiment of the nectar of the six perfect attributes.
37. Because He is the inner self of all and the controller of all, the meaning is that He possesses all forms.
38. As the inner self of all entities—distinguished as sentient or insentient, existent or non-existent, and so forth—He is the locus of each respective seat of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
38. That very point is stated by the words "as the inner self," and so forth:
"By some cause that is inconceivable and beyond questioning, it exists in two ways through the relation of the possessor of power and its power. 39.
He who is designated by the two—the word and the cognition—as "I" alone shall become Nārāyaṇa; and that which is his supreme egoity (ahaṃtā) [is he].
That Śakti, who possesses those attributes, is Lakṣmī; she is of the nature of existence.
She alone is the performer of all actions; that very Śakti expands the universe.
Having taken hold of the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān), just as moonlight clings to the cold-rayed moon,
she formerly desired to expand herself in the form of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).

42. By stating that the Goddess’s agency in the activity of the world depends solely upon the Blessed Lord and not independently, it is shown that there is no inconsistency in the Blessed Lord’s unique defining characteristic of being the cause of the world’s birth and so forth.
It is thus stated that the Impelling Agent (prayojaka-kartā) is the Lord of All, while the Goddess is the Impelled Agent (prayojya-kartrī). By this, his...
There is no room for the suspicion that the Pāñcarātra Siddhānta has entered into the Śākta doctrine.
Having first expanded herself, she then extends herself through the path of objects—that which is the primordial emergence, consisting of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman). (43)
Free from blemish—or, according to some, consisting of the blemish (kalaṅka)—and consisting of the path of the arts (kalā), it is experienced by those established in yoga.
Having the nature of a continuous stream of phonemes, that is called the path of phonemes (varṇamārga). || 44 ||

44–45. The path of *kalās* consists of the nature of the qualities such as the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). The expression "continuity of the stream" is the designation for the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*).
Having presided over the path of *kalās*, he [the Lord] then arises by means of the path of mantras, taking up the entire wheel of Vaiṣṇava powers.

45. The wheel of powers (śakticakra) consists of Lakṣmī and the others. It is supreme, consisting of light through the Supreme Self, characterized by bliss, and has been described to you previously in its threefold form. 46.
That very supreme form then proceeds by way of a subtle path in the form of the expansion of mantra; and that shall be shown to you.
That subtle [body], moreover, exists in three ways through its gross course;
and that which is the gross body is distinguished by its limbs and minor members. (48)
This is the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, augmented by the six divine qualities;
herein, indeed, the entire universe—both sentient and insentient—is to be contemplated. (49)
49. Here, however, the meaning is "in the gross form consisting of mantra. That which bestows various sovereignties is precisely the state of being their presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*).
The Vaiṣṇava form of the mantra should indeed be understood by the wise.
50. He describes the abiding of all principles within the mantra-form with the words beginning "tattat" (that and that), etc.:
"I am that lotus-born one who is the power (śakti) of that [mantra] which effects each respective effect.
Indeed, that which is the consciousness (caitanya) of the mantra, they declare to be the Person (puruṣa). 51.
The capacity for the production of fruit is called the natural form (*prakṛti-rūpa*);
that which is firm resolve is the quality (*guṇa*) belonging to the Great One (*mahat*). (52)
52. Of the Great (mahat), that is, of the principle of the Great (mahattattva).
140) That which is the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃyutva) among the mantras is indeed the quality of ego (ahaṃkāra).
The nature of mantras is mental, yet they serve as the cause for sensory cognition.
That which is the nature of sound within the mantra should be known as abiding in the ether;
trembling during the immersion into the mantra is said to be the form of wind. (54)
The state of being an illuminator in meditation, which consists of the mantra and is of the nature of light—
that satisfaction found in the true essence of the mantra should be understood as being in water.
"For that entity which abides in the mantra is said to be the earthly quality (guṇa).
In this way, the practitioner of mantra should clearly recollect the all-pervading extension of the mantra-nature. (56)
Soon, through the power of the mantra, he is born with that very disposition;
thus, by the power of consciousness, the pervasive energy of the Tārikā arises.
57. "By that state" means by that particular quality.
One should first perceive the throbbing [light] within the hollow of the heart-lotus, in the previously mentioned radiance of consciousness, like lightning in the sky. 58.

58. "As previously stated" means that which was stated on the occasion of defining the *ādhāraśakti* and so forth. One should contemplate the eternal, divine couple within the *tārikā*-form as it vibrates, within the *śabdabrahman*; understand this correctly. [Ā, B, C: correctly]
59. By this, it is stated that the Tārikā is of the nature of Śabdabrahman.

One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment, whose form consists of portions of the Sun and Fire, seated upon the seat of consciousness (cid-āsana), with eyes as broad as lotuses. 60.
60. To describe the mental worship of the Supreme Person known as Nārāyaṇa, he states his form with the words beginning "sūrya":
"Clad in yellow garments, with noble limbs, and adorned with a girdle and anklets."
Resplendent with necklaces, earrings, armlets, crowns, and bracelets.
Or with a luster conforming to the age (yuga), or resembling a dark blue garment;
the god bearing the conch and discus, bestowing the boons of granting wishes and fearlessness.
Like a gem filled with its own radiance, like the ocean in its profundity,
like the sun in its brilliance, and like the moon in its moonlight.
Having first meditated upon Hṛṣīkeśa, whose lotus-face is serene,
one should worship Puruṣottama with the eighteen offerings.
Then, O Vāsava, [one should worship] with the Puruṣasūkta,
with the Praṇava, and likewise with those consisting of twelve, six, four, and three syllables, as well as with the Jitatā.

65. "With the two-six," etc., means with mantras consisting of six, eight, and twelve syllables. "With the *jitantā*" means with the mantra in the form of the verse beginning "Victory is yours, O Lotus-eyed One" (*jitantaṃ te puṇḍarīkākṣa*).
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should then meditate upon Lakṣmī as pervading all his limbs.
Then, having worshipped with the nature of absorption (laya), one should thereafter invoke Lakṣmī.
Then, one should worship her as she sits upon the left lap of the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow,
with various offerings according to the injunctions prescribed in the scriptures.
Śakra said: O beloved of the gods, O goddess of gods, salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one!
Tell me the ritual procedure for the Puruṣasūkta and for the Tārā-mantras and others.
Śrī said: "The one god is Nārāyaṇa, the glorious, lotus-eyed;
I alone am the supreme Śakti of Hari, the accomplisher of all his tasks. (69)
We two, the lords of all, seated in the supreme ether for the welfare of all beings,
are always served by the wise.
A certain resolve arose in the hearts of those two:
"Let a means be sought for the deliverance of living beings. (71)
The great ocean of the Śabdabrahman is the splendor produced by the two of us;
from that which was thus churned, the nectar of these two hymns emerged. (72)
The hymn of Puruṣa and likewise my own hymn are intertwined with each other’s powers and adorned by each other’s syllables.

73. "My well-spoken hymn" (mama sūktam) means the Śrīsūkta. It is held that the Pauruṣa Sūkta has Nārāyaṇa as its seer and is unmanifest; whereas the other hymn which they call the Śrīsūkta has me as its seer. 74.

74. "Nārāyaṇa" means that Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *Puruṣasūkta*. "Madārṣakam" means that I, Śrī Rāma, am the seer. The five mantras beginning with the *praṇava* have been correctly demonstrated previously.
Now listen briefly to the sequence for their propitiation.
75. "Five" means Tārā, Anutārā, Ṣaḍakṣarā, Aṣṭākṣarā, and Dvādaśākṣarā.
Eighteen verses have been proclaimed in the Puruṣa-sūkta, the most excellent of hymns;
by means of those [mantras], beginning with the Praṇava, one obtains eighteen supreme enjoyments. 76.
One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation; these are recorded as eighteen:
the invocation, the seat, the offering of water (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and likewise the water for sipping (ācamana). || 77 ||
Bathing, clothing, along with an upper garment and a sacred thread; perfume, flowers, a lamp, incense, and the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka). || 78 ||
The offering of sweet betel-leaf with a moon, a handful of flowers at the feet, the gift of self-offering, and the contemplation of one's desired abode. (79)
79. The offering consists of food and other items to be presented. Indu is camphor.
She who is endowed with all auspicious marks, who consists of the support of all, who is eternal, and who possesses the six perfections in their entirety—she is the radiant form of Viṣṇu. 80.
This very form is called the "mantric form" (māntrī mūrti);
it is that which the practitioner of mantra causes the deity to accept through the mantras consisting of consciousness, by means of his own splendor.
That is called "invocation" (āvāhana) by those who have reached the further shore of mantra-knowledge:
Hari, by his very nature, brings forth all things, sentient and insentient, for the sake of performing auspicious rites.
82–83. "He causes [the deity] to descend" means he causes [the deity] to accept the body of mantra; this is the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*).
That upon which the universe presides is the seat (*āsana*); following that is the ritual action (*kriyā*).
My power, consisting of bliss (*ānandamayī*), is the deity by which [the seat] is nourished.
That very [power] takes the form of the arghya, ācamanīya, and so forth; thus one should contemplate the arghya and other offerings.
All worlds consist of water, and living beings likewise have that as their support.
[They have] a common basis. || 84 ||

84. "She herself" means that she is indeed the power consisting of bliss (*ānandamayi*). [The term] "watery" (*ammayāḥ*) refers to those things which are transformations of water, since it is stated that "in the beginning he created waters alone," thereby indicating that all worlds have water as their material cause (*upādāna*).

"Dependent on her" (*tadāśrayāḥ*) means those who maintain life by means of water. The statement regarding their being dependent on her is made because living beings (*jīva*) are not themselves transformations of water.
By the offering of water for the feet (pādya), it is illuminated that the remaining portion belongs to both;
thus, having divided my own form into six parts, I satisfy the Eternal One. 85.

85. The meaning is: "I alone, in the form of sound and the other [objects], propitiate the Blessed One. 86. By means of the five entities beginning with sound, and also internally through the sense of ego (abhimāna), one should worship with enjoyments—such as those pertaining to this visible world—that have been infused with the true state of being (sadbhāva).
One should propitiate the Lord of the World with a mind full of attentiveness;
those for whom joy is produced by the mere sight [of him] are considered "those who are pleased by the sight" (sāṃdṛṣṭika). || 87 ||

87. He describes the fourfold division of enjoyments (*bhoga*) by distinguishing them as those pertaining to the visible, those pertaining to ingestion, those pertaining to touch, and those pertaining to conceit—beginning with the words "by sight alone," etc. (p.
Beautiful women, lamps, vehicles, and the like—these enjoyments are auspicious and constantly satisfy one with their essences. (88)
Those things such as water for sipping and water for rinsing the mouth are called *ābhyavahārika*;
they are pleasant, delightful, soft to the touch, and satisfy the Unborn through their tactile qualities.
Those enjoyments consisting of tactile contact should be preceded by water for the feet, the guest-offering, and a seat;
some of those tactile enjoyments consist of perfumes, while others consist of food.
The winds and other elements are established in their respective orders; the last [elements] possess the fragrance of what is produced by ripening.
Indeed, those enjoyments consisting of sound, such as hymns, instrumental music, and song, are of the nature of sound.
Those who offer their palms joined in supplication out of wretchedness and so forth are known as those characterized by pride (ābhimānika).
Thus, through these four kinds of offerings, according to the path seen in the scriptures, || 92 ||
One should propitiate Puruṣottama with Ṛg verses preceded by the Praṇava;
at the end of the mantra, there is the assignment of the enjoyment, and immediately thereafter, satisfaction.
Having performed the preliminary rites and uttered the five [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava, I invoke Lakṣmīśa, the imperishable Supreme Self. (94)
94. "The five beginning with the *praṇava*," that is: Tārā, Anutārikā, the six-syllabled, the eight-syllabled, and the twelve-syllabled [mantras].
"May the divine Lord of the World, the Supreme Person Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, abide in this form out of a desire for my grace. 95.

Having thus brought [the deity] down from the flowers held in his joined palms onto his own form, and having prostrated and asked whether he has arrived well, he should ask for forgiveness with this mindset: || 96 ||
96. Having prostrated before my own form— that form imagined by myself— I then worship the Blessed One with a seat.
Having spoken the mantras and then uttered them three times, one should point this out with the words "iti" (thus). || 97 ||
Afterwards, having specified the name, one should express affection;
thereafter, "May the Blessed One be pleased," and after that, "Vāsudeva. (98)

98. *Sanāma* (with name): preceded by the designation of the names of the offerings in this manner—"this is for the feet," "this is for the water," and so forth—one should pour out the *arghya* on the altar; this is the sequence of the ritual procedure for the offerings (*bhoga*).
One should assign the seat, the *arghya*, and the other offerings among the *bhogas* according to their respective characteristics (*liṅga*). 99.
One should perform the invocation with the first [verse] and the offering of a seat with the second;
the guest-offering (arghya) should be given with the third, consisting of water mixed with flowers poured upon the head.
100. He states the application of the verses of the *Puruṣasūkta* for the bestowal of enjoyments, beginning with "by the first," and so forth: 101.
Water for the feet (*pādya*) should be given with the fourth verse, while water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) is offered with the fifth;
the ritual bath (*snānavidhi*) is performed with the sixth, and the lower garment (*paridhānaka*) with the seventh.
On the eighth day, the upper garment; on the ninth, the application of fragrant unguents;
on the tenth, garlands and ornaments; and on the eleventh, the lamp.
On the twelfth day, fragrant incense is offered; on the [next] day, the supreme honey-mixture (madhuparka);
on the fourteenth day, the meal offering (prāpaṇa); and on the fifteenth day, the anointing (anuvāsana).
103. That which is called *anuvāsana* is fragrant betel-leaf and the like, to be offered immediately after the meal.
On the sixteenth [day], however, there is prostration with a supreme handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*). And on the eighteenth, there is the offering of the rite of complete propitiation. 104.
One should provide water for bathing, garments, and lamps, as well as the act of offering water for sipping (ācamana);
first, the honoring (arhaṇa) should be performed by giving the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and food.
105–106. *Arhaṇa* is the ritual water-offering (*āpośana*). After the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should perform these with two *praṇavas*.
In this manner, during bathing and other such activities, one should act according to the requirements of place, time, and other factors.
The practitioner should perform the conduct like that of a king with the respective mantra;
there are three [elements]: intention, offering, and affection—each being a triad.
One should perform [the offering] with regard to all enjoyments, taking into account the place, time, and other factors;
then, being composed and having joined the palms in *añjali*, one should say: "Oṃ Bhagavan... (108).
Having said, "I shall honor you with a seat," one should then offer the seat;
having uttered the mantra, one should designate it by saying, "This is the seat. (109)
Saying, "Oṃ, may the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva be pleased," and taking the water for the arghya and other offerings, he should place it in the presence of the deity.
With these [waters] for the arghya, and likewise with these for the pādya, with these for the ācamanīya, and also with these for the arhaṇīya. || 111 ||
111–112. In the verses beginning with "ābhirarghyābhiḥ" (with these waters for the *arghya*), the qualifying term "adbhiḥ" (with waters) from the subsequent sentence must be supplied.

[The construction is: "with waters for the libation (*tarpaṇīyābhir adbhiḥ*)" and "with waters for bathing (*snānīyābhiḥ*). Regarding the intention of satisfaction, it should be stated as "these are the *arghya* waters."
The words should be uttered at the time of offering according to their respective genders; this is the sequence.
Furthermore, the preparation of the *arghya* and other offerings will be prescribed later in the section on the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*).
Thus, with the six [offerings] beginning with the garland, one should worship Janārdana, the God of gods, with five, four, three, or even two [of them]. || 114 ||
114–115. "By six"—this means by means of garlands, lamps, incense, honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), food offerings (*prāpaṇa*), and fumigation (*anuvāsana*).

Or, having worshipped [the deity] with even one of these, according to the requirements of place and time, and having meditated upon Janārdana, the God of gods, as being worshipped by me alone— ||| 115 ||
Like the ocean swelling at the rising of the moon, she will always be fully developed in all her limbs,
indescribable, incomparable, and infinite.
116. "Anaupamyām" means incomparable (*anupamā*). *Aupamya* is simply *upamā*; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*).
It is like the fragrance residing in a flower, or like the radiance residing in a lamp.
I am inseparable from the Supreme Person, such that it is impossible to extract me from him.
117. "To extract" means to cause [the deity] to emerge.

Meditating thus according to the rule, the mantra-practitioner should worship me through the yoga of dissolution (*layayāga*). Having sought out the procedure for the *Tārikā*, he should worship me, the *Tārikā*, by means of her. 118. [The verse continues: ...having sought out the procedure for the *Tārikā*, he should worship me, the *Tārikā*, by means of her.
Then, like lightning rising from a cloud, the wise one should mentally visualize [the goddess] emerging from Puruṣottama by His will.
One should contemplate me seated on the left lap of the God of gods,
perceiving us two as one and our nature as perfectly cool.
120. "Aikadhyam" means being of one kind.
One should take refuge in Janārdana with the two verses beginning with "hiraṇya-"; and one should console her with the following two verses: "Console me, who am as yet not separated from you. 121.
121. "With two *ṛc*s" means with the two verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇām" and "tāṃ ma āvaha.
And with the fifth [verse], one should enter while contemplating her with a serene mind, having understood the actual power of the *Tārikā* as previously described. 122.
O Lord of the Gods, the mantra known as "invocation" (āvāhana), when accompanied by its mudrā, should be recited mentally while performing inhalation (pūraka).
Then the God shall carry me upon his lap, the lap of the Supreme Self—
me, whose face is ever serene and who am endowed with all auspicious marks.
Resembling the interior of a lotus, lovely, with dark and long eyes, she was adorned with shimmering bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and earrings. || 125 ||
She possessed a deep navel and a slender waist adorned with three folds;
she had breasts that were very firm, solid, high, full, rounded, and dense. || 126 ||
Her mass of curls was overspread by a swarm of hovering bees;
her bimba-like lower lip was slightly reddened, and her teeth were like bamboo seeds and pearls.
127–128. Her teeth were like white lotuses; she wore a shining forehead-ornament (lalāṭikā) shaped like a half-moon upon her brow;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks, and her hair was black and curled.
128. *Lalāṭikā* means a forehead mark (*tilaka*). [The suffix] *kan* is used in the sense of an ornament.
[She is] the bestower of boons, with hands holding lotuses, adorned with a garland of lotuses, embraced by the left arm of Viṣṇu, and with her lotus-hand resting upon his shoulder. 129.
Carrying a divine cluster of blossoms in her left arm,
she may have hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, or alternatively, she may hold a noose and a goad. (130)

Having meditated upon me, who am seated in the half-svastika posture, adorned with a shimmering crown, and facing [the practitioner], one should bring forth my eternal form as the embodiment of the mantra.
131. The *svastika* is a particular type of posture.
With the root mantra and all other mantras as before, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon my body, omitting the placement on the hands. 132.
Then, with a truly respectful mind, one should offer flowers, the arghya water, a lamp, incense, garlands, and ointment, as well as water for the feet and water for sipping.
Then one should perform prostration with the eight limbs, mental utterances of "Victory!",
and the mudrās that were previously shown.
Welcome to you, O lotus-eyed one; take up residence in my proximity, O lotus-like lady, and accept this mental worship, which is conceived according to the true reality.
Having then obtained permission from me, one should perform the mental sacrifice with pure,
ultimate enjoyments produced by mere resolve.
One who is well-versed [in the teachings] should constantly worship me with external rites, as will be described further below, using enjoyments such as those of touch and so forth. 137.
Having performed the rites up to the final offering, one should then call to mind the Guru who performed the consecration—
whether he is living or deceased— and then offer everything to him.
The knower of mantras should distribute his wealth according to the portion for guests,
whether for those living or for those deceased, with a mind focused solely on the goal.
One should especially remember all the attendants who are about to be described,
as being merged within me, their cause, like seeds within a tree.
One should worship by means of the application of the respective mantras through the process of dissolution (layaprakriyā);
one should perform the auspicious oblation (homa) in the kitchen, which bestows the fortune of liberation.

Having churned the fire-drill of meditation within the triangular fire of the three qualities, which rests in the center of the support of the three qualities, and having brought down the fire of consciousness; 142.

Having consecrated [the fire] with the ritual purifications (saṃskāras) according to the wisdom to be described, the wise one [should act] toward the Vaiṣṇava Jātavedas situated within the substratum of the three characteristics.

143. "By means of the *saṃskāras*" means by the procedure of the *vaiṣṇavīkaraṇa*. Having taken the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) of Brahman that has flowed forth from the ether at the end of the *nāda*, one should then enter through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). 144.
Then, having gone to the fire-chamber and having prepared clarified butter according to the scriptures,
one should perform the entire ritual with the ghee and fire according to the prescribed rule.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the wise one should, with devotion and the mindset to be described, mentally renounce that ritual action within me through its underlying intention.
Whatever sequence has been prescribed for the external [practice], all of that should here be performed mentally,
or else with attention by means of collections of substances consisting of myself.
This mental sacrifice (mānasa-yāga), which pacifies all calamities and bestows all fruits, has been described; it should be performed until the fall of the body. 148.

148. Regarding the phrase "until the fall of the body": by this, it is stated that for the *paramaikāntin* (the most exclusive devotee) who is devoted to the five-fold daily duty (*pāñcakālika-dharma*), the worship of the Lord must necessarily be performed every day for each individual life; this constitutes his obligatory duty (*nitya-karma*).
Then, having diligently transformed all substances into the nature of mind,
one should perform the external ritual for the sake of pacifying the latent impressions arising from external objects.
Thus, O Śakra, my internal sacrifice (antaryāga) has been described;
now listen to me regarding the true nature of the external sacrifice (bahiryāga). 150.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Internal Sacrifice," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (36)
Chapter Thirty-Seven: Śrī— (p. 145)

If I am worshipped with substances situated outside the sacrificial altar and other locations, perceived through the contemplation of Me and serving as objects of enjoyment, that is traditionally known as the external sacrifice (bahir-yāga).
1. "By those perceived through my contemplation" means by those contemplated as being of my own nature. "Existing as objects of enjoyment" means existing as the instruments of enjoyment.
Impression (*vāsanā*) is said to be of two kinds, arising from external and internal causes.
The mental sacrifice is supreme; it drives away all internal [impurities]. || 2 ||
For the sake of purifying external dispositions, the external sacrifice is prescribed;
having established oneself upon ground prepared according to the scriptures, in that adorned pavilion. (3)
3. *Āśaya* means latent impression (*vāsanā*). It means [the place] purified by the contemplation of Brahman in the station of Brahman.

Regarding the station of Brahman: "Then, on the sacrificial altar of knowledge, endowed with all qualities, measuring eight cubits, or half of that, or even half of that, which has been prepared... 4.
One should stretch a perfectly white thread from end to end across the middle of the altar;
on both sides of that [thread], as well as in the middle and at the two half-middles.
Having made three marks, one should drive five stakes:
at the two ends, in the three middle points, and there, in the two penultimate points.
One should cause a stake to be placed at that point where the middle of the cord was reached;
then, having fastened two loops, one should bring them together at the central mark.
Having established marks there on both the right and the left,
and having fixed two [pins] in the middle, one should bring the center of the thread together.
And at the location above the mark, one should gradually place a gnomon (śaṅku) at the point where the middle of the thread reaches on both the right and left sides.
Having fixed one cord at the eastern point and the other to the south,
one should then form a clockwise corner by joining these two at the central mark.
One should likewise perform the rite for the northeast corner, and then, having released [the thread],
proceed further; in this same manner, one should do so for the west and south, as well as for the west and north.
Having released the two cords in succession, one should likewise form the other two corners;
then, for the sake of clearly defining that field, one should stretch threads in the four directions.
One should fashion a nine-petalled lotus within the sixteen-fold field of devotion by means of the four intermediate squares and the regions starting from the east.
13. This means it is divided according to the portions. Listen as to how the middle lotus should be made with eight petals:
one should rotate the field fourfold, excluding the eighth [part].
Outside. || 14 ||
The pericarp, the filaments, the junction of the petals, and the node are, respectively, each four parts in measure; one part is left out, and beyond that is the void.
Upon that [ground], one should cast eight threads situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions upon the lotus;
furthermore, one should likewise cast another eight threads within the intervals of those threads.
By means of the thread situated at the lotus-junction, the eight petals are arranged according to the sequence of the directions.
The lines of the innate ones are known as the multitude of sky-lines. (17)
In this very same manner, there should be eight other lotuses;
thus is the delightful, excellent city characterized by nine lotuses.
It should be constructed with an outer gate, endowed with the beauty of the *kāṇa* and other features;
it should be fashioned with four colors for the purpose of distinguishing the pericarp and other parts.
19. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the pericarp and so forth," the filaments, the joints of the petals, and the nodes are included.

[One should worship] on a flower-bed, or on a cloth that is very white or fumigated, or on a consecrated ground (*ahata*), or on a surface smeared with fragrant substances, or on a plastered altar (*sthaṇḍila*). 20.

20. Even a bed of flowers and the like, like a mandala, should be accepted as a place of worship. For the sake of the ritual, the mantra-practitioner should visualize a nine-petaled lotus; and according to the teachings of the scriptures, he should fashion an image situated upon the path of meditation. 21.
In a firm vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, free from cracks and other defects,
one should worship— or invoke— the deity within a full jar filled with curd, milk, or water.
Having visualized a new lotus upon a seat covered with excellent sprouts and provided with cloth bands and the like, the best of mantra-knowers should perform worship. (23)
In the jar, in the city, and likewise in the image, the mantra-practitioner should worship,
in due order, that which consists of all worlds, which is the supreme refuge of all the gods.
One should meditate upon the supreme city consisting of the support of all, which is a nine-petalled lotus;
then, it should be worshipped with the syllables of the Tārikā and the word "namaḥ," along with the water for honor (arghya) and other offerings.
Then, there should be four vessels made of gold or other precious materials,
filled with pure water, scented water, garlands, gems, medicinal herbs, and kuśa-grass water.

26. He clarifies what was previously stated regarding the offering of *arghya* and so forth with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*). One should place [the deities] upon the altar situated in front of the image, in the four corners, starting from the northwest (Vāyu) and ending with the southeast (Agni).
One should arrange it in this manner in due order. || 27 ||

27. "One should place [the vessels]"—the remainder of the sentence is "as the vessels for the *arghya* and so forth. Regarding "starting with the *yātavīya*": [it refers to] the northeast (*aiśāna*). "28. The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), uttering these mantras, should prepare in due order the *arghya*, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and the water for bathing (*snānīya*)."
One should clearly form the mental designations "this is the Tāra" in the center;
there, the arghya for the many deities should be prepared in a vessel in the middle.
29. The meaning is that [the offering] is performed according to the sequence beginning with "Oṃ, I present the *arghya*," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of manifold purpose":
its traditional renown is that it serves all purposes (*sarvārtha*). White mustard seeds, sesame, *dūrvā* grass, barley, and white rice [are the ingredients].
Water, milk, and fruit are declared to be the materials for the *arghya* offering.
Having filled the vessel with the Tārikā, whose body consists of a mass of nectar,
one should contemplate the wheel of mantras within that state which is free of parts (niṣkala).
Having first worshipped the partless (niṣkala) middle arghya with flowers and other offerings,
it should be properly meditated upon as having the nature of both fire (agni) and moon (soma).
32. That which is to be honored, having been honored; that which is to be cultivated, is to be meditated upon.
This is the first refinement; now attend to the second:
one should burn it with the masses of the sun’s fierce rays. 33.

33. "The second" means that which is to be described, consisting of burning, flooding, and so forth. Regarding the word "dahet" (one should burn): the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) is that one should burn it after first drying it.
Then one should extinguish what has been burnt with the rays of the cool full moon.
One should fill that [space] with the waves of the nectar-ocean of the bliss of Brahman. || 34 ||
Having consecrated [the water] with the primary mantras of those [deities], beginning with the Tārikā,
one should then take the water and place it into other vessels. (35)

35. "From that" means from the vessel filled with consecrated water. Alternatively, one may perform such a sequence of consecration for each individual [vessel] as well; from this, one should effect the filling of the vessels and the propitiation [of the deities]. 36.
36. "Pratisvam" means that each individual vessel for the *arghya* and other offerings [should be prepared].
A cow, the wish-fulfilling *Kāmadughā*, should be fashioned from one's own mantra;
she is Surabhi, resembling the snowy mountain (the Himalayas), standing in the supportless state (*nirādhārapada*). 37.
Having meditated upon it, one should display that mudrā, which resembles her breasts, with both hands smeared with fragrant paste and with a mind full of vigilance. (38)
Having sprinkled the mandala and the pavilion with water from the arghya vessel,
one should strike all the sacrificial materials without exception with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
39. "With the weapon [mantra]" means with the mantra *oṃ vīryāyāstrāya phaṭ*. Afterwards, one should sprinkle everything with the root mantra; all that shall then become an object of enjoyment.
Then, having paid homage to Viṣṇu and the lotus-born goddess seated upon his lap, [one should proceed]. 40.
40. "With the root" means with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). One should worship with the root mantra using loose flowers and so forth.
Then, taking the vessel for the *arghya* offering, [one should offer] flowers, incense, and unguent. 41.
41. "Āmukta" means not strung together, that is to say, sparse.

One should likewise offer a lamp and food offerings (naivedya), and then perform the sacrifice at the gateway. At the base of the udumbara tree, in the middle of the outer door— 42. [The text continues: ...at the base of the udumbara tree, in the middle of the outer door.
42. The word *udumbara* refers to the two wooden beams placed above and below the door.

However, one should worship the Field-Protector (Kṣetrapāla) stationed on the ground, endowed with meditation and other qualities, resembling a dark blue cloud, holding a staff in his hand, and possessing a massive body. 43.
43. He describes the form of the Kṣetrapāla: "Blue," etc.
The Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśvara) should always be meditated upon with his left hand forming a fist;
and here the mudrā should be displayed. Such is the procedure for others in due order. 44.
One should worship Lakṣmī, who stands above the door-post and is situated upon the Udumbara tree,
holding a lotus in her hand and seated upon a lotus.
45. The worship of Lakṣmī is now described—beginning with "above the door": Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are at the base of the southern and northern door-posts;
likewise, Jaya and Vijaya are outside and inside the door [respectively]. 46.
46. A *śākhā* is a wooden panel on the side of a door.
All deities beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Vijaya should be known as having four arms.
And those of great strength, bearing maces and discs, with conchs in their hands. || 47 ||
Indeed, threatening those who are not devoted and striving for the destruction of all defects—thus should the mudrās be meditated upon, worshipped, and displayed. (48)
48. "Those who are not devotees" means those who are not devotees of the gods.
Then, between the two branches, on the left and right respectively, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā immediately thereafter. 49.
49–50. She holds with both hands a water-pot filled from the sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*) at the two door-posts—the two wooden sections flanking the doorway.
Possessing the beauty of fresh youth, she is white in complexion and has a smiling face.
50. The forms of Gaṅgā and Yamunā are described by the verse beginning with "with the two hands" and so forth:
Gaṅgā is to be meditated upon as serene, with a face resembling the full moon;
such is the river Yamunā, who resembles a dark blue cloud. 51.
By that same sequential method, one should worship with offerings of water, flowers, and so forth, the two Lords of Treasures named Śaṅkha and Padma, who stand inside the doorway.
Those two lords of treasures (Nidhīśas) are to be meditated upon as seated upon treasure-vessels,
with stout bellies, tawny eyes, two arms, and being identical with the Blessed One.

Having thus performed the sacrifice at the door, one should then [offer] a flower facing [the deity] with the three fingers— the thumb, index finger, and middle finger— while reciting the Astra mantra.
Having taken [the water] and consecrated it with mantras, one should then visualize that wheel above it—
possessing sharp spokes, blazing in form, and raining down fire and thunderbolts. (55)
One who destroys the web of obstacles should place [the hand] within the sacrificial hall;
then, one should properly position the right index finger facing upwards.
Having remembered her, who is joined with the *śikhā* mantra and possesses a radiance flashing like lightning, he should enter the sacrificial hall while whirling that [garland] around.
One should sprinkle one's own seat with water from the *arghya* vessel using the *astra-mantra*.
Upon that, one should worship the mantric seat beginning with the *ādhāra-śakti*.
Wherever and whichever mudrā is to be displayed,
having sat down there, one should worship the Lord of Gods who resides in the heart.
One should cause that supreme light known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, which resides within the heart,
to pervade both eyes as an inseparable divine couple.

60. He should cause [the time] to pass; the meaning is that he should let it go by. Having brought everything to that state, he should look with steady eyes in the pavilion, on the altar, or wherever he wishes to sacrifice. 61.
Having worshipped with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and so forth, one should perform the visualization of the support and other elements;
thereafter, one should worship the [deities] such as Dharma, who reside in their respective directions.

Then, having meditated through yoga upon the lotus, the sun, and the mandalas, one by one in succession up to the seat of the deity (bhāvāsana), one should worship them with flowers and other offerings.
To the right of the deity situated in the maṇḍala, upon the maṇḍala, starting from the beginning of the Kṛta age and ending with the Vāyu-tattva, proceeding in order up to Īśa; || 64 ||
Having first divided the site into seven parts,
one should worship Gaṇapati seated upon a lotus posture (padmāsana) in its pericarp, within the petals of that lotus.
Holding a rosary and an axe with his two upraised arms,
while his first two hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

However, having thus meditated upon the mudrā— [B: "one should meditate upon that which is endowed with mudrās"]— the form of the Vyākhyā-mudrā arises from the contact of the index finger and the thumb in the hands that grant boons and fearlessness.
One should place the six limbs— plump, pot-bellied, stout, single-tusked, and elephant-faced— upon the filaments of the six petals of the lotus.
Having formed the mudrā, the wise one should worship it with flowers and other offerings using his own mantra;
thereafter, the wise one should worship the goddess Vāgīśvarī with her own mantra.
Seated upon a white lotus situated within the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire;
though liberated from all limiting adjuncts, she has yet assumed a formal manifestation.
[One should meditate upon] my own Śakti, who is directly of the nature of sound,
arisen first, having two eyes, two arms, white in color, and holding a conch and a lotus. || 71 ||
Then [he saw] the Guru and his Guru, whose ornaments and garments resembled shimmering waves of nectar, and those two who possessed forms established in the world.
Afterwards, one should worship the Guru who is the Supreme Preceptor (Parameṣṭhin) in his world-established form;
thereafter, the group of ancestors (Pitṛgaṇa), which is formless yet resembles a physical offering (piṇḍa), is to be worshipped.
Afterwards, one should worship the eternally perfected ones (ādisiddhas), who are intent on meditation upon the Blessed One,
peaceful, with eyes closed, possessing beautiful limbs, and preeminent in splendor.
Having obtained permission from them and having received their authorization in due order, he should subsequently worship me, who am seated upon the lap of the God of Gods, after having invoked me;
listen, O Lord of the Suras, to the various ways in which this is done. 75.
75. "Having obtained permission" means having kept in mind the permission received from the guru, the paramaguru, and so forth.
Thus ends the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra* [or *Śrīpañcarātra*; *B*: *Śrīpāñcarātre*].
The thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the External Sacrifice," in the Lakṣmītantra. || 37 ||
Chapter Thirty-Eight: Śrī—p. 149)
The god Nārāyaṇa alone is the embodiment of the six perfect attributes;
I am his supreme power, the one eternal ego.
For the sake of favoring practitioners, I have assumed a formal form;
listen now to how I, seated upon the lap of the God of Gods, am worthy of worship.
Having obtained permission from Gaṇeśa and the other deities, one should then invoke the Supreme Self residing within the heart,
who has been worshipped through the internal sacrifice; He is the full and tranquil possessor of the six attributes, filled by me with my own power.
Having worshipped Śakti and the others, one should utter that Tāraka three times and then utter the Tārikā three times.
Then, reciting the masculine mantra, one should invoke the Puruṣa,
the lotus-eyed one, who has four full and noble arms.
5. "The masculine mantra" means the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
One should slowly utter the supreme mantra with the *recaka* breath.
By way of the path situated between the two, Agni and Soma, from the nose and the belly.
One should cause Lakṣmīśa, the abode of divine power,
to descend from the unstruck (anāhata) plane, or from the feet, or from everywhere as that which has attained equanimity.
7–8. One should meditate upon the unstruck (anāhata) twelve-petaled lotus situated in the heart. One should then visualize the Lord emerging from it like a mass of lightning from a cloud;
seated upon the conceptual throne (bhāvāsana) in the midst of a handful of flowers, one should install him there.
Performing the four mudrās— namely, *saṃnidhi*, *saṃnirodha*, *saṃstambha*, and *sthāpana*— one should properly carry them out mentally.

9–10. The mudrās for *saṃnidhi* and the others will be explained immediately hereafter. Having placed the two hands together with palms facing upward, one should touch each respective little finger with the two thumbs; that is the *saṃnidhīkaraṇa* [mudrā].
Likewise, one should perform the cleansing (unmārjana) between the two middle fingers;
at that time, both stabilization (saṃstambha) and restraint (saṃnirodha) are accomplished.
Having formed two fists with the four fingers of both hands, and having turned them sideways toward each other, one should place them upon one another.
O Śakra, the placement of the two thumbs constitutes this *saṃsthāpana* mudrā;
one who is thus disposed becomes such [as desired] while reciting the mantra beginning with *Tārā*.
One should meditate on Hari as having arisen after the rites ending with the offering of water for the feet and the guest-offering (arghya);
likewise during the offering of the bath, ornaments, garments, and garlands, as well as during the act of adorning Him.
14. "At the [proper] time" (kālam): this means "at the right time. The accusative case is used here to denote duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

In other instances, such as during the sacrifices of enjoyment (*bhogayāga*), one should do so according to the requirements of each specific enjoyment. One should remember the deity’s scriptural form, full of compassion and well-facing [the practitioner]. 15.

15–16. "Compassionate" (*sānukampa*) and "well-facing" (*susammukha*) are epithets of Hari. When the body has been fashioned, he remains in that form [of compassion and presence]. Among the enjoyments being offered, there is a supreme power consisting of the Self (*manmayī*).
Standing there, one should visualize her as if she were actually present, just as Hari did when she was summoned;
then, one should offer a full añjali of flowers along with arghya water. (17)
17. "Of one who has been summoned" means one who has been brought into presence.

18. Having scattered [flowers], one should worship in sequence with the two hands joined palm-to-palm and facing downward upon the head, using the syllables *tāra* (oṃ), *tārā*, the two [syllables *tāre*], and *namaḥ* (or *manasā*).
One should perform the rites, both in brief and in detail, at the appropriate time, using flowers, water-offerings, incense, and ointments, along with the root mantra and other formulas. (19)
19. Anointing (lepa) refers to the application of sandalwood paste and other unguents.
One should subsequently worship Śakti—who is complete in all her limbs, formless, and incomparable—with the [mantra] Tārayā; thereafter, one should worship the deities within her limbs. 20.
20. "Anūpamām" means incomparable.
One should worship the weapons, ornaments, powers, and so forth, each with their respective mantras.
This sacrifice, known as "Laya," is great and bestows the accomplishment of all goals. 21.
Then, from the body of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, which was fully endowed with power,
there emerged one divine, supremely radiant form consisting of all powers.
The Goddess, who embodies the sixfold policy of statecraft, who is indefinable and incomparable, and who is in every way never departing from Viṣṇu at all times and in all places. (23)
Out of compassion, for the sake of the practitioner, she herself assumed a formal appearance; yet, without ever abandoning that very form of the deity, she remained distinct from it.
The pure practitioner should first invoke me with the mantra according to the stated sequence;
one should perform the entire procedure as prescribed for the rite of invocation. (25)
One should meditate upon me as Viṣṇu’s beloved, seated on his left lap;
and my form, which is to be meditated upon, has already been described previously. (26)
In that [state], one should sacrifice everything into me gradually by way of dissolution;
then, one should remember that which has issued forth from me, beginning with Śakti and so forth, in due order.
Just as one would [observe] a multitude of sparks from a well-blazing flame,
listen now to how each [of these] should be placed individually in the place of enjoyment.
One should meditate upon the lotus-eyed Puruṣa seated upon the conceptual throne in the center of the pericarp of the central lotus, and the Lotus-born Goddess (Paṅkajā) seated upon his lap.
One should meditate upon Lakṣmī, who has emerged from the body of [the central deity] in the middle of the pericarp of the eastern lotus;
she has two arms, two eyes, and beautiful earrings. (30)
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with necklaces and armlets, endowed with all auspicious marks, and possessing full, elevated breasts. || 31 ||
Her wide eyes were like blossomed blue lotuses, her face was graced with a beautiful smile,
and the rows of her locks of hair were lovely with swarms of hovering bees.
She had a tilaka-mark upon her forehead, lips as red as young shoots, and black, curly hair; her teeth were like bamboo and pearls. (33)
One should meditate upon her seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with two hands holding a noose and a goad,
her form resembling the interior of a lotus, and facing toward both of us.
One should remember her as residing within the center of the pericarp of the lotus on the right side,
identical in dress, ornaments, and so forth to Lakṣmī, or perhaps white like a jasmine flower.
[He saw] Kīrti, who had emerged from my form, supreme and consisting entirely of glory,
seated upon the pericarp of the western lotus, which served as her throne for both of us.
One should meditate upon Jayā, who is similar [to herself] and reddish, as having emerged from my own form;
one should remember her situated within the center of the pericarp of the northern lotus.
One should contemplate Māyā, who has emerged from my own form, as being of such a red hue;
her heart is in the lotus of the southeast, and her head is in the water-born flower of the southwest.
One should place the *śikhā* on the western lotus and the *varma* on the northeastern lotus;
the *netra* on the front petal of the central lotus, and the *astra* in the corner.
One should contemplate the god Vāsudeva in front of the eye;
one should remember the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa on the petal in the middle of the south.

One should meditate upon Pradyumna on the western petal of the central lotus, and Aniruddha on the northern petal; [and the others] on the pair of corner petals situated in the two [remaining] directions. (41)
Behind the weapon, one should visualize serpents showering nectar;
likewise, [one should offer] guggulu, aguru, madana, and śalala.
42. Gulgulu and others are the names of the *nāgas*. [B, C:
omit three lines from here] Those who hold jars of nectar, who are as white as a conch shell or a jasmine flower, and who have four tusks;
One should place the Kaustubha gem on all sides upon the lotus petals of Lakṣmī.
In this manner, one should place the forest garland upon the petals of the heart-lotus;
one should place the ornamental lotus upon the petals of the fame-lotus.
One should thus place the armor on the petals of the Jayā lotus,
and likewise on the petals of the Padma lotus, distributing it across the four petals of the lotus.
One should place the supreme goad upon the petals of the lotus of the head;
one should place Garuḍa, the best of birds, at the front of each of the four doors.
Or one should station the *nāgas* there at the front of one's own gates;
on the ground of the eastern gate, one should place Balākikā, who holds a lotus in her hand.
Likewise, from the southern gate, one should [visualize] the white Vanamālikā, who has eyes like lotus petals, is serene, and is of short stature; she is blue in color.
In the middle of the western gate, one should place Vibhīṣikā, who is red in color;
and in the middle of the northern gate, Śaṅkarī, whose luster is like honey.
From the eastern direction up to the northeast, at the outer entrance area,
one should visualize the eight world-protectors, Indra and the others, together with their vehicles.
Above that, one should contemplate Nāgeśa and Brahmā;
and outside of that, one should contemplate their weapons, such as the vajra and others.

One should meditate upon the Lord Viṣvaksena, whose limbs are magnificent, situated in the sky in the direction between Soma and Śaṅkara (the northwest), as he approaches from the midst of the firmament.
Now, O Purandara, hear from me the meditation upon those [deities] not yet mentioned:
[one who is] of the nature of nectar, whose limbs are like clouds, and whose eyes are as long as lotuses.
One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus; who bears the Śrīvatsa mark on his chest; who is clad in yellow garments; and who has four arms. (54)
One should meditate upon the supreme Saṃkarṣaṇa, who has the appearance of a mass of snow, wears blue garments, possesses four arms, and holds a plow and the Śārṅga bow.
55. The Saunandaka is the mace of Kāmapāla.
One should meditate upon Pradyumna, the Lord, who is red in complexion, clad in red garments, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and capable of lifting up those submerged [in distress]. 56.
One should meditate upon Aniruddha, who holds the Śārṅga bow and arrows, bestows boons and fearlessness, is yellow in color, and is clad in pure white garments.
Holding a sword and a shield in their hands, and with their supreme hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
all these lotus-eyed men were seated.
Beholding the northern direction, as well as myself and Viṣṇu the eternal,
elephants resembling the snowy mountains drenched us both with jars of nectar.
His body is white and red in color, he wears white garments, and has four arms;
he is seated upon a lotus throne and is marked by a lotus and a conch in his hands.
His hand is adorned with the heart-mudrā, while his left hand always bestows fearlessness;
he is richly endowed with white ornaments and garments, and his body is smeared with camphor.
The wise one should meditate upon the heart-mantra seated before us both—
the supreme one, red like a bandhujīva flower, and bearing a lotus and a discus.
Dark as the soot of a crow's eye, bearing the lotus and the kaumodakī mace,
adorned with his own mudrās in the right hand and granting fearlessness with the other.
63. "Dark" means as dark as a crow, as a bee, or as soot; or alternatively, *kākāli* refers to a specific type of crow that is an extremely black color.
It is smeared with musk alone, yet endowed with black flowers and other such items.
One should remember the Lord, clad in armor, seated before us both.
Resembling the reddish hue of turmeric, holding a mace and a lotus in sequence,
with his two front hands occupied in forming his own mudrās. (65)

One should remember the Weapon-mantra (Astra), which is richly adorned with gold, garments, and ornaments, possesses the prowess of the fire of universal destruction, and sits facing us both with great vigor.

Or the best of practitioners should visualize these [deities] as women—beginning with the Heart [mantra]—richly adorned with the aforementioned ornaments and attire, and anointed with perfumes suited to themselves. (67)
Thus has been described the auspicious meditation on the limbs [of the deity], which removes all sins.
One should meditate upon the Kaustubha gem as having two arms and possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns. (68)
Richly adorned with garments and ornaments set ablaze, he bears his own mudrā at his heart;
he wears a beautiful five-colored forest garland and possesses auspicious eyes. (69)
69. Regarding "the forest garland" (*vanamālā*): the word "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) is to be supplied.
One should meditate upon her holding in both hands a *mudrā* resembling a mature woman, [and] a lotus with a lotus-like face, serene and resembling the moon. 70.
Two-armed, with all limbs beautiful, holding a ring in both hands,
dark as fresh dūrvā sprouts, the Lord of the Noose, with the face of a serpent (or:
devourer of serpents).
Two-armed, holding his own mudrā with the right hand and likewise the hand of boon-granting, he is of terrible form and inspires fear.
