72–73. With his right hand— that is, with his right hand— one should visualize [the deity] holding a sharp, long-nosed, and terrifying goad (aṅkuśa) in his southern hand,
and in his left hand, the boon-granting gesture (vara-mudrā).
Those world-protectors were well-known by their dress, form, and ornaments;
they bore human-shaped weapons marked with insignia upon their heads. (74)
74. The female door-keepers, such as Balālikā and others, were mentioned previously in verses 47, 48, and 49.
Viṣvaksena, bearing the conch and discus, four-armed, equal to Viṣṇu himself, should be meditated upon with his two other hands engaged in performing mudrās. 75.
Then one should meditate upon Garuḍa standing at the front of the door, with terrifying eyes,
a red beak, a large nose, and the luster of molten gold.
"Having broad fangs, a vulture-like face, and adorned with a circle of wings"—thus has the meditation upon your retinue been described in brief. (77)
Above us two, who are gross, one should remember the subtle Tārikā;
she bears the form of a divine couple, subtle, as if both visible and invisible, and sinless.
Above that, however, is the supreme Tārā, who consists of the fullness of the six divine qualities;
she is our divine couple, the supreme state of the Paramaśiva.
It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere.
It eternally shines forth, manifesting both sound and meaning by its own splendor, ever-risen.
In this [receptacle], the entire wheel of mantras appears like a reflection;
thus, the supreme Tārīkā is expanded through the forms of both direct and reverse order.
Having understood this through the state of being according to reality, one should worship them as they were arranged;
from the beginning, one should worship the two sinless ones together with all their abodes by means of the intellect.

Then, the knower of mantras should worship the retinue, beginning with Śakti and ending with Viṣvaksena, by means of a multitude of offerings starting with the *arghya* and ending with the presentation of enjoyments. || 83 ||
At the very beginning, [one should place] Garuḍa, the Goddesses, and the four female gatekeepers;
O Śakra, this sequence of installation (nyāsa) has been shown to you according to the procedure for the sacrificial enjoyment (bhogayāga).
Learn from me what those enjoyments are, how many they are, and of what kind they are. (84)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the External Sacrifice," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (In the version cited as Ā: *Śrīpañcarātra*; in version B: *Śrīpāñcarātre*) 38.
Chapter Thirty-Nine:
Śrī (Glorious Fortune) — page 153.
Listen to the enjoyments of the lords of the gods by which I am satisfied when they are given;
it is in these that my power remains extended for the sake of experiencing those objects of enjoyment.
1. "She remains" (tiṣṭhate) means she remains manifesting her own intention (*svāśaya*); the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is used in the sense of manifestation.

[This occurs] through the various diverse divine powers (*divya-śakti*) which have attained a state of solidity (*styānatā*) in providing the respective objects of enjoyment according to [the soul's] capacity. 2.
That excellent seat, completely filled with soft coverings spread upon it, worthy of the Lord, should first be meditated upon in its entirety.
3. The specific enjoyments are described beginning with the word "soft" (*mṛdu*) and so forth. Regarding the worship of the Blessed One, there are six seats as follows:

the seat of mantra (*mantrāsana*), the seat of bathing (*snānāsana*), the seat of adornment (*alaṃkārāsana*), the seat of food (*bhojyāsana*), again the seat of mantra, and the cross-legged seat (*paryaṅkāsana*). Among these, the first, the seat of mantra, is described here.
Having first offered water for the guest (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and likewise water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
one should thereafter offer oneself and one's possessions preceded by a prostration.
4. Regarding the things to be offered upon that seat, he says with the words beginning "arghyam" (the water of honor).
He describes the manner of offering oneself and one's possessions in the *Pādmapurāṇa* (4.3.140):
"O Lord of the World, I am your servant, together with my sons and all my dependents; command me as your messenger in whatever must be done."
"Always employ me in what is beneficial.
Having thus obtained permission, he should thereafter provide an excellent seat for bathing,
a footstool, the arghya offering, and then the reception of the water for washing the feet.

5. Second is the bathing seat here. Regarding this, the mantra in the *Sāttvata* (6.26) is as follows: "O Lord, while you are intent on bathing, I have made manifest for you this supreme, auspicious, and great bathing seat, complete with a footstool. Please occupy it quickly for the sake of bathing, out of a desire for my grace. Thus it is said.
Water for the feet, sandals, a cloth for bathing, a small measure of rice,
a mirror, scented water, and water for washing the hands.
6. "And *mātrā* is *śālikā*. Here, the meaning of the term *mātrā* is a vessel filled with unbroken, fresh, and bright-colored *śāli* rice grains. Thus it is said in the *Pādmapurāṇa* (4.6.36):
"with a measure (*mātrā*) of *śāli* rice grains. And this—

The taking of food is for the sake of propitiation, and the chewing of a tooth-stick, as well as water for rinsing the mouth and sipping, are for the purpose of avoiding defects that have arisen. Likewise, there is scented oil and powder made from rice and wheat. (7)

Then, for the purpose of anointing with fragrant unguents, [the body] should be mixed with turmeric powder and slightly infused with padmaka; thereafter, for the purpose of bathing, it should be joined with khalī.
8. *Khali* is the dregs of concentrated fragrant oil, perfumed with musk and other scents.
Warm water mixed with sandalwood and camphor is for the purpose of anointment.
Likewise, there are cow’s milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugarcane juice. 9.
9. Camphor, sugar, and fragrant *āmalaka* fruits; after that, *lodhra* water, then *raktacandana* water, and excellent *rajanī* water. 10.
Afterwards, [he should offer] the milk of granthiparṇī, then water infused with tagara,
and water containing priyaṅgu, jaṭilā, siddhārthaka, and all medicinal herbs.
Flowers, leaves, fruits, and water; likewise seeds and fragrant water; gold, jewels, river water, and water from sacred fords; and pure water—in this sequence.
These waters, together with the water for bathing, should be offered;
likewise, the *arghya* water from the *arghya* vessel is to be offered at intervals between the baths. (13)
One should perform the washing with water containing flowers from time to time.

[Regarding the phrase "snānaśiṣṭāmbusaṃpūrṇaṃ haridrāśālisaṃbhṛtam": after the ritual bathing (snapana), the waving of lights (nīrājana) is prescribed; this refers to the water remaining from the bath, filled with turmeric and śāli rice.]
Holding a water-pot adorned with garlands and other ornaments in his hand, and then, on the other side, having whirled a vessel containing white mustard seeds and incense above his head; || 15 ||
15–16. [The water] in the left hand is for the right hand; elsewhere, it is for the right hand.
Then, one should cast it outside and give two well-washed lower garments (*aṅgaśāṭikā*):
a cloth for the purpose of removing hair and water, and a garment for removing water from the body.
Then one should offer two beautiful, well-washed garments, one for the lower body and one for the upper body, purified with perfumes and incense, followed by a noble seat.
17. The auspicious seat is the bathing seat.
One should purify it with full water-pots and meditate upon Hari as if immersed in the sky.
Afterwards, the ornamentation seat should be provided, abundant with a soft carpet. 18.
18. *Kha-pluta* (the letter *kha* with the vowel *u*) is situated at the *dvādaśānta*. He describes the third seat, the Ornament (*alaṃkāra*), saying "Ornament" (*alaṃkāra*).
Therein, everything such as the *arghya* and *pādya* offerings should be presented as before. Furthermore, "arranging the hair" (*vivecanam*) means cleansing the hair with a comb (*kaṅkata*). 19.
19. A comb and a hair-pin; flowers for the head, and then the arrangement of the topknot;
fragrant substances such as sandalwood, and a fan.
It has the meaning of drying up. || 20 ||
Most wonderful ornaments, such as crowns and others, should be offered, along with garlands of various forms composed of pure, virtuous flowers. (21)
A handful of flowers was offered at his two feet, a rampart was built with heaps of blossoms,
and his eyes were anointed with collyrium cooled by fragrant substances.
Likewise, there is also the act of touching [the body], as well as the tilaka mark on the forehead;
a polished, stainless mirror, and looking all around.
Lamps, incense, vehicles, animate and inanimate objects, hymns of praise, auspicious songs, and the sight of dance and instrumental music; || 24 ||
24. "Conveyances, whether animate or inanimate," refers to elephants, horses, and so forth, fashioned from gold and other materials.
"And measures filled with jewels" refers to those various activities appropriate for a king of passion, which fill the gaps in one's enjoyment and are mentally contrived. 25.
For [the deity] seated upon the ornamented throne, these enjoyments indeed consist of myself;
then, the seat for the meal, as well as the water for honor (arghya) and the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, should be offered.

26. By the phrase "consisting of me" (*manmaya*), the subject matter mentioned at the beginning of the chapter is recalled. The fourth seat for the guest (*bhojyāsana*) is now described—beginning with "Now" (*atha*).
Listen attentively to how one should honor him with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
The mixture of milk, honey, and curd is called madhuparka. || 27 ||
27. He describes the *madhuparka*: "With milk," etc.
Having placed the vessel before [the guest], it is filled with *madhuparka*.
The *arhaṇa* (honoring) and the *tarpaṇa* (satisfying) should be performed separately from the *arghya* in two separate vessels. 28.
First, there is worship with the *arhaṇa* offering, followed by the *madhuparka*;
then the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the substances suitable for libation, and finally the purification (*niṣpuṃsana*) performed upon the hand.

29. The *arhaṇa* consists of water for sipping (*āpośana*). The *tarpaṇa* is the water for drinking. The *niṣpuṃsana* is the wiping of the hands. Water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) should be given afterwards; the cow intended for the *madhuparka* is the [final] measure.
One should perform the sacrifice with the *annayajña* complete in its parts, just as in the *madhuparka* rite. 30.
30. Furthermore, the taking of the cow as a substitute is prescribed here in order to avoid any deficiency resulting from the offering of the *madhuparka*.
Portions of cooked rice made from *śāli* rice should be offered for the sake of the food-sacrifice (*annayajña*);
likewise, betel-leaf with camphor should be offered as an after-treatment (*anuvāsana*).
31. On the fifth seat of mantras, betel leaves and other offerings should be presented.
Thereafter, for the sake of rest, a most wonderful celestial chariot (vimāna) should be offered;
there, everything such as the arghya and other items should be given as before. 32.

32. The sixth is called the paryanka posture—thereafter [it is said]: "Then one should perform the recitation (japa), unobserved by other people, using an auspicious rosary that has been properly consecrated with mantras. 33.

33. Among the implements for counting the number of recitations (*japa*), the rosary (*akṣamālā*) is most highly praised. Counting with the fingers is considered common; however, by means of the joints [of the fingers], one may count up to ten more [than that]. Indeed, it should be understood that counts of one hundred or more are to be performed with a rosary. 34. [The preceding verse is part of this continuous passage. Counting with the fingers is considered common; however, by means of the joints [of the fingers], one may count up to ten more [than that]. Indeed, it should be understood that counts of one hundred or more are to be performed with a rosary.
The vocal [recitation] is for the purpose of minor rites; the whispered [recitation] is for the rite of accomplishment;
the mental [recitation], consisting of meditation, bestows the fortune of liberation and grants all perfections.
35. The specific types of recitation (japa) are vocal and so forth.
The rosary should be made in such a way that it is not visible to ordinary people.
The beads should be the size of a bone; these are proclaimed to be the best. 36.
Those resembling the stone of the *dhātrī* fruit are proclaimed as middling; those with the appearance of the stone of the *badara* are inferior. The best consists of one hundred and eight.
Half of that is declared to be the middling size, and half of that again is remembered as the lowest.
[An image] made of gold is for the sake of attaining wealth, for nourishment, and for rites concerning the ancestors.

38. He describes the specific types of beads for the rosary with the words beginning "sauvarṇam" (golden) and so forth: "Silver [beads] or those of copper form are for the sake of attaining wisdom and heroism; those of tin are for the accomplishment of yakṣiṇīs; and those of lead are for [dealing with] rākṣasas and piśācas. (39)
For the purpose of accomplishing the Vetāla, the rosary should be known as being made of brass or bell-metal; it is used for the accomplishment of Nāgas and Pannagas.
40. *Rīti* is a specific type of brass or bronze.
Iron is for minor purposes; thus, a gem made of metal is for such uses.
Every gem made of precious stone (*maṇi*) is for the sake of longevity, health, and prosperity—or, as some say, for increase. 41.
A crystal gem is said to be for liberation and peace;
one made of coral should be used for good fortune, while one made of pearl should be used for emancipation.
42. A *sautra* [amulet] is one made from thread.
For peace, liberation, and nourishment, an amulet born from the root of *tulasī* is used.
The *pādma* amulet bestows all supernatural powers (*siddhi*), while the *śāṅkha* amulet is considered to grant prosperity (*śrī*). 43.
A pearl is the most excellent gem; it bestows longevity, progeny, and fame.
One should take one of these [gems] at an auspicious time when its qualities are preeminent.
Immediately thereafter, one should wash it with water scented by the Astra-mantra.
Then, having prepared a new, firm thread made of hemp, cotton, or wool, [one should proceed]. (45)
Having tripled [the cord] and made it fourfold as firmly as possible,
and having washed it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra), one should string the beads with that very same cord.
Neither deficient nor excessive, equal, immovable, and linked together,
they are like a string of desired numbers of gems threaded on a cord with two ends.
One should fashion a *maṇi* [bead] from Meru; this is the procedure for the rosary (*akṣamālā*). || 47 ||
47. Meru is a large, special jewel situated at the principal knot of the *japa*-string.
Thus ends the "Illumination of the External Sacrifice" (*bahiryāgaprakāśa*) in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the venerable *Pāñcarātra* [or *Śrīpañcarātra*]. [Variant: *bahiryāga*].
The thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Nāma."
Chapter Forty. Śakra:
Salutations to you, O one born from the waters; salutations to you, O one born from the lotus.
O Lotus-born One, tell me the method for the consecration of the rosary.
Śrī said: One should place the accomplished rosary in an auspicious vessel;
having worshipped it with water for the guest (arghya), flowers, and other offerings, one should perform its purification.

Having accomplished and manifested it, one should burn it with the weapon-mantra (astra) and extinguish it; then, one should nourish it with the armor-mantra (varma) by means of the supreme nectar-form of Śrī. Thereafter, one should meditate upon that garland.

3. Having extinguished and dried [the impurities], one should meditate—that is, visualize—with splendor by means of the Śrī-mantra, in the form that is about to be described: "The four-armed, incomparable one, who is composed of me (manmayī) like another version of myself, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, and with her two hands joined in the añjali gesture. 4.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who resides in the lotus of the Brahma-door, resembling a tuft of hair;
she is that supreme Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, composed of my own essence, who pierces through my ego.

5. The "Brahma-door" is the channel known as the *brahmarandhra*. The "crest" (*śikhā*) is the crest of fire. Having contemplated [the deity] at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], one should then meditate in sequence upon the heart-lotus.
[One should contemplate her] having risen again from the heart-lotus and emerged through the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*). 6.
6. At the *dvādaśānta*, in the place twelve finger-breadths above the crown of the head,
one should contemplate her slowly arising and situated upon a garland,
endowed with the sequence of limbs and secondary limbs [and the ritual actions].
Consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
O Lord of the Gods, one should meditate upon me there as the Śakti in the form of the Tārikā;
likewise, one should meditate upon the jewels, the thread, the rosary, and the Vaiṣṇavī residing within the rosary.
O Lord of the Gods, one should meditate upon all illusion as having been turned into a single ocean;
having contemplated this rosary of beads given by me as being consecrated.
Thereafter, one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the previously mentioned procedure,
[focusing] upon the unmanifest, the supreme, the subtle, and the gross Self itself.
One should contemplate this pentad as having the form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa:
the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), the fourth (turya), deep sleep (suṣupti), dreaming (svapna), and waking (jāgara).
Likewise, there are the five states, as well as their agents and instruments;
similarly, the emergence of the agent, that which resides therein, and the external instrument. (12)

One should likewise meditate upon every syllable of the mantra as being gross and composed of that [essence], situated in the center of the heart-lotus and emerging from the lotus-face of the Mantra-deity. 13.
One should remember the power of Viṣṇu, consisting of sound, which pierces through my [the Guru's] ego;
one should meditate on Mātṛkā, the mother of mantras, as having emerged from her.
Then one should meditate upon the rosary as consisting of the Self and composed of the mantra to be recited;
indeed, one should contemplate the mantras there as flowers upon a creeper.
Visualizing the throbbing upon the touch of the jewel and its dissolution within the heart when that [touch] ceases,
the wise practitioner should perform the recitation of the Lord of Mantras.
Recalling that it issues forth from and returns to the luminous form within the heart, both outwardly and inwardly, in forward and reverse order—
one who thus remembers and recites it even once obtains the merit of ten million recitations. || 17 ||
Having completed the recitation according to the rules, one should consign the recitation performed to me;
one should contemplate that Power (śakti), which resides within my mouth, in the form of the recitation. (18)
One should employ the ringing of the bell during the offering of the lamp, incense, and water for honor (arghya);
likewise, during the invocation, the offering of arghya, the food offering (naivedya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
And for the purpose of pleasing [the deity], the wise one should employ the ringing of the bell;
it should not be moved without worship, nor should it be worshipped without being moved.
For those desiring the accomplishment of their goals both in this world and the next, she is indeed the power named Ghaṇṭā, the mistress of speech, Sarasvatī. (21)
All mantras reside in speech, and everything that is to be spoken resides within the mantras.
When this [speech] is set in motion, the mantras follow swiftly, like calves [following their mother].
Desiring [liberation], they come to that bell, the mother of mantras;
one should meditate upon the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as being face-downward, containing the worlds, both the Kula and Akula.
Above that stalk, however, the wise one should meditate upon a circular lotus—
auspicious, white, with eight petals, and endowed with a pericarp and filaments.
In the center of that, one should contemplate the Goddess endowed with eight arms,
holding in her four principal hands a noose, a conch, a lotus, and a goad.
Holding in her four right arms a rosary, a book of wisdom, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise the gesture of granting boons; || 26 ||

Seated in the lotus posture, with eyes like lotuses, possessing a luster equal to the interior of a lotus, wearing a garland of lotuses, and adorned with yellow and white garments and unguents. || 27 ||
One should cause this [goddess], who vomits forth a flood of mantras and is praised by Brahmā and the other gods, to move while reciting the long *tārikā* in pairs. 28.
By worshipping with this, the practitioner of mantra attains the perfection of mantra.
Then, having invited gurus—whether they are identical with me (Śiva) or devotees of Viṣṇu— || 29 ||
While reciting my mantra, one should offer them half of the food portion;
then, one should properly offer the supreme [oblation] consisting of Agni and Soma, which has entered the fire.
30. The propitiation of the fire is now described, beginning with the word "atha" (now).
"O Lord of the Gods, listen attentively as I describe how you should satisfy me.
Then, in the northern direction, either outside the temple of the deity... 31.
On a portion of ground endowed with auspicious characteristics, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing the proper marks—
either square and level, or heart-pleasing in the shape of a lotus.
For a number of fifty oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be twelve finger-breadths;
for one hundred and eight, it should be equal to a cubit (aratni); and for a thousand, it should be one hand (hasta).

33. The width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the number of oblations is stated [in the verse] beginning with "śatordha" and so forth: 34. For that which is called ten thousand (ayuta), it should be two cubits; for a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma), four cubits; and for ten million oblations (koṭihoma), it should be eight cubits. One should have it constructed in accordance with the scriptures.
Or one may construct a triangular fire-pit for the oblation, provided with three tiers;
having first cleared it with the *tāra* (OM), one should sprinkle the ground three times with that same mantra.
35–36. By means of that Tārā: one should properly perform the drying, burning, and flooding by means of Tārā.
Beginning from the Ādhāra-śakti and so forth, the worship should be carried out up to the Bhāvāsana.
36. The Bhāvāsana has been previously described in the section on the Ādhāraśakti.

Therein, one should contemplate the supreme Śakti known as Nārāyaṇī, who consists of light, is composed of the Self (manmaya), has the form of nectar, and possesses a nature that transcends all else. 37.
Having brought down from the heart-lotus the eternal [Deity], who abides within the totality of all powers and resides within the interior of all things, by way of the path of emanation; 38.
Having descended from the heart-lotus in the form of a radiating *tārikā*,
one should cast it into the center of the lotus within the *kuṇḍa* by means of the exhaling breath (*recaka*).
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having displayed the lotus-mudrā,
one should meditate upon the Śakti who is in her fertile season, well-bathed, and clad in new garments. (40)
40–41. By the words "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) and so forth, the transformation of the fire into the Vaiṣṇava state is described.
One should meditate upon that very power (*śakti*), which is the self of all, as the lower friction-stick (*adharāraṇi*);
and one should meditate upon Hari, who consists of all splendor, as the upper friction-stick (*uttarāraṇi*).
One should properly worship with Tārayā, and likewise with Anutārayā;
having taken up the fire produced from Śakti by means of Tārayā, [one should offer it]. 42.
Having grasped [the child] with his fingers, he should perform the consecration (saṃskāra) known as Vaiṣṇava;
and he should perform the tonsure (cūḍā), preceded by the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), with the Tārā mantra.
43. Having embraced and concealed [the child], [one performs] the first feeding of solid food; by this, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and the naming-rite (*nāmakaraṇa*) are also included.
Then, having initiated [the child] (*upanīya*), one should cause him to cross over the fire with the *tārā* and *anutārā* [mantras].

Then, with the two goddesses *svāhā* and *svadhā*, [one worships] Jātavedas (Fire). 44. One should perform the marriage ceremony with either the *tārā* or the *anutārā*;
all rites such as the naming ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others should be performed consisting entirely of meditation.
When fire has been produced from iron, stone, or gems for a specific purpose,
or even in a common worldly fire, one should perform the sacraments beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception rite).
Having placed [the offerings] in a vessel made of metal, or one of clay, or even a new one,
the wise man should worship the Lord of Svāhā together with the Goddess using *tāra*.
Having withdrawn [the breath] by means of *pūraṇa*, one should lead it to rest within one's own self;
then, by means of the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), one should gradually unite it with the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Having again brought him down step by step along the path of emanation,
one should lead him to the earth situated within the lotus in the center of the sacrificial pit by means of the Tara-mantra.
One should worship Vahni with Svāhā, Sva, Īśāna, and the one consisting of Agni and Soma,
uttering the Tāraka mantra with three fuel-sticks, one by one.
Thereafter, with offerings of rice, sesame, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should then offer three oblations of clarified butter (ājya).
Having first uttered the Tārikā, one should then say "awaken" twice.
While staying there, the fire itself is awakened according to the proper rite;
then the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) must be performed by her with wet hands.
One should spread the darbha grass with *tāra* mantras, arranging it in three sets each toward the four directions;
one should spread a heap of darbha grass in the northern part of the fire-pit.

One should cause all of these to be placed there: the vessels for the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* waters, the wooden ladle and the fuel, the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, as well as the vessel for clarified butter and the two strainers.
Having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with fragrant water and having purified it three times with two strainers (*pavitra*), one should meditate upon me, Śrī, by means of the *tārā* mantra. (55)
Having established the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to the north of the fire, one should fill it with water for prosperity;
then, having purified it and sprinkled the sacrificial implements equally with that water.
Having taken up the vessel for the clarified butter (ājya) and having placed the clarified butter within it—
visualizing that [butter] as originating from the ocean of Brahman’s ghee— one should place it to the north of the fire.
Having kindled it with the *tāraka* [mantra] and placed it on the tip of a *darbha* blade,
and having kindled it again with that same [mantra], one should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having established it behind the fire, one should purify it with the pair of pavitras;
then, having purified it with the Tāra mantra, one should cast that pair of pavitras into the fire.
One should enclose [the site] in the four directions with sacrificial boundary-sticks (paridhi);
then, having placed two fuel-sticks (samit) in the middle of the fire-pit between the directions of Agni and Śarva.
Then, having arranged the dry fuel consisting of fifteen pieces,
he should sprinkle the fire with water using the *tāra* mantra and heat the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
Having wiped [the ladle] with the *tārā* [mantra], they should subsequently sprinkle [the offerings] with that same *sruk* from the west as far as the southeast,
reaching up to the northeast.
One should cause it to flow in a stream into the fire; one should offer a ladle-oblation (sruvāhuti) in the center,
either one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or half of that again.
(159) One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the *Tārikā* mantra ending in "svāhā";
this fire shall then become fit for the sacrificial offerings to the Blessed One.
Then, the wise practitioner should first place seven fuel-sticks made of sacrificial wood derived from trees belonging to the *brahma* and *kṣatra* classes, using the *tārikā* mantra. (65)
65. The *brahmataru* is the *palāśa* tree; the *kṣatrataru* is the tree named *mucukunda*. Regarding the phrase "the remaining ten": this means the ten remaining fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
One should offer these ten remaining sticks, which are in the form of wood, along with the *tārā* [seed-syllable].
One should meditate upon me alone in the center, as the supreme goddess seated upon the lap of Viṣṇu.

One should offer all the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidhs) while meditating upon Lakṣmī seated on the lap of the All-pervading Lord, who resides upon the pericarp of the lotus consisting of the bliss of Brahman.
Then one should offer that which consists of flowers and likewise that which consists of incense materials;
these three kinds should be offered by the wise person with their own hand alone.
Thereafter, the wise one should offer the madhuparka with the *sruva* ladle;
having taken four portions of food into the *sruc* and filled it with clarified butter as before, [he should proceed]. (69)
With that same [ladle], one should offer oblations of food while reciting the Tārikā mantra ending in "svāhā";
one should likewise perform oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, equal in number to the previously mentioned fuel-sticks.
Taking a handful of flowers, one should mentally worship her who resides in the fire;
this much constitutes my daily sacrifice (nityayāga), and thereafter one may cast the oblation for specific desires (kāmyāhuti).
If he should have a desire, he should sprinkle the fire with water using the *tāra* mantra in accordance with each specific injunction, and then offer an expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
Saying "Tārā, forgive me" ten times with his mind, he should withdraw the Praṇītā vessel and lead it—or place it—in a pure location. || 73 ||
Having offered all the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one should perform the pouring of the residue (*saṃsrāva*);
and having offered the grass-bundle (*stara*) into the fire, one should fill the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) with clarified butter.

Reciting the Tārikā ending with "svāhā," one should offer the long final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to that supreme Tārā, who is united with Śakti, established in the fire, and composed of the essence of mind.

And having drawn me, who was seated upon his lap, through the path of the junction of Viṣṇu’s nostrils by means of the power of the vital breath (marucchakti), he placed me within the lotus of his heart.
Then, having gone to the sacrificial ground, one should unite that creative act with me, who am situated upon a fresh lotus, and deposit it within me, who abide as the object of worship.
One should divide the food beforehand, even before its distribution as a gift;
with that food, one should properly worship the four-armed Viṣvaksena.
Having brought him to the edge of the mandala and summoned him from the midst of the sky,
[he saw one] resembling a fresh mango leaf, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes.
Having worshipped the god who wears yellow garments, possesses four tusks, is endowed with his own two mudrās, and holds a mace and a sword, the wise one should proceed in due order.
Then, having displayed the *sāṅga-mudrā* and gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
Viṣvaksena should then be propitiated with devotion using sesame seeds and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
81. From this point onward, the [verses] up to the middle of the fifth [chapter] follow the words of the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*.
Then, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having worshipped in the mandala, one should then perform its dismissal (*visarjana*). 82.
O best of gods, reciting the words "Forgive me" with his own mantra,
he should display the mudrā and visualize him as having flown up into the sky.
One should cast all the materials for the worship of Viṣvaksena into deep water,
and one should drench that maṇḍala with water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited.
Then one should worship all the guardians of the world (lokapālas) without exception,
with flowers, water-offerings (arghya), and gifts of food, and with a single oblation into the fire.
p.
160) Or with fire-offerings, or with grains such as rice, according to one's capacity, using their respective mantras and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped and dismissed these, one should likewise worship those weapons.
One should worship all those attendants according to the sequence of their respective positions; one should honor the Kṣetrapālas and others, and offer libations into the center of the fire.
Beginning with the foundational power (Ādhāra-śakti) and including all the powers of the sacred seats (Pīṭha-śaktis),
as well as Gaṇeśa and the others, they should be fully worshipped and gratified with ghee and other offerings.
Having performed [the rites] once or thrice, one should then pour full [libations] into all [the vessels];
prior to the worship of Viṣvaksena, one should worship all [deities], beginning with Lakṣmī.
After the worship of Viṣvaksena, one should perform the worship of the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in sequence;
then, having purified the altar and spread the sacrificial grass (darbha) facing south.
One should worship the ancestors in their proper order with the remnants of the food intended for them;
having prepared three pindas, one should offer them to the ancestors upon the sacred grass.
Likewise, one should offer water for the *arghya*— one *añjali* for each individual—
or else one should give it to a Vaiṣṇava, or especially to a distinguished Brāhmaṇa.

92. Regarding the phrase "to a distinguished Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya viśeṣiṇe*): this means "to an eminent Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, this refers to cases other than those involving a creditor. However, regarding the case of a creditor, it is stated in the *Sāttvata-tantra* (6.167–179) that one should feed four Brāhmaṇas according to the rules of the *śrāddha*, or, if they are unavailable, just one.
Having dedicated that food intended for the ancestors, mentioning each of their names in turn,
and having offered it all into me while observing its disappearance, [one should proceed].
Having withdrawn the water for the guest-offering (arghya) and the rest, and having retracted the armor (varma) and weapon (astra) [mantras],
and having withdrawn the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the subsequent sacrifice (anuyāga).
94. The *anuyāga* (concluding sacrifice) is the utilization of the remnants of what has been offered, such as the food and so forth.

Having sprinkled [the food] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and having sprinkled it around with the *tārā* [mantra], one should spread a base [of ghee] with that same [mantra] and offer the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) with that same [mantra]. 95.
95. "Having spread it with her" means having drunk with Tārā.
However, one who is uninitiated, while performing the subsequent sacrifices, should recite the *Tārikā* joined with each respective mantra and should visualize me as abiding within. 96.

96. The aforementioned acts—sprinkling, circumambulatory sprinkling, the *āpośana* rite, the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*), and so forth—are intended for those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*). For those who are uninitiated, however, these must be performed using only the mantras prescribed by the respective authors of the Sūtras.
[One should contemplate] the divine [food], consisting of the essence of Soma, which has sequentially attained the nature of food.
Having the form, taste, and appearance of vigor, she consists of the essence of brilliance, energy, and strength. || 97 ||
One should meditate upon the self as the imperishable enjoyer, whose nature consists of sovereignty, power, and wisdom—the lotus-eyed Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). 98.
Then, while reciting the *tārikā*, one should cover the food with water;
having performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) twice, one should thereafter perform the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) within oneself.
99. "Having covered [the mouth] with water" means having drunk the *uttarāpośana* (the final sipping of water).
Then, the wise man should practice his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) for the remainder of the day, as well as the fourfold scriptures and the *tārikā* and other [mantras] arising therefrom. 100.
100. *Svādhyāya* is the study of the Vedas, divine scriptures, and so forth; as well as all fourfold *siddhāntas*—namely, the *Āgama-siddhānta*, etc.—with an undistracted mind.
For the sake of purifying one's own disposition, one should examine [the matter] with one's own intellect. || 101 ||

Having performed the twilight devotions according to rule and having approached me with devotion, one should practice yoga according to the prescribed method with a mind purified by the scriptures. (102)
"During the two watches of night, from the first to the last, one who possesses the equilibrium of the bodily constituents [should practice];
thus, O Śakra, the procedure for sacrifice has been shown in detail. (103)

103. The first watch of the night and the last watch are the time for yoga. Even the sleep that occurs in the middle should be cultivated as being of the nature of yoga by means of the surrender of one's own self to the Blessed One. Now, listen again to me regarding the summary of this procedure. [B: I shall tell it to you.]
One should perform it either in brief or in detail, according to what is appropriate for the place and time. || 104 ||
One should never cause a deficiency; one may even worship me with a mere handful of water.
One should worship both of us together with the Puruṣa-sūkta.
105. *Apaccheda* means severance.
Likewise, one should worship them separately with my own *sūkta*, or with both of us;
or else, in the place of all mantras, one should employ the *tārikā* alone. 106.
One should perform both the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) separately at the beginning and the end;
or, without specifying the enjoyment [of results], one may sacrifice with those [offerings] alone.
One should act in whatever way one is able;
however, one must never let the sacrifice lapse, even if one must give it as a mere handful of water.

108. "He should be able to... [This implies that] because the propitiation of me is obligatory (*nitya*), and because there must be performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśakty-anuṣṭhāna*) for what is obligatory—[the wise one], in the absence of material offerings, should recite the *Tārikā* or even meditate mentally upon her form, whatever its nature may be.
109. ...or even recite the *Tārikā*; in the absence of material wealth, the discerning one should meditate in his mind upon her form, whatever its specific characteristics may be.
For one who is free from worldly desire, pure, and has indeed attained the goal in that state, all the ritual actions shown by the scripture lead only to agitation. (110)
And for one who has attained equanimity toward all things, who is ever-expanding, who could perform what action, for whom, for what purpose, or in what manner? (111)
Having abandoned the two paths pertaining to all the worlds— those of Agni and Soma—
one should enter the space between them and practice the upward path.
The evil path burnt away by the fire of absorption, he has become cooled and free from affliction;
he is expert in treading upon the states that transcend the gross, the subtle, and the supreme. || 113 ||
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing;
speaking, releasing, grasping, as well as opening and closing the eyes—(one should know that it is the Self alone which acts). 114.
Indeed, being absorbed in me and not consisting of this world, he performs all that [action] without being constrained by any conditions such as state, place, time, and so forth. (115)
115. "Unpierced" (anavasyūtayā) means "unbounded. It is as if overwhelmed by the sense of "I-ness," like one who has inhaled smoke and then drunk fire;
for it exists in the interval between the two, the sun and the moon. 116.

116. "Smoke-drinker" and so forth: the meaning is that just as one situated between smoke and fire becomes connected with both the smoke and the fire, so too he is situated between the sun and the moon.
Having clearly extracted the palate [or, having extracted the jewel from the palate].
Establishing [the mind] in the station of the fixed,
he should abide in a state consisting of emptiness, which is commensurate with dissolution.
Thus, the yogin who conducts himself in this way, intent upon the meditation on Tārikā—
he is a master of ritual action, he is indeed a follower of Sāṃkhya, he is a yogin, and he is a devotee of the Sāttvatas. || 118 ||
"He is to be known as a Pāśupata, and he has reached the culmination of all philosophical systems.
Thus have I declared to you my ultimate nature;
now hear from me the remainder of what I wish to say to you in its entirety. (119)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Daily Rites," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (40)
Chapter Forty-one: Śakra— (p. 162)
Homage to the Mother of all embodied beings, who is eternally faultless,
whose nature is that of the Ādhāreśa, and who is the ground of all paths, both pure and impure.
The sacrifice, with all its details, has been heard by me according to the distinction between external and internal;
now I desire to hear from you the definitive exposition of initiation (dīkṣā).
Śrī said:
"Nārāyaṇa alone is glorious, resplendent with the majesty of his sixfold attributes; I am his single, eternal Śakti, whose form consists of those sixfold attributes. (3)
O Vāsava, by means of divine consciousness, I, though one, divide myself fivefold:
through the forms of sound, form, and meaning, as well as through the form of mental activity.
In the same way, by means of the other [form] known as initiation (dīkṣā), which takes the form of the Teacher (ācārya),
it tears asunder the afflictions, karmas, and so forth, and bestows the entire state.

5. The etymological derivation of the word *dīkṣā* is given by the verse beginning with "yat" and so forth: "It cuts (*dyati*) [or] shatters; the root is *do* in the sense of 'to cut apart' (*avakhaṇḍane*).
Having exhausted all impurity (*mala*), it bestows the supreme state."
Therefore, initiation is described by those who know reality and have mastered the Vedas.

6. The initiate (samayin), the spiritual son (putraka), the third, the practitioner (sādhaka), and the teacher (ācārya)—these are those to be initiated; the details regarding them are found elsewhere.
Furthermore, this initiation is threefold: through the sacrifice of the great maṇḍala, or by means of oblation alone, or even by speech alone. (9)
Having brought one who possesses firm resolve and has been tested over a long period— whether he be wealthy, of small means, or destitute of resources— respectively.
The teacher, having first fashioned a fresh lotus for the disciple—who is bowed down and scorched by the fire of *saṃsāra*—and having worshipped (*samijya*) the water-pot (*kumbha*) therein;
Regarding "having worshipped" (*samijya*): it means having fully honored (*saṃpūjya*).
To his disciples, whose sins had been cleansed by various kinds of expiations,
who were well-bathed, wearing washed garments, and whose bodies had been made pure; || 12 ||
Having brought the devotees of the Blessed One, auspicious maidens, and women,
he purified them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) following the preliminary cleansing of the teeth.
13. Regarding the girls and women, he states that they too have the qualification for Tantric initiation (*tāntrikadīkṣā*).
14. Having them hold handfuls of flowers, with their eyes bound and dressed in new garments, one should apply a single thread from the soles of their feet up to the crown of their heads.
Having made three strands and three knots on that thread according to the number of the principles (tattvas),
one should contemplate the sequence of the principles from the head down to the feet.
15. "Consisting of the three qualities" (triguṇā) means consisting of the knots made of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The number of principles (*tattva*) is twenty-seven.
From Īśvara down to Earth, the number is twenty-seven.
The principles are to be known as the knots, while the three qualities reside within those knots. 16.
Māyā, avidyā, and kriyā—these are proclaimed to be the bonds (pāśas).
The body, consisting of both gross and subtle aspects, bestows the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions. (17)
(163) This [soul],
colored by various qualities and the abode of all impurities,
itself [assumes] a body made of threads at the conclusion of the ritual of the *saṃpāta-homa*. 18.
18. The *saṃpātahoma* is the offering to the principles (*tattva*).
Having cut [the bonds] again and again, one should offer oblations as the cause for uprooting enjoyment.
One should meditate on the Lord on the forehead, whose form is consciousness and who faces in all directions. 19.
19. He describes the meditation on the principles (tattva) according to the division of their parts, beginning with "on the forehead":
Having meditated upon [the principle] established by its own seed-syllable, one should offer oblations according to the number of the principles.
One should remember Pradhāna, resembling a mass of vermilion, situated between the two eyebrows. 20.

One should contemplate the intellect (buddhi), resembling the rays of the full moon, situated at the root of the palate; and within the middle of the palate, one should meditate upon the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) as having the luster of a flower.
One should meditate on the mind, possessing the luster of a royal gem, between the palate and the ears;
it is situated between the lotuses of the throat and the heart, divided equally into five parts.
22. The king’s stone is the diamond (vajra).
One should contemplate the five [senses], such as hearing, which have the form of shimmering stars;
likewise, one should remember speech and the others fivefold in the center between the heart and the navel. 23.

One should remember the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound and the rest at the navel, the base of the genitals, and the middle [of the body]; one should remember the gross elements starting from the two thighs down to the pair of feet.
Having pronounced the Praṇava over those [deities] as well, which are in the form of stars and joined with their respective forms, one should then utter each of their specific seed-syllables (bīja).
Then, with the syllable *tattva-saṃjñā* followed by *svāhā*, such is the oblation of the remnants (*saṃpāta-huti*).
At the conclusion of the homa of the remnants, the Guru himself becomes composed of Lakṣmī.
Then one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *tāra* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Thus, at the conclusion of the *saṃpāta-homa*, that firm thread with its knots [is prepared].
Having offered [the oblation] placed within a pair of shallow bowls (śarāva-sampuṭa) at the end of the *mada* [rite],
one should then remove the blindfold from the initiated disciple who has been brought forward.
Having properly saluted his own guru who has bestowed the book upon him, that disciple, standing near the fire, should offer oblations with a mind focused on the *tāra* mantra. (29)
Thus, through the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, and the entire retinue beginning with Lakṣmī,
one indeed becomes qualified for the recitation, the fire-ritual, the hearing, and the worship.
Then, for the purpose of purifying the path during initiation, one should offer oblations with the [mantras] beginning with the Mūla-mantra;
furthermore, one should offer sesame seeds, starting from a hundred and ending at ten.
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with ghee alone and cause it to fall through a ladle;
this constitutes the Mantric initiation (māntrī dīkṣā), which empowers the application of all mantras.

Within this much of the scope of authority, however, one should cause disciples who are solely addicted to worldly enjoyment to grasp the desired mantras, whether they be of the *prakṛta* or *prākṛta* type. (33)
All mantras arising from primordial nature (prakṛti) become effective when present before one;
however, their essential principles (tattvas) must be purified according to the method that will be explained.
The reception of mantras is prescribed for the category of the path of the pure principles (śuddhatattvādhvan).
This is the initiation pertaining to mantras (māntrī dīkṣā); now learn from me the initiation of the principles (tattvadīkṣā).

Oṃ! Purify the seed-syllable and the designation of reality through the sequence of the name [and the purification by *svāhā*], by means of ten repetitions of oblations in conjunction with perfect meditation. (36)
The group of principles (tattvas), beginning with earth and ending with Īśvara, is purified;
in the fire-oblation and other rites for the one to be initiated, the designations should be applied according to their true meaning. (37)

While the disciple is seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) close to him, the true guru should meditate upon the entire sequence of principles (tattvapaddhati), beginning with Īśa and ending with the earth element.
Having gazed [upon it] with the two eyes of Lakṣmī, one should touch it with the hand of Lakṣmī;
then, having withdrawn [the elements] beginning with Earth, one should create again those beginning with Īśāna.
39. Since it was previously stated that the Guru consists of Lakṣmī, his two eyes are called "the eyes of Lakṣmī. By "Lakṣmī’s hand" is meant the hand joined with the *tārikā* [syllable].
In this way, this initiation consisting of meditation quickly brings about the awakening of the insentient principles residing within the body of the disciple. (40)
Then, having placed the cord of the noose between two shallow bowls,
one should go near the sacrificial pit, remove those bowls, and set them down.

Having offered into the fire one thousand or more, but at least one hundred, oblations of *tārā* together with its ancillaries, and then taking a single flower and consecrating it many times— || 42 ||
One should strike the disciple on the heart with the *tāra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having recollected the disciple as abiding in the principle of the elements (*bhūtatattva*), one should mentally cause him to enjoy their respective experiences. (43)

Then, having extracted [the soul] from that state where the enjoyment of all worlds has been completed, one should join it to the water-element (aptattva). Having likewise considered this with respect to Īśa, such is the procedure.
Having offered oblations with the *tārā* mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*), and having severed the earthly knot,
one should place [the vessel] in the *sruc*, fill it with clarified butter, and offer it with that same mantra.

When the Tārikā is in the state beyond [the subtle body], situated in the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) with the luster of a blazing flame, one should cause the subtle water-element (aptattva) to ascend; one should likewise offer that as a sacrificial oblation (homa).
One should transfer that subtle fire and offer it with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
having thus offered the succession of full oblations in this sequence, [one should proceed]. (47)
Having led [the disciple] from primordial nature (prakṛti) to the person (puruṣa), one should lead that person to the Lord (īśvara).
Beyond the Lord, no further reality exists within the collection of principles. 48.
The power (śakti), which takes the forms of gross, subtle, and supreme, is the very nature of the Lord (īśvara);
for the person (puruṣa) has descended below that principle of the Lord and is therefore impure.
Having attained that supreme reality, he becomes pure;
as the self of the universe with eyes on all sides, he then becomes fit for initiation.
Then, for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, there should be two *pūrṇāhuti* offerings;
having meditated upon the disciple as both *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts), one likewise [offers] clarified butter into the *sruk*.
Unifying that duality, the Guru indeed stands transcending the supreme;
meditating, his nature being consciousness and sound, he abides in the form of the most excellent Paśyantī.
Beyond the Tārikā, one should equalize the disciple with that which is beyond conceptualization, unarisen, and unstruck (anāhata), using the Tārā mantra ending in vauṣaṭ.

Then, for the sake of the disciple's stability through the falling away of the body, one should offer many oblations with the *pūrṇāhuti* mantra beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "Namaḥ," using the *tārā* [mantra]. 54.
There, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and then casting the *mahāpūrṇa*,
the Guru [unites] the disciple, himself, and me, the eternal Lakṣmī.
One should meditate on everything as being unified within me, like milk poured into milk;
thus, having made the disciple consist of *lakṣmī* by means of the wind of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), [one should proceed].
Having drawn [the disciple] forward, he should again cause him to hear this mantra in sequence;
then, having established me, Tārā, within his heart, he should instruct him.

One should instruct everything pertaining to the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga), as well as the scriptural sequence, the conventional dharma, and indeed that which concerns the secrecy of the mantra and so forth. (58)
Then one should place the hand of Viṣṇu upon the head, the back, and within the heart;
having touched that limb with the mudrā, the disciple should worship me. (59)

Taking the water-pot with Tārā, and mentally reciting the Tārikā mantra together with its limbs (aṅgas) and subsidiary limbs (upāṅgas), he went to wherever he had previously been instructed by his Guru.
The guru should consecrate the disciple with a serene inner mind;
having thus attained his true form, the disciple then crosses to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Then, with great magnificence, one should perform the Guru-yāga;
having established the foundational powers (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth, and having seated the Guru therein.
One should worship with all offerings such as *arghya* and so forth, as well as with gold, jewels, and the like;
thereafter, one should worship the guest who has been fed and satiated with this mantra.
Salutations to the Guru, who is the embodiment of the sun, moon, and fire that illuminate the dense thicket of ignorance, and who brings peace to the torment of the three fires of suffering. 64.
Having then received permission, one should thereafter repeat the mantra;
and one should accomplish it according to one's desire, for as long as one wishes. (65) [After verse 65, the]
The Telugu printed edition contains the following additional passages within brackets:
Śakra:
O Padmā, those enemies of Madhu who have been initiated by you into the initiation [you] described—
O Īśvarī, the right to perform worship belongs to them or to no one else.
Śrī said: O Indra, out of affection for you, I shall tell you this supreme secret:
there are those on earth initiated for the sake of liberation among the three castes.
For all of them are indeed disqualified from performing sacrifices for the sake of others;
among them, however, those of great fortune are they whose hearts are dedicated to the feet of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, there are eight hundred sages in this world who are supremely devoted;
they are knowers of the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions and are solely intent upon the Pañcarātra.
They were knowers of the Dharma of taking refuge, devoted to the two foremost and unsurpassed [truths],
and adhered to the performance of the ritual actions according to the sūtras proclaimed by the sage Kātyāyana.
Then Kāśyapa, Gautama, Bhṛgu, Āśvalāyana, Aṅgiras,
and other such preeminent sages [were engaged] in the sacrifice for Hari for the sake of others.
Others possess the qualification for performing sacrifices, but they are not qualified [for this];
these are my devotees, dear to Hari, these are the Bhāgavatas.
Other Bhāgavatas do not at all worship us two;
rather, other Bhāgavatas worship with devotion the Blessed Lord Hari.
Those others in the world who are devoted to [the Lord] are called Bhāgavatas;
for even the worship of the supreme [deities] is performed by those born in the lineages of the best of sages, such as Kāśyapa and others.
If other devotees of the Lord perform worship to another deity out of delusion, it will result in the downfall of the kingdom and its people through their own power.
Therefore, with every effort, those devoted to the Lord (Bhāgavatas) should always [initiate] one born of the lineage of Kaśyapa and others who has been initiated, even if he is illiterate.
"He is indeed worthy of propitiation, a purifier, a great knower of Brahman.

65. Beyond this point, a text intended to establish that only those born of the lineages of Kāśyapa and others are authorized to perform sacrifices for the sake of others is not seen to be universal; rather, it is found only in the edition printed in Telugu characters.

Thus it is seen; moreover, it is coiled. Therefore, this section may have been appended by certain people desiring to establish their own right to perform sacrifices for the sake of others in temples—this is the opinion of the Unnetṛ.
Thus, O slayer of Bala, initiation and consecration have been described to you.
What more do you wish to hear regarding that which is to be accomplished through right concentration?

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Method of Initiation and Consecration," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (Variant readings: *Śrīpañcarātra* or *Śrīpāñcarātre*; Ṅ: *prakāśaḥ*) || 41 ||
Chapter Forty-Two: Śakra— (p. 166)
Repeated salutations again and again to you, the queen of Hṛṣīkeśa, whose two lotus feet are a boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
O Goddess, by your grace I have heard the sequence of the initiation rites; now tell me,
O lotus-dweller, the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* of the *Tārikā*.
2. Puraścaraṇa is the name for the preliminary practice of a mantra received through the instruction of a guru, performed for the sake of attaining one's desired fruit.
— Śrī — I am the Power named Nārāyaṇī, who rests upon Nārāyaṇa.
Her supreme form is Tārikā Bhuvaneśvarī. || 3 ||
Listen now to the perfection of the practice for me, who have become a mere lump of flesh,
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
4. "Of her who has become a mass" means: of her who has the form of the *piṇḍa-mantra*.
That time for the accomplishment of Tārikā has been demonstrated by those learned in the Tantra.
[One who is] untouched by great sins and by the well-known heinous crimes; 5.
Fallen from his state due to atheism, yet avoiding the practice of censurable acts,
he cultivated friendliness toward all beings and felt remorse for the evil he had committed.
One should bring various high and low sins to pacification through expiatory rites,
remaining a celibate student, eating sacrificial food, speaking the truth, and being firm in one's vows.
In the presence of Viṣṇu, one should mentally recite the syllable Oṃ one million times;
one should perform ten thousand oblations with clarified butter accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
A *niyuta* is ten *lakṣas*; an *ayuta* is ten *sahasras*. One should perform an oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds using the *Sāvitrī* mantra that many times.
Having abandoned [the effects of] great sins and heinous crimes, these two are rendered celebrated [as purified].
9. "Renowned as a *vihāra* (monastery)" means not made public.
Having performed such a rite with the triad beginning with the *praṇava* (OM), one is liberated from non-public [sins] such as great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and extreme sins (*atipātaka*). 10.
Likewise, through fasts and other such illuminating practices,
or else one who knows the reality of the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra should fast for three nights.
11. By the phrase "through fasting and so forth," the expiation for those who have committed acts of public disclosure is stated:
"Three times during the day and three times during the night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
at each junction of the day (saṃdhyā), immersing himself, he should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times. 12.
One should thus spend those three nights performing ritual ablutions;
on the fourth day, one should indeed give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
In this way, one becomes purified of all sins without exception, as previously stated;
or else, one should consecrate oneself with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) at the three junctions of the day.
Having passed three nights in this manner, one is liberated from all sins;
or else, by means of the intellect, one may focus on each one of those five [deities], beginning with Tārā.

15. Regarding "the pentad beginning with Tāra": this means the Tāra, the Vyāhṛtis, the Sāvitrī, the Tārikā, and the Anutārikā. While reciting [these] and drinking, one should indeed gaze upon the Vaiṣṇava [form], which is stainless and radiant.
By performing [this] for a day and night, one is thus liberated from all sins.
16. "One should look upon a Vaiṣṇava"—this was said for the sake of ensuring the excellence of the performed rite.
17. Those who go to Viṣṇu in this world, being sinless and devoted to dharma—even one sitting in their row, having eaten there, is liberated from all sins.
17. He describes the greatness of the Vaiṣṇavas with the verse beginning "In the world" (bhuvane), etc. The meaning is that the Vaiṣṇavas are those who have taken refuge in Viṣṇu as their protector.
Having brought evil to destruction through those dharmas esteemed by the hosts of great seers,
one should thereafter take refuge in the Tārikā, who delivers one across the ocean of existence.
Having observed the fast according to the rules on the seventh day of the dark fortnight, the practitioner,
remaining at the twilight hour, should perform the recitation of the Tārikā on the eighth day.
Having abandoned other desires, one should perform the prescribed action without yielding to distraction in the divine, perfected, and likewise rishi-made, stainless abode of Viṣṇu.
On a mountain peak, by a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or even in a grove of bilva trees,
one should eat any one of these— milk, barley-meal, or sacrificial food— only once.
One should indeed perform the recitation twelve thousand times for seven days;
one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that number, as well as oblations (āhuti) with clarified butter.
By this procedure for the present time, if one beholds a favorable vision at midnight on the fourteenth day during the rite of the Tārikā, [success is attained].
Either the acquisition of a jar of liquor, or the drinking of liquor, or the ritual sprinkling of a woman out of desire, or else the sight of Sudṛśī. (24)
Either an embrace with her out of passion, or enjoyment together with her;
or else, through the perfection of mantra, speech with her, or from that, the attainment of the fruit. || 25 ||
Or even the sight of a gentle person, or a handsome couple,
or the sight of a king, or the sight of a queen.
Either the direct vision of Nārāyaṇa himself, or my own vision of him in a dream, or the sight of a devoted wife, or meeting with Vaiṣṇavas—[these are the means]. (27)
And whatever other auspicious vision is described in the treatises on dreams, having obtained that [dream], he should rise up, cast off sleep, and overcome fatigue. (28)
Having sipped water and become purified, the practitioner should remember me while lying on his bed during the night;
then, having risen in the morning and performed the sequence of the sandhyā rites, he should proceed. (29)
29. On the bed upon the grass mat; "the night" (*niśām*) is in the accusative case to express duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
They were equal in character, age, and form, handsome, and devoted to the Dharma. They were neither dejected nor miserable in appearance, beautiful, and high-minded. 30.
Having summoned the husband and wife— who were in the prime of youth and spoke with pleasant gentleness— and having bathed them, he regarded them as the very embodiments of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.

Having adorned them with garments and other finery, they practiced a deception regarding their wealth; once the two were fed and their limbs anointed with fragrant scents, they were gratified with sacrificial fees.
One should pray for the accomplishment of the *tārikā* while identifying with Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
at the conclusion of the words "May it be so," one should take refuge in those two after bowing to them. (33)
33–34. "Those two of us" means that couple known as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, who are our very forms.

Having had [the text] recited, and having then gratified the Vaiṣṇavas—who are most learned in the Vedas—and the foremost of the twice-born with auspicious blessings, one should proceed for the attainment of one's desired goals.
If one does not see a dream-vision on the night of the fourteenth day,
then beginning from the new moon until the seventh day of the dark fortnight, one should continue.
Furthermore, one who observes the vow should pass that same amount of time,
reciting the mantra three thousand times while subsisting on a single meal per day.
36. He ate but once a day, taking his meal only one time.

In the interim, he did not neglect the fertile season of his youthful wife, nor did he reproach her conduct; rather, with a wise mind, he brought joy to both husband and wife. 37. [He remained] pleasing the couple through his intellect, while not transgressing the seasonal period of his young wife.
Doing what is pleasing to the passionate women without being greedy for them, and avoiding sin, he should then reach the eighth day of the dark fortnight and perform his recitation as before. (38)

Performing all [rites] such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth, one should cause them to cease upon seeing [the signs] in a dream; one should practice in this manner for as long as the signs are not fully perceived. || 39 ||
When the Tārikā is accomplished, a man obtains everything;
he becomes a perfect practitioner of the scriptures and one who is skilled in the realization of the inner self.
He was a knower of the ordinances of all tantras, one who had reached the further shore of all Vedānta, a piercer of all doubts, and one who had mastered all definitive conclusions. || 41 ||
(168) He who speaks according to reality, who is straightforward, eloquent, and has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of Dharma—
such a person indeed desires to employ [this] for the sake of another or for himself. (42)
Whether in subduing or in favoring, he always attains success.
Śakra said:
"Obelisance to you, O beloved of Hari, whose very form is the complete set of six political expedients (ṣāḍguṇya)! (43)
O you whose home is the lotus, O housewife of Govinda!
From the lotus of your face, I have heard the Siddhi that is the specific excellence of Tārikā.

The gross, subtle, and supreme forms of Tārā, who possesses a threefold nature, have been demonstrated according to the rule as they truly are, once she has been accomplished through the prescribed ritual. (45)
"O Lotus-born One, you should now tell me my specific application (viniyoga).
Śrī said: "The one, self-perfected with the six qualities, the swan-like Nārāyaṇa, the self-controlled... (46)
I am the Haṃsī-Śakti, his Vaśinī who grants all desires;
both we, the Haṃsa and the Haṃsī, are delighted in our nature as Tārikā.
Learn from me the application of that [Śakti], who is my own essential nature, within various mantras according to their external and internal divisions. (48)
Whatever mantras there are, of whatever kind, whether superior or inferior; and whatever applications of them there are, of whatever kind—[all these he knows]. (49)
There are as many such applications of her as there are [beings], of this there is no doubt;
nevertheless, O Śakra, listen to some of my applications.
[He saw those] who produce immediate conviction regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
[he saw her] with a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and [her] dwelling in a black antelope skin. (51)

Having meditated upon her, who is clothed in a black antelope skin, whose auspicious eyes are like those of a frightened black fawn, who resembles the full moon, and who holds the Brahma-mudrā and a rosary of beads; 52.
And holding two lotuses in her other two hands—
thus [one should meditate] upon me, the lotus-eyed one, or upon Janārdana, the God of gods.
Having meditated, one should recite the mantra of Tārā one hundred thousand times; then the Dharma will become manifest.
[One should offer] five million *prasthas* of rice in the form of husked grains.
One should cook that many *prasthas* of clarified butter and *palas* of sugar— or likewise that many *palas* of jaggery— all together in a single vessel.
An oblation of clarified butter, well-boiled according to the prescribed rite and equal in quantity to that milk,
[should be offered] on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight when half the sun has risen.
One should offer the oblation situated in the great vessel with a single oblation alone,
using a *triṣṭubh* verse addressed to Jātavedas, with the *tārikā* mantra placed at the beginning and the end.

57. With the verse beginning "jātavedasya" (jātavedase sunavāma somam), the wise one [should perform the rite] in the great fire within the great sacrificial pit by means of the application of the yantra. Then, beginning at dawn until the setting of the sun— 58.
The wise one, free from fatigue, should offer oblations continuously with the *sruva* ladle alone, using consecrated clarified butter and employing that same *triṣṭubh* meter. (59)
Beginning from morning, one should continuously feed one brahmin at a time, starting from the morning, with śāli rice prepared with milk, curd, and clarified butter.
Having caused the twice-born who are most learned in the Vedas to recite [the texts], he should at the conclusion offer libations;
likewise, he should honor a Vaiṣṇava couple under the names of Lakṣmī and Lakṣmīśa.
The hero who acts in this manner, supported by his resolve,
obtains a treasure that is beyond compare, inexhaustible, and numbering ten million.
O Pākaśāsana, listen to this most wonderful application:
first, having taken the word *tārā*, one should join it with the word *subhage*. (63)
One should then join it with *svāhā*; this six-syllabled mantra belongs to Tāriṇī. Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should commence the practice on the full moon day.
One should recite that [mantra] ten thousand times while seated properly in the middle of a beautiful tree in a grove, between a full water-pot and a lamp.
Meditating upon me, who have the luster of the interior of a lotus, who hold a pair of lotuses,
who am two-armed, with dark-cornered eyes and dark, curly hair. (66)
Her face was filled with a smile; she was beautiful, with full and elevated breasts, adorned with all ornaments, and clothed in the finest silk garments.
Meditating thus upon her who is most beautiful and auspicious, one should then perform the recitation (japa);
one should likewise offer libations (tarpaṇa) and oblations (homa), each being a tenth part [of the japa], with this Tārā-mantra.
The wise man should offer a bali-oblation consisting of śāli rice mixed with milk, ghee, and jaggery; he should also feed a woman endowed with auspicious marks who has been duly honored.
The student himself should eat sacrificial food once at night;
in this manner, he should perform this vow for thirty nights without fail.
Undertaking the recitation, libation, fire-offering, and so forth without interruption and with diligence,
one should complete the vow on the following full moon day.
At the conclusion of the vow, she who is composed of the essence of Manmatha and named Subhagā will arrive;
that Yakṣī will say to the practitioner, "What shall I do? (72).
One should regard her as a mother, a sister, a wife, or a friend;
having approached her with the attitude of a mother, she protects one even from all calamities.
73. "One should fashion" means one should meditate upon her.
As a "sister," she who has been sought as refuge grants all worldly benefits;
as a "beloved," she who has been accepted grants all desires for as long as life lasts. 74.
Accepted as a friend, she indeed leads one in every direction;
one desiring liberation should constantly recite [the mantra] consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme Self. (75)
I, being well-pleased, shall cause you to attain that divine station of Viṣṇu;
as for the applications belonging to the supreme mantra, they will be stated hereafter.
76. He also states that the worship of Tārikā has liberation as its fruit: "That state...

etc. "All those [deities] who are the effects of Tārikā, as well as those who rely on other mantras—the path of *puraścaraṇa* has been declared to you, along with its ritual applications (*viniyoga*)."
In order to establish confidence in her, learn from me the path to accomplishment.

77. "Of her" means of Tārikā. Thus ends the section on the transmission of the Tārā mantra in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra* (or *Śrīpañcarātra*). [B: the transmission of the Tārā mantra; F: the worship of the Tāraka mantra]
The forty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Tārā Mantra."
Chapter Forty-three: Śrī—p. 170)
Listen, O Lord of the Gods, I shall declare the supreme accomplishment arising from various yogas, pertaining to the Tārikā, who is the personified essence of the Vidyā.
The yogi should duly apply the Tārikā within the range of the body—at the tip of the nose, at the tip of the tongue, and at the middle and root of the tongue. || 2 ||
One should maintain the sequence of the principles (tattva-paddhati),
beginning with earth and ending with intellect, each possessing its own nature according to its respective effects; here,
"intellect" refers to the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva).
Moving from one principle to another principle, one should recite [the mantra] according to the number:
twice, four times, six, eight, ten, and sixteen times respectively.
4. "From the *tattva* of earth," and so forth; the meaning is that one proceeds in this manner from the *tattva* of earth to the *tattva* of water, and so on.
One should contemplate *prakṛti* twenty-four times. One should then recollect the eighty *tārās*, and therein one should meditate upon the *jīva*. 5.
Whatever its extent, whatever its nature, and whoever it may be—within that one should perform a hundred recitations;
one should then contemplate the Puṣkara lotus situated below, which is the support for the unmanifest consciousness.

Having meditated upon this [mantra] as being in the form of a lotus— serving as the support for the constituent parts beginning with the *tattvas*, infinite, and conveying the reality— the wise person should recite it one hundred and fifty times.
Then, that which consists of the unmanifest, time, life-force, and the imperishable (akṣara) is the stalk;
but where there is space (kha), there time is the inner darkness characterized by a hollow.
Having reflected correctly upon that which consists of those three— thinking "this is he who is consciousness within"— one should then perform two hundred recitations.
Below the navel, while recollecting me— the power (śakti) named Aniruddha who consists of the Blessed Lord— through forms, time, and other means, one should perform a hundred recitations.
Below that is the power of Pradyumna, and the number of recitations is likewise;
below that is the power of Sāṃkarṣiṇī, and the number of recitations is likewise. (11)
At the very bottom is the couple known as Vāsudeva, which is the gross form;
beyond that is the subtle, and beyond that is the supreme, which transcends everything.
It was the manifestation of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, indefinable and incomparable,
vibrating everywhere as the power and the Lord of power, and entirely pure.
Having attained the sleep consisting of yoga, one should thus enter into that very sleep;
then, having risen during the latter part of the night, one should maintain these twelve [concentrations].

14. Regarding "twelve": there are twelve *dhāraṇās*, consisting of the four beginning with Vāsudeva—namely, the individual soul (*jīva*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*), intellect (*buddhi*), and the elements (*bhūta*)—along with those starting from Vāsudeva down to the earth (*bhūmi*). This follows the sequence of the method for their enumeration.
Or one may hold all these meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) within the heart.
These twelve indeed are the dhāraṇās, whether in the Tārikā or otherwise;
this yoga is beneficial to all, insofar as one abides therein through the essential principles (tattvas).
Or, having withdrawn everything consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, and having made the mind supportless, one should enter the state of emptiness. || 17 ||

17. He states another method: "Having withdrawn," etc. Having dissolved all principles (tattva) back into their respective causes, one should make the mind free from objects. That experience of supreme bliss which occurs when the mind is objectless is itself the supreme yoga.
I enter the Great Yoga, which is like the ocean filled with the form of emptiness and the equal form [of all things], established in the meditation on emptiness. (18)
When the yogi, while practicing yoga, becomes like the bliss of a still, silent rain-cloud, that yogi is always dear to Me. (19)
Where there exists nothing whatsoever that is a delimited object of meditation,
that undelimited state which is beyond cognition— that is clearly my own form.
20. The limited and finite; the yogi assimilates the entire object of knowledge simultaneously. That vast, great flame is my waveless body. 21.
