Wherein all beings and worlds are invoked by the mind,
then my eternal state of being as the essence of all things unfolds.
22. All existence exists as the universal self; "existence" (bhāva) means being (sattā).

Having offered the elements, the senses, the worlds, and so forth into the sacrificial ladle of the mind, and having then cast that ladle away, I exist as a yogi. 23. [The verse continues: "Having offered the elements, the senses, the worlds, and so forth into the sacrificial ladle of the mind, and having then cast that ladle away, I exist as a yogi."
23. "I exist" and "I exist as my own self"—this is an impersonal (bhāve) usage.

That by which something is delimited is greater than that [delimited] thing; for everything that exists and does not exist is delimited by the intellect (dhī). 24. [The same applies: "By me it is being done," "by my self it is being done"—this is an impersonal usage. That by which something is delimited is greater than that [delimited] thing; for everything that exists and does not exist is delimited by the intellect.
24. The nature of the Goddess as the essence of knowledge is stated [in the verse] beginning with "That which is delimited," and so forth:
"She is not delimited by anything else; that form of mine is stainless.
These two—intellect and the object—are not external to Her, whether they be non-existence or existence. 25.
That which is not touched by my intellect is not pleasing to me;
for if the ocean were to transgress its bounds and submerge the world, [what could be done]? 26.

26. Regarding the fact that during the stage of the maturation of yoga (*yogaparipākadaśā*), the entire world appears as nothing but the form of consciousness (*dhīrūpa*), he states a worldly illustration: "When [the eye] has transcended... and so forth.
At that time, there are no longer high places or depressions; likewise, the entire world [is seen] in me.
This supreme state cannot be attained by one of small soul. || 27 ||
One should repeatedly sever [the mind] in order to attain this yoga, whether in a present state, a past one, or a future one—be it auspicious or otherwise. (28)
One should remember the most essential form, the supreme form of the Supreme Lord;
just as bees collect honey from all flowers. (29)

29. He provides an illustration regarding the fact that all things are to be meditated upon as one's own self: "They bring together... and so forth. "They bring me, who am one, together within all things; wherever the mind goes, there one should contemplate my splendor. (30)
Having moved, where does it go? For everything is composed of that [mind].
One should contemplate the sequence of the principles as a garland strung upon my thread.
Or, with me acting as its wall, one should perceive the world as a painting;
it is like a mass of foam upon the ocean, which is motionless, boundless, and profound. (32)
One should remember the fourfold group beginning with the subject (pramātṛ) both in forward and reverse order,
as well as that [power] which arises from the form of the "I" and returns to it again.

33. "The tetrad" means the fourfold set consisting of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the instrument of knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*). This connects with the phrase "the unfolding path of the principles. "The Person, the primordial unfolding of me, is fashioned by my own volition."
Another manifestation of my power, known as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), resides upon the ground of the lower lip.
Another, the third, located below that on the earth, consists of externalization;
this fourth is of the nature of existence, consisting of the object of knowledge, and is the lowest of the low. || 35 ||

By the power of my own resolve alone, constantly meditating with my intellect— both sequentially and out of order— upon that which is eternally of the nature of blissful consciousness, [I remain] perpetually.
Having abandoned these four, one attains my state, either within the thirty-two lotuses that serve as the support for consciousness. (37)
37–46. The word division is *dvātriṃśati ambujeṣu* ("in thirty-two lotuses"). He indicates the thirty-two lotuses:
*ādhārā* and so forth, six; *paśyantī* and so forth, five; *bodhayantī* and so forth, five; *ghoṣayantī* and so forth, five; *grāhayantī* and so forth, five; *praṇayantī* and so forth, six.
One should meditate upon me as having the luster of a lamp’s flame, or as Rūpasundarī,
beginning from the support-lotus (ādhāra-padma) down to the earth below the navel-lotus.
p. 172) Six lotuses are to be contemplated by yogins; hear their names from me:
Vyucchantī, Vyuṣitā, Vyuṣṭā, Vyuṣuṣī, Vyoṣuṣī, and Ramā. (39)
From the navel-lotus and the heart-lotus, they declare five lotuses:
Paśyantī is called the navel-lotus; Paśyā consists of the other [four].
The visible and the being seen are the heart, which is called the lotus;
now hear about those called the five lotuses from within the middle of the heart and the throat.

Awakening, the awakener, the being awakened, and likewise the other [state], as well as resonance and manifestation—these are the designations for [the states] residing in the lotuses of the throat, the heart, and the middle [of the body]. (42)
Listen to these, known as the five lotuses situated between the throat and the palate:
Ghoṣayantī, Ghuṣyantī, Ghuṣṭā, Puṣyantī, and Puṣṭā, as well as Ghoṣā and the other.
These are called the five lotuses located in the region of the palate and the space between the eyebrows.
Causing one to grasp, the desire to grasp, and the act of grasping. || 44 ||
"Nirṇīti" refers to the throat, the space between the eyebrows, and the lotus-cluster;
now hear these names for the six lotuses located at the root of the brows, the crown of the head, and the center. (45)
Prāṇayantī, Prāṇatī, Prāṇā, and Prāṇāvabodhinī—these supreme powers awaken [the soul]; they reside within the lotus situated between the eyebrows.
One should meditate upon me within the crest-jewels of the lamps, proceeding in both direct and reverse order,
while reciting my long *tārikā* mantra, which resembles the resonance of a long bell.
Thinking of me in this way, or even remembering my beautiful form, the yogi abandons all affliction and attains my own state. || 48 ||
Or one may observe them within nine lotuses in direct and reverse order:
three lotuses in the *ādhāra*, and three lotuses below the heart. (49)
Below the head, there are three lotuses; this is the sequence for the arrangement of the nine lotuses.
Alternatively, in twelve lotuses, they are placed in pairs at the locations beginning with the head.
Or one should contemplate the Tārikā, the resonant sound of the syllable Om, within the six first lotuses, or in the three—the root, the heart, and the earth—or even between the eyebrows. (51)
One should first contemplate that drop as being the size of a mung bean and intensely radiant;
then as the size of a mustard seed; then as variegated and formless.
Whatever object is perceived, whether it has the form of a jar, a wall, or the like—[it is all that].
Therein, one should contemplate those principles (tattvas) which exist according to the scriptures, as many as there are.
Having made these one with oneself, one should contemplate them there through the sense of "I," as well as whatever objects exist in the world that are either causes or effects.

Those which consist of the supported and the support, which are either transparent or dense, whose natures are both the entity and its possessor, and which are composed of the auspicious and the inauspicious; 55.

Whether consisting of the produced and the unproduced, or appearing as qualities and the possessor of qualities, or existing as the container and the contained, they are all composed of Śakti and its Possessor (Śaktimān). || 56 ||
They consist of the nature of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, or the forms of woman and man;
they consist of the nature of the action and the agent, or the means and the goal.
Whatever forms of words exist in the form of feminine and masculine genders, or whatever things in this world exist as dual entities; ||| 58 ||
The yogi should perceive those [elements] with his intellect as being of the nature of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
O Purandara, hear now the supreme secret vow of this tantra. (59)

That which is to be performed by the yogin in the sequence of the ritual procedure for the yoga of Lakṣmī was previously set forth by the Primordial God for the sake of the creation of the world. (60)
Desiring to do what was pleasing to me, the yogi, who is expert in the Lakṣmī-tantra, assumed the form of a woman with great resolve. (61)
One should not, through action, mind, or speech, recall the censure of those who desire women;
where I am, there are the principles (tattvas), and where I am, there are the deities.
"Wherever I am, there are meritorious deeds; wherever I am, there is Keśava.
Since I am in the woman, therefore the woman embodies the entire world. (63)
He who reviles that woman reviles Lakṣmī;
he who welcomes her welcomes the three worlds. || 64 ||
He who hates any woman hates the beloved of Hari;
he who hates the beloved of Hari hates the entire world. (65)
He whose mind becomes serene upon seeing a woman like moonlight,
and who does not harbor any ill-will toward her, is considered by me to be most dear.
Just as there is no sin in Nārāyaṇa, nor in me, O Śakra, just as there is none in a cow, in a Brahmin, or in one who knows the Vedānta; || 67 ||
O Śakra, likewise no evil whatsoever exists in a woman;
she is as stainless as the Gaṅgā and as meritorious as the Sarasvatī.
For just as the river Aruṇā is [the source], so too is Sīmantinī the most excellent;
since I am the mother of the three worlds. (69)
This [is achieved] through reliance on the noble lady, for she is my supreme strength—the goddess who is the mother of the three worlds and the fulfiller of all desires. (70)
Why should a yogi not worship a slender-limbed woman who is Yoga personified?
He should not commit sin against a woman, nor should he dwell upon the misconduct of women. (71)
One who desires to attain yoga should not do anything pleasing to a woman except for what is sinful;
he should regard her as a mother, as a goddess, or as myself.
He who, out of delusion, hates a woman and does not provide her assistance—listen to this as well, O Lord of Gods, for you are dear to me. (73)
Having heard this, you too must carry it out and never speak of it to anyone.
Any woman of beautiful form who has come within the range of your vision— (74)
In her, the yogi should meditate upon me while reciting the *tārikā* mentally;
with a mind free from longing, he should contemplate her form. (75)
One should meditate there upon Prāṇa as the Sun, the Supreme Self, the Person within the heart of the woman, and as Fire, endowed with the perfection of beauty and charm.
One should remember that woman endowed with every perfection;
having remembered her and reciting the sacred word (brahman), one should indeed contemplate me through the intellect.
Then, upon the attainment of samādhi, I become possessed therein;
the loosening of all stiffened limbs is the characteristic sign of my possession. (79)
Having diligently propitiated me with a mind free from greed, one who practices yoga should indeed desist from worldly activity, completely avoiding all evil. (79)
But this [practice] must never be performed by a wise man regarding the wives of others;
for wherever this concentration exists, she certainly becomes enamored with him. (80)
One should perform [the rite] with one's own wife, or even with a common woman;
even a transgression here is not a fault, because she possesses the contemplation of my nature.
Regarding the great surge of joy that arises from enjoyments born of sensory contact,
one should meditate upon my form with an undistracted mind.

One should cultivate that state of being which consists of the intense joy one feels when recollecting the pleasure arising from an excellent object, such as that produced by rubbing or churning. (83)
The joy that arises when an object is seen with the eye, or when it is tasted, heard, or smelled—that is my body consisting of bliss. (84)
This method of attainment has been described for the ascetic who subdues the mind, even when sounds, touches, tastes, and so forth present themselves by chance. (85)
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, so one should not delight the mind in them.
That supreme happiness which is manifested within by the internal organ (antahkarana), when it abides in sattva, having cast off rajas and destroyed tamas; || 87 ||
That bliss of mine, whose nature is knowledge, is devoid of beginning and end;
such as it is, it is never manifested by contacts dependent upon sense objects.
The objects that bring pleasure bind one to suffering, just as honey mixed with poison is sweet when consumed. (89)
What is gained by that which subsequently kills its devourer—he who, afflicted by the heat, takes refuge in the shade of an angry serpent? (90)
That man may enjoy those pleasures arising from touch for his own happiness—
pleasures that are to be accomplished through the exhaustion of effort and suffering, and which, though seemingly pleasant, are mixed with pain. (91)

What happy person would resort to objects of sense, which are so subtle and subject to decay, when the body has been refined by divine beings through the purification of breath-control and the restriction of food by means of recitation? 92.
Diminishing the qualities of rajas and tamas through conduct and actions dear to Me,
the yogi should constantly subdue the mind with effort for the sake of meditative absorption.
When the mind is ever-conquered, the entire universe is thereby conquered;
when the mind is conquered, my pure body manifests of its own accord.

Śakra: O Creator, seated upon the lotus, who ordains the entire system of the machinery of distinctions between consciousness and the unconscious, and who provides all enjoyments—salutations to you! (95)
By what means can that mind be tamed, which is ever inclined toward sense objects, restless, powerful, firm, swift-moving, far-reaching, and indistinct? (96)
Śrī said:

O Śakra, that mind is difficult to subdue, difficult to restrain, eternally subtle, hard to comprehend, and prone to transgression; it is restless and can only be brought under control through the practice of dispassion. 99.
Attachment, however, is a longing for an object born of nature, habit, or association;
its absence is dispassion, which is produced by the knowledge of reality. (98)
The wickedness of the sense objects is that which is known as the knowledge of reality;
the wise person should discern that wickedness through wisdom in four ways. (99)
One should reflect: "Of what nature is this entity, from where does it arise, and for what purpose?
For sense objects are of the nature of bondage; they ensnare those who serve them. (100)

100. "They ensnare" means they bind; the verbal root is *ṣiñ* (to bind). All those who have attained manifestation from the unmanifested [nature] are subject to pleasure and pain. And those objects of the senses do not exist by their own inherent nature for those who merely desire sense-objects. 101. [The verse continues: "But for those whose intellect is fixed on the Supreme, the senses, being turned away from external objects, bring about peace. For them, the objects of the senses, even though present, do not produce attachment or aversion because their minds are withdrawn from the external. Therefore, it is said that the senses are like snakes with venomous fangs. Thus, one should restrain the senses through the practice of yoga. One should not allow the mind to wander among objects. By restraining the senses, one attains the highest state. Therefore, one should always control the senses. This is the teaching of the Lord. Thus ends the tenth chapter.
For those [pleasures] arise from means that involve uncertainty, exhaustion, and suffering;
they do not produce happiness alone, for they surely flow with pain.
And that pleasure, perishing in an instant, is equated with the suffering of its own state;
this variegated form should be reflected upon by the wise person in every single phenomenon. 103.
This knowledge of reality has been declared both by way of summary and by way of detailed analysis;
yet attachment to sense objects arises from the conviction that they are the cause of happiness. (104)
Because it consists of false cognition, it is sublated by the cognitions of reality;
and when that [false cognition] is refuted by such ascertainment, its status as a logical reason is not established at all. (105)
No one should take up causeless sense objects for the sake of their own accomplishment;
rather, that which is the knowledge of reality and its repeated cultivation [or reflection],
is called "practice" (abhyāsa) by the knowers of reality in the treatises on reality.
In the subtle and the great, in the minute atom and in the gross, stable, and moving object. || 107 ||
Wherever the mind abides and is held through the practice of these [methods],
by the striving yogi through the yoga of dispassion and practice— 108.
The unrestrained mind is tamed; therefore, it certainly attains peace.
Śakra said:
"O you whose gait is skillful in wandering through the multitude of the lotuses of reality! (109)
Homage to you, O dweller in the mind of the Conqueror of Madhu, seated upon the lotus!
Just as the mind is tamed through practice, so may it become powerful and firm.
"Show me that path; salutations to you, O Lotus-born One! Śrī said:
"When the arrow, having become slender in the upper sky, falls with speed—" (111)

111-112. Having first directed the mind toward objects exactly as they are perceived, and having gradually attained detachment from them, one should subsequently direct it toward the investigation of reality (*tattva*).
To explain this point with an illustration, he says "viyati" and so forth. [The phrase] "become attenuated" (*tanūbhūta*) means...
The meaning is that it is visible due to its leaping to a distant place and its small size.
In the same way, one should restrain the mind upon a subtle object such as Arundhatī;
or one should contemplate the mind upon a great mountain or upon the infinite. 112.
Or, whatever subtle atom exists that revolves upon the wheel,
one should fix the mind right there and cause it to revolve along with that which is revolving. (113)
113. The same applies to the analogies of the wheel and so forth.
Likewise: "One should move the mind with the moving tip of an ashvattha leaf;
when it stands still, one should stabilize the consciousness; when it goes away, one should cause the mind to follow. 114.
O Purandara, this method has been described to you for the sake of illustration;
by subduing the mind through this, one will attain supreme yoga.

One should meditate upon that form of the Supreme which, though consisting of both the Lord and the one to be ruled, is both supreme and subordinate; it resides in the sun, possesses a male form, and likewise has a female form consisting of five points (bindus).
Thus, O gentle one, this form of the Tārikā has been shown to you in its entirety.
For one who has realized the truth in this manner, no other object of knowledge is required. (117)

Thus, O Śakra, this accomplishment of the *piṇḍa* has been shown to you in brief; now hear from me the procedure for the manifestation of names and forms, as well as the means of realization (*sādhana*). || 118 ||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Illumination of Various Yogas," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (In the version A: *Śrīpañcarātra*; in version B: *Śrīpāñcarātre*). 43.
Chapter Forty-four: Śakra—

Salutations to you, O Goddess expert in protecting the realms of both the conscious and the unconscious; salutations be to you, the consort of Viṣṇu, the architect of the creation of the universe. || 1 ||
The divisions consisting of the gross, subtle, and supreme selves have been previously demonstrated.
O Lotus-born One, show me the divisions of Tārā’s seed-syllables, clusters, and so forth. (2)
Śrī:
The glorious Nārāyaṇa alone is the embodiment of the six perfect attributes;
I alone am His supreme Śakti, the embodiment of the six attributes. (3)
Desiring to show compassion for the worlds, I, who am eternally of the nature of knowledge and action,
nourish and purify them through my form as Tārikā.
O Śakra, her state as the supreme (para) and so forth has already been shown to you;
now listen to me as I explain the various divisions, such as the seed-syllables (bīja) and the clusters (piṇḍa).
O Śakra, that supreme *ahaṃtā* which was previously shown to be threefold in nature—just as it is, it is called the seed-syllable of Tārā. (6)
Abiding in the fire of the sun, with Viṣṇu as her mass and the Lord of the Sky (Īśvara) as her crest-ornament—
her preparatory yoga and its accomplishment have been revealed.
7. "Hrīṃ" is the seed-mantra (bījamantra).
O Śakra, it is indeed the Tārikā known by that name who is served by yogis. Listen to me as I speak while you fix your mind upon her. 8.
Taking the single pure [syllable], O Śakra, one should join it with *svāhā*;
this is the mantra of the name, worshipped by yogis, gods, Brahmā, and others [or:
worshipped by Brahmin sages]. (9)
9–10. "The meaning is that it is a pure seed. O Lord of the Thirty-three, whether by striving yogins, or by me, Nārāyaṇa, it is possible to describe the power of this designation."
But the supreme imperishable is intended as the mere continuity of the auspicious;
and for this [goddess], when she is condensed, there are likewise the accomplishments and the means of accomplishment. (11)
11. The auspicious letter is *śa*. Its specific connection [to the preceding] is the distinction. "Śrīṃ svāhā" is the name-mantra (*saṃjñāmantra*).
By constantly remembering it through practice, one’s body becomes identified with that [mantra].
The yogi, having attained identity with Me, reaches My own state of being.
Or, having been awakened by him and having attained direct realization, I fulfill every desire—that is, all desires—whatever that yogi wishes for. (13)
Thus, O Śakra, the mantra of Saṃjñā has been briefly demonstrated to you. Now listen to me regarding the word-mantra that accomplishes everything. (14)
Although this [object] is neither to be extracted by analysis nor to be written down,
nevertheless its true nature is taught so that its form may not be lost.
Oṃ 3 hrīṃ 3 śrīṃ 3 oṃ āṃ 3 hauṃ 3 haṃsaḥ 3 oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namo viṣṇave | Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namo nārāyaṇāya | Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ |
To the Blessed One Vāsudeva: Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ [O Conqueror, O Lotus-eyed One, O Primordial Being of Great Men!
Homage be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa; homage to you, O Creator of the Universe! Victory to you, O Lotus-eyed One; homage to you.
O Creator of the Universe! Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! O Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Lord of Lakṣmī, Supreme Person, Origin of the World, Center of the World. (p. 177)
I approach the Blessed One, Śrīnivāsa, the refuge of the world. I take refuge in the Blessed One.

I have gone unto the Blessed One. I entreat the Blessed One. I am meditated upon by the Blessed One. I am become an attendant of the Blessed One. I am permitted by the Blessed One. I am created for the Blessed One.

By the grace of the Blessed One, I shall cause the Goddess Lakṣmī—who is identical with the Blessed One and consists of the Tārakā mantra—to revolve through these words. It is as follows: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, to the gurus and the wives of the gurus;
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, to the supreme gurus and the wives of the supreme gurus; Oṃ śrīṃ...

Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) and the Supreme Goddess (Parameṣṭhinī). Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the ancient perfected ones (Pūrvasiddhas) and the ancient perfected goddesses (Pūrvasiddhās). Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, repeated salutations to Lakṣmī and the Yogins, and to Lakṣmī and the Yoginīs.
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Īṃ! Salutations to her who bestows the perfection and abundance of all accomplishments, to the supreme state of absolute unity, to the Supreme Haṃsī,

who transcends the speech and mind of all people and their own individual selves, whose nature is the great ocean of the mass of supreme bliss that is stainless, motionless, and free from all undertakings, and who is the highest of the high.
To Viṣṇu and the Consort of Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu, to her—svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ [Ā: Īśaḥ], salutations to her whose primordial state of aesthetic identity (sāmarasya) is eternally and incessantly expanding.

At the commencement of the succession of openings and closings manifested by one's own sovereignty, [I bow] to the one whose form is the manifestation of the power of existence through the penetration of His own will,

possessing the four qualities. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ īṃ namaḥ* to the one who has manifested the pervasion of the Blessed Lord through the power of His own volition, and who is skillful in fashioning the forms of the manifestations of the glory of existence as they expand through the immersion of His own desire.
Svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hiṃ hiṃ hiṃ [ī:
omits hiṃ hiṃ], salutations to the manifestation of the form of the Blessed One, which is eternally arisen, supremely blissful, and most beautiful.

Salutations to the Consort of Viṣṇu, whose abode is the various ointments of supernatural powers (*siddhāñjana*); who is the supreme reality consisting of the expansion of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*); whose nature is skilled in the transformation of the manifold, pure, and beautiful web of enjoyments and bliss; and who is subtle within her extremely subtle and gross forms.

Pañcabindave hiṃ hiṃ hiṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ namaḥ to her who is the mass of foam-like fragments of the conceptual distinctions between Time and Kali, stirred up by the wind of one's own volition; [O Sarveśvarī] (according to B and F).
To the one who is a single great ocean of the perfection of enjoyer, the enjoyed, the instruments of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment, as demonstrated by her playful grace;
to the wife of Viṣṇu, whose form is both supremely subtle and gross; to the five bindus: Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ.
Svāhā!

Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the one who has taken upon herself the intellect, mind, limbs, and minor members for the benefit of the entire world; to the bestower of enjoyment and good fortune to all people; to the pacifier of various calamities arising from sense objects; to Nārāyaṇī!
Svāhā! Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Oṃ!
Thus has this most wonderful Padamantra been shown to you;
it should be received from the mouth of the Guru alone by wise men who have undergone initiation. || 16 ||
While this knowledge is being studied, which is as stainless as a mirror, I shall manifest clearly—exactly who I am, how much I am, and what I am like. (17)
Listen as I describe the sequence of her limbs, she who has realized the meaning of her own true nature, who is celebrated by all the Siddhas, and who is well-awakened. (18)
I am the essence of light and bliss; at the end of that is the All-Seeing One, who manifests true being; and near her is the Supreme Brahman.

19. Oṃ, O essence of light and bliss, O all-seeing one, O manifester of true beings, O you whose form is the Supreme Brahman, O Blessed One, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutation to the Heart for the sake of knowledge. The word *svāhā* denotes the caste (*jāti*).
Then, [the mantra continues] with "O Blessed One" and likewise "O Consort of Viṣṇu" at its end.
Knowledge should be declared as being joined with birth; this is the most wonderful heart-mantra. || 20 ||
O Supreme Goddess, at its end lies the state of unimpeded bliss;
situated above all, the remainder is like the *hṛdaya*-mantra joined with its *jāti*.
21. Oṃ, to the one whose blissful state is unimpeded, the Supreme Goddess, who stands above all; for the sake of knowledge, salutations to the head. And I [B, c:
indeed] am likewise in her who is full of power and the primordial nature of the universe;
in the flame of the fire of knowledge, the remainder is intended as before. 22.
And [it is described] as consisting of the great vibration (*mahāspanda*) of the unfolding of *prāṇa* and *aprāṇa*;
this armor (*kavaca*), like the preceding [sections], transcends all stages of life (*āśrama*). (23)
Furthermore, when one is afflicted by transformation, one's own true nature is thus described as "consisting of great heroism"; this is the weapon, as previously stated for the remaining cases.
"With capacity independent of others," "the progenitor of all," and finally, "consisting of awakening"—thus [is] the Eye, as the remainder of what was previously stated. (25)
On the peak of the Brahmās in Pañcaka, this Māyā named Brahmaśrī, who dwells within the fire of tranquility and has Vyomeśa as her crest-ornament, [is present]. 26.
26. Oṃ Śrīṃ—this is the mantra of Brahmaśrī.
In the quadruple peak of concentration (dhāraṇākūṭa), she who dwells in the subtle fire is this Dhāraṇāśrī, whose crest is fashioned by Mahāvyomeśa. 27.
27. *Aṃ* 4 *yrīṃ*: this is the Dhāraṇā-Śrī mantra.
Residing on the seat of Pradhānānala, adorned with the crown of Vyomeśa, she is to be known as Puruṣa-Śrī, who extends the flood of consciousness. 28.
28. "Mrīṃ" is the mantra of Puruṣaśrī.
Residing in the fire of the Pole Star (Dhruva), with Māyā and Vyomeśa forming her crest, she is to be known as Pradhānaśrī, the one who brings consciousness to all. 29.

29. *Bhrīṃ* is the primary Śrī-mantra. [She is] she who goes to the sacred fire at the end of the purification rites beginning with Vāmana; she is the glory of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śrī*), whose crest-jewel is made by Māyā and Vyomeśa. 30.
30. *Baṃ phaṃ paṃ prīṃ*—this is the Śrī-mantra of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). From "man" (narāt) to the end of the "tāla-lakṣmā," she is Sragdharānalacāriṇī;
adorned with Māyā and Vyomeśa, she is designated as Jñānaśrī. 31.
32. *Naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ trīṃ* is the mantra of Jñānaśrī.
In the *kūṭa* (syllabic peak) preceding Vaikuṇṭha, she resides within the fire that nourishes the universe.
This is declared to be Karmaśrī, adorned by Māyā and Vyomeśa. || 32 ||
32. *Ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ṭrīṃ*—this is the *Karmaśrī* mantra.
From the letter *Uttamā* (Ū) to the end of *Karālā* (Ra), she moves through the fire of tawny hue (*kapilānalacāriṇī*).
This is declared to be *Bhūtaśrī*, adorned by *Māyā* (I) and *Vyomeśa* (H). 33.
33. *Ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ krīṃ*—this is the mantra of Bhūtaśrī.
Preceded by Brahmaśrī, these eight [syllables] reside upon the eight petals of the lotus.
The retinues of the Tārikā of the Foot-form have been proclaimed. || 34 ||
All of them possessed the luster of the interior of a lotus, with faces like serene lotuses, and held a pair of full-blown lotuses in their two arms. (35)
Brahmaśrī is auspicious, forming the Brahmāñjali mudrā with her two front hands;
Dhāraṇālakṣmī, who distinguishes between the pure and the impure, is present with the two preceding hands. (36)
With her two front hands, Puruṣaśrī forms the gesture of respectful salutation (añjali);
with her two front hands, Prakṛtiśrī wields the noose and the goad. || 37 ||
The beauty of the inner organ (antahkarana-lakshmi), however, wears the seal of reasoning (tarka-mudra):
with the palm of the hand facing downwards, the two fingers—the little finger and the ring finger—[are joined]. 38.
One should contract and hold the other two fingers together;
likewise, having separated them, one should forcefully hold the thumb raised high.
When it is elevated on its right side and facing outward, the arrangement should be made in that manner; this is the Tārkikī mudrā.
When such a pair of hands forms what is known as the *vyākhyā-mudrā*, that is the mudrā of Jñānaśrī; now learn from me the mudrā of Karmalakṣmī.
O high-minded one, when the hands are always engaged in activity with forceful exertion, this is declared to be the mudrā of Karmalakṣmī.
The first two hands of Bhūtalakṣmī bestow various enjoyments;
this single peak (kūṭa), consisting of Mahālakṣmī, brings all happiness. (43)
Listen with an attentive mind, O slayer of Bala:
a man should gradually extract that [mantra], beginning with Garuḍa and ending with Karāla. (44)
44. The Mahālakṣmī Mantra: Having recited from *kṣam* up to *kam*, one should then recite *krīṃ*.
One should then utter the Māyā-bīja (*hrīṃ*) situated in the fierce fire, followed by the Savyom-eśā (*hūṃ*).
The peak consists of Mahālakṣmī; Mahāśrī is its presiding deity. || 45 ||
She possesses both a single and manifold nature; she is with form and yet formless;
she is the supreme state of infinite bliss and likewise the one who brings about the infinite.
She is eternally present everywhere through the relationship of the support and the supported;
she possesses various colors and is crowded with a multitude of diverse collections of weapons.
Cruel yet gentle, seated in equilibrium, and preeminent with manifold prosperity;
easily accessible everywhere, she is to be meditated upon as radiant as the interior of a lotus.
O Mahāmati, this very same [deity], ending with Garuḍa, when reversed, should be meditated upon as before according to her form; she bestows the previously mentioned fruit. (49)
The seventy-two vowels of the Goddess exist as her rays;
the Bindu exists as the foundational support; and Emanation is her own powerful form.
Thus has the form of the Tārikā, known as the "Word" (pada), been revealed to you;
always fix your mind upon it with focused attention. (51)
This essence has been extracted from the great ocean of the Lakṣmītantra, which extends for a hundred crores [of verses], and presented by me with affection. (52)
52. "A hundred," and so forth. By this [it is shown that] the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the fundamental source, consists of one hundred crore verses.
53. "Formerly, in my very presence, the god of gods, Janārdana, the lotus-eyed one, extracted this supreme knowledge for my pleasure."
Just as the hearts of men become serene upon seeing moonlight, so too does the heart of yogis become serene upon seeing this knowledge. (54)
There is no affliction from the restraints (yama) and so forth, nor any failure regarding the postures (āsana);
there is no distress from breath control (prāṇāyāma), for nothing at all is required here.
Seated comfortably, with a serene mind and assuming whatever posture he desires,
one who practices this vidyā with the mind attains perfection.
Just as rivers and streams flow together into the great ocean,
so do all supreme sciences converge within the Self that is the Word (padātman).
Just as there are innumerable jewels in the lord of rivers and streams, so too are there countless qualities within that Supreme Reality.
They likewise know that there are innumerable splendors within the form of the Foot. || 58 ||
Just as food mixed with honey and honey combined with food [are mutually enhancing], so too are the seed-syllables and other such entities bestowers of pleasure upon Tārā. (59)
Seated upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa, I am the Great Sovereign of all the worlds;
consisting of every perfection, I am the intended object of meditation as the embodiment of the supreme state.
Furthermore, O Śakra, I myself am exerted by supreme compassion for the sake of the welfare of practitioners and for the cultivation of the mind. (61)
For I, who am indivisible and complete, desiring the welfare [of beings], divide this very form consisting of knowledge into a fourfold self by means of myself. 62.

62. "In four ways": O Purandara, the fourfold modes known as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā will be explained in the following chapter. You ought to hear from me, exactly as they are, the ritual procedure for these four forms consisting of my own essence, once they have been differentiated.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Secret," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, which is the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (F: in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence). 44.
Chapter Forty-Five: Śrī—(p. 180)
I am the goddess Nārāyaṇī, the progenitor even of those who came before;
I am Lakṣmī, the inseparable Śrī of the Lord Viṣṇu himself.
By my own power, I divide myself fourfold through myself;
those four forms are Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā.
She who is that supreme power, Lakṣmī, the supreme Śakti— I am she, the ego of Viṣṇu, Hara, and Hari; for the welfare of the world, she divides her own self into fourfold.
I alone am the Supreme Ego, the first body;
I am the highly fortunate one named Lakṣmī, the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty. || 4 ||
My second body is named Kīrti, the bestower of good fame;
my third body is named Jayā, the bestower of victory. || 5 ||
The fourth of my bodies is named Māyā, which causes all wonders;
Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā—these are the ones who take refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
My forms, which take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, are supremely radiant;
endowed with the totality of my own powers, they are indeed formless and partless.
Just as the rays of the sun or the waves of the ocean [are ever-present],
so too does Lakṣmī abide within the sovereign power and majesty of the Lord of Lakṣmī.

8. The meaning is that the Lord of Lakṣmī’s sovereignty, power, and so forth are dependent upon Lakṣmī. Yet, by this much, there is neither dependence nor deficiency on the part of the Blessed One. For an excellence bestowed by a quality increases the preeminence of the possessor of that quality. And the learned have said: "O Śrī, you are Viṣṇu's own; you are his very self."

Therefore, although this Blessed One’s prosperity was dependent upon you, he remained one whose majesty was not subject to another; for even though a jewel is of great value by its own luster, it is neither devoid of quality, nor does it have its independence blunted, nor does it acquire qualities bestowed by another. Thus it is said.
Surrounded by millions of various specific glories,
Fame likewise exists as if divided into the distinct forms of the Lord.
There is indeed nothing that is not pervaded by her, whose body is the universal;
and whatever fame arises for anyone, anywhere, through its own inherent power, it is she.
Each particular form of hers has arisen from her universal self;
thus Jayā exists as the pervasive power of the Lord of Victory (Jayendra).
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, know me to be whatever illusion exists in this world among the gods and others—me, who have been brought forth by your own Māyā. (12)
"O best of gods, apart from his partless form and my own, what else exists in this ocean of principles (tattva) in its fourfold aspect? [13]
13–14. They exist in fourfold ways, consisting of Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and so forth, as well as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and so forth.

Fully permeated by these divine powers (bhagavat-śaktis) through the manifestation of yoga, they have attained embodied form (sākāratva) by virtue of the capacity of their own self-luminous knowledge.
14. The connection is that prosperity, fame, and so forth, when manifested through yoga, are to be meditated upon.
15. They are to be meditated upon by the best of practitioners, and they are to be worshipped and honored for the sake of accomplishment;
behold the form [or forms] of Lakṣmī, who is the first among them.
15. First, he describes the form of Lakṣmī with the words beginning "tāsām" (of them):
With a gentle face and gentle eyes, having two arms and beautiful earrings, resembling the interior of a lotus in luster, she is adorned with a girdle and a string of jewels. 16.
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
she is endowed with all auspicious marks and possesses full, lofty, and firm breasts. (17)
Her wide eyes were like blossomed blue lotuses, her face was graced with a gentle smile, and she was adorned with locks of hair that moved like swarms of wandering bees. || 18 ||
18. "Caras" means those who move; the meaning is those whose nature is to wander.
And she bore a beautiful, variegated tilaka-mark on her forehead, was charming, possessed ruby-like lips that were slightly reddened, and had teeth like bamboo-seeds and pearls. 19.
With a crescent moon upon her forehead and dark, curly hair,
the Goddess holds a noose and a goad, bestowing dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Seated in the lotus posture and adorned with a magnificent crown,
I, the Sovereign Goddess, should be meditated upon in this way as the virtuous one abiding within the array of Lakṣmīs.
I shall proclaim her mantra; listen as I recite it to you. That seed-syllable named Tārikā is my supreme heart-mantra. (22)
22–23. The *tārikā* is the *hrīṃ* mantra. Having first taken the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should join it at the end of that.
Then, the two-syllable [seed-mantra] follows, and at the very end, one should join "namaḥ śriyai" (salutation to Lakṣmī).

23–26. *Oṃ hrīṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ paramalakṣāvasthitāyai hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*. This twenty-syllable mantra is the Mūrtimantra. Then, one should add the word "parama" at the end, followed by "puruṣeśvara."
And one should extract Ānandin, Garuḍa, and Varuṇa.

At the end of this [mantra], one should recite the word *sthita* for her; then again, my heart-mantra (*maddhṛdaya*), followed by the secondary seed-syllable (*anubīja*), and finally, at its conclusion, my supreme seed-syllable (*madbīja*). || 25 ||

At the end of that [seed-syllable] is the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, Svāhā); such is my Mūrti-mantra, remembered as consisting of twenty syllables, which is directly called Lakṣmī herself. || 26 ||
O slayer of Vṛtra, learn the limb-mantra of this [goddess] as it truly is:
having first taken the syllable Śānta (ŚAM), one should place Puruṣeśvara at its end.

27–29. Regarding the phrase *aṅgamantra*: this means the mantras for the limbs (*aṅga*), such as the heart and so forth. He extracts these mantras with the words beginning with *śāntam*. By joining each of these—*ślraṃ*, *ślriṃ*, *ślruṃ*, *śllraṃ*, *ślreṃ*, *ślroṃ*—individually with *ṭaṃ*, the mantras are extracted.
The fire, that which is situated below it, and this aggregate— these three are traditionally taught.
At the end, one should join the illusion of the beginning of the Yugas within the six vowels at the beginning and the end.
One should place Candrin and Vyāpin above all others;
know, O Vāsava, that these six, beginning with Hṛdaya and ending with Astra, [are the limbs]. (29)
Now, listen to these mantras of the companions of Lakṣmī:
SATYAṂ, TATSTHAṂ, VARĀHAṂ, and likewise MĀYĀNTAṂ and AMṚTAṂ. (Or: MĀYĀKTAṂ. 30.

30. Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Samṛddhi, and Vibhūti are the four friends of Lakṣmī. Their seed-mantras are Ṛṃ, Vṛṃ, Siṃ, and Viṃ, each joined with Ṭaṃ. Varuṇa joined with Ra (Ra) constitutes the four leaders of the seed-mantras.
Then, the Moon and the Pervasive One (Vyāpin) should be joined in sequence upon the heads of all.
Ṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Samṛddhi, and Vibhūti are her group of friends; Tāra is their seed-syllable (bīja), followed by their names and Svāhā—this is remembered as their mantra. || 32 ||
32. Oṃ ṛṃ ṭaṃ, svāhā to Ṛddhi, and so forth are the mantras. These four female friends (sakhīs) have two arms and a gentle appearance;
they resemble the interior of a lotus bud and are marked with the Śrīvṛkṣa and the yak-tail whisk (camara). 33.
Seated in the lotus posture and gazing at my face—thus are those female companions to be meditated upon; now hear of the four male attendants.
Avācya, Sumanas, and Saubhāgya as the third,
and Somanastha as the fourth— these four are my attendants. (35)

35. Beauty (Lakṣmī) is followed by Loveliness (Lāvaṇya) and the others. They have four arms and gentle faces, and are dressed in blue silk garments. They hold a lotus, a conch, a sword, a noose, and likewise a lotus and a discus.
36. [They hold] a fruit, two jars, and likewise a lotus and a discus.
I shall explain it truly through my auspicious arms or by means of mantras; listen to that from me.
Vidu, Tvādi, Devāḍhya, Soma, and Bhuvanasthiti.
Having taken it as it has become twofold, one should employ it with the two who move upon the earth. || 38 ||
38. The mantras for the attendants are now stated, beginning with "vibudha": *lāṃ*, *suṃ*, *sauṃ*, *sauṃ*, *ṭaṃ*—these are the seed-mantras (*bījamantra*).
One should meditate upon these seed-mantras as being truly endowed with the pervasive moon.
The door, the seed-syllable, then the name, and "namaḥ" at the end—this is remembered as the mantra. || 39 ||
39. *Oṃ lāṃ ṭaṃ, obeisance to Lāvaṇyā*, and so forth are the mantras.
This form of Lakṣmī, together with her limbs and retinue, has been shown.
Now hear the form and other attributes of the second image, known as Kīrti. [Ā, Ṅ: form and other attributes]
Listen to that. || 40 ||
In form she is similar [to Lakṣmī], in fortune she is like Campaka in radiance, and in her remaining beauty she is equal to Lakṣmī; know me now as the personified Mantras. (41)
First is Tāra, then my heart (Hṛdaya), then Karāla joined with Viṣṇu, then Sragdhara mounted on Anala, adorned with sovereignty. || 42 ||
42. Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ traiṃ namaḥ sadoditānandavigrahāyai hrīṃ krīṃ svāhā—this is the twenty-syllable mantra.
Then follows the phrase: *namaḥ sadoditānandavigrahāyai*.
My seed-syllable is mounted upon Kamalā, with Anala and adorned by Viṣṇu. || 43 ||
One should remember this seed-syllable joined with Vyāpin at the end;
this mantra, ending with the word "svāhā," is proclaimed to consist of twenty syllables.
Now learn the limb-mantras; listen to my final [instruction]:
having placed Karāla upon the fire and joined it as before. (45)

45-46. The limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) beginning with *krāṃ* and *krīṃ* should be known as belonging to Lakṣmī, just as they are for Śrī when joined with the vowels beginning with *ānanda* (a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ) and the moon (*i*). These are the limb-mantras; now hear the mantras of her companions, Kīrti and the others.
46. "O friends," and so forth; the meaning is: "Listen to their forms and names. These are remembered as the friends Dyuti, Sarasvatī, Medhā, and Śruti.
They have two arms, possess a golden complexion, have the form of Kīrti, and have smiling faces. 47.
Listen as I describe the mantras of my companions, Kīrti and her friends, while she holds a fine book in her left hand and a fly-whisk in her right.
Having placed Madana, Amṛta, and likewise Pradhāna and Śaṅkara upon the fire-altar, one should adorn them with Māyā.
49. "Madanam" and so forth. *Mrīṃ*, *srīṃ*, *mrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *ṭaṃ*—these are the mantras.
One should bestow the pervasive Candrin and recollect these mantras of the female companions (*sakhīs*).

Now hear the names, forms, and other attributes of the followers of Kīrti. 50. [The mantras are: *mrīṃ*, *srīṃ*, *mrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *ṭaṃ*. One should give the pervasive Candrin and remember these mantras of the female companions. Listen now to the names, forms, and so forth of the attendants of Kīrti.
Vāgīśa, Jayada (or Śramapada), Prasāda, and Trāṇa—
these should be meditated upon as having the hue of *kiṃśuka* flowers and possessing beautiful forms.
Captivating. || 51 ||
51–52. The attendants of Kīrti are Vāgīśa and others.
They are clad in white garments, have four arms, and are adorned with all ornaments.
Among them, one should meditate upon [the principal deities] with their two primary hands, the left and the right.
Learn from me through the other two [hands] that there is a great tree called Kadamba, shining like a hundred moons and conch shells, adorned with flowers and frequented by bees.
With beautiful eyes, they hold a mirror resembling the full moon in their left hand and a bright peacock-feather fan in their right hand.
(183) It is rich with the primordial god Varāha, immeasurable and absolute;
it is pure, mounted upon fire, and likewise wears a garland. || 55 ||

55. The syllable *va* is Varāha; the syllable *pa* is the Purifier (*pavitra*); the syllable *ta* is Sragdhara. Having joined them with the Primordial God (A), one should properly join them above those [syllables]—[or, according to manuscript Ā and Ṅ: "one should join them at their heads"].
At the end, the mantras are dependent upon the attendants, [namely] Candrin and Vyāpin. || 56 ||
This sequence has been proclaimed for Kīrti, who is indeed my second form; now listen to me regarding the form and other attributes of Jayā, my third form.
Equal in form and fortune to Jayā, she is supremely beautiful; she is Tārā and Tārikā, the destroyer of birth, and the one who transcends the four states of existence. || 58 ||

58. *Tāra* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ). *Tārikā* is the mantra *hrīṃ*. *Janmahantā* is the letter *ja*. *Caturgati* is the letter *ya*. Followed by the *Ādideva*, that very [letter] is then conjoined with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Having taken the *tāra* (the syllable Om), at its end one should place *kāla* together with *parameśvara*.

59. Kāla is the letter *ma*; the Supreme Lord is the *visarga*. He is the all-pervading one, the destroyer of birth, as well as Sarāma, Sragdhara, and likewise the one endowed with the Primordial God (Ādideva), the Sustainer, and the Primal Matter (Pradhāna). 60.
60. The letter *a* is the pervasive one; *Rāma* is the letter *i*; the Sustainer (*Dhartā*) is the letter *dha*; the Primal Matter (*Pradhāna*) is the letter *ma*.

Then there is Varuṇa, who abides in the nectar, the archer adorned by Rāma, the Vairāja, enriched by the Primordial God, and the conch adorned with sovereignty. 61. [The mantra is: *a-i-dha-ma-varuṇa-amṛtastha-dhanvī-rāmavibhūṣita-vairāja-ādidevāḍhya-śaṅkha-eśvaryabhūṣita*.
61. The letter *tha* is Dhanvī; the letter *ta* is Vairāja; the letter *ya* is Śaṅkha;
Tārikā is the eternal Viṣṇu, the support of the entire world. Then follows [the letter] adorned by Vyomeśa, and thereafter the wife of Vahni.
62. [The letter] adorned by Vyomeśa is [the letter *va*]; thereafter is the wife of Vahni (the letter *ra*).
62. The letter *ja* is Śāśvata; *i* is Viṣṇu; the *anusvāra* is Vyomeśa; and *svāhā* is the consort of Vahni. This is the root mantra of Jayā; now learn from me her limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*).
Taking up the destroyer of births, which was adorned with the fire of time.
63. The letter *ra* is the fire of time (*kālapāvaka*). One should adorn it with vowels as before, conjoined with the moon-pervader (*candrivyāpin*).
One should contemplate those limbs, beginning with the heart, belonging to Jayā. 64.
Jayantī, Vijayā, and the third, Aparājitā;
the fourth is to be known as Siddhi—these are remembered as the companions of Jaya. (65)
Ajita joined with Viṣṇu, Varuṇa joined with Ceddha,
and likewise Soma, the all-pervading one, adorned with his desired ornaments. || 66 ||

66. Ajita is the letter ja; Varuṇa is the letter va; Idhdha is the letter i; Soma is the letter sa; Iṣṭa is the letter i. Having joined them together with the name, one should unite them with the pervasive moon.
Having joined "svāhā" at the end, one should recollect these mantras for the female friends (sakhīs). || 67 ||
Having the luster of the color of a jasmine bud, with serene faces and eyes, all of them wearing yellow garments, their lotus-like faces radiant;
having the luster of the color of dark blue clouds, with serene faces and eyes.
All her female companions were wearing yellow garments and golden earrings.
68. He describes the appearance of Jayā’s companions: "With white chowries in their hands and variegated cane-staffs in their grasp, they were gazing upon the faces of Jayā and Ajita. 69.
Pratāpin, Jayabhadra, and the third, Mahābala, along with Utsāha—this group is known as the attendants of Jaya. || 70 ||
70. The followers of Jaya are described as follows, beginning with "Pratāpin" and so forth:
"All of them wear red garments, have four arms, and possess great strength; they hold bows and arrows in their hands, as well as maces and discs. 71.
71. He describes the appearance of the attendants of Jaya with the words beginning with "red" and so forth:
"In this way, those attendants are to be known—[or, according to manuscript B, meditated upon]—adorned with flower ornaments.
Padmanābha, Anala, Ajita, and likewise Kāla... 72.
72. Padmanābha is the letter *pa*; Ajita is the letter *ja*; Kāla is the letter *ma*; Uddāma is the letter *u*. (p.
184) And Uddāma, Sureśa, Ete, Candi, Vyāpin, and Vibhūṣita [are likewise].
They begin with the syllable Om, end with "namaḥ," and are accompanied by their respective names.
O slayer of Vṛtra, those mantras following Jayā should be known;
this is the wonderful ritual for my third form, Jayā. (74)
Listen to my arrangement for the fourth [night], concerning my illusory form;
it is a goddess who brings about every wonder for the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Māyā is my great power, my supreme fourth body;
she is equal to Lakṣmī in form. Now listen to the mantra of her embodied form.
Having first taken the *tāraka*, one should then remember the *tārikā*;
afterwards, "māyāyai namaḥ," with the syllable *kāla* situated within *odana*. (77)

77. Odana is the syllable *oka*. Joined with the left eyebrow (*vāma-bhrū*), it is Sūrya; adorned with a garland, he is embellished by Viṣṇu. This same [syllable] alone is Narāntya; then Madana is joined with Gopanā. 78. [The syllable] is *madana* (ma) accompanied by *gopanā* (ga). It is the first of the vowels (*akārādya*) and is endowed with the letter *ka*. It is the first of the consonants (*kādya*) and is joined with the letter *na*. It is the first of the letters *ca* (*cādya*) and is joined with the letter *tha*. It is the first of the letters *ta* (*tādya*) and is joined with the letter *pa*. It is the first of the letters *pa* (*pādya*) and is joined with the letter *ya*. It is the first of the letters *ya* (*yādya*) and is joined with the letter *va*. It is the first of the letters *va* (*vādya*) and is joined with the letter *la*. It is the first of the letters *la* (*lādya*) and is joined with the letter *ra*. It is the first of the letters *ra* (*rādya*) and is joined with the letter *ṣa*. It is the first of the letters *ṣa* (*ṣādya*) and is joined with the letter *sa*. It is the first of the letters *sa* (*sādya*) and is joined with the letter *ha*. It is the first of the letters *ha* (*hādya*) and is joined with the letter *kṣa*. It is the first of the letters *kṣa* (*kṣādya*) and is joined with the letter *ya*. It is the first of the letters *ya* (*yādya*) and is joined with the letter *va*. It is the first of the letters *va* (*vādya*) and is joined with the letter *la*. It is the first of the letters *la* (*lādya*) and is joined with the letter *ra*. It is the first of the letters *sa* (*sādya*) and is joined with the letter *ha*. It is the first of the letters *ha* (*hādya*) and is joined with the letter *kṣa*. It is the first of the letters *kṣa* (*kṣādya*) and is joined with the letter *ya*. It is the first of the letters *ya* (*yādya*) and is joined with the letter *va*. It is the first of the letters *va* (*vādya*) and is joined with the letter *la*. It is the first of the letters *la* (*lādya*) and is joined with the letter *ra*. It is the first of the letters *ra* (*rādya*) and is joined with the letter *ṣa*. It is the first of the letters *ṣa* (*ṣādya*) and is joined with the letter *sa*. It is the first of the letters *sa* (*sādya*) and is joined with the letter *ha*. It is the first of the letters *ha* (*hādya*) and is joined with the letter *kṣa*. It is the first of the letters *kṣa* (*kṣādya*) and is joined with the letter *ya*. It is the first of the letters *ya* (*yādya*) and is joined with the letter *va*. It is the first of the letters *va* (*vādya*) and is joined with the letter *la*. It is the first of the letters *la* (*lādya*) and is joined with the letter *ra*. Following that is *Puṇḍarīka* mounted upon fire (*ra*) and joined with *Rāma* (*la*).
It is enriched by *Tāla*, *Lakṣmī*, and other deities, and is endowed with the conch (*śaṅkha*) and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

79. Puṇḍarīka is the letter Śa; the letter Ta is marked with the sign of Tāla. Then, Kāla (Ka) mounted upon Anala (Ra) and conjoined with Māyāvyāpin (Ū), one should meditate upon this divine seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), situated above the Tārikā (Hūṃ). 80. [The resulting mantra is: Hrīṃ Hūṃ.]
The wife of Vahni (Svāhā) should follow at the end; this is remembered as the mantra of twenty syllables.
I shall now declare its limbs; listen to them from me. (81)

Having taken the seed-syllable of Māyā and having sequentially differentiated it with the vowels beginning with 'ga' and ending with 'na', the wise practitioner should perform the arrangement of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) as previously described. 82.
O Lord of the Gods, Mohinī, Bhrāmaṇī, Durgā, and Preraṇī—these four should be known as the companions of Māyā, resplendent with jewels. (83)
In charm, prowess, beauty, and splendor,
these goddesses, clad in white garments and anointed with unguents, are equal to Māyā.
Holding chowries and goads in their hands, they remain seated in the lotus posture;
I shall proclaim their mantras—listen, O slayer of Bala! (85)
The principal [syllable] is established upon *odana* (the letter *u*), followed by *dhruva* (the letter *o*) and the letter *ra*;
then *madana* (the letter *ma*) is established upon *bhuvana* (the letter *u*), joined with the power of fire (*analaiśvarya*, the letter *ra*). || 86 ||
86. The syllable *bha* is *dhruva*; the syllable *u* is *bhuvana*.
Indeed, all these, joined with *candri* and *vyāpin*, reside upon the seat of the *praṇava*.

When conjoined with *saṃjñā*, *svāhā*, and *āyu*, these are remembered as the mantras of *māyāsakhī*. 87. [The mantras are: *bhūḥ saṃjñāyai svāhā*, *bhuva āyuryutāyai svāhā*, and *svaraḥ vyāpinyai svāhā*. These are known as the mantras of the friends of Māyā.
Māyāmaya, Mahāmoha, Śambara, and Kalīśvara—these four attendants resemble crows, black collyrium, and soot. (88)
Four-armed and large-bodied, with gentle faces and smiling countenances, they are adorned with armlets and wear yellow silken garments. (89)
Adorned with necklaces and anklets, decorated with various flowers, white as the dust of snow, they held swords and nooses raised in their hands. (90)
He holds an arrow and a bow in one pair of hands, and a parasol in the other two;
he is the primary [form], accompanied by Gopana, and immediately following that is the solitary [form].
One should place Śaṅkara, Kevala, Kamala, Candrī, and Vyāpin, respectively, upon the heads of all.
O slayer of Bala, the mantras of the four beginning with Māyāmaya are preceded by *tāraka* (the syllable Om), end with *namaḥ*, and are endowed with their respective names. (93)
O Vāsava, the meditation for all the limb-mantras has been declared to be common; so too, O Indra, are the mudrās for the deities together with their limbs.
A man who worships these goddesses—whether individually or all together—should display them exactly as they were previously described by me. (95)
According to my understanding and according to my zeal, I apply myself with supreme splendor;
these four slender ones of mine are of the nature of the rays of the Blessed One. (96)
By means of those [powers] through which that Blessed Lord, the God, abides in his full form,
there are for each one of them innumerable powers, whose nature corresponds to each respective [power]. (97)
These [goddesses] have infinite retinues; thus, the world consists of power (śakti).
Of these four powers, one is the Supreme Goddess. (98)

[I bow to] that Māyā, who is the fundamental supreme egoity of Viṣṇu, who possesses his attributes as her own, who consists of all powers, and who is the leader of the circle of powers (śakticakra). 99.
One should remember her as pervading the interior of both light and bliss,
situated between the pair of fire and moon, and following the central path.
A wise man should contemplate with a non-averted state of mind,
having caused the sun and the moon to set in the path of Suṣumṇā. 101.
One should establish one's abiding in me through a mode of conduct that is not directed outward.
Śakra said:
O Goddess who consists of the God of gods, O Goddess seated upon the lotus! 102.
"Tell me the mudrās of the goddesses' companions and of my servants. Śrī said:
"O slayer of Bala, the mudrās of the goddesses have already been shown to you."
Now, learn from me regarding the sixteen companions of that [goddess]:
having brought the two hands together, making them very distinct and well-extended. (104)
One should indeed take the pair [of fingers] from both the little finger and the ring finger;
one should join them at the tips of the nails so that they become like a single mass.
With the four fingers in the middle of the palm held without support, one should place the two thumbs like a staff, extended and touching at their tips. || 106 ||
Having rested the four fingers at the level of the abdomen,
one should carefully form the two index fingers like a serpent's coil.
O Lord of the Gods, having extended the two middle fingers forward so they touch,
and having straightened the two little fingers while joining both hands together— 108.
And one should join them very closely from the ends of the wrists;
the wrists [should meet] slightly at the base of the thumbs from both hands. (109)
One should perform it fully blossomed; this is the mudrā called Mahāyoni, O slayer of Bala, the supreme mother of the three worlds. (110)
If she is employed according to one's desire, she can bring the entire world under her control;
a woman intent on this practice should bind [the object] from afar and display it. 111.
A man who is engaged here, or one who displays himself among women, instantly causes agitation even in sages who have transcended all attachment. (112)
O Sage, even women whose passionate nature has ceased become agitated before a sage; yet they remain free from desire themselves—what then can be said of those who are full of passion?
O Vāsava, this is the common mudrā for all of them; now I shall describe, in brief, the mudrās of the sixteen attendants.
Having placed the two hands joined behind the back, one should then release them;
likewise, the pair of index fingers and the pair of little fingers [should be released]. (115)
O Mahāmati, with those two [fingers], the middle [fingers] should be clearly positioned facing downward;
the two little fingers are joined together, and the pair of index fingers is held apart.
One should hold the middle and ring fingers in pairs; joined together at the nail-base, they should extend as far as the middle joint. 117.
O best of gods, with the face turned upward and the ground level, the two thumbs should be clearly visible, hanging down and facing downward. (118)
But when they are situated far apart from one another, this mudrā grants all desires;
it should be performed accompanied by their respective mantras, for this is the single [mudrā] common to them all. (119)
(186) These two mudrās are said to be common to those who follow as friends.
Thus, [he saw] me accompanied by these four [goddesses], together with their retinues.
120. "By four"—this means by Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā.
"Having thus worshipped me through these manifestations (vibhūtis), one attains me alone at the end;
for my manifestations are infinite, resting upon the reality of ultimate truth. 121.
O Vāsava, each one of them has a retinue of ten million times ten million;
these four are proclaimed to be the principal ones.
Thus, I have described to you the summary of the mantras of the forms along with the limb-mantras and so forth; now hear from me the means of accomplishment and other details.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Forms," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. || 45 ||
Chapter Forty-Six: Śrī—p. 187)
O Lord of Gods, learn from their mantras the sequential means of accomplishment for Lakṣmī and the others, as well as their various rites.
1. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā are included.
Having constructed a square city with four gates as previously described, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus in its center, possessing a white and reddish luster. 2.
2. He describes the construction of the city with the words beginning "caturaśram" (square):
"Having drawn four white [squares] and svastikas in the corners, the city is [constructed] by pervasion, starting from the wrist and the mouth. 3.
Having placed the root mantra solely upon the hand and the body,
one should subsequently and first likewise place the Lakṣmī mantra with both hands.
Then, having performed the placement of the limbs upon the hand and the body as before,
one should subsequently place the quartet of goddesses that follows it.
5. *Anugati* means the mantra of the fourfold group beginning with *ṛddhi*.

Following that, [the mantras are placed] on the two hands starting from the index fingers (*pradeśinī*), then on the body, on the head, in the center of the heart, and likewise on the two thighs and the two knees. 6.
O Vāsava, having placed the four [fingers] beginning with Lāvaṇya on the two hands starting from the ring finger (anāmā) up to the thumb, one should likewise place them on the body.
7. He states the placement (*nyāsa*) of the attendant mantras: "Lāvaṇyā and the others... [He says:
"Then, having performed the placement according to the rule on the right and likewise on the left shoulder and on both wings, one who desires prosperity (*śrī*) should then worship in the heart. 8.
Having performed the Lakṣmī-mantra alone by means of the application of the layayāga, one should then perform the visualization and other rites, and subsequently place it externally.
O Indra, the root mantra joined with the form-mantra is upon the pericarp;
it is the all-pervading Lord, whose body consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and who is endowed with all mantras.
10. "Upon the pericarp" means upon the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus. "Partless" (akala) means devoid of parts (niṣkala).

Having caused Lakṣmī, who has come into his lap, to descend by means of her own mantra, one—endowed with the previously mentioned meditation—for the sake of attaining both enjoyment and liberation: 11. [One should worship her.]
Then, [one places] the four [mantras], beginning with the Heart, in the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest; the Eye [mantra] is placed upon the expanse of the filaments.
One should place the four [deities], beginning with Ṛddhi, in sequence at the front, the right, the back, and the left side; they are two-armed and of such form.
Resembling a lotus in complexion, marked with the śrīvṛkṣa and the yak-tail whisk,
seated in the lotus posture, he was gazing at that face.
Having placed the four [deities] beginning with Lāvaṇyā in the positions of the corners starting from the northeast,
they have gentle faces and four arms.
Clad in blue silk garments, holding a lotus and a water-pot in his hands,
with a lotus-stalk banner in his hand, and bearing a fruit-bearing *āmalaka* tree.
Having placed the weapon-mantra at the gates in the four directions and worshipped it as before,
O delighter of the gods, one should worship the goddess Lakṣmī accompanied by the root-mantra. (17)
One should display all the mudrās wherever they are prescribed;
then, having performed the recitation (japa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and ghee.
When available, one should perform the oblation with *sāmalī* fruits, *śrīphala* fruits, or lotuses,
using them innumerable times according to one's capacity at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice.
O slayer of Vṛtra! || 19 ||
Then, having assumed the form of Lakṣmī, the practitioner, firm in his resolve,
should recite [the mantra] five hundred thousand times, subsisting on pure food and with his senses subdued.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with bilva, āmalaka, and lotus flowers,
according to one's capacity, either in unlimited numbers or by counting ten thousand for each.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, O Śakra, the Supreme Goddess grants her vision, saying:
"O son, I am accomplished for you; tell me what is desired in your mind. Perform all your cherished tasks by means of my mantra."
From this day forward, I shall be free from fear and devoid of the afflictions of dualities.
Having spoken thus, that goddess quickly departed to the place from which she had come;
thereafter, one should perform the rites with the permission of Lakṣmī and myself.
When pleased, he bestows desired prosperity upon supplicants just as they seek it;
when enraged, he can render even the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) penniless by a mere word.
One should fashion a golden image while meditating once, through the recitation of the mantra;
then, having filled a jar with water, or with milk, or else with honey, [one should immerse it].
Having placed the right hand [downward] and the left hand upon it,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while endowed with meditative concentration.

For one who is established in devotion to the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra), single-minded and composed, attains the state of the Lord of Mercury; indeed, even the water drawn into his vessel becomes so.
O Purandara, one who pierces a target from a lake with weapons and the like becomes immortal;
he makes his body ageless and free from disease. (29)
First, one should take a stone the size of a thumb with the right hand and the belly, and [a stone] the size of a jujube fruit with the left hand. (30)
Having consecrated those two fists with mantras, two hundred and sixteen stones situated on the right side attain the state of jewels.
And on the left, there shall be two pearl-like fruits of great value;
whatever kind of jewel one desires, that very jewel shall then appear.
Likewise, taking in his hand the bones produced from cows, elephants, and horses, he makes them appear as various pearls. (33)
Having consecrated it fifty times, it indeed becomes endowed with life and attains the state of a sprout;
likewise, having consecrated tin, lead, or iron one hundred times, [it attains that same state].

34. "Having done so"—the phrase "if he maintains it" is to be understood as the ellipsis. 35. "O Lord of Gods, whatever mineral he takes up and desires, whether gold or exceedingly pure silver, that very thing is produced."
Whether angry or well-pleased, he would act accordingly;
thus, a difference in the nature of things made of stone is established. (36)
Whatever prosperity appears in the mind of anyone, He quickly bestows that very thing upon him— be it wealth, grain, cattle, or the like. (37)
Having written it on birch bark according to the sequence of the sacrificial placement (yāganyāsa),
whoever always wears it with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), || 38 ||

38. "With *rocana* and saffron"—this connects with the preceding word "having written. 39. O Śatakratu, if one wraps the *lakṣmī-mantra* on the body with gold, there shall be an increase in his lifespan, and he shall become a great victor everywhere.
Wherever he may enter, he shall receive great honor;
this is declared to be the means of propitiation especially for those who desire prosperity,
O tiger among gods, for Lakṣmī is my first manifestation.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Accomplishment of the Lakṣmī-mantra," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (In versions A and Ṅ, "Lakṣmī-mantra" is omitted. 46.
Chapter Forty-Seven: Śrī—p. 190)
That which is indeed declared as the first glory of the arrays, known by my own name—that is called its accomplishment; now listen to that of the second.
Know that the entire method of ritual placement (nyāsa), the lotus sacrifice (padmayāga), and so forth, have been previously explained.
Having constructed the previously described mandala, one should place white and yellow [powders] within it.
However, one should indeed fashion a lotus and subsequently place it;
one should place Kīrti upon the lap of the Lord, and the heart and other limbs as before.
Listen now to how she gradually meditated upon her companions:
she was two-armed, golden-hued, the very embodiment of fame, with a smiling countenance.
One should meditate on him who has a beautiful book in his left hand and a fly-whisk in his right, who possesses the luster of a *kiṃśuka* flower, and who is lovely in form and enchanting.
Therein, one should contemplate the fourfold Anuga, measuring four cubits and clad in white garments, with his primary left and right hands [placed] upon them.
Learn from me through the other two [hands] that he holds a conch shell with the luster of a hundred moons and a great tree called kadamba, adorned with flowers and frequented by bees.
Having meditated upon her as resembling the full moon, with a mirror in her left hand and a bright peacock-feather fan in her right hand, one should then display [the mudrās] in this manner.
Then the practitioner should worship all the individual mudrās;
having properly recited the mantras with water for offering, flowers, and so forth, he should then perform the fire oblation according to his capacity.
Having offered sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter and mixed with fragrant śāli rice,
and having fashioned an image of the Goddess at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should adorn it with flowers, collyrium, and garments.

Staying in a solitary, secluded place, observing silence and subsisting on roots and fruits, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
O Lord of the Gods, [one should perform] one hundred thousand oblations with rice mixed with sesame seeds,
using the ghee of Kapila cows combined with an equal amount of milk.
One should then offer a thousand oblations for each of the [mantras] beginning with the heart;
afterwards, one should present the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with milk mixed with clarified butter.
When the vessel is full and [the drop] has fallen, the Supreme Goddess arrives and, standing before the practitioner, says, "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu sādhu).
Come, come to the supreme abode; abandon this material city.
Even while dwelling in the midst of mortals, enjoy the divine pleasures. 15.
"O practitioner, perform my entire ritual with the mantra.
Having spoken thus, that goddess then departed for the sky.
The practitioner should perform whatever rite he desires with the Kīrtimantra;
whatever he gives to anyone shall become inexhaustible for that person as well. || 17 ||
By that, he gains renown as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure,
provided that he remains mindful even while standing in the midst of fierce men.
If he speaks something in an assembly, he shall obtain vast fame;
having surpassed all people, he attains preeminence. || 19 ||
Having recited [the mantra] over a vessel of prepared food during a time of food scarcity, even in a short period of time,
whatever people desire shall become their meal according to their wish.
If one gives [this] incessantly for seven days, his merit becomes inexhaustible;
he shall attain great fame until the dissolution of all beings.
Having taken a mere fragment of gold when there is an abundance of it, and having recited the mantra a thousand times according to the prescribed rite while standing all around, || 22 ||
That abundance proceeds and is bestowed upon those who seek it;
for two weeks, without interruption, one does not encounter any doubt. (23)
Having taken a water-pot from the lake in the abode of the Lord of Nagas, he shall thereby attain great fame honored by the world. (24)
One should indeed go to a desert region; there, on low ground or on a mountain peak, one should cast [the substance] after it has been consecrated a thousand times with mantras.
There, that lord of serpents, accompanied by his retinue,
remained guarding the water for as long as the earth endures.
Because of that, O Vāsava, he attains great fame in the world;
for even when the god does not rain, he remains one who causes seeds to sprout at the proper time.
Having taken a lump of clay from the edge of a pond that has been softened by its water,
or one already moist within it, he should recite the mantra over it three hundred times.
Having heated it with mouth-breaths, one should recollect the Kīrtimān mantra;
indeed, when that is thrown into the sky, it attains the state of a cloud.
That cloud-king shall fill the entire earth with water;
by his command, he shall dwell in that region for as long as required.
As much water as falls during the year and becomes available for his use, by that he shall attain great fame extending throughout the three worlds. (31)
O best of gods, he accomplishes whatever is desired by the mind of anyone; such is the power of the king of mantras known as Kīrti.
Having written it as before and bound it upon his right hand,
he shall attain great fame,
worship, prosperity, and the goddess Sarasvatī herself.
O Vāsava, O best among embodied beings, this procedure for the second mantra of Kīrti has been declared by me to you in brief. (34)
By following this auspicious ritual procedure for the Kīrtimantra, one shall obtain stainless fame that bestows prosperity even upon one's progeny. (35)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Attainment of the Kīrti-mantra," in the Lakṣmītantra, the essence of the Śrīpāñcarātra. || 47 ||
Chapter Forty-Eight: Śrī—p. 192)
O slayer of Vṛtra, hear from me the ritual procedure for the victory of Jayā, along with the method of accomplishment praised by the hosts of Siddhas. || 1 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before and having worshipped Jayā in the heart,
one should construct the mandala as previously described and draw a lotus in its center.
With a powder equal to blue lotuses and with beautiful petals,
one should place Jayā upon the lap of Viṣṇu, originating from his heart.
One should place the mantra-parts upon the pericarp according to the previously mentioned sequence;
however, listen attentively to the meditations for all of them as they truly are.
They were the color of dark blue clouds, with serene faces and eyes;
all the female friends wore yellow garments and golden earrings.
Holding white chowries in their hands and raising variegated cane-staffs,
they gazed upon the faces of Jayā and Ajitā.
Having the luster of the color of a closed bud, with lotus-faces full of serenity, wearing red garments, four-armed, and possessed of great strength. || 7 ||
The four attendants should be meditated upon as holding bows and arrows, and equipped with maces and discs, adorned with flower ornaments.
One should display all the mudrās that have been proclaimed for each [deity] respectively, and then worship with devotion; immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
With sesame seeds mixed with white mustard, clarified butter, and guggulu resin,
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the practitioner, having assumed his own form as the embodiment of victory, [should perform the rite].
Then, perceiving with his mind that a great victory had indeed arrived,
he reached a place on the shore that was secluded from people and free from fear.
Having performed the binding of the directions with the armor-weapon mantra (*varmāstra*) for the destruction of evil beings,
one should thereafter commence the recitation (*japa*), always subsisting on milk, food, and fruit. (12)
