O Vāsava, having first prostrated before Hari with devotion using his own mantra,
he remained devoted to solitude, eating sparingly, observing silence, and intent on meditation.
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa).
The sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) should be one span (prādeśa) in length and made from red sandalwood.
One should offer ten thousand of those [seeds] smeared with ghee without distraction;
and, O Great-minded One, two million of white mustard seeds mixed with honey.
Then one should offer ten thousand and a hundred thousand oblations with black sesame seeds mixed with the three kinds of honey; at the end, there should be three full oblations (pūrṇāhuti).
O Śakra, one should perform oblations in sequence with honey, milk, and ghee;
then the Blessed Goddess Jayā herself arrives.
And, my son, perform whatever task you desire with my mantra, being free from doubt and devoid of anxiety, thinking "I have succeeded. (18)
Having spoken thus, the Śakti whose essence is Nārāyaṇa vanishes from sight;
thereafter, one should perform various kinds of rites in manifold ways. (19)
O Wielder of the Vajra, listen as I describe in brief those things which are desired in this world by oneself or by others; hear them according to their true nature.
The practitioner should meditate on the goddess with her tongue like a flame by means of the mantra;
indeed, she causes whatever object—whichever it may be—to be raised up.
Having conquered that [enemy] through righteous means, one indeed attains victory without effort,
even over an army endowed with strength and filled with elephants, horses, and weapon-bearers.
Having seen another engaged in battle, prepared to strike, (p. 193) [ā, F, ṅ: approaching; B: risen up].
Having consecrated the bow, sword, shield, and five arrows by reciting mantras over them. || 23 ||
Having indeed bestowed this upon someone, he who impels it shall go to the front of the army;
even alone, he rends asunder the foe and attains eternal victory. 24.
Having meditated upon the triangular mandala of fire held in the right hand,
one should contemplate the Goddess in its center, accompanied by her retinue.
Upon seeing intoxicated elephants, lions, serpents, or thunderbolts,
they quickly turn their backs and flee once they behold that palm of the hand.

Having touched and taken up the *kādira* and the pestle (*musala*), having consecrated them one hundred times with mantras, and having gone to the entrance of the cave which possesses four colors and is endowed with victory; || 27 ||
O Lord of Gods, one should there gradually offer eight blows with a pestle,
using the mantra of the Goddess encapsulated by her own weapon-mantra.
Then, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, he should worship the *bilayantra*;
thereafter, the most excellent of practitioners, accompanied by all the people, should enter.
Having shattered numerous mechanical engines and conquered the foremost of the Dānavas,
he established a settlement for the people there along with his groups of beloved women.
Having drunk the sattvic beverage with his own hand, that one of great strength departed by that very same path of his own to his own dwelling.
O Lord of Gods, if the minister (mantrin) sets his mind upon victory in the three worlds without hesitation, he shall prevail, with mace and discus raised in hand.
Or else, holding a noose and a goad, he attains victory; it is not otherwise.
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, and thick ink.
Having indeed encapsulated his name and placed it in the midst of the people,
he then easily attains victory over all divine beings through mere play.
Having drawn [the design] with sandalwood paste, milk, and saffron,
one who wears it on the neck, the mouth, or on the left or right hand—
O Śakra, one who seeks victory anywhere at any time will certainly attain it without hesitation or obstruction by means of this mantra, O Lord of the Thirty-three. (36)
The practitioner should employ this constantly; wherever he does so, he shall obtain victory.
This is the procedure for my third form, which is celebrated as Jayā;
thus has it been shown to you, O Śakra. (37)

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Accomplishment of the Jayā-mantra," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. (In the *Śrīpañcarātra*: *Śrīpāñcarātre*) || 48 ||
Chapter Forty-nine: Śrī (Fortune) — page 194.
O Vāsava, that fourth body of mine which is mantra-natured and called Māyā—
now hear the procedure for it, accompanied by the ritual application of mantras.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the lineage of mantras pertaining to Māyā— numbered by the forms, limbs, and perspiration— as before, upon his own hand, he should subsequently perform it upon the body.
Having performed the ritual within the heart with all enjoyments as before,
one should then construct a mandala externally, with an auspicious lotus in its center.
There, having brought down Māyā from the lap of Viṣṇu and from his heart, one should then worship her together with her companions, such as Aṅga and the others.
Then, the four lotus-eyed female friends, Bhrāmaṇī and the others, should be meditated upon; they wear white garments (or yellow garments), are divine, and shine with jewels.
Likewise, the four attendants beginning with Māyāmaya should be meditated upon, holding chowries and goads in their hands and seated in the lotus posture.

6. By the phrase "holding fly-whisks and goads in their hands," their state of having two arms is indicated. Their attendants, such as Māyāmaya and others, are mentioned here by name in the forty-fifth chapter;
they possess all limbs complete and are glossy like a swarm of bees.
They have four arms and large bodies, with gentle faces and smiling countenances. || 7 ||
Adorned with armlets and wearing yellow garments,
they were likewise equipped with necklaces and anklets, and decorated with various flowers.
White as frost and dust, they held swords and nooses raised in their hands;
one pair of hands bore an arrow and a bow, while another pair held a parasol.
Having thus displayed the mudrās prescribed for each respective deity,
one should thereafter perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds combined with white mustard.
Then, O Vāsava, having undertaken the observance and subsequently assuming the form of the Goddess with unwavering devotion, he transformed his own self.

Accompanied by mature and capable assistants, the practitioner, observing the vow, should proceed to a place inhabited by twice-born men and recite seven hundred thousand mantras according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Subsisting on milk, roots, and fruits according to the requirements of place and time, he may indeed eat a single alms-meal that is unasked for, or even live on barley-gruel.
When the time of twilight has arrived, he should eat food prepared by his own disciples, purified by mantras and free from salt, oil, and meat. (14)

The practitioner of mantra should consume it until satisfied, having consecrated it with honey and ghee; at the conclusion of the recitation, he should diligently perform the fire-oblation according to the rules. 15.
Balā, moṭā, māṃsī, cakrāṅgī, nāgakesara, sandalwood, powdered saffron, and the powder of turmeric; || 16 ||
Then, one should mix well-ghee with sesame seeds and honey;
having thus prepared it with ghee, one should then perform three hundred thousand oblations.
O Purandara, with the middle and ring fingers together with the thumbs,
one should finally offer three ten-thousand oblations of sacrificial fuel sticks.
First, ten thousand [offerings] of *kādira* trees originating from the *arka* tree,
then those made of *suradāru* wood, and after that, a third [set] of ten thousand.
19. The *rājataru* is the *karṇikāra*; the *suradāru* is the *devadāru*.
One should properly offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with a perfectly purified inner self. When the full oblation has been poured, [the deity] descends from the midst of the sky. 20.
Accompanied by her retinue, Māyā spoke: "Excellent, excellent!
Now perform your desired task; go forth with my mantra. (21)
Having said this, the goddess shall depart quickly for the abode of Viṣṇu. Then, O Śakra, that best of practitioners should immediately begin various rites, whichever are desired by his mind.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, listen to them from me in brief.
Having recited over an *āmalaka* and a *bilva* fruit once, one should enter the king's palace;
having placed them before the treasury, wherever he may be stationed, he shall remain there.
Whatever wealth he desires, whatever praiseworthy ornament, or whatever auspicious garment, may that fall swiftly from the sky. (25)
In this very way, one should likewise cast a ball of rice, or similarly sesame and rice,
into a full granary, a cow-pen, or a pit.
Whether in the royal treasury or his own property, from wherever he may be situated,
whatever grain, crop, or rice-filled produce he desires— || 27 ||
Then, at the very moment one desires, it falls from the sky right before them;
in this very same way, having consecrated a pill of prepared food with the mantra, [it likewise falls]. (28)
Having cast it into the area of the kitchen, one should draw forth prepared food in an instant;
having made a pill from cow dung, indeed the size of a jujube fruit.
Having cast [the vessels] within the cow-pen, consecrated seven times with mantras,
they were filled with curd, milk, and clarified butter at the end of a mere moment through the power of meditation alone.
Wherever the observer of the vow stands, he should look at the vessels behind him after having properly recited [the mantra] over a jujube fruit or some other fruit.
One should cast [the seed] into Madhuvana, and it produces a fruit for the king;
however, in Supuṣpavāṭikā, one should designate a single flower.
Having recited the mantra three times, the practitioner should instantly attract flowers;
wherever those arising from his limbs fall, he should cast them there after having consecrated them seven times with the mantra.
But wherever one forms a mental resolve, there that [mantra] shall abide;
once drawn forth according to one's desire, it shall go to whatever place one intends.
Furthermore, that excellent practitioner never becomes indebted at any time;
having performed the rite with a single ember and recited the mantra a hundred times with a concentrated mind,
he should cast it into the middle of water, and that water will be seen to blaze.
A drop of water resting on the tip of a blade of kusha grass, consecrated with a hundred recitations [of the mantra].
Having prepared it, one should cast it into a blazing mass of fire;
in an instant, that fire will appear like water.
And having seen a forest filled with sand and devoid of grass, one should cast there a blade of grass over which two hundred mantras have been recited.
One should make that place, strewn with flowers and leaves and crowded with foliage and sprouts,
equal to the Nandana grove, surrounded by a body of water.
It was filled with various birds, endowed with city parks and groves,
complete with city walls, and possessed of temples for the deities.
Accompanied by the sounds of songs and the Vedas, and graced by beautiful women—
this wonder of kings is indeed always worthy of being seen.
Indeed, in forests where water is scarce and food is entirely absent, they always obtain water, food, and various enjoyments according to their wish. (42)
While the enemy stands face-to-face holding his weapons, one should strike with eight clods of earth or cow-dung consecrated by mantras. (43)
If, moreover, one remains alone and intent upon wrath, while reciting the mantra and forming a great resolve in the mind; (44)
And his own army, consisting of a multitude of infantry, chariots, horses, and elephants, quickly becomes a host of formidable prowess. 45.
O Śakra, upon seeing that the enemy's army has turned away, its vigor destroyed, whatever one does with the mind while reciting the mantra brings about that very result. (46)
That which is false appears as if it were true, and that which is true is seen in that same way.
Having seen a withered tree, one might even strike it with one's foot. (47)
Reciting the great mantra, he shall be filled with flowers and fruits;
uttering the mantra with both hands, he is endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits.
If the practitioner of mantra stands upon a mountain peak and recites the mantra for the purpose of its destruction, the tree he oppresses shall undergo withering. (49)
The mountain shall remain beneath his feet for as long as the practitioner desires;
then, being satisfied, it shall subsequently raise that best of mountains from the netherworld (pātāla).
One should place the mantra within the heart of a lotus using sandalwood paste;
then, on an auspicious day, one should draw the ancillary limbs (aṅgas) upon the petals.
Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, one should likewise encircle it with binding threads;
by wearing the yantra as before, all his prosperities—indeed, all his supernatural powers—shall be attained.
In this world, these things manifest correctly for him, and he becomes free from thorns;
moreover, being fortunate and long-lived, he shall attain happiness in the next world.
O enemy of Vṛtra, this most wonderful power of Mūrti has been shown to you only in brief; its entirety is difficult for me to describe. (54)
This collection of accomplishments belonging to the four goddesses has been briefly stated; it is described here in brief fragments for the sake of attaining benefit for practitioners. (55)
To them he grants divine and elemental auspicious things,
as well as stainless purity of mind and, at the end, the supreme state.
He reveals to his devotees the imperishable Vaiṣṇava nature,
and me, Lakṣmī, as being so vast through these manifold manifestations.
One should worship her with various dispositions, having established the mind in tranquility.
Śakra said: "Homage to you, the primordial goddess of the gods; homage to you, the beloved of Vaikuṇṭha. (58)
"Upon what mark (lakṣa) having fixed my mind, O Lotus-born One, should I worship you?
Śrī said: "There is one Nārāyaṇa, the Swan, the ocean of the nectar of the six divine attributes. (59)
I am his supreme power, never departing from Viṣṇu;
I am she who sits upon his lap, as was previously described to you.
O Śakra, that very hundred thousand [gold pieces] is the cause for the stability of your mind;
it is endowed with all auspicious marks and made of gold, silver, and other precious materials. (61)
Having fashioned me as one seated upon the lap of the Lord according to the teachings of the scriptures,
and having established me through the prescribed rites, worship me with those various sentiments.
Śakra said: Homage to you, O abode of the world, who bring delight to the mind and the eyes!
What kind of image is this in which the two of you are established, fashioned from the six divine attributes?
Śrī said: Just as the god Viṣṇu is composed of all beings and is the embodiment of the six divine attributes,
so too am I, the wondrous one, abiding as the self of all beings— indeed, most wondrous.
Since I and Nārāyaṇa are established everywhere, what indeed could be the formal installation of the image? For all that is truly the glory of Viṣṇu.
When the mind of the ascetic has ascended to this true reality,
these conceptual constructions such as "worship" and "consecration" cease to manifest.
Listen, O slayer of Bala, to my instruction regarding the installation ceremony as it truly is, by which, when performed, an embodied being attains the fulfillment of his purpose. (67)
Having properly fashioned our two forms according to the scriptures as described in the Yoga-tantras,
one should bathe them with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) while reciting two well-spoken hymns accompanied by purifying grass (pavitra).
Having clothed him in a new garment, he should have him instructed by pure Brahmins who know the true nature of dharma and are learned in the three Vedas and the Sāttvata scriptures.
(197) They should likewise study the *Tāraka*, the *Tārikā*, and the *Anutārikā*, as well as the *Śākuna Sūkta*, as purificatory texts. 70.

70. The *Śākuna Sūkta* in the *Ṛgveda* (Maṇḍala 2, Sūkta 42, Ṛk 1) should be consulted. Having reached the setting of the sun, one should [consecrate] its orb wrapped in cloth with the hymn beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca" and likewise with the *Sārasvata* hymn. 71.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) with verses from the Rigveda concerning gold;
then, when the pure sun has risen, one should perform the ritual installation of the directions (diksthāpana).
Saying "Arise, O Brahman," they should lead him to the altar;
then, having removed his garment, they should bathe him with pure water.
And on the southern part of the altar, which is beautified by a covering of soft grass,
one should lay the image with its head toward the east, preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Then, having taken a golden probe consecrated with mantras, one who has recited the eye-mantra should scratch the eyes with that probe. (75)
The artisan, having bathed and wearing clean garments, being beheld with a divine vision,
should open the eyes with a weapon consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
One should fill it with honey and ghee and display it in that vessel;
at that time, one should offer a pair of cows adorned with ornaments.
One should give all that to the artisan once it has been opened;
then, having tied it with white thread and fine garments, [one should proceed].
78. A *rāji* is a black mustard seed. One should tie its protective amulet (*kautuka*) on the right hand with a thread.
Then, having placed the image upon a stable and auspicious pedestal, [one should proceed]. 79.
When it has been properly worshipped with a state of right devotion according to the sequence beginning with the support (ādhāra),
one should then contemplate the image with the intellect as being filled with the six qualities.
Having struck it with the weapon-mantra and having enveloped it with the armor-mantra,
one should bathe it with water containing all medicinal herbs alone.

Then, having wiped [the image] with a new, unwashed cloth, one who knows the mantras should release the auspicious thread (kautuka) and offer water for honor (arghya) upon the head with the Cakramantra.
Then, having meditated upon the image as if it were the form of one with lovely luster,
[one should perform the rite] with pure, consecrated jars filled with the ritual substances and offered in worship.
With sixteen [deities] stationed upon the sixteen petals arising from a sixteen-petaled lotus,
one should first [bathe the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the second time with cow urine.
The third [layer] with cow-dung water, the fourth with the ashes of the three sacred fires (tretāgni),
and the final one with earth from the tips of the horns of an elephant, a cow, or a bull, and from an anthill.
The seventh [rite] is performed with water from rice fields, rivers, lotus groves, and so forth;
the eighth is with water containing all medicinal herbs.
The ninth [consecration] is with milk, the tenth with curd, the next (eleventh) with clarified butter;
the twelfth is with honey, and the thirteenth with the water of all seeds.
Having first consecrated each jar with fruits, various grains, and highly fragrant waters, he should fill them one by one while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (88)
One should reverently bathe [the deity] with those sixteen substances using the root mantra,
alternating them with water, along with offerings of arghya, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Then, having rubbed it with the powders of lentils, black gram, and wheat, and having washed it with milk, one should place the supreme *tārikā* upon the head. 90.
Then, the wise one should [visualize] the subtle and then the gross [forms] in these places in sequence:
on the head, the face, the two shoulders, the ear, the heart, the navel, and behind the back. (91)
One should likewise place the *tāraka* at the base of the hips, the thighs, the knees, the ankles, and the feet; and in the same manner, one should also place the *anutārikā*.

Having thus performed the placement of the *puruṣasūkta*, one should then perform the placement of the *śrīsūkta* as well; with the *yajus* mantras, one should place "Śrī is my head," according to the specific characteristics of the parts.
93. "May glory be my head," and so forth; this is to be found in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (2.6.5.3).
And one should perform the placement of the Hotṛ priests as prescribed in the Yajurmayī;
having thus performed the placement within me, the Puruṣa, one should thereafter proceed.

94. Regarding "the placement of the Hotṛ-mantras": this refers to the placement of the mantras beginning with the Daśahotṛ, as recited in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. Having first performed the placement [of these], one should [place] the Śrīsūkta: "May Śrī be my head, and the Yajus-mantras... and so forth.
And then, having thus performed the placement of the Hotṛ priest upon the two bodies, [one should proceed]. (95)
At the conclusion of the previously described procedure, one should offer oblations into the fire-pit for the sake of universal pacification;
this applies to all classes of mantras, whether those already mentioned or those currently existing. || 96 ||
One should offer oblations with that many [verses] for the pacification of all defects;
the Ṛg verses in the eastern direction and the Yajus verses in the southern direction. (97)
And in the west, O gentle one, he should likewise teach the Sāmans and the Atharvaṇa hymns, as well as the Sāttvata mantras, to the twice-born in their vicinity.

First, one should bathe [the deity] with water from jars placed at the four directions within the pericarp of a sixteen-petaled lotus, using mantras that consist of the Tara mantra repeated three times.
With the mantra "vasavas tvā," one should [sprinkle] with a jar of flowers and water;
with the mantra "rudrās tvā," one should [sprinkle] with fragrant water using a jar of golden water.

100–101. With the mantra "May the Vasus [anoint you]," with "May the Rudras [anoint you]," with "May the Ādityas [anoint you]," and with "May the Viśvedevas [anoint you]," the knower of mantras should perform the consecration using a water-pitcher filled with jewels,
accompanied by the Tāra, Tārā, and Anutārā mantras.

101. [Reciting] "ādityāstvā" and "viśve" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.7.15.5), he should then take pure water and, with the threefold mantra beginning with "parā," consecrate him with Tārā; likewise, he should pour the arghya water upon his head. 102. [He should then recite: "ādityāstvābhiṣiñcantu" and so forth. Having taken pure water, he should then consecrate him with Tārā by means of the threefold mantra beginning with "parā," and likewise pour the arghya water upon his head.
Then, having anointed the image with ointments such as sandalwood paste,
one should worship it with offerings beginning with garments and ending with food.
Having formed the mudrās, one should thereafter worship the pedestal (pīṭha) together with the Brahma-stone;
one should meditate upon the radiant Vaiṣṇava pedestal as consisting of the entire path (adhvan). 104.
One should meditate upon the divine Brahma-stone as the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti).
Thus, the pedestal and the Brahma-stone are fashioned together in a state of coexistence.
One should prepare those [materials] separately for the superior bed;
the method for the bed of a stable image is prescribed as follows.
The ascent to the palace, the placement of the pedestal and the Brahma-stone, the consecration thereof, and then the invocation of the image. || 107 ||
The ritual placement of the twelve-limbed digits, the means for the festivals beginning with the three-day rite,
as well as the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) and other such rites—
all this is prescribed here.
Listen attentively to how one should perform the installation of the *kalabimba*, the sprinkling with the four jars, the propitiation, and the invocation. (109)
Prior to the invocation, one should perform the triad of enjoyments in sequence within the nature that is unmodified,
pure, waveless, and free from affliction. (110)

Having remained as the Guru in the heart-lotus of the one who has passed beyond, he should again contemplate the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu, which consists of pure existence and is conformable to his own nature.
One should recollect that conditioned image which was previously [established], consisting of that very [nature];
one should recollect the two states consisting of fire and moon residing within one's own body. (112)
Abiding as all-pervasive above and below, they are supremely luminous;
as it is in the self, so it is in the reflection, and as it is in the reflection, so it is in the self.
Then, one should depart from the body by way of the right channel, the path of fire;
with the intellect, one should enter the heart of the image by way of the left channel.
Just as the incomparable Self has been personally experienced within one's own heart,
so too should one constantly recollect that Self residing within the heart.
Having beheld that light, which is inlaid with its own rays and filled with bliss,
one should contemplate its oneness within each and every Supreme Brahman. (116)
Having thus turned [the universe] into a single ocean, that supreme Vaiṣṇava light should remain,
concentrating upon it and fixing his own mind in that state of motionlessness.
Then, when the mind was vibrating, having again remembered that [Self] through his own intellect,
he emerged from the reflection by way of the right path with his wisdom.
One should enter one's own heart-lotus by way of the left side;
this is the yoga of the substance-image (dravyabimba) which sets the multitude of channels (nāḍī) in motion. (119)

119. Regarding the phrase "the multitude of channels" (*nāḍībṛnda*): here, this statement of the Supreme Lord (*Pārameśvara*) should be kept in mind: "O tiger among sages, this yoga is the manifester of the multitude of channels from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, both of the [inner] image (*bimba*) and that which is born of material substances (*dravyaja*). O Brahmin, I shall now describe that yoga by which mastery over this entire image is produced."
"Fix your attention one-pointedly. (15-447, 448) Thus it is said.
Then, for the sake of attaining the state of the Lord of All, he should abide in another yoga;
from the lotus of his heart, he should meditate while reciting the *tārikā*, the Savior. (120)
One should proceed by the upward flow to the supreme, painless state;
then one should remember that supreme state and the enjoyment attained through one's own will.
Then, taking up that vibration which possesses the power of consciousness and sovereignty,
one should again proceed undisturbed along that same path to the lotus of the heart.
122. *Spanda* is agitation (*kṣobha*). And so it is said in the *Pārameśvara*: "Though uninterrupted, it is nonetheless unagitated;
yet by its own will, it undergoes agitation" (15.451).
Having emerged through the right [channel], accompanied by mutual assistance, [it proceeds].
One should enter that lotus-heart of the image by means of the left [nostril] alone. || 123 ||
Having meditated as before on the state of oneness, having emerged by way of the upward path, having entered the *dvādaśānta*, and having attained vibration (*spanda*) as before; || 124 ||
Just as the reflection [enters], the wise one should enter the heart-lotus by that same [path];
then, having emerged through the fire on the left, he should enter the heart.
One should then remember vibration and sovereignty as the two eyeballs,
gazing at each other while, as it were, manifesting a state of oneness.
One should contemplate those two as being interpenetrated by their mutual gazing;
this is described as the yoga known as "union with the Lord" (īśvarasaṃdhāna). || 127 ||
By means of which there may always be universal sovereignty over all images;
now, the connection with the word "atha" is indeed that which is the identity of the mantra and the image. (128)
That subtle power of Viṣṇu, which is stainless and known as Sattā,
having become identical with that universal essence, causes its own resonance to dissolve therein.
Know that to be devoid of all conceptual constructions, free even from the mere word, peaceful, supreme, subtle,
and produced by awakening.
Then, one should remember that supreme and subtle state of Paśyantī which is emerging, characterized by the effort of a half-throb of the refinement of word and meaning.

Having ascended the path of conceptualization and being colored by various latent impressions (saṃskāras), that which arises directed toward one's own object of expression after having separated it [from the underlying reality]—that indeed is [the nature of the world]. (132)

One should remember that intermediate form, which is verbal in nature, situated within the lotus of the heart, produced by various places of articulation and efforts, and impelled by the breath through the organs of speech. (133)
p.
200) That which manifests clearly through waves in the form of phonemes, words, and so forth,
as the very nature of the signifier— that word they know as *vaikharī*.
Therefore, having contemplated the body as consisting of consciousness and sound, and possessing distinctions such as the supreme, the subtle, and so forth,
one should then meditate upon that reflection.

Through the application of the withdrawal of sound, one should likewise remember that pair: one’s own body and that reflected image, which consist of the essence of unfluctuating consciousness and sound (or word and meaning).

By means of the application of the sequence previously described, one should indeed contemplate the unstruck Śabdabrahman as consisting of the reflection of sound through the very sequence beginning with Paśyantī.
Having thus performed the coordination of sounds and the coordination of mantras, the wise one should begin the ritual action; this is called his yoga. || 138 ||
The supreme unstruck sound (anāhata), having reached the state of Paśyantī at the navel,
resides within like a lotus fiber in the central heart-lotus.

Having remained there, one should remember [the Self] entering within the reflection by means of that *vaikharī* speech, as having the nature of the throbbing *nāda*, and likewise pervaded by all mantras. (140)
One should meditate upon the Lord of the World, whose essence is mantra, situated within the center of the heart of the *bimba*.
Thus established, the *bimba* bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (141)
Then one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) into this image of Hari,
first saying "I invoke," and likewise with the mantra for all the limbs.
One should visualize the entrance and exit of Lakṣmī from the body of the Lord;
her invocation is prescribed with the first five Ṛg verses. (143)
One should perform the placement of the twelve parts and the digits (kalānyāsa) as in the ritual of deity-placement (devanyāsa).
One should console the two [deities] with the mantra: "May you both be well-disposed toward us. (144)
While such is the case for a movable image, for an immovable one, the knower of the Sāttvata and other rites should perform the installation according to the previously mentioned method.
Regarding this triad of connections previously mentioned, it is my conviction that this alone constitutes the foundation in both cases. (146)
Thus, when these two images have been perfected through ritual consecration, the wise man perceives with his intellect Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī as being present before him.
With his mind fixed on them, devoted to them, sacrificing to them, intent on their recitation,
and constantly practicing yoga toward them, he attains those two alone at the end.
This supreme state, consisting of pure knowledge, is declared to be the direct means of firm establishment;
for men, nothing other than knowledge is considered to be the deliverer. 149.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Consecration" (or "The Illumination of the Attainment of Māyā"), in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. 49.
Chapter Fifty. Śakra:
Salutations to you, the source of the universe; salutations to you, the manifestation of all prosperity.
Salutations to you, the fundamental cause of all spiritual accomplishments. || 1 ||
1. O you who are the source of all! That is to say, O you who are the locus of the origin of the universe.
O consort of Nārāyaṇa, whose very self is the primordial God;
O lotus-born one, who is worshipped by the entire world—salutations to you! 2.
2. To her who has become [my] very self; that is to say, to her who is as dear as life.
"By your grace, your mantras have been heard by me, and their accomplishments attained; furthermore, the propitiation of them all has been correctly understood. 3.
Now I desire to hear the entire procedure for your well-spoken words as they issue from your lotus-like mouth; I have approached you as a student—teach me, O Lord! (4)
4. Of your hymn, the Śrīsūkta. Śrī said:
The Lord named Nārāyaṇa is the master of all that moves and stands in the world.
And he is the Self of all worlds, whose form consists of the bliss of the six qualities.
5. "Of the world," and so forth. This means the Lord of all moving and stationary beings.
He is the source of all nature, the Sovereign, the omniscient, and the performer of all actions. He is free from suffering, blameless, and the refuge of all auspiciousness. 6.
6. *Prakṛti* is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
It is the illuminator of both darknesses and lights by virtue of its own self-luminosity;
it is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) and the ruler, manifested through existence and non-existence.
[The state of] thorough discernment. || 7 ||
7. Herein is the expansion of the meaning of the Śruti passage: "By its light all this shines. Regarding the phrase "existence and non-existence":
the meaning is that [the Lord] is determined as having the nature of both existent and non-existent categories.
"The possessor of power, the support of all, the omnipotent, my Lord."
I am his supreme, singular, and eternal power, named Śrī.
It is free from all defects, it is the cow of plenty for all desires of the Lord,
and it manifests upon the wall of the Self as the entire range of the pure and impure paths.

9. "Sarvakāma" (one who has all desires fulfilled): the sense is that he alone has attained every desire. "Ātmabhitti" (the wall of the self): the meaning is that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), whether pure or impure, has me as its sole support. Anuvratā [is] Hṛṣīkeśa, having attained equanimity in every respect.
Thus we two are the supreme parents of the universe, dwelling in the highest heaven.
Established in heaven with supreme splendor for the sake of blessing the worlds,
they were once moved by compassion, desiring the welfare of all living beings.

"May these living beings be happy; how indeed might they attain us?"—thus, with supreme concentration (*samādhi*), he was intent upon seeking the means. (12) 12. *Samādhinā* means by means of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

We have churned that exceedingly profound great ocean of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma), which is filled with the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus [Vedas]. From that ocean, as it was being churned, [the Veda emerged]. || 13 ||
13. "We have churned," they said; the meaning is, "we have not churned.
That divine pair of hymns arose like clarified butter from curds—unstruck, unambiguous, clear, and imperishable. 14.
14. The *sūkta* pair consists of the *puṃsūkta* and the *śrīsūkta*. It is unstruck (*anāhata*) and unimpeded (*avyāhata*); it is not manifest (*anaspaṣṭa*) and yet exceedingly manifest (*atispaṣṭa*).
Endowed with all sovereign qualities, its words and syllables are unconfused;
from beginning to end, it is eternally intermingled with one another's syllables.

omits this line] Pervaded by power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat), and intermingled with various syllables (akṣara), that which is well-spoken therein possesses the characteristics of the Person (puruṣa) and is adorned with the qualities of the True Brahman (sadbrahman). || 16 ||
The lotus-eyed Lord accepted there the well-spoken definition of womanhood, which was established in its own greatness and adorned with the qualities of the True Brahman.

17. "He accepted" (svīcakāra): the meaning is that he contemplated himself as the seer of that mantra, as its ṛṣi, as its subject matter, and as its deity. By the term "lotus-eyed" (aravindākṣa), it is indicated that his eyes are described in the Śruti as being "like a lotus flower with its stalk still attached" (yathā kapyāsaṃ puṇḍarīkam evamakṣiṇī).
I, remaining undisturbed, accepted [the world] as established within my own glory—these two verses from the supreme hymn (sūkta) frequented by hosts of great seers (maharṣi). 18.
Both when studied and when reflected upon, these lead to the supreme goal;
they are the ordinances established by the ancient authors of the Kalpasūtras. (19)
19–20. It has been studied according to the words and reflected upon according to the meaning by the authors of the ritual manuals (kalpakṛt), such as Śaunaka and others.
O Lord presided over by the Immortals, those various [mantras] number in the thousands and are free from inauspiciousness.
Now, listen to the procedure for my hymn (matsūkta) as it is prescribed therein.
20. *Aghorāṇi* (The Non-Terrible Ones). The meaning is that they are supremely enjoyable not only in the state of fruition (*phala-daśā*) but also in the state of practice (*sādhana-daśā*).
"One should know me alone as the first sage of this [mantra]; the meter is said to be named Śrī;
the deity is the support of all, I, the Sovereign, the consort of Viṣṇu. 21.
The application of this hymn is in the worship of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
one should meditate upon me, the Supreme Goddess Lakṣmī, seated on the lap of Viṣṇu. (22)
22. "Seated on the lap" means seated on the left lap; she is constantly embraced by the Supreme Self with His left arm, and her arm is resting upon His shoulder.
Holding a divine lotus. || 23 ||
Then, being self-restrained, one should worship me, the Supreme Goddess, with Ṛg verses—
me who am seated upon the left lap of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
With the first *carcā*, one should unweariedly perform the invocation;
with the second, one should offer a seat to the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should offer the *arghya* with the third [mantra] to Īśāna, and likewise arrange the *pādya*;
with the fourth [mantra], the *ācamana*, and with the fifth, the *upahāra*.
On the sixth day, the best of practitioners should perform a bath together with his consort;
on the seventh day he should offer two garments, and on the eighth day, ornaments.
On the ninth day one should offer perfume; on the tenth, a heap of flowers;
on the two following days, incense and a lamp; and on the final day, the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
28. "By the two following" means by the eleventh and twelfth verses.
And with the fourteenth and fifteenth [verses], there are salutations;
then, at the very end, one should employ the *tārikā* and the *anutāra*. 29.
29. "The *tārikā*," and so forth. This means the two mantras *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*.
The practitioner, being disciplined, should recite them according to the ritual procedure and to the best of his ability for each verse (*ṛc*).
Afterwards, he should contemplate the dissolution of the hymn (*sūkta*) within the *tārikā*. 30.
Having meditated on the two as being established upon the *tārikā*, one should remember our universal course;
or else, the rite of invocation is performed first with the four *ṛc* verses.
31. He states another alternative: "With the *ṛc*s... and so forth.
"But with the fifth [verse], one should approach me, Śrī, with a pure mind;
with this [verse] beginning 'āpaḥ', one should perform the rites of the arghya, pādya, and ācamana. 32.

32. Regarding "āpa" (waters): this refers to the twelfth [verse], beginning with "āpaḥ sṛjantu" (may the waters release). "Ārdrām" (the moist) refers to the bath; "kardamena" (with mud) refers to the garment; and "gandhadvārā" (by means of the gate of fragrance)—fragrances should be applied. May [it] approach.
It may be an ornament. || 33 ||

33. Regarding "ārdrām" and so forth: the meaning is "on the thirteenth and the fourteenth. Regarding "kardamena": the meaning is "on the eleventh. Regarding "gandhadvārā": the meaning is "on the ninth. Regarding "upaitu": the meaning is "on the seventh. (p. 203)
"I shall offer incense and lamps, as well as an oblation on the sixth day; such is the desire of my mind"—with these words, one should prepare the madhuparka offering.
34. "kāṃsosmi" (I am gold): this refers to the fourth [verse]. Its application even in the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) has been stated previously.
"ṣaṣṭhyā" (with the sixth): this means with the verse beginning "ādityavarṇe. "manasaḥ" (of the mind): this refers to the tenth [verse].
For this [verse] is the one that establishes the attainment of freedom from hunger and thirst.
But with the final [verse], one should perform the salutation; the rest should be performed as before. || 35 ||

35. "Kṣudh" and so forth; the meaning is "on the eighth [lunar day]. "By the last one"; the meaning is "by the fifteenth," as in the phrase "bring that to me. In this hymn, there are fifty-three names of mine;
hear their etymological explanation from me, O destroyer of Jambha. 36.
36. "Fifty-three" means fifty-three. It is deposited within all beings like a female bee in a wound (*raṇa*);
it produces a supreme sound that is unceasing, like a stream of oil. 37.

37. By the words beginning with *nihita* and ending with *hiraṇyavarṇā*, the etymology of the name is provided. The word *hi* has the sense of *nihita*; the meaning is "I produce sound in battle. This is an elaboration of the immediate sound: "like a female bee. *Acyuta* means "uninterrupted."
Situated between the opening and closing of the eyes of the sun and the moon,
she extends from the root foundation (ādhāra) up to the end of the twelve [fingers].
Resembling many thousands of rising suns, fires, and moons,
the peaceful *madhyamā* is then seen emerging from the wheel that is the support of the wind. 39.

39. He explains the word *varṇa*: "From the wheel" (*cakrakāt*), meaning from the *ādhāra-cakra*. "The Supreme Peace" (*śāntā parā*) means the *parā* [state]. "By the vision" (*paśyā*) means by the *paśyantī*.
Having reached the locus of *vaikharī*, she resides there in the eight locations.
Having become the mother of the social classes, I yield enjoyments like a cow. (40)
40. The locations of *vaikharī* speech are the eight places beginning with the throat.
Having praised me with the hymn beginning "Hiraṇyavarṇā," the noble-minded Prajāpati then, by my grace, spoke on the dharma of yogas. 41.
This nine-syllabled mantra of mine begins with the Praṇava and ends with "namaḥ";
it consists of the Śabdabrahman itself and is the direct means for achieving yoga for practitioners. (42)
42. "Oṃ hiraṇyavarṇāyai namaḥ"—this is the nine-syllable mantra. 43. I go from afar to a place even further away than the minds of yogis; yet yogis of firm vows bind me with their own devotion.
43. Here the name "hariṇī" is etymologically explained: it is called *hariṇī* because she runs far like a deer (*hariṇī*), and there is a second etymology: "yogins capture and bind her.
Sixty-eight thousand yogins are devoted to me as their supreme goal.
Having meditated upon me, the golden-hued one, they have attained supreme withdrawal of the senses.
Clad in a deerskin, with a deerskin for her bed, with a deer embracing her waist, she had eyes as long as a deer's. || 45 ||

45. He states another etymological derivation—beginning with "hariṇa," and so forth: "Her waist is embraced like that of a deer," meaning it is unadorned; or alternatively, the etymology is "her waist is embraced by Hari" (Viṣṇu). "By recollecting me, Hariṇī, one shall attain supreme peace."
"I lead Hari to my tasks, and I am led by Hari himself" (46).
This is another etymological explanation for the word "Hari. As the learned say: "He who, being dependent on the subtle gestures [of others], ordains everything.
Furthermore, "I am always like a deer (*hariṇa*); I am one who captivates (*hāriṇī*) the sins of the virtuous."
This six-syllabled mantra of mine begins with the syllable Om and ends with "namaḥ. (47)
47. There are two etymological derivations: *hariṇabhāsā* and *hāriṇī*. Oṃ, obeisance to Hariṇī.
She is the direct accomplisher of all aims and the supreme means for the practice of yoga. (p. 204)
My garland is always fashioned from golden lotuses.
48. "Suvarṇasrak" and "Rajatasrak" are two names. I create beautiful colors, or I thoroughly choose the universe to emanate.
Furthermore, those unborn beings who are bound and liberated have also been constantly created by me. || 49 ||

49. With the words "I create" (*sṛjāmi*) and so forth, another etymology is given. With the words "the universe well" (*suṣṭhu viśvam*) and so forth, the third etymology is provided. Since "Viśva" is listed as a name for Viṣṇu, the etymology should be understood either as "I choose Viṣṇu as my husband" (*viṣṇuṃ patitvena vṛṇe*) or as "I choose the universe as my dwelling place" (*viśvaṃ lokaṃ vāsasthānatayā vṛṇe*).
He states the etymological derivation of the word *srak* (garland): "They have flowed forth" (*sṛtāḥ*).
Having worshipped for a long time on Mount Meru with a golden garland, the lord of the Guhyakas attained the status of the Lord of Wealth (*dhaneśa*). (50)
50. An explanatory narrative is told: "Of the Guhyakas. Silver garlands, lotuses, and stainless garlands shine; all these creators of the worlds have been honored by me. 51.

51. The name *rajatasrag* is etymologically explained as "those who are made of silver" (*rājataiḥ*). Another derivation is "those who shine" (*rājante*), and yet another derivation is "those who have shone" (*rājitāḥ*).
In ancient times, the foremost among the Rudras was indeed known as *Rajatasraj*.
Having arrived at Kailāsa, he attained sovereignty over the silver mountain. || 52 ||
52. An explanatory narrative is told: "Of the Rudras," and so forth.
These two mantras consist of eight syllables each, joined with the *tāra* (oṃ) and with *namaḥ*.
Through recitation (*japa*), worship (*arcana*), fire-oblation (*huta*), and meditation (*dhyāna*), they will accomplish one's desired goal. 53.
53. Oṃ, homage to Suvarṇasrajā! Oṃ, homage to Rajatasrajā!
As I walk to and fro, I dissolve the evil deeds of my devotees;
like the moon, I constantly melt the hearts of my devotees. 54.

54. The etymology of the name *candra* is explained as "one who walks" (*caṃkramyamāṇa*). From the verbal root *kram*, with the suffix *yaṅ*, the form *caṃkramya* arises. Taking the syllable *caṃ* from that and joining it with *drā*, the word *candra* is formed.
He explains the word *drā*: "I cause to run" (*drāvayāmi*). Another etymology for this very term *drā* is "like the moon" (*candravat*).
I overflow within the yogis as the characteristic of the vibration of inner bliss;
indeed, I illuminate their fourth state like the moon. (55)
55. He states another etymological derivation: "udemi" (I emerge). The fourth state is the *turīya* condition.
Vasiṣṭha, the supreme sage, who has conquered the ground of other yogas, [perceives] within himself the pure lunar [nature], a great ocean of consciousness-bliss. 56.
56. By means of a narrative, he states another etymological derivation with the words beginning "yogena":
"Having recollected me, who resides in the channel [or: who resides in the navel], he again attained his own yoga."
This six-syllabled mantra of mine instantly produces bliss.

57. Oṃ, salutation to Candrā. This golden one, possessing the luster of the sun, brings about the cessation of suffering for those scorched by the forest fire of worldly existence, extending from the foundational lotus to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]. 58.
58. The etymology of the name *Hiraṇmayī* is explained as follows: "The Support," and so forth. *Dviṣaṭkāntam* means "the end of twelve" (*dvādaśāntam*).
The word ending in the vowel *ā* is *bhāsā*, meaning "whose splendor is like that of the sun.
She is declared to be constantly arising through the buds of sound and mental constructs (*śabdasaṃkalpakorakaiḥ*).
And in the supreme ether beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), within the mandala consisting of the three Vedas.

59. The conceptualizations of sound (*śabda-saṃkalpa*) are [the levels of speech] beginning with *paśyantī*. The instrumental case in the word *tadātmanā* is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūta-lakṣaṇa*), meaning "by means of that nature. There is another etymological explanation starting with "of the primordial matter" (*prakṛteḥ*). "I abide eternally in the golden [egg] for the welfare of the worlds."
The sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas know me as "the golden one" (hiraṇmayī).
Having offered praise, the yogis attained their desire through this supreme yoga;
for this seven-syllabled mantra is the accomplisher of all desires and goals. (61)
61. Oṃ, salutation to Hiraṇmayī. (p.
205) As the witness of all beings, I observe their auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
I am the eternal Lakṣmī of Hari, and I am the object of perception for all measurement.

62. From here follow seven verses devoted to the etymological definition of the name Lakṣmī. He states the derivation from the verbal root *lakṣ*, meaning "to see," with the words "the witness" (*sākṣiṇī*) and "and Lakṣmī. The meaning is that Lakṣmī is the all-encompassing prosperity (*sarvasampad*) of Hari. In this regard: "Through faith, a god attains godhood; for his splendor is indeed immeasurable."

One should contemplate [the verse] beginning with "She who is that daughter of Janaka. Regarding the term "the object" (*lakṣya*): the meaning is that she is the object of all valid cognition (*pramiti*).
"I am the giver, the thrower, and the eternal one; likewise, I am the triple impeller."
Likewise, I am of the nature of consciousness, to be characterized in every act of cognition. 63.
63. He states the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the root *kṣip*: "the thrower" (*kṣepaṇī*). Its further explanation is "the three-fold impeller" (*tripreranī*);

the meaning is that she is the impeller of body, speech, and mind. Here, the formation is intended to be derived from two roots: *lā* in the sense of "giving" and *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling. Thus, I am to be characterized as having the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpā*).
In the creation of the abode of dissolution, I am the impelling force of primordial nature (prakṛti),
appearing in the form of the various stages of manifestation such as the kalās and kāṣṭhās of the state known as lakṣaṇa.

64. Regarding the word *laye*: "I am Lakṣmī, who impels Prakṛti during the processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. All entities (*bhāva*) are called *lakṣaṇa* because they are perceived (*lakṣyante*) and measured (*pramīyante*). I am their constant impeller; such is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*). I am the one who always impels that which abides in the unmanifest, the manifest, and the quality of goodness (*sattva*).
I lead myself to the goal, I take it up, and at the end, I cast it away.
65. "Lakṣam" and so forth is another etymological derivation (*nirukti*). Likewise, "lāmī" is also used; it means "I become dissolved" (*līnā bhavāmi*).
"Kṣipāmi" means "I impel" or "I cast. This etymology is formed by taking the verbal roots *lī* and *kṣip*. "I alone destroy, I exhaust, and I annihilate the misdeeds of the virtuous."
For forgiveness is indeed the strength of all beings; I forgive both them and me.

66. He states another etymological derivation: "I cast" (*kṣipāmi*). He explains the derivation from the root *kṣam* with the words "I am patient" (*kṣame*). He explains the derivation of the word *mī* with the words "I measure," and so forth.
Having perceived these meanings within himself, the supreme seer of noble intellect—
"O Lakṣmī, mark me!"—thus spoke the sage Kapila to me, who am marked by the signs of Lakṣmī. || 67 ||
67. "O Lakṣmī, do not look at me; do not cast a sidelong glance at me"—this is the meaning of what the sage Kapila said.
For this five-syllabled mantra is the means for attaining the subterranean realms (Pātāla) and the provider of enjoyments pertaining to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial spheres. 68.
68. Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī.
That body of mine, consisting of knowledge, exists within the heart of Viṣṇu (or, like that of Viṣṇu, it manifests).
This is the meritorious knowledge of the Self; this is the supreme knowledge of Yoga.
Endowed with the form of yoga. || 69 ||
69. He explains the etymology of the name *Anapagāminī*: "Tanu" [refers to the body]. Because she never departs from Viṣṇu, she is named *Anapagāminī*.
Just as the radiance of the stars always resides in the moon, so too [does she reside in Him].
I am the power of Viṣṇu, the possessor of power, abiding as his inseparable consort.
I alone am the one who moves without a trace; having become the Great Quality (guṇa), I flow. And in the beginning, having become Sarasvatī, I brought forth the sage.

71. He states another etymological derivation: "apaśca" (and water). The meaning is: "In water, I am the quality called fluidity; therefore, I do not depart from them. He states another etymological derivation: "apāvāhayam" (I caused to flow away). This is the aorist (*laṅ*) of the root *vah* with the prefix *apa*.
Formerly, while she was flowing through the waters of the Sarasvata region as declared by Viśvāmitra, the Sarasvatī, true to her promise, carried Vasiṣṭha away from that pure-souled Viśvāmitra.

72–73. Having been told by Viśvāmitra, "I carried his adversary Vasiṣṭha away in the water," Satī replied using the perfect tense (*liṭ*). When the sages said to her, "Vasiṣṭha has been swept away by the current," she said, "O Satī, protect Vasiṣṭha, who is dear to the truth, from his enemy."
73. Having thus derived the word *apagāminī*, he now states its opposite meaning with the words "The sages," etc. The syntactical connection is: "The sages said to me, 'Protect [us] from the enemy.
Having become Sarasvatī, I carried her away from that enemy;
for then the sages gave me the name Anapagāminī (She Who Does Not Depart).
74. I carried Vasiṣṭha away from his enemies; that is, I removed him or drove him away.
For this nine-syllabled mantra is the warder-off of all calamities. I am the morning dawn, and I always dwell in the city. 75.

75. Oṃ, salutation to Anapagāminī. In the city whose form is intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, I am the horse, the city, and the vehicle. I dwell there. Because she draws the intellect toward various objects and causes it to run, she is the "Horse" (*aśvā*). Because she is the abode of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), she is the "City" (*pūḥ*). Because she carries the body as the Self (*ātman*), she is the "Vehicle" (*vāhanī*). Therefore, she is called "Aśvapūrvā" (She who has the Horse as her Precedent).
I utter a sound like the neighing of horses at the commencement of yoga, within the threefold [body]— consisting of mind, vital breath, and physical form— which itself is of three kinds. (76)

76. He states another alternative: "Of horses," etc. Previously, at the commencement of yoga, she was like a horse; thus: "Salutation to the one preceded by a horse (aśvapūrvā). Having entered the center of the channels, I produce a sound like that of a chariot.
Having reached the opening of the sky, it resounded with the trumpeting of elephants.

77. The etymological explanation of Rathamadhyā—namely, "Nāḍī. He explains the name Hastinādaprabodhinī with the words beginning with "Vyoma": Oṃ, obeisance to Aśvapūrvā; Oṃ, obeisance to Rathamadhyā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Hastinādaprabodhinī.
The striving yogins have attained me in this threefold manner:
the first two are mantras of eight syllables each, and the last is one of eleven syllables.
For these three mantras, consisting of myself, are indeed the bestowers of desired objects;
I hear the compassionate speech and I destroy the misfortune of the virtuous. (79)

79. He begins the etymological explanation of the name "Śrī" with the words "I hear," and so forth. The verbal roots are *śru* (to hear), *śṝ* (to injure), and *śṝ* (to expand). [The verse continues: "I pervade the universe with my qualities (*guṇaiḥ*), and I am the eternal refuge."
And I am the body of Hari, served with faith and desired by the gods.
80. Regarding "by faith" (śraddhayā): the sense is that by taking the letter *śa* and the letter *ra* from this word, and joining the vowel *ī* from the desired word, one obtains the word *śrī*.
I abide in the station of the support of Peace (*śāntādhārapada*), and I am the observer (*paśyantī*) who sports within the navel-born [Viśvatantrī].
She is the impeller of thoughts, the center of the intellects, and likewise the source of the syllables from her mouth.

81. Regarding "śāntā" and so forth: the sense is that by taking the letter *śa* from the word *śāntā*, the letter *ra* from the word *rantī*, and the vowel *ī* from the word *preraṇī*, one obtains the word *śrī*. This is called the "creation of phonemes" (*arṇasāṃ sṛṣṭiḥ*), which refers to the form of *vaikharī* speech;
and thus, abiding in the four places of articulation, it is differentiated as *śāntā*, *paśyantī*, and the others.
I take refuge; I am worthy of being taken refuge in; by my powers, I rejoice and I delight. || 82 ||

82. I take refuge in Viṣṇu. She who is to be resorted to (śrayaṇīyā) by powers such as Jayā and others, and who is to be served; I am she who destroys (remi) the sins of those who have taken refuge, and I am she who bestows (rāmi) all desired objects. I am the one who kindles power (śakterujjvalinī), the most auspicious (śaṃtamā), and the desired delight (ratirīpsitā).
Thus, those who know the truth of the three Vedas immediately recognize me as Śrī.

83. She is the illuminator of power (*śakti*). Most auspicious (*śantamā*), most blessed. She is the embodiment of delight (*rati*). She is desired and to be prayed for. Here too, by combining the letters *śa*, *ra*, and *i* from the three words, the formation of the word *Śrī* is intended. [“O Lord of the Gods, I am the Master, the Sovereignty, and the Three Worlds. Furthermore, “I am the Master and the Sovereignty.”
The three worlds, together with their lords and immortals, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the excellence of my own caste. 84.
In the first three words, the syllables *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *oṃ* consist of my own essence;
by these four, my body is sustained. (85)
85. "Or this" means the mantra "Oṃ śriyai namaḥ. "With these four" means with these four: Śrīṃ, Hrīṃ, Oṃ, and Oṃ śriyai namaḥ.
Whether recited, worshipped, offered as oblations, or meditated upon individually, in pairs, in groups of three, or all together, they shall accomplish whatever is desired.
This quartet of jewels must be guarded with great effort;
it bears fruit through one another and is superior by virtue of all its qualities without exception. (87)
[Ī: My power is indeed mighty through all my illusory powers at the dissolution of the universe.
At the dissolution of the universe, the entire world is measured by all measures within me;
and since I am the sovereign of the Self, when I am all-pervading, there arises the realization "I am Mā" (the measurer). || 88 ||

88. The etymological derivation of the name "Me" (meti) is given by the passage beginning with "mima" and so forth. "I measure everything" (*sarvaṃ praminomi*); "I am measured" (*mīye*) or "I am fully measured" (*pramīye*);

"it is measured" (*māti*), meaning it becomes limited. Regarding the passage beginning with "ātma," the meaning is described by taking the syllable *ma* derived from the word "asmad" (we/I). "Me is the intellect" (*meti dhīḥ*) means the intellect whose object is the "I-sense" (*ahamarthadhīḥ*).
Therefore, those who know me understand that I am exceedingly desired like one's own self;
for this five-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of all desires. (89)
89. Regarding "like myself" (ātmavat): the intended meaning is that it is derived from the sense of "like me" (mā iva mām). Om, salutation to Māyā.
I am the bestower of all desires and the protector of all actions; I am the beloved of the God. The sages know me as the Goddess. 90.

90. He explains the etymology of the word *devī*—as "the giver" (*pradātrī*). It is derived from the roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place), and is explained as "the beloved of the God. The intention is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied here due to her union with a male (*puṃyoga*). Om, salutations to the Goddess (*devyai*). Indeed, this five-syllabled mantra bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
She is always the conscious one, dwelling within all beings, and she makes them hear.
91. Regarding the phrase "kāṃ sosmitām," the word *kā* is a separate term. The word *ke* explains the etymology of the name: it means "I call out" (*śabdāye*). The meaning is "I make a sound.
Furthermore, she is sought by all the Vedas as *kā*, and she is sought by all as *ke*.
And I bear the form of Brahmā, wearing a mass of matted locks.

92. Regarding the word *kāye*: the meaning is "in that which is to be established. Taking up the word *kim*, he says: "anviṣye" (I shall seek). Thinking that *ka* is a name for Brahman, he says: "brahmetyādi" (Brahman, etc.). *Oṃ kāyai namaḥ*.
I create various beings who are intent upon the study of their own Vedic recitation. [Ā, B, C]
Therefore, the sages who have mastered the Vedas call me "Kāma. || 93 ||
For this five-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of its own study:
"ud" is the name of Brahman, while "vikasti" is his smile. (94)
94. He explains the etymology of the name *Sosmitā*: "She has risen" (*uditī*). The meaning of the Vedic text, "That is His name, 'The Risen' (*uditi*)," is intended here.
That which is the unfolding, the expansion, or the vastness (*bṛhattva*) of that Brahman—that very unfolding is the smile.
The form is *usmitam*. She who is accompanied by that is *Sosmitā*. That which is the vastness of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is...
This is what is meant by saying that [the world] is dependent upon this. As they say: "That which is the Supreme Brahman above the many side-glances (apāṅgas) became that. Oṃ, salutation to Sosmitā.
Since the expansion of the universe is dependent upon me, they therefore know me as Sosmitā.
For this seven-syllable mantra shall bring about even greater expansion. || 95 ||
My supreme nature is both beneficial and delightful;
by taking refuge in that which consists of the quality of *sattva*, sages cross over the darkness.

96. The etymology of the name *Hiraṇyaprākārā* is explained as follows: it means "beneficial" (*hitā*) and "enclosure" (*prākāra*). Here, the word *prākāra* refers to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Om, salutations to Hiraṇyaprākārā.
[The manuscript *Ī* omits this line. Therefore, the seers worship me as Hiraṇyaprākārā.
For this ten-syllable mantra bestows the fulfillment of all desires. || 97 ||
(208) She is the one who dissolves all remaining defects for those who have approached me,
by means of a stream of nectar flowing from the downward-turned lotus of her head. 98.
98. He provides an etymological explanation for the name Ādrī: "Ārāt" means "from afar.
Another etymological derivation is "from one with a downward face.
[She says: "I am consecrated (ārdrā) and yet moist with compassion; my inner self is softened by mercy."
I blaze eternally within the sky of all beings, in the supreme beyond.

99. He explains the etymology of the name *Jvalantī*: "I am burning. Pure, stainless, and true, I illuminate the world with my radiance; I am without crest, yet three-crested, and possessed of five times five crests. 100.

100. He states that [the Goddess] has the nature of Śabdabrahman: "Pure," etc. "Unlearned" (aśikha) refers to her supreme form (*parārūpa*). She is three-crested through the divisions of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. She is twenty-five-crested by way of the nature of the consonants (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, abiding within the body, she blazes sevenfold and again threefold.
The two mantras consisting of six syllables, which are all-pervading, bestow liberation and radiance. || 101 ||
101. This means that she exists in seven ways through the nature of the array of the internal retention (*antardhāraṇā*), and in three ways through the nature of *ha* and *lakṣa*.
Oṃ, salutation to Ārdrā. Oṃ, salutation to Jvalantī.
She is eternally full of love for Hari and always satisfied among her devotees.
And without worldly enjoyments, I am eternally satisfied by my own nature.

102. He states the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of her name, "Tṛptā," with the words "in Hari" (*harau*). "Without the worldly" (*prākṛtairvinā*) means "with the non-worldly" (*aprākṛtaiḥ*). Om, salutation to Tṛptā.

Meditating upon each respective form of Tṛptā, the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas—[F, ṅ, ī: yoga]— *Note: The bracketed portion indicates a fragmentary or corrupted reading from the manuscript source.*
They have attained the supreme, eternal satisfaction consisting of nectar, which is rooted in knowledge.
For this six-syllabled mantra satisfies the entire world;
I satisfy Viṣṇu with his qualities, and myself also with those same qualities.

104. He says "I satisfy" regarding the name "those who satisfy. And he describes the act of satisfying many [deities] by means of many instruments with the words beginning with "by qualities" (guṇaiḥ).
Within the ocean of the body, there are seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs).
I constantly satisfy them with essences by virtue of the impulsion of the vital breaths (or, always by virtue of the regulation of breath). || 105 ||

105. There are seventy-two channels (nāḍīs) in the body, as well known in the Yoga scriptures. Here, the intended metaphorical identification (adhyavasāya) is of the body as the ocean, the channels as rivers, the vital breaths (prāṇas) as wind, and the fluids (rasas) as water.
For those who have eternally attained the supreme state by way of the suṣumnā path,
I have become the reflected image within the stainless mirror of yoga.
106. He states another method: "By means of the *sauṣumna*... [and so forth].

107. With the nectar-essences of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which consist of consciousness (*cinmaya*) and have emerged from the reflection of the Self (*ātma-bimba*), I satisfy the supreme being (*sattva*) within the yogis.

Always tending toward transformation from the stage of primordial nature (prakṛti) up to the specific evolutes (viśeṣa), it has attained the state of being an effect, yet it does not exhaust itself through its own powers.

108. He states another perspective with the words "prakṛtyādi" (beginning with primordial nature). By the phrase "always inclined toward transformation," it is stated that primordial nature has the inherent nature of constant transformation.
By the phrase "like rivers [flowing] into the ocean," the support of the vital breaths is indicated.
I shall satisfy the sense organs of living beings with the gift of life, just as one always nourishes a lamp with oil. 109.

109. He states another intended meaning with the words "by affection" (snehena): "I satisfy [the deities] solely by the nectar of my own consciousness, which is of an imperishable nature; the yogis who have reached the further shore of yoga say that they are thus satisfying me. 110.
For this seven-syllabled mantra satisfies the entire world incessantly.
Because it measures (minoti) time as it proceeds (padyamānam), they call it *padma*. 111
111. Oṃ, obeisance to Tarpaṇyā (She who Satisfies). He explains the etymology of the name Padme-sthitā (Abiding in the Lotus): "That which is being measured" (*padyamāna*).
The meaning is "the entire object of cognition. She measures, that is, she delimits. Oṃ, obeisance to Padme-sthitā. (p. 209)
Constantly measuring out all time and ever remaining present,
by praising me with these names, one shall become a virtuous person who has transcended time.
By the power of my own splendor, I eternally describe myself as the Supreme Lord, the primary source of all beings;
my body is adorned with excellent colors in the form of lotuses.

113. Because they are being manifested (*padyamānatvāt*), the meanings of the word *padma* are the Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and Īśvara. Another intended meaning is "those having the form of a lotus. Oṃ, salutation to the one of lotus-color (*padmavarṇā*). By praising me as "of lotus-color," one shall attain clarity regarding the scriptures.
He who was the first ray to emerge during the churning of the ocean of milk.
114. The etymology of the name "Candrā" is explained as "the one who has risen" (*udgatā*). Oṃ, salutations to Candrā.

That ray of mine known as Candra is the precursor of her who is rising; however, the sages, knowing my power, designate me as Candrā. 115. [The verse continues: "That ray of mine named Candra is the forerunner of her who is rising; yet the seers, aware of my majesty, declare me to be Candrā."
That moon which is born from ten million times ten million times ten million parts of my rays—this six-syllable mantra indeed bestows purity of mind. (116)
My light, being drawn forth in all states and at all times, is concealed by that which it desires to conceal; thus is my light obscured.
117. Regarding the passage beginning with "being drawn forth" (*prakṛṣyamāṇā*): here, there is no etymological definition (*anirvacana*) for the word *prabhāsānām*.

He states the excellence of light itself with the words "by which": by that splendor (*tejas*) by which the sun and others desire to obscure the light of others, even that [splendor] is eclipsed by my splendor.
For just as the shadow of one's own head cannot be overtaken by one's own feet, since it moves ahead of the feet even as one desires to overtake it. (118)
118. He provides a worldly illustration regarding invincibility: "Just as... (yatheti).
My rays of light, which are eternally risen consciousness-bliss, are perpetually blazing;
they are, respectively, faith, Soma, water, food, virility, and the oblation (havis). 119.
119. He states another method with the words beginning "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth, and "faith" (*śraddhā*) and so forth. This is well known in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*.
The words ending in the accusative case, such as "faith" and so forth, are syntactically connected with the subsequent verb "they cast away" (*asyanti*).
These [elements], which are the manifestations of the power of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya-śakti-prabhā*), are cast away into the six fires.
It is called Prabhāsā by the sages who have reached the further shore of the Tantras and Vedānta. || 120 ||
120. "In the six fires" means in [the worlds] such as Svarga and so forth. The etymology is "she who casts forth radiance" (*prabhā asyati*). Oṃ *prabhāsāyai* namaḥ.
Indeed, this seven-syllable mantra is the means for accomplishing the continuity of splendor.
Whatever radiant fame arises in the world from the giving of knowledge and other such acts, [belongs to him]. (121)
121. The name "Yaśas" is thus explained: it is "fame. That fame of mine is divided into various forms.
Know me alone to be the vessel of that fame, splendor, and glory. 122.
122. And that fame becomes manifold in form. He says this very thing with the words beginning "of fame" (*yaśasaḥ*).
Therefore, the wise know me as Yaśasvinī because of that fame;
for this seven-syllable mantra bestows fame upon the one who recites it. [It also bestows splendor.]
123. Oṃ, obeisance to Yaśasā. According to this, the recitation of the hymn (*sūkta*) is: "The radiant, the luminous, the glorious, the blazing.
[She is worshipped] through the divisions of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, male, female, and Vaiśvānara.
Accepting the oblation that has arrived, which is designated as faith, Soma, and so forth.
124. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) for the name "Jvalantī" with the words beginning with "svarga":
"Having divided myself sixfold, I have attained the state of fire; I am celebrated by the sages as Jvalantī, blazing with the power of the enjoyer and the radiance of the Lord. (125)

125. By the phrase "the power of the enjoyer" (bhoktṛśakti), it is established that there is no distinction among the manifestations whose purport is the power of the object of enjoyment (bhogyaśakti). Oṃ, salutation to Jvalantī.
Through the division of Agni and Soma, I thus divide the entire universe. [Ā, B, Ṅ]
I am [he who is thus invoked].
Having praised me with this mantra, one shall accomplish whatever is desired. || 126 ||
She is always cherished by the god Hari and served by the gods;
and the gods, relying upon me, remain established in their respective domains.

127. The etymological explanation (*anirvacana*) of those things favored by the gods (*devajuṣṭānām*) is given by the words "by the god" (*devena*), and so forth. As for the word "god" (*deva*), it refers here to the sense organs (*indriya*);
because they are specific transformations (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), they are indeed insentient (*acetana*).
Therefore, having taken up my own power, which consists of the activity of pure consciousness, || 128 ||
The ear, speech, mind, and other faculties operate toward their respective objects;
yet they know me alone as the one served by the senses for the sake of their functioning, and as the one cherished by the gods. 129.

129. Since the word *deva* (divine) here refers to the sense organs (*indriya*), he says "with the ear," etc. Regarding the meaning of "function" (*vṛtti*), it means the state of being occupied with the objects of the senses. With the *akṣas*, that is, the sense organs. Oṃ, salutation to the one cherished by the gods (*devajuṣṭā*).
She who bestows all powers, who dwells within as the one cherished by the gods.
By constantly meditating upon me, one conquers all the gods. || 130 ||
From that very source alone have arisen here the cognitions of the great seers,
as well as the powers and the activities of men, which are both high and low.
131. The etymological explanation of the name *Udārā* begins with the words "mata eva" and so forth. *Oṃ udārāyai namaḥ*.
The wise know me as *Udārā*, who grants even the most unrestrained desires.
This seven-syllabled mantra bestows everything desired. 132.
I perform the five cosmic acts through her, who is the soul of the universe;
those who know reality and have reached the further shore of the Vedanta declare: "She is she, and I am she."

133. Regarding the term *padmanemīm* here, the author provides an etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) by taking *tām* as a distinct name: "I expand" (*tanomi*). The five functions are emanation (*sarga*) and so forth. The meaning is: "I become expanded for her sake. The root is *tāyṛ*, meaning "to extend" and "to protect. *Oṃ tāyai namaḥ*.
For this five-syllabled mantra spreads forth auspicious expansion;
by my own splendor, I lead both Prakṛti and Puruṣa [to that state]. 134.

134. The etymological explanation of the name Padmanemi—by means of the passage beginning with "prakṛtim" and so forth. The meaning of the verbal root *pad* is "I lead. The meaning of the word *nemi* is "outside. Om, salutation to Padmanemi.
And because he has come forth even from Time (*kāla*), they therefore know him as Padmanemi.
For this seven-syllabled mantra bestows the fulfillment of all prosperity.
I shall describe Āditya, who is of solar hue through his splendor, fame, and glory;
having become the very soul of light, he stands as the Sun, divine and composed of the three Vedas.

136. Regarding the name "ādityavarṇā," he says "ādityam" (the sun). "Varṇayāmi" means I describe her as possessing color, that is, I make her radiant. Intending for the word *varṇa* to refer to syllables (*akṣara*), he says "varṇātmeti" (whose self is the syllable).
She illuminates all objects, even those past and future.
Among the ancestors, gods, and humans, I am the eternal eye.
137. Regarding "the eye": the meaning of the Vedic text, "The eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni," should be understood.

Furthermore, my first syllable is the *tāra* (the sacred syllable *om*), the primary designator. Therein, through the states of the tranquil (*śānta*) and the emergent (*udita*), I rejoice in the Self by means of the Self. 138. [The verse continues: "And the primordial letter of mine is the *tāra*, the first designator. Therein, through the tranquil, the emergent, and bliss (*ānanda*), I rejoice in the Self by means of the Self."
138. Thinking that the syllable *tya* is established at the beginning, he says: "The primordial one.
Like a stream of oil, uninterrupted, sounding like a long bell— That subtle crest of the *praṇava*, consisting of sound, is my body. 139.
One who is proficient in that Brahman will quickly attain me;
for I have manifested as sound, born with the luster of the sun.

140. Regarding the phrase "therein, the Brahman": this means within the crest of the *praṇava*. "Born with the color of the sun" means that all speech (*vāṅmaya*) is born from the *praṇava*. *Oṃ*, salutations to her who has the color of the sun. In the form of *śāntā*, *apaśyā*, and so forth, she is *vaikharī*, the one who utters the phonemes.
Yielding all objects of desire, the wish-fulfilling cow stands ready; the seers know these objects to be within me through the mantra beginning with "ādityavarṇā."
For this nine-syllabled mantra is the fulfiller of all desires.
Scattering rays throughout the world, and scattering them ever higher and higher, by means of the wind, the divine friend, the jewel, and the supporting fire. || 143 ||

143. The etymological explanation of the name *Kīrti*: "They scatter," and so forth. The root *kṛ* means "to scatter. Scattering refers to both rays and sounds. Regarding those sounds, he says: "successively. [This refers to] Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.
The explanation of the term "by the jewel" is: "by the fire of the substratum."
Having rested repeatedly and slowly upon the petals of the twelve lotuses,
I thereafter resort to that which is beyond the twelfth.
144. An explanation of the meaning of "upaitu" in the Śruti: "I worship. Om, salutations to Kīrti.
Therefore, wise sages proclaim me as Kīrti.
Indeed, this five-syllabled mantra bestows the purity of Yoga. 145.
I am successful through the qualities of Viṣṇu, and I surpass the yogins who move within the inner support of the yoga-lotuses upon their petals. || 146 ||

146. He provides an etymological explanation of the term *ṛddhi*: "It means *samṛddhi* (prosperity). I cause to prosper; that is, I delight. He states what prosperity itself is: "In the petals... [I attain] an ever-increasing prosperity, enjoying supreme expansion.
Then the elders spoke of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), which illuminates yoga for practitioners of yoga. (147)
147. I prosper; I attain growth. Oṃ, salutation to Ṛddhi.
