Fragrance and the other [objects], as well as earth and the other [elements], are the gateways to my perception.
I am the eternal one who has become the gateway to all meritorious fragrances. 148.

148. The word "scent" (*gandha*) is also indicative of form, taste, and so forth, and thereby points to their substrata, earth and the other elements. In the passage, "He understood that food is Brahman," the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*) is prescribed in the Śruti as a means for the knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, the Śruti itself, stating "Earth is indeed food," declares that the word "food" refers to the earth. Therefore...
In the knowledge of the Goddess, earth and the other elements serve as the doorways. Om, salutation to the one whose door is fragrance.
The Brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta call me Gandhadvārā;
I am invincible to all the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas. (149)
I am pure consciousness and action, incapable of being sublated by anything;
for all beings who have become my very self, I am the essence of consciousness and action. (150)
How indeed will he who wishes to remove both the state of being a knower and the state of being an agent explain that [negation], since he himself is the knower and the agent of the negation? (151)
151. That is its removal. No one at all is able to violate my state of consciousness (*saṃvid*).

Having reflected thus on the absence of that [violation], for in the absence of it, that very thing is consciousness itself. 152. [The verse continues: "Therefore, O King, you should not grieve; this is the nature of reality. Thus he spoke. The king, having heard these words, attained supreme peace. Then, having bowed his head to the feet of the sage, he departed from that place. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Non-existence of the Self," in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
152. The meaning is that because of the absence of that [obstruction], there is the state of being unassailable. *Oṃ durādharṣāyai namaḥ*.
Those who are experts in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya call me "Durādharṣā" (Unassailable).
This eight-syllabled mantra indeed releases one from the path of darkness [or: from fear]. 153.
Nourished by the eternal Viṣ�ṇu, and eternally nourished by excellent qualities, consciousness—devoid of my objects of sense—is the eternal, supreme body. 154.

154. The non-definition of the Ever-Nourished (Nityapuṣṭā): by the words "by the eternal," etc. [The meaning is: "Even without objects, my supreme body, which is of the nature of consciousness, is nourished by the true qualities, namely the qualities such as knowledge and power. Om, salutation to Nityapuṣṭā.
She alone nourishes the objects of the senses for those whose nature is inert by means of her own non-inert powers;
yet the Siddhas, who are experts in consciousness, declare me to be eternally nourished. 155.
For this eight-syllabled mantra constantly nourishes consciousness;
its performers are called "Kariṇas," who are purified in three ways and devoted to the threefold action.

156. He provides the etymological derivation of the name *karīṣiṇī*: "kariṇa" means "doers. The sense is that the word *karin* is derived from the verbal root *kṛ*. They are "pure in three ways," meaning pure in body, speech, and mind. Their "three activities" consist of sacrifice, giving, and study.
I desire to see them always; with my mind I go ever to those who are sustained [by me].
Resembling the lord of snowy mountains, these lordly elephants are my vehicles.

157. Taking up the verbal root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire," he states the meaning: "I desire those. With the intention of [the root] *iṣ* in the sense of "going," he says: "I go with my mind. Regarding the word *kari*, its conventional usage as referring to an elephant is well known.
Because I am always the sovereign, the agent, and the one who possesses all things (annavatī), the knowers of reality call me "Karīṣiṇī. || 158 ||
For this seven-syllable mantra bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
and I am always the mistress of all beings through my beloved Lord. 159.

159. He utters the name *Īśvarī* with the words beginning with *bhūtānām*. The form *īśvarā* is derived from the root *īś* (to rule) with the suffix *varac* according to the rule *stheśabhāsa-* etc. The word *bhūta* refers here to all sentient and insentient beings.
In the phrase *priyeṇeśena*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). The meaning is that she was meditated upon as the beloved consort. *Oṃ Īśvaryai namaḥ*.
She is the bestower of boons, the sovereign of the worlds, and is always praised by all beings;
she is the giver of prosperity, ever-increasing, and the destroyer of all sins.
"My name is indeed 'Īśvarī'; thus it is established in the Veda. For this six-syllabled mantra bestows the abundance of all sovereign powers. (161)
Those known as terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial, as well as those which are extraordinary and supreme—
all these desires, consisting of eternal bliss, are centered in me.
I am the supreme ground of delusion for all desires;
I am the object of Viṣṇu’s mind, and I transcend everything.
163. He states another etymological derivation for the name *kāma* of the mind: "of the desires of the mind. *Oṃ*, obeisance to the desire of the mind.
By saying "the desire of the mind," the gods thus praised me.
For this nine-syllable mantra bestows the fulfillment of all desires. || 164 ||
Furthermore, those words that are proclaimed—whether worldly, Vedic, or arising from external scriptures; whether silent or vocal—are all [contained therein]. || 165 ||
165. He provides the etymological derivation (nirukti) for the name of Speech as "Intention" (ākūti): "They are worldly," etc. All those [worldly] acts of utterance are directed toward me;
every person intends me, who abide as the Self of all. 166.

166. Regarding the word *abhipretya*: the sense is that the word *ākūti* refers to intention (*abhiprāya*). The meaning is that it is the ground of the intended purport (*tātparya*) of all speech. *Oṃ, salutation to the intention of speech.* In each respective manner, according to the sequence of the utterance of words.
By that [speech], I have been inspired in my intentions by those who know the Vedas.
This eight-syllabled mantra indeed bestows the accomplishment of all words and their meanings;
it is that which perceives the world as twofold—both "being" (sat) and "non-being" (tyat)—through the means of valid cognition.
168. He utters the name "Truth" (satya), saying "the Real" (sacca). The Śruti passage, "It became the Real (sat) and the True (tyat)," is intended here. Om, salutation to Truth.
"I am all that," thus did the Ṛṣis declare me to be Truth.
For this six-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of all truths. || 169 ||
Living beings, established in three modes, perceive;
but their true form, O Śakra, is consciousness devoid of anything to be rejected.
170. He declares the name "the form of the bound souls" (paśūnām rūpam) by saying "they see" (paśyanti). The word *paśu* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the three modes": these are the forms of gods, animals, and humans; or, they consist of the states of being bound, liberated, and eternal. [The text continues:
"I myself am that very form, whose nature is the mass of consciousness and bliss."
All those living beings are mere fragments of My power, designated as the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 171 ||
For that power of mine which belongs to Agni has indeed arisen in various forms;
thus the Sāṃkhyas declare me to be the very form of the sacrificial animals.
172. The fiery power (āgneyī śakti) is the power of the enjoyer (bhoktṛśakti). *Oṃ paśūnāṃ rūpāya namaḥ*.
This nine-syllable mantra bestows the fruit of perfect knowledge.
The three qualities (traiguṇya), arising from the six attributes (ṣaḍguṇottha), and the two-fold food.
Thus it has been fully proclaimed. || 173 ||

173. Regarding the statement "the name of food is glory," he says: "It is the threefold nature" (*traiguṇyam*). Food characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) is the collection of objects of enjoyment belonging to *prakṛti*. Food characterized by the six qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is the collection of non-material objects of enjoyment; with reference to this, the Śruti declares the song of the liberated: "I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food."
(113) For those bound by the three qualities (guṇas), there is one [type] and for others, the other;
and of both kinds of food, that which is famous is the most excellent form. 174.
Thus, I am proclaimed by those who know reality as the Self of all beings;
mundane and supramundane enjoyments are the manifestations of my power.
That power of mine which is Soma has indeed arisen in such and such a manner;
those who contemplate the ultimate reality know me as the glory of food. 176.
176. Soma-śakti is the power of enjoyment (bhogya-śakti). Oṃ, salutation to the glory of food.
Indeed, this nine-syllabled mantra bestows the entirety of all enjoyments.
I have measured out these six paths; thus I am measured by all means of measurement. 177.
177. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) for the name "Mātā" (Mother) occurring in the phrase "mātaraṃ padmamālinīm": *mime iti*.

The meaning is that she measures (*paricchinatti*) the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), which are known as the worlds (*bhuvana*), words (*pada*), mantras, principles (*tattva*), energies (*kalā*), and phonemes (*varṇa*). Furthermore: "She is the measure of all measures, and within her everything is measured."
I shall ferry across the entire world, the boundless ocean of existence.

178. *Miti* means knowledge (*jñāna*). It exists as that which measures (*māti*) or limits. Having thus explained the meaning of the word *mā*, he states the meaning of the word *tṛ*: "I shall cause to cross" (*tārayāmi*). The verbal root *tṛ* signifies "floating" and "crossing.
[The mind] has crossed over the ocean of all defects, having become a boat for all beings.
Having assumed the form of a cloud, I flood the entire universe with water.
179. He speaks for the purpose of immersion: "I immerse. *Oṃ*, obeisance to Mātṛ.
"I contemplate and I perform what is dear and beneficial to all;
therefore, yogins know me as the Mother of all beings. 180.
For this five-syllabled mantra bestows the abundance of all enjoyments;
it is the channel named Suṣumnā, the mistress of the wheel of channels. (181)
The vehicle of liberation is known as the Mahāyāna and the Yogiyāna;
it is indeed proclaimed as the subtle Vaiṣṇavī power, consisting of my own self. (182)
182. He states the synonyms for Suṣumnā: "the vehicle of liberation" (muktiyāna), etc.
It is that which, having been relied upon, remains as the object of all volitional constructions;
and it is that which, piercing upwards and downwards, follows the movement of the body for every living being.
[again, the state of existence] || 183 ||
Pervading the supreme ether, she is celebrated as Suṣumnā,
for the liberation of all living beings who are weary of the entire cycle of worldly existence.

184. The supreme ether is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). I exist within the bodies of embodied beings in the form of the Suṣumṇā. From the top of the bladder to the head, O Purandara, I abide in that power. 185.
185. The *vasti* is the region below the navel.
There are indeed thirty-two lotuses situated there, known as the *ādhāras*.
Since I am pervaded by a garland of these lotuses, I am therefore called *Padmamālinī*. 186.
186. "Thirty-two" refers to the lotuses of the *ādhāra* (foundation) well-known in the Yoga scriptures.
187. "Because I sustain Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and eternal Time in their own essential forms, I am therefore called Padmamālinī (the One Garlanded with Lotuses)."
187. It has already been stated previously that *prakṛti* and the others constitute the meaning of the word "lotus" (*padma*). Om, salutation to Padmamālinī.
This eight-syllable mantra indeed bestows the fruits of all actions.
I provide nourishment for all by means of my form, fame, and splendor.

188. He provides the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) for the name *puṣkariṇī*: "poṣam" and so forth. The intended derivation is formed by taking the verbal roots *puṣ* (to nourish) and *kṛ* (to do/make).
"I alone lead forth the lotus-form known as Time (*kāla*), which is the *puṣkara*."
Therefore, the sages call me "Puṣkariṇī. || 189 ||
189. He explains the etymology from the word *puṣkara* as a synonym for *padma*: "It is *puṣkara*. Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣkariṇī.
This seven-syllabled mantra indeed bestows the fruit of all nourishment;
I am beloved by all the gods and am ever united with Hari. (190)
190. She said, "My name is Yaṣṭi," meaning "I am desired. The sense is that I am worshipped by all the gods.
I am the bestower of all desires and the support for everyone;
relying upon me, Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and the others abide. 191.
191. With the intention that the word *yaṣṭi* signifies the meaning "staff," he says: "the support. Oṃ, obeisance to Yaṣṭi.
Because of this [meaning], the seers therefore designate me as *Yaṣṭi*.
For this six-syllabled mantra bestows the fruit of all yogas. || 192 ||
I am Piṅgalā by my own radiance, which has the luster of molten gold;
and in former times, I bestowed great fortune upon Piṅgāya, the lord of the Yakṣas.
193. Piṅgalā said: "To Piṅgā. Intending the verbal root *lā* in the sense of "to give," she said: "I have given (*adām*). Oṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalā.
O Śakra, in former times the Lord of Yakṣas addressed me as "Piṅgalā."
For this seven-syllable mantra bestows the abundance of the splendor of yoga. || 194 ||
I satisfy Viṣṇu with my virtues, and I am satisfied by the virtues of Hari;
when I am praised for my own deeds, there is satisfaction for all beings.
195. The etymological definition of Tuṣṭi (Contentment): "I shall satisfy," and so forth. *Oṃ tuṣṭaye namaḥ*.
Contentment has been defined by those who have reached the further shore of the ocean of Yoga;
indeed, this six-syllabled mantra bestows satisfaction of the mind (*manaḥ-saṃtoṣa-dāyaka*). 196. [The mantra] is the cause [of that satisfaction].
I utter well-formed phonemes, either those that are supreme or even those that are not; these phonemes, which have no beginning in time, are beautiful and expressive of my meaning. (197)
197. He utters the name "Suvarṇā," saying "suvarṇayāmi. The analysis is "suvaḥ nayāmi" (I lead to heaven). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).

Furthermore, "suvaḥ" means heaven; "paraṃ suvaḥ" means the supreme state. He explains the etymology as "that which has beautiful (*su*) syllables (*varṇāḥ*) as its designators," beginning with the words "anidam," etc.
Having become the eternal Sarasvatī, I describe that which is beautiful;
therefore, she is proclaimed as "Suvarṇā" by the Brahmins who know the truth. 198.
198. He states another meaning: "Excellent," and so forth. *Oṃ suvarṇāyai namaḥ*.
This seven-syllable mantra bestows the abundance of all prosperity.
And [it reveals] the divine golden mountain filled with the moon, sun, and planets.
199. The name Hemamālinī is explained as follows: "Haimam" means Mahāmeru. Oṃ, salutations to Hemamālinī.
Having become the Earth (Dharā), I sustain [the world] for the sake of the maintenance of the Creator.
In former times, Viriñca praised me as Hemamālinī because of that.
Indeed, this eight-syllabled mantra bestows steadfastness upon human beings;
for the welfare of all living creatures, I shall now set forth the path of reality.
201. He explains the etymology of the name "Sūrya" with the words "for the sake of welfare" (*hitāya*). The meaning of the word *sū* is "I bring forth" (*prasūye*).
202. Furthermore, I delight [beings] therein through enjoyment and liberation as is appropriate;
likewise, by means of time, I regulate the sequence of the principles (*tattva-paddhati*) together with the individual souls (*sa-jīvam*).

The meaning of the letter *ra* is "I delight" (*ramayāmi*). "According to what is fitting" means according to the distinction of those qualified [to receive the teaching]. The meaning of the letter *ya* is "I restrain" (*niyacchāmi*).
And she is eternally beneficial to the wise, residing in the solar orb in the form of the Sun.
"Therefore, I am called 'Sūryā' by the wise who contemplate the truth. (203)
203. He states another meaning: "And from the wise" (sūribhyaśca). The intention is that the suffix *-yat* has the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*). Om, salutation to Sūryā;
for this six-syllabled mantra bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, fifty-three names situated within the hymns have been proclaimed. (204)
Having reached me, the wise fulfill their respective desires;
even though the arrangement regarding the scope of their fruits has been declared by me for them. (205)
The greatness of these [mantras] should not be considered by the wise to be merely that; until liberation, they are to be contemplated without doubt, for they bestow all fruits upon all. (206)
For from this series of names, I, the supreme goddess Śrī, am indeed [manifested], just as stars are in the sky or as jewels are in the ocean. (207)
As enjoyments exist upon the earth, as desires exist in the celestial tree, as greatness exists in cows, and as splendors exist in a Brahmin; 208.
Just as the divine qualities in Janārdana, the God of gods, are infinite,
so too are the glories in this hymn of mine boundless.
For as long as time exists— characterized by its divisions of kalās, kāṣṭhās, and so forth— I am simply unable to fully describe his excellent qualities.
This is the final goal of those who know the Vedas; this is the path of those who know the Tantras (or mantras).
A human being should constantly take refuge in me with this hymn.

211. To the word *saiṣā* ("this very one"), the word *yat* ("that which") must be supplied as its correlative. The feminine gender used in the expression *māṃ prapadyeta* ("she who takes refuge in me") is in accordance with the nature of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), just as in the phrase *śaityaṃ hi yat sā prakṛtir jalasya* ("for that which is coolness is the very nature of water").
Having recollected the meaning of the hymn and having studied the hymn for a long time, once serenity of mind has been attained, one should indeed take refuge in me as the goal. || 212 ||
Taking refuge in me constantly—whether as the God or as the Supreme Person—one who is faithful and has conquered the senses should reflect in this manner. (213)
213. "In this manner" means by the method that is about to be described.
"Hostility has been abandoned and favorability resorted to by me toward all beings, according to my ability and according to my understanding. 214.
214–215. By the words beginning with "prātikūlya" (hostility), the auxiliary practices (*aṅga*) taught in the seventeenth chapter are here recalled.
"I have turned away from misfortunes and from sinful acts within the ocean of worldly existence;
nevertheless, may even that activity toward this world which arises from the remembrance of You perish. 215.
For one who is indolent, of little strength, and lacking correct understanding, even the means enjoined by the scriptures will not be capable of delivering me from these three [sins]. (216)
216–217. The meaning is that there are three means, such as action, knowledge, and devotion.
Nevertheless, whatever engagement occurs here is indeed the fulfillment of Your command.
Therefore, because I lack these means, I am wretched, destitute, and without refuge.

217. "Even so" (tathāpi) means even though the [prescribed] rites are not the means (*anupāyatva*). Here, regarding the means: "the fulfillment of the command" refers to such scriptural injunctions as, "The Brahmins seek to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting," and "Meditate thus: 'Om'; one who desires liberation should indeed unite the Self with 'Om' as its refuge."

"I take refuge; perform your duty with self-restraint; come to me alone for shelter"—the meaning is the fulfillment of such commands in the form of injunctions, as in "one who takes refuge with self-restraint attains prosperity.
I abide taking refuge in your shadow, which removes all suffering.
Our Mistress is free from all limiting conditions, independent, and a treasure-house of compassion. || 218 ||
218–219. "Shelter" (chāyā) means, in effect, your compassion.
You alone are extolled as the refuge in all the scriptures.
Whatever is considered difficult to abandon or difficult to sustain—whether it be the self or that which belongs to the self—[is entrusted to you].
All that has been entrusted by you to your two auspicious lotus-feet;
therefore, I choose you as the very means for my attainment.
220. By the phrase "everything is surrendered," the relinquishing of both self and what belongs to the self is expressed.
"O Goddess, be my means; be my refuge, O Lotus-born One!
Burn away all my evil; nourish my mind that is fixed upon you. (221)
221. By the words "puṣya dhiyam," the devotion for the fruit is prayed for. (p.
216) Having reflected thus, one should indeed take refuge in me as the goal.
Or [he may worship] Ādideva, the Lord of the World, the Sovereign, or Puruṣottama. || 222 ||
O Śakra, at the times of performing rituals, a person should cause this supreme rite of well-being, which destroys all misfortune, to be recited according to the procedure for my hymn.
It validates all actions and nourishes the listener;
it dispels all illusion, misfortune, and impurities along with their stains.
224. *Samarthayati* means he renders them capable of bestowing their fruits. *Māyām* refers to the connection with *prakṛti*.
By the phrase "and *alakṣmī* along with the impurities," the meaning of the *Śrīsūkta*—namely, "I destroy the impurity of hunger and thirst, and the elder *Alakṣmī*"—is recalled.
For this, when practiced through action, mind, and speech, protects one from great evil and certainly brings about prosperity. (225)
225. By the words "He protects" and so forth, the cessation of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable are expressed.
Thus, O Śakra, this unsurpassed tantra has been told to you, wherein all the insights of the wise reside. 226.
Just as the treatise on liberation is the best among various types of scriptures, as the Brāhmaṇa is the best among bipeds, and as the cow is the best among quadrupeds; 227.
Just as gold is the best among metals and the Kaustubha gem is the best among jewels, so is the mother the best among elders, and the son the best among those who speak. (228)
Of the senses, the mind is the foremost, just as the wind is among moving things;
Meru is the best of mountains, and the triple-streamed Ganges is the best of rivers. (229)
Among the stages of life, the householder is foremost, just as Vasiṣṭha is among those who recite prayers;
among the principles, total renunciation is foremost, just as wisdom is the best among gains.
230. Regarding the phrase "of the stages" (āśramāṇām): it means "of those belonging to the stages" (āśramiṇām).

May he—having attained spiritual wisdom through service to the lord of ascetics named Śrīvāsa, and having reached the pinnacle of the tradition of the *Āmnāyānta*—explain the *Lakṣmītantra* by way of a pure and excellent path for the delight of the virtuous; may he be pleased!
She is skilled in the method of protecting her beloved devotees and is dear to Mukunda.
Likewise, this is the supreme tantra among all tantras for those who speak of reality;
herein, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, is the Guru. (131)
And we two have been correctly glorified by our true nature, qualities, and majesty;
for those who are devoted to us in this [devotion] possess pure knowledge and certainty. (232)
Taking hold of this ladder, they indeed ascend to the supreme state;
it is the supreme tantra among tantras, sealed with my own name. (233)

It should not be given to one who has not observed the vow nor to one who has broken his vow, nor indeed to an ungrateful person; it should never be given to one who does not know the ritual manual, nor to one defiled by malice.
This should not be given to one who is not a devotee of Vāsudeva, nor to one who lacks devotion toward me;
it should be given to one of virtuous conduct, who has bathed well, and who is an ascetic.
To one who has determined the Vedas and Tantras, and especially to my devotee who bears even greater devotion toward Vāsudeva Janārdana.
To you, who are pure in vows, skillful, and habituated to constant practice— to you,
all this that I was asked here by you has been told.
"I am pleased with you, O Lord of Gods; what more do you wish to hear? (237)

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Power of the Śrīsūkta," in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the essence of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*. [B: The *Lakṣmītantra* is completed. The number of verses is 3,500.]
217) In the manuscript designated as (Ī) held in the Oriental Manuscripts Library of the Madras Government, the following chapters are read in addition:—
Fifty-first Chapter. Śakra—
[It appears that one or two verses are missing at the beginning]— Origination and Dissolution.
And their fruit has been determined, as well as the specific modes of practice that apply to each of them accordingly. (1)
For you, there are five constant duties as well as those that are occasional:
the two feet consisting of the conduct section (caryāpāda) and the action section (kriyāpāda), and the two feet consisting of wisdom (jñāna) and yoga.
Thus, the various kinds of tantras are augmented by four components,
and are consistent with ancient deeds, ancient traditions, and historical narratives.
This work, titled the Lakṣmītantra, contains the convergence of many secrets and is adorned with various statements; it correctly provides immediate conviction to human beings.
While in a state of meditative concentration, I have understood this exactly as it is;
yet, because its form is so extensive and due to the complete reversal of time, [it has not been fully grasped]. (5)
And because of the feebleness of the mind, it does not shine forth exactly as it is;
[yet] from this great ocean, O Goddess, which is filled with your knowledge, [it shines].
Having extracted the essence from all [teachings] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, please explain this compendium of the Tantra; homage to you, O Lotus-born One! (7)
Nārada:
Thus urged, the goddess Padmā, like a milch-cow by her calf, spoke to the subduer of Pāka with an affectionate mind. (8)
Śrī said:
"Well spoken, O child, slayer of Vṛtra; you have been perfectly enlightened.
Listen as I relate in brief that which has been extracted from this tantra."
I am the eternal ego-consciousness of all beings; through ascent and descent, I am remembered as the accomplisher of the universe.
That which is called the supreme egoity (ahaṃtā) is said to be beyond the fourth state (turyātīta);
it is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, namely Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
In that state, there is no distinction between us two established in existence and non-existence;
whatever expansion occurs there is like the swelling of the ocean at the rising of the moon.
I am the power of Nārāyaṇa, characterized by the desire to create;
likewise, I am his fourth state (turyāvasthā), which consists of the nature arising from transformation.
At that time, every state consisting of both the pure and the impure is contained within;
as are the Vyūhas, the Vibhavas, and likewise the various other Vyūhas and so forth.

This is the nature consisting of purity, O Blessed One, which is also that which consists of [the Lord], both in the manifestation (*vyūha*) and the sovereign power (*vibhava*), as well as in the intermediate manifestations (*vyūhāntara*) and so forth. (15)
In this same manner, one should understand each of my states, beginning with deep sleep;
likewise, the unmanifest, the mahat, and so forth, as well as the world of transformation.
This entity consists of both the pure and the impure, and there are indeed three states therein;
one should likewise elevate each of these individually in their respective places, O Lord of Heaven. (17)
These fourfold states are to be understood as existing in both the elemental (bhūta) and the stable (sthita).
However, there is another sequence in this way regarding the path consisting of the pure and the impure.

Within the ascending stages consisting of myself, which are the knower, the instruments, and the objects of knowledge, there are ten groups of subjects (mātṛgaṇas) in sequence, distinguished as the void (śūnya), the vital breath (prāṇa), and so forth. 19.
Know that the instrument is twofold: external and internal.
For in both cases, there is indeed a sequence beginning with silence and so forth. (20)
The objects of knowledge have been declared to be manifold; therein one should likewise infer the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the realization of the nature of the Blessed One.
This descent has been described; now hear from me also about the ascent. Beginning from the final extremity, it is established as ending with me. (22)

That, however, should be understood as the ascent (āroha) upon the path consisting of both the pure and the impure; a person who constantly contemplates both the ascent and the descent [attains success]. (23)
With his mind fixed on Me, his life-breath absorbed in Me, he attains My own state;
for there is no limitation of Me by form, time, or space.
O Indra, they are pervaded by me alone, who am the embodiment of knowledge;
by my will, I manifest the entire universe upon the wall of the Self. (25)
The establishment of the grasped and the grasper occurs according to the gradations of that [consciousness's] form;
this transformation of the nature of the expressible has been shown to you in brief. (26)
With a concentrated mind, listen to its nature as the Speaker:
first consisting of pure consciousness, it subsequently undergoes transformation into the form of vital breath.
Through the occurrence of those respective locations, speech manifests as the differentiated [vāk]:
the *śāntā*, the *sūkṣmā*, the *madhyā*, and the *vaikharī*. (28)
I, who am peaceful and evolving, resort to that subtle state which is fourfold in form, expressed in four forms, and self-created as the object of speech. (29)
The subtle form is established in two ways: as Śakti and as Nāda.
I, the subtle one who am undergoing manifestation, attain the state of Madhyamā. (30)
The perfection of the refinement of the *bindu* is that state of the continuity of the imperishable (*akṣara*).
I, who am the evolving *madhyamā*, attain the state of *vaikharī*. 31.
Meditating continuously on these two— the ascent and the descent— of the continuous stream of syllables through its divisions beginning with fifty;
One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains that which transcends sound.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, an extraction from the *Lakṣmītantra* within the illustrious *Pāñcarātrasāra*. 51.
Chapter Fifty-Two: Śrī (Fortune) — p. 219)
Now listen, O child Purandara, to the path consisting of mantra:
"I am the nature of manifest bliss; I am the fullness of egoity; I am Hari. (1)
Know me as Mantramātā, known as Prāṇa, consisting of pure consciousness;
these [worlds] arise from me alone and certainly set within me.
And I, knowing their strength and my own true nature,
am empowered as one, as two, and indeed as threefold.
In four ways, five ways, six ways, and likewise seven ways;
and likewise in sixteen ways, and also in twenty-five ways. (4)
Furthermore, I arise in fifty ways, and again in sixty-three ways;
indeed, I manifest in many forms like the wish-fulfilling gem, O Sovereign Lady.
Vowels and consonants, the combination of vowels and consonants,
syllables, words, as well as sentences together with chapters— thus [is the structure].

The systematic arrangement of the daily rites (āhnika) and the chapters (adhyāya), as well as the structure of the scriptures and systems; the various types of traditions (āgamas), and the distinction between those that are external and those that are internal.
Know that worldly and Vedic languages, as well as various other tongues,
are all of the nature of mantra for those who know my true form.
The establishment of the grasped and the grasper, as well as proximity and distance, occur through the gradations of cultivation. (9)
Mantras are of four kinds: seed-syllable (bīja), aggregate (piṇḍa), word (pada), and name (saṃjñā).
Know, O Vāsava, that among these the five jewels are preeminent.
O Pākaśāsana, those seed-syllables are contained within my hymn like clarified butter placed in curd;
they arise from the fragments of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, and are endowed with the Nāda.
That which is the form of the sun here is declared to be the state of waking;
fire is the dream state, and the moon is deep sleep, as well as that called Māyā and Parā.
The fragment known as Indukhaṇḍa is the fourth; beyond that is Nāda.
Śakti is the state consisting of the tranquil self, which is the very abiding of Nāda. || 13 ||
Beyond that, however, is the Brahman which is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
it consists of six, four, and six vowels, arising from the Sun, Fire, and Moon.
The remaining consonants are produced from the vowels; such is the arrangement of the phonemes.
This is the supreme seed-syllable that bestows the fruit of all desires. 15.
It bestows sons upon those desiring sons, a kingdom upon one desiring a kingdom,
prosperity upon those desiring prosperity, and liberation upon one desiring liberation.
It destroys enemies and attracts whatever is desired;
it is named "Cintāmaṇi," yet this jewel is not merely a cintāmaṇi gem.
And following that very [mantra] is the seed-syllable beginning with Śakra (Ś), which grants all desires;
it consists of pairs of illusory syllables (māyākṣara) positioned at the beginning and end of the six vowels.
This arrangement of the limbs (aṅgas) should be performed together with the seed-syllables and the mudrās;
the same rule applies to the remaining four seed-syllables as well. (19)
Through immersion in the fullness of I-consciousness and through union with the primordial seed-syllable,
the manifold host of mantras attains its state of being mine.
Whatever deity belongs to the mantras, that deity is established in my power and partakes of my nature;
therefore, it is indeed I who am to be meditated upon therein.
There, one should indeed recollect each respective deity in the form of a woman,
endowed with their particular colors, weapons, forms, ornaments, and so forth.
"Having attained my own nature, they likewise bestow their fruits swiftly.
Thus, O Śakra, this path of mantra has been described to you in brief.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*, the *Lakṣmītantroddhāra*, which is a compendium of the meaning of the Tantras. 52.
Chapter Fifty-Three: Śrī (Fortune) — p. 220)
O Purandara, I shall proclaim the Kriyāpāda in brief:
one who has bathed, having cast off impurities according to the vision of the scriptures.
O Śakra, having reached a secluded place and preceded by the purification of that place,
one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) through the meditation on primordial wisdom.

That which is known as the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti), beginning with earth and ending with primordial matter (prakṛti) itself, is traditionally held to possess two forms through the distinction of gross and subtle. (3)
The configuration existing within the range of the eye is described as gross form (sthūlarūpa);
therein, the state of having the form of the cause is called the subtle [element], the *tanmātra*.
This reality consists of sixteen principles, divided into gross and subtle;
one should assign the objects, the senses, and their functions to their respective places therein.
Among the five [senses] beginning with the genitals and smell, one should lead each triad respectively by means of the five great elements beginning with earth. (6)
One should bring the conceit of the mind to rest within the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra),
and one should conceal the determination of the vital breath within the principle of the intellect (buddhi).
One should bring sattva, rajas, and tamas to rest within the unmanifest root;
in this group of sixteen, one should contemplate the eightfold root.
O Indra, the respective designations beginning with Dhruva and ending with *huṃ phaṭ* are:
flesh, fat, blood, semen, space, and the three syllables.
One should meditate upon the eight subtle [syllables], each followed by the next and joined with the Bindu;
within this group of eight seed-syllables, one should place Māyā conjoined with a crescent moon.
The wise one should understand these mantras as residing within the eight powers (śaktis):
namely, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti; || 11 ||
The wise one should remember these powers: Śāntyatītābhimānā, Prāṇā, and likewise Guṇavatī, beginning with Earth and ending with Prakṛti. (12)
In that same [context], having joined the eight seed-syllables with fire, māyā, and the half-moon,
one should know these mantras as belonging to the presiding deities.
Having meditated upon me, who possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns at the time of universal destruction and resembles smokeless embers,
one shall consume the earth with the fire arising from my mouth.
One should likewise sprinkle with water produced from one's own mouth, which has the luster of ten thousand moons;
thus the purification of the site is accomplished. Now hear the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). || 15 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, an extraction from the *Lakṣmītantra* within the *Śrīpāñcarātrasāra*. 53.
Chapter Fifty-Four: Śrī—p. 221)
Having drawn forth the Earth—quadrangular, level, yellow, and marked with the vajra—with the mantra, one should cause her to dissolve into her own place within the body. || 1 ||
Then, one should cause that [scent] to dissolve into its own seed-syllable by means of the mere scent;
upon its cessation, one should cause that [seed-syllable] to dissolve by means of its own mantra.
While I have become the locus of empowerment, one should cast me and that [image],
which resembles a half-moon and is marked with a lotus, from the body into the external water while reciting the mantra.
Having brought [the deity] situated in its own place into dissolution by means of one's own mantra into the mere essence (rasa),
and having established it there with that mantra, one should then bring that [essence] into dissolution within oneself.
And then, through me, fire, non-return, and primordial nature (prakṛti) in succession, the wise man should realize that everything is not manifold; he should understand the dissolution of my power.
For just as one might pour clarified butter into milk produced by churning it,
and that butter is one thing while the other milk is another, so too is that clarified butter distinct from the other milk.
Thus the wise man should meditate upon Prakṛti as the presiding power;
likewise, he should meditate upon me, the Supreme Śakti, endowed with the sevenfold Śaktis.

Having raised [the breath] up to the end of the *dvādaśānta*, one should cast it into me, who consist of mantra; I am resplendent with the brilliance of ten million fires, moons, and suns, with eyes, heads, and mouths on all sides.
"For the benefit of all living beings, this body of mine consists of mantra.
Śakra asked: "Which are the locations within this body where dissolution should be performed in sequence?"
"And what are the forms of the Earth and the other elements within the lotus? Please tell me.
Śrī said:
"The station of the Earth is from the knees upward; that of Water is remembered as being up to the waist. (10)
The place of fire is up to the navel, the place of air is from there up to the heart;
the place of ether is up to the throat, and that of the ego-sense is up to the base of the palate.
The great place above the eyebrows is remembered as the supreme space;
the great earthly orb is square and marked with a thunderbolt.
That which resembles a half-moon, is white, and is marked with a lotus is said to belong to water;
that which is triangular, marked with a svastika, and red is declared to belong to fire. (13)
Smoke-colored and joined with six dots, the circular [mandala] is said to belong to Vāyu;
likewise, the space [of Ākāśa] has the luster of collyrium, and its station is remembered as being merely the size of a disc.
Thus, when the summary of reality has been made, [the breath] which has emerged from the hollow of the heart,
supported by the rope of knowledge, proceeds along the central path of the *suṣumnā*.
Having raised [the self] upward from the soul by means of the series of steps that are the powers,
one should cast it into me, who abide in the center of the great lotus at the limit of the twelve.
The great lotus at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] is endowed with a thousand petals;
it possesses the brilliance of a thousand times ten million suns and the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons.
Abiding within the duality of Agni and Soma, my body consists of great bliss;
that consciousness, which is beyond description and comparison, is my own body. 18.
From this [source], the excellent river Jīvānandā flows forth in part;
having brought this self-bliss, she leads one to the state consisting of great bliss.

Then, one should burn from all sides that lump, which resembles a mound of salt, with networks of great flames consisting of masses of rays emerging from one's own mouth, which are composed of pure consciousness (cinmaya). || 20 ||
Then, one should flood the body-fire— the sixth [cakra], which is red like a lotus and possesses a dot— with nectars arising from my moon-like mouth.
When my desire to create arises, embraced by consciousness and vital breath,
one should remember those powers impelled [by it], which reside within the body composed of mantra.

Then, one should meditate in sequence upon the creation of everything from primordial nature (prakṛti) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa), preceded by the impelling of those powers through the gateway of the command.
Then, having thus produced the great *piṇḍa* consisting of pure *lakṣmī*, which arises from the *piṇḍa* and is radiant with causes and manifestations; 24.
By the path of movement previously described, one should bring [the self] into the heart in reverse order;
from a state of bliss, one should realize one's own self as characterized by the bliss of pure consciousness. (25)
Then, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the hands and body,
on the joints of the fingers starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
[He should touch] both palms, both backs, and both hands;
from the knees up to the feet, and likewise from the navel up to the head. (27)
Having placed my seed-syllable (m-bīja) in the joints, one should place the limbs beginning with the heart;
then again, with the six [syllables] beginning with the heart, [one should place them] on the navel, back, hands, and thighs.
The wise one should assign the sixfold attributes, beginning with knowledge, to the calves and feet.
When the body has been thus produced— pure, auspicious, and consisting of Lakṣmī—
he should perform the assignment of the six supports (ādhāra-ṣaṭka) with the vision of wisdom.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, an extraction from the *Lakṣmītantra* within the illustrious *Pāñcarātrasāra*. || 54 ||
Chapter Fifty-Five: Śrī—p. 223)
I shall fully explain the supports; listen, O Pākaśāsana.
Now, O Lord of Wealth, they are within the meḍhra, in the meḍhra itself, and in the middle of the navel.
The wise man should meditate upon six lotuses in the pit of the heart and between the eyebrows,
[visualized] by means of the Vedas, the Rasas, the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), the Suns, and the Vikāras.
And [he saw] those joined with petals for the two Aśvins, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
conjoined with the vowels from *ka* to *ta*, and with the two ending in the color of the Sun.
One should meditate upon me, the Goddess, appearing like a jewel-lamp amidst these lotuses;
wherever there may be a desire, one should practice yoga while remaining in that very place.
Starting from the first support and extending to the lotus at the end of the twelve,
one should meditate on the single, supreme, primordial [power] residing within the body, having the form of a lamp-flame.
When the mind reaches dissolution by recollecting this supreme, conscious [reality] through both direct and reverse orders,
that indeed is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
If you have a desire for the bond of a body, listen to my description of that body:
one should contemplate the water of the Mahendra [ocean] within a single heart as a pavilion.
There, one should visualize [the city] endowed with four gates and the female gatekeepers:
Balākinī in the east, Śyāmā, and likewise Vanamālā in the other [directions].
One should subsequently recollect the white Vibhīṣikā, whose color has been described;
and in the north, O Śakra, one should recollect the smoke-colored Śāṅkarī.
There, in the center of the pavilion, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus, radiant like a thousand suns, shining with its pericarp and filaments.
Vāsudeva on the eastern petal, Saṃkarṣaṇa on the southern,
Pradyumna on the western leaf, and Aniruddha on the northern.
One should remember all of them bearing conchs and discs, adorned with forest garlands, possessing beauty according to the respective ages, and facing toward me.
One should meditate upon Gulgulu, Gurunya, Madana, and Śalala in the corner, as they sprinkle me, Sudhā, with nectar. 13.
One should remember me, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds, situated in the center of the seed-syllable within the pericarp, possessing the luster of molten gold and holding two lotuses.
She has hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, is adorned with all ornaments, is indescribable and incomparable, the blameless consort of Viṣṇu. (15)
She sprinkles the three worlds, scorched by heat, with cool rays born from her dark outer corners— divine rays accompanied by the moonlight of her smile.

Having produced enjoyments through knowledge, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with them—enjoyments that consist of the bliss of Brahman, are truly composed of the Self (Manmaya), and are free from defects. (17)
Or else, she who sits upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa, adorned by the joy of his union,
closely embracing the Lord with her right hand.
Then, one must practice in a celestial body;
our state as husband and wife is beyond doubt, for it is a mystery profound as the Vedas.

It is evident that the end of the fifty-fifth chapter, the entirety of the fifty-sixth chapter, and the beginning of the fifty-seventh chapter are lost. ...........................
Chapter Fifty-Seven: Śrī (Fortune) — p. 224)
"Who is the god who establishes existence and dwells within all beings?
It is the power (śakti) that transcends the three forms (trimūrti)—this is the supreme recitation (japa). (1)
Through the distinction between word and meaning, the Goddess Lakṣmī manifests in two ways,
known by the names Śāntā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.

This manifestation of sound is fourfold, and the manifestation of meaning is likewise. [The supreme state] is that in which all latent impressions have subsided and which is devoid of vowels, consonants, and the like. (3)
That primordial state which is verbal is peaceful and has peace as its means;
it is the unrefined form of the power of sound that brings about the cognition of meaning.
That which is the pure unfolding is proclaimed as Paśyantī;
that which consists of the form of the awakening of meaning is proclaimed as Śabda (Speech). || 5 ||
When the formative forces do not cause harm, that is then the Middle Way;
thus, when perfected through these formative forces, it possesses hundreds of conceptual distinctions.
Then, having divided her form into parts, she took delight in various ways among those [eight] places, and not among ordinary women. || 7 ||
That which is called *vaikharī* is said to be the one that speaks variously through the letters;
that which is called *śāntā* is the supreme (*parā*) which has attained equanimity everywhere.
A thousandth of a ten-millionth part of that is the speech known as Madhyamā;
and a thousandth of a ten-millionth part of that is the speech known as Vaikharī.
Phonemes, words, and sentences constitute the threefold mode of articulated speech (vaikharī);
this very [speech] undergoes progressive contraction by way of the phonemes and so forth. (10)
This fourfold power, born of the inverse and direct orders,
proceeds in four ways along with its increase through the stages of śāntā, paśyantī, and so forth, in succession.
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, and the others cause it to set in four ways;
furthermore, that [Speech] should be known as threefold: manifest, unmanifest-and-manifest, and unmanifest. (12)
That which exists within the bodies of living beings, which arises and sets, and which is made manifest by means of the lute, the flute, the drum, and so forth—that indeed is what is manifested. (13)
Then, through the efforts of living beings exerting themselves with the desire to speak, that [sound] became equal to it [the cosmic sound],
as rivers flow from the ocean and from mountain caves due to the agitation caused by the wind.
That power of word which is manifested is said to be "unmanifest" (avyakta).
Regarding their arising and setting, the previously mentioned "disorder" (vyutkrama) and "non-disorder" (utkrama) apply. (15)
The fourfold object of expression (vācya) should be known as being distinguished by [the states] beginning with tranquility (śānta).
Thus established is the determination that Śakti is the Savior (Tārikā). 16.
That recitation is called "middling," which consists of the description of the phonemes on all sides;
it is the power that takes the form of the phonemes and that which arises from their combination. (17)
That which is bound by power, that which is permeated by power, and that which arises from the desire to speak—this is the tetrad of powers, preceded by their definitive determination. (18)
The final superimposition (adhyāsa) upon the word is that of the object;
having cognized the denotatum separately, one then cognizes it as existing in three forms. (19)
For that awakening by means of mantras is indeed the supreme and inferior recitation (japa),
which is described in the Lakṣmītantra as consisting of Agni and Soma.
Having transcended those respective forms designated as the signified and the signifier, and having crossed the night consisting of Lakṣmī, which takes the form of the syllable Tārikā; || 21 ||
In the great ocean of the consciousness of waveless supreme bliss,
having purified all the mantras and being joined with the placement (nyāsa) of their essential nature, || 22 ||
Having worshipped those [deities] therein, which are radiant through their respective nourishment,
one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra by means of both its general and specific aspects.

Thus disciplined, one should mutter the mantras; this daily recitation is considered worshiped when it is endowed with the sequence of consecrations and postures as prescribed in the respective scriptures. (24)
Endowed with those various states of being and meditating upon the deities of the mantra, one who sees all should perform recitation; this is remembered as the supreme recitation. (25)
Nārada said:
"This supreme secret must not be given to one who is unworthy. Having spoken thus, she vanished from sight like lightning in the sky. (26)
Having obtained supreme wealth, Śakra rejoiced, freed from his feverish distress. Atri said:
"O blessed lady, having spoken thus, the venerable Nārada ceased. (27)
O fair-faced one, having been worshipped by Indra, the fortunate Śrī departed;
and Indra too, filled with wonder, went constantly to the abode of Brahmā.
And being questioned by Brahmā, he then explained it to him according to the rules;
and being questioned by the Prajāpatis, Brahmā, the knower of reality, explained it to them.
Then, on Mount Malaya, the sages were made to hear it by Nārada;
subsequently, Aṅgiras caused Pāvaka to hear this supreme tantra.
Pāvaka [instructed] Kātyāyana, and he [instructed] Gautama in the hermitage;
then Gautama [instructed] Bharadvāja, and he [instructed] Garga, the great sage.
Garga [taught] Asita Devala, and he [in turn taught] the sage Jaigīṣavya;
that sage then caused his ancestors to hear [the teaching], and thereafter he, the conqueror of greed, attained liberation.
Ekāñjanā, the daughter of Annapika, who was born of her mind, caused the great sage Pārāśarya to hear [the work]. || 33 ||
Pārāśarya also caused his son Śuka, the supreme yogi, to hear it;
and Śuka, in turn, recited it to the Prajāpati named Svarbhānu.
Vasiṣṭha instructed the wise Arundhatī in the teachings of Nārada;
from her, the yogis beginning with Kapila obtained that system concerning Lakṣmī.
Śaṅkara, the moon-crested Lord, caused Pārvatī to hear it,
as did Hiraṇyagarbha, the speaker of Yoga, who caused Sarasvatī to hear it.
For those goddesses who are devoted to their husbands—the wives of gods, brahmin-sages, and yogis—it is traditionally held that the perpetual study of them is known as the Lakṣmī Tantra. (37)
Having heard this from the presence of Brahmā, O wise one, I have related it to you;
that you are dear to me and beloved—nothing remains further to be told.
Listen further, Anasūyā, to this summary with a mind free from envy;
having heard it, strive to practice it and protect yourself with vigilance. (39)
Your state of mind will become one whose form is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, having completely abandoned misfortunes and sins within the ocean of worldly existence. (40)
Whether by fate or through delusion, when one is overwhelmed by calamity,
one should likewise worship both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
She herself abandons all misfortunes that have been committed, both constant and sudden;
she is free from greed regarding their commission and is devoted to the welfare of the world.
Having personally established non-existence through a firm intellect alone—
at all times, in all places, in all states, and in every way— (43)
With the firm conviction that "the glorious Hari will protect those who have taken refuge in him," they place themselves, their own possessions, and everything else at the feet of the Lord of Śrī.
"Choose a means; contemplate Him, the Lord of Lakṣmī, as the one to be approached.
O auspicious lady, all this—the scriptures, the meaning of the scriptures, and their fruit—has been told to you. (45)
The supreme reality has been revealed with an attentive mind;
this is the supreme Lakṣmītantra, complete with its secrets and its summary. (46)
"You must never, under any circumstances, give [this] to one who is not a devotee of Vāsudeva;
for Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī do not depart from his heart. (47)
To whomever it may be, this unsurpassed teaching should be spoken by you;
however, it must never be studied in the presence of atheists.

It is not for those who do not observe vows or bathe [at sacred sites], nor for those who hate their mother and father, nor for those who hate various scriptures, and likewise not for those who hate their guru. (49)
Likewise for those who hate their spouses and those who hate women;
for he who has performed the ritual bath after completing Vedic vows is indeed dear to his mother, father, and guru.
He was free from blame, a knower of the higher and lower ordinances of the scriptures,
a believer, full of faith, and beloved by Lakṣmī and the Lord of Lakṣmī.
One who knows the divisions of ritual and sacrifice, who is conversant with the prescriptions of other tantras,
who knows the rules for yoga along with its ancillaries, and who understands the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures. (52)
He was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a master of the doctrine of Paśupati,
skilled in the methods of reasoning and refutation, and a scholar of the categories of valid cognition and logic.
One who knows the true reality of the meaning of all internal sciences deserves to attain [this]:
Om, salutation to Vāsudeva, for whom Śrī is the beloved. 54.
Oṃ, salutations to the consort of Viṣṇu, whose beloved is Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the eternally faultless one, the universal cause of all;
salutations to the waveless knowledge, the very self of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (55)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Essence of the Meaning of the Secret Scripture," in the *Tantrārthasaṃgraha*, which is the extraction of the *Lakṣmītantra* from the glorious *Pāñcarātrasāra*. 57.
The Lakṣmītantra is completed.
